# FILE: BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1
# BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 — BASS-II hardware, O2 dilution, combustion products, thin PMMA films, Nomex and PMMA rods (BAS-01 p.9–61)

## Scope
Covers: BAS-01 (Olson et al. 2021, BASS-II summary report) as gathered from p.9 to p.61, with the context pages it borrows (p.12–13, p.111–115 Tables A.1–A.3, p.123): chapter 1 (glovebox flow-duct hardware, N2 dilution of the MSG and its CSTR model, ISS gas sensors, O2/CO2/CO stoichiometry, heat release rate, global equivalence ratio, crew and repairs), chapter 2 (Bhattacharjee, RTDFS: thin PMMA films in opposed flow on the ISS, the critical-velocity paper with its 2D model and scale analysis, and the microgravity-versus-1-g downward paper with the SDSU ground rigs), chapter 3 (Ferkul: Nomex III and a BASS-I wax candle) and chapter 4 (Fernandez-Pello: opposed-flow spread over PMMA rods, microgravity against 1 g); plus the also-routed SAF-06 Table 1 description that lists two BASS SIBAL concurrent tests.
Not here: BAS-01 from p.62 (end of chapter 5 on PMMA slabs, chapter 6 PMMA rods in stagnation flow, chapter 7 SIBAL fabric, Tables A.1–A.4 row by row) → BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_2; Tables A.5–A.6, BAS-01 p.123–136, BAS-03 and BAS-04 → BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_3; BAS-05, BAS-07, the OVR-13 SIBAL slide and the PSI records PSC-01, PSD-01, PSD-02, PSD-03 → BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4; the Saffire rows and results of SAF-06 → LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2; general Earth-versus-space statements and BAS-09 → EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1 and EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2.

## Findings

### 1. Report layout, hypothesis and objectives (chapter 1)
- BAS-01 opens with an overview and then gives one chapter per principal investigator (five PIs, alphabetical); its appendices hold each PI's test matrices (A), the dilution model and its verification tests (B), anomalies met (C), thermal analysis (D) and the BASS and BASS-II papers and talks produced up to summer 2020 (E). [BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED]
- BASS-II tests the hypothesis that a material in microgravity, given enough ventilation, burns as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity when the other conditions (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature and so on) are the same. [BAS-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA screens and controls materials for flammability with an upward-burning test in normal gravity, held to be the worst-case geometry on Earth; the authors state that this test may not be conservative for flammability in space. [BAS-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- One BASS-II objective is to find the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft environments and how it compares with the terrestrial upward-burning screen used to clear materials for spacecraft use. [BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED]
- The main BASS-II variables were ambient O2 concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness and geometry; the ambient O2 variable was made possible by diluting the working volume with gaseous N2. [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.19 · MEASURED]
- Many tests looked for the minimum O2 concentration or flow velocity at which a material burns in space, for comparison with Earth-based limits; flame growth rates were also sought, to learn how fast a fire in space grows and whether flames reach a finite size or keep growing. [BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that flame growth rate matters for spacecraft firefighting strategy. [BAS-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors state that data from the simpler microgravity flow environment can validate detailed combustion models, which can then be extended to the more complex models that normal-gravity flames need, with broad use for terrestrial combustion problems. [BAS-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- 126 BASS-II tests were run, more than the 103 planned, because some samples were burned more than once; some samples could still be burned further if operations time becomes available. [BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED]
- The authors describe the chapter 1 data as the first extensive data on the stoichiometry and toxicity of combustion products in microgravity. [BAS-01 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### 2. BASS-II hardware in the ISS glovebox
- The BASS hardware is a small flow duct that contains small-scale burning of solid samples inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the ISS; the MSG, in the ISS Destiny Lab, gives a contained atmosphere for fire safety experiments (Ref. 9). [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The MSG filter banks capture particulates and convert CO to CO2 with an ambient-temperature catalyst; Fig. 1.1 shows the BASS-II hardware in the MSG working volume, which was diluted with ISS N2, and the CSA-CP (O2, CO) and CDM (CO2) sensors used for gas concentrations before and after each burn. [BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.12 · Fig. 1.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The BASS-II hardware is made of the flow duct, a still camera, a video camera, video and power boxes, an external control box with its plumbing, and mounting systems. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The flow duct is black anodized and rectangular, 7.6 × 7.6 × 17 cm with rounded corners; it was first built for gas-jet diffusion flame studies (Ref. 10) and adapted to hold solid samples for BASS. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- A variable-speed fan blew the flow through the duct, and up to two extra flow restrictors at the fan inlet raised the pressure drop to bring the duct flow down to the test point; the flow then went through a honeycomb straightener and an inlet screen to reduce swirl. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Maximum duct flow velocity was ~55 cm/s with no restrictor and ~35 cm/s with two restrictors (BASS-II duct in the MSG, ISS). [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED]
- An omnidirectional spherical airspeed transducer (TSI 8475) between the honeycomb and the screen measured the steady-state duct flow; its probe response time was about 1 min. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The 17-cm test section held an N2 nozzle, a movable scale and an Oriel 71768 thermopile detector (Newport) with a CaFl window (spectral range 0.13–11 µm), set in the downstream top back corner and looking upstream. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The test section had two orthogonal windows; for BASS the top one was replaced to give a mounting-rail system for the solid samples, and the top window was used by a Nikon D300s 12.3-megapixel colour still camera with a 60-mm lens (4,320 × 2,968-pixel images). [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The duct exit held a perforated copper plate followed by a brass screen, for heat rejection and as a cold surface for soot deposition; the flow turned 90° to leave the duct, which helped the hot combustion gases mix with cool ambient air. [BAS-01 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The front window opened for sample and igniter change-out and carried interlocks for the igniter and the N2 flow; a Panasonic WV-CP654 colour video camera (760 × 480 pixels) looked in through it by a turning mirror. [BAS-01 p.12–13 · MEASURED · nominal]
- A video camera with a data overlay and a 35-mm still camera recorded the burns; the overlay showed the N2 flow rate (cm3/min), fan voltage (10× V), airspeed transducer reading (cm/s) and radiometer signal. [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The fan voltage was calibrated against the airspeed transducer at the end of every operations day. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED]
- The radiometer signal was not calibrated; it served as a measure of flame dynamics and steadiness. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · ctx]
- An astronaut worked the controls (ignition, fan speed and others) while the PI team watched from the ground and spoke directly with the astronaut; the external control box held the fan-voltage and N2-flow controls, enable switches for the igniter and N2 flow, and a radiometer gain setting. [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Samples and ignition
- BASS-II burned cast PMMA shaped as rods of several diameters (6.35–12.7 mm), thin to thick slabs (0.125–5 mm) or a section of a 4-cm-diameter sphere, plus flat cotton-fiberglass blended fabric samples. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED]
- Samples could generally be mounted to burn in either opposed or concurrent flow; flat samples were 1 or 2 cm wide. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Ignition was manual, by a Kanthal A-1 29-gauge hot-wire coil of nominal resistance 0.8–1 Ω, powered at 3.5–3.8 A when the astronaut pulled the deployment lever that moved the igniter into place. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Samples burned inside the duct, and the combustion products left the duct and mixed with the working-volume gas; samples were returned to Earth and weighed for mass loss. [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 1.2 shows BASS-II flame geometries, forced flow upward in every image: (a) opposed thin slab, (b) spherical section, (c) opposed rod at higher flow, (d) flat fabric at higher flow, (e) opposed thick slab, (f) concurrent rod, (g) opposed rod at low flow with an open tip, similar to a concurrent rod, (h) flat fabric at low flow (BASS-II duct in the MSG, ISS; not reported in the pages read for these images: O2, pressure, flow values). [BAS-01 p.13 · Fig. 1.2 · MEASURED]

### 3. Setting the test O2: N2 dilution of the glovebox and the CSTR model
- For the first time on the ISS, BASS-II diluted the MSG working volume with ISS gaseous N2 (GN2), taking it from standard ISS "air" down to the low-O2 flammability limits. [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- A perfectly stirred (continuously stirred tank reactor, CSTR) dilution model was built to give the N2 flow time and flow rate that bring the working volume to each test's target O2 in a controlled way. [BAS-01 p.9 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.11 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.14 · MODELED · nominal]
- The model was calibrated with CSA-CP O2 readings offset by that day's Major Constituents Analyzer (MCA) reading of the ISS ambient atmosphere, because the CSA-CP O2 sensor is not recalibrated on orbit. [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED]
- The authors report that the dilution worked very well for operations and added a new key variable, ambient O2 level, to the test matrices; the conclusions state the CSTR model was verified against sensor readings. [BAS-01 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Working-volume O2 was varied from ambient ISS levels (~21 % O2) down to ~14 % O2 for very near-limit flames. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED]
- A diluted atmosphere, needed by many tests, typically took 1–3 h to reach, using ISS N2 from the hose linking the BASS-II duct to the MSG back wall (Fig. 1.1); a small MKS 179A mass flowmeter (<0.5 LPM) regulated the N2, which entered the duct through a small nozzle just downstream of the fan. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · nominal]
- During the N2 flow the duct fan ran at maximum (>100 LPM) to mix the gas, blow it into the working volume and keep it circulating through the hours-long dilution. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Model assumptions: mixing in the working volume by the BASS-II duct fan is taken as instantaneous, so the "leak" outflow from the MSG work volume to the ISS cabin carries the perfectly mixed concentration; pressure, temperature and volume of the work volume are constant, so the leak rate equals the N2 supply rate r. [BAS-01 p.14 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.14 · MODELED · ctx, nominal]
- Validity check: perfect mixing holds while the residence time (V/R) is at least 5–10 times the mixing time, which the text says the 100 LPM N2 flow rate during dilution meets (250 L / 100 LPM ≈ 2.5 min mixing time); for the MSG volume and N2 flow rates the residence time V/R is 500+ min and the mixing time under 50 min, so the authors judge the assumption valid. [BAS-01 p.14 · MODELED]
- Appendix B symbols for the model: Cin, O2 concentration entering the work volume, = 0 (pure N2); r, GN2 flow rate, 0.0005 m3/min maximum, adjustable; V, MSG working volume, 0.25 m3; the model is a mole balance on O2 with the working volume as control volume, an N2 input and a leak of well-mixed gas. [BAS-01 p.123 · MODELED · ctx]
- The model details and its on-orbit validation tests with the MCA (Ref. 11) are given in Appendix B. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED]

### 4. Gas sensors
- To measure O2 depletion and completeness of combustion (CO and CO2) in microgravity burns under spacecraft ventilation flows, and so give data on flame stoichiometry and heat release rates, BASS-II used onboard ISS sensors read before and after each test: two portable battery-powered instruments in the working volume, the Carbon Dioxide Monitor (CDM, CO2) and the Compound Specific Analyzer-Combustion Products (CSA-CP, O2 and CO) (Refs. 3–5). [BAS-01 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.13–14 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors state that these sensor readings allow the completeness of combustion to be judged. [BAS-01 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CSA-CP O2 resolution was 0.1 % O2; its CO sensor is zero-calibrated every 60 days, with a 0–1,000 ppm range and 1 ppm resolution; the CDM CO2 sensor was within its calibration window, with a 0–5 % range and 0.1 vol% resolution. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · ctx]
- The sensor data gave initial and final conditions for repeated tests in a sealed working volume and showed when the working volume needed purging. [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED]
- O2 fell during each burn while CO and CO2 rose accordingly (BASS-II tests in the sealed MSG working volume, ISS; initial O2 ~21 down to ~14 %; total pressure not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED]

#### O2 depletion and CO2 production (Fig. 1.3)
- Sensor readings taken before and after each test gave the O2 depletion and the completeness of combustion (CO, CO2) of each microgravity burn under spacecraft ventilation flows; for every BASS-II test with PMMA fuel, the O2 depletion is set against the CO2 produced (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · nominal]
- PMMA stoichiometry (Eq. 1.1): C5H8O2 + 6 O2 → 5 CO2 + 4 H2O (PMMA C5H8O2; molar coefficients; a stoichiometric relation, not a fit). [BAS-01 p.14 · Eq. 1.1 · MODELED]
- Over a wide range of initial O2, opposed or concurrent forced-flow velocities and sample geometries, the O2 depletion against CO2 production agrees very well with the 6:5 stoichiometric O2:CO2 ratio for a one-step gas-phase reaction (Fig. 1.3 dashed line, slope −6/5 = −1.2; conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.9–10 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.15 · Fig. 1.3 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 1.3 legend series: opposed rods, concurrent rods, opposed thin slabs, opposed thick slabs, spherical section in stagnation flow; caption: data from all geometries, flows and initial O2 follow the expected stoichiometric trend (conditions C2). [BAS-01 p.15 · Fig. 1.3 · MEASURED]

#### CO production (Fig. 1.4)
- Apart from unburned fuel (mainly methylmethacrylate vapour, which holds some O2, Eq. 1.4), the authors name CO as the only other non-trace species that could hold O2; CO was measured (Figs 1.4–1.6). [BAS-01 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CO against CO2 followed a linear trend for some data sets but not for all the fuel geometries and flows tested (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.10 · MEASURED]
- Concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm CO for every 1 % CO2, opposed thick slabs on average 370 ppm CO per 1 % CO2 (between the two rod series), and opposed rods showed a very nonlinear CO-versus-CO2 response (conditions C1, flow direction as named). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest the opposed rods' very nonlinear response may point to a flow effect. [BAS-01 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The longer the burn, the more CO2 formed; the nominal procedure for most samples turned the flow down in steps (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At very low velocities the tail of the opposed-flow flames opened up (PMMA, opposed flow, BASS-II duct in the MSG, ISS; velocity values not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED]
- The authors presume the opened tail let incomplete-combustion products escape the flame zone. [BAS-01 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The concurrent procedure was very similar, but the concurrent flame always had an open tail, so incomplete-combustion products left throughout the burn (PMMA rods, concurrent flow, BASS-II duct in the MSG, ISS). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 1.4 caption: CO generated appears clustered by geometry and flow configuration; concurrent rods produced the most CO per CO2, opposed rods showed a very nonlinear trend and thick opposed-flow slabs fell between the two; legend series as Fig. 1.3, with unlabelled dotted trend lines (conditions C3). [BAS-01 p.16 · Fig. 1.4 · MEASURED]
- The Fig. 1.3 outlier at 2.8 % CO2 is left out of Fig. 1.4 because its CO over-ranged the sensor (>1,000 ppm full scale), so there is no quantitative CO value for that test (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED · single-test]

#### Completeness of combustion: CO/CO2 ratio (Fig. 1.5)
- The authors take the CO/CO2 ratio as a measure of completeness of combustion, of interest to the combustion community; Fig. 1.5 plots it against the initial O2 in the working volume. [BAS-01 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For efficiently burned flue gases (boilers, furnaces and similar) the ratio is typically below 0.004, a value given without a reference. [BAS-01 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most BASS-II CO/CO2 data lie well above 0.004 (conditions C1; initial O2 ~13.6 to ~22.2 vol% as plotted in Fig. 1.5). [BAS-01 p.16 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.17 · Fig. 1.5 · MEASURED · ~fig]
- The authors read this as microgravity flames being comparatively inefficient, and conclude that the CO/CO2 ratios of these fires are an order of magnitude above those of efficient flue gases. [BAS-01 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors state that a smouldering event of similar size would produce significantly more CO. [BAS-01 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On the Mir space station, a smouldering carbon bed in the Trace Contaminant Control System raised CO to very high levels throughout the station before it was detected (no reference given). [BAS-01 p.16 · CITED]
- Absolute CO values were very high in the 250-L MSG free working volume, but the MSG contained the CO and converted it to CO2 during the post-test purge of the work volume (BASS-II tests, ISS). [BAS-01 p.16 · MEASURED]
- Diluted into the ISS U.S. Lab alone (106 m3 pressurized volume), the products of a fire the size of a BASS-II test would give only 1.5 ppm CO. [BAS-01 p.16 · MODELED]
- 1.5 ppm is well below the spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) for long-term exposure (10 ppm) and the 1-hour SMAC of 55 ppm (Ref. 12). [BAS-01 p.16 · CITED]
- Fig. 1.5 caption: the data show some clustering; lower O2 gives more CO per CO2 for concurrent rods, while opposed rods show the opposite trend; opposed-slab data trend like the concurrent rods but with large scatter; legend series as Fig. 1.3 with unlabelled dotted trend lines (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.17 · Fig. 1.5 · MEASURED]

#### Heat release rate (Fig. 1.6)
- Heat release rates were calculated from the O2 consumed and the burn time of each test, with 13.1 kJ released per gram of O2 consumed (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.10 · MODELED · nominal]
- The 13.1 kJ/g O2 constant and the method are Huggett's O2 consumption calorimetry (Ref. 13), applied with each test's burn time. [BAS-01 p.16 · CITED · nominal]
- Most tests had heat release rates well below 100 W (conditions C1; initial O2 ~13.6 to ~22.2 vol% as plotted in Fig. 1.6). [BAS-01 p.10 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.16 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.17 · Fig. 1.6 · MODELED · ~fig]
- HRR tends to rise with ambient O2 concentration (Fig. 1.6, conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.16 · MODELED]
- The authors attribute the HRR scatter to the different duct flows between, and even within, tests. [BAS-01 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The one long opposed thick-slab test that damaged the front window's lower downstream corner, the Fig. 1.3 outlier at 2.8 % CO2, released close to 100 W (initial O2 of this test not reported in the pages read; other conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.15–16 · MODELED · single-test]
- An earlier, fairly brief concurrent-rod test released almost 110 W and caused no damage (initial O2 of this test not reported in the pages read; other conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.16 · MODELED · single-test]
- Fig. 1.6 caption: the Fig. 1.3 data converted to watts with burn time and Huggett's constant, plotted against initial O2; HRR generally rises with ambient O2 and is modest for these small flames under the conditions tested; legend: opposed rods, concurrent rods, opposed thick slab, spherical section in stagnation flow, with unlabelled dotted trend lines (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.17 · Fig. 1.6 · MODELED]

#### Fuel mass loss and global equivalence ratio (Fig. 1.7, Eqs. 1.2–1.4)
- To date 34 burned BASS-II samples have come back to Earth for postflight analysis; 8 of them, used for several tests, were altered on orbit (burned fuel cut off and/or built-in igniter leads removed), so their pre- and postflight weights cannot give combustion mass loss, and 7 more had burns so short that no O2 consumption was measured, so they cannot be used for equivalence-ratio estimates; Fig. 1.7 compares mass loss with O2 consumption for the remaining 19. [BAS-01 p.18 · MEASURED]
- O2 consumption and CO2 generation show clear trends against measured fuel mass loss (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.18 · MEASURED]
- The authors find it unsurprising that the O2 and CO2 trends mirror each other, given the stoichiometric O2–CO2 relation. [BAS-01 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CO data are more scattered, but CO generation generally rises with fuel mass loss and O2 consumption (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.18 · MEASURED]
- The test with 7 g of fuel mass loss had over 1,000 ppm CO, above the sensor range (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.18 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Fig. 1.7 caption: O2 consumed, CO2 generated and CO generated per gram of fuel mass loss for the two fuels; legend: O2 consumed, CO2 generated, CO generated, and linear fits to O2 consumed and CO2 generated (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.18 · Fig. 1.7 · MEASURED]

- The observed slope of O2 consumed against fuel mass loss is 0.4582 O2 vol% per gram of fuel (conditions C6; MSG free volume V = 250,000 cc). [BAS-01 p.19 · MEASURED]
- Eq. 1.2: the global equivalence ratio, for cellulose or PMMA stoichiometry, is Φglobal = (gmol_fuel / gmol_O2) / (1/6), with gmol_fuel the fuel consumed (Eq. 1.4) and gmol_O2 the O2 consumed (Eq. 1.3); fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.18 · Eq. 1.2 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.19 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1.3: by the ideal gas law, gmol of O2 consumed = PV/RT = [1 · (ΔO2 vol%/100) · 250,000] / (82.05 · 300), with MSG free volume V = 250,000 cc, R = 82.05 cc·atm/gmol·K, P = 1 atm, T = 300 K and ΔO2 vol% the change in O2 percent by volume; fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.19 · Eq. 1.3 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1.4: gmol_fuel = grams of fuel / molecular weight (g/gmol); a PMMA molecular weight of 100 g/gmol is used for most of the data. [BAS-01 p.19 · Eq. 1.4 · MODELED · nominal]
- With the 0.4582 O2 vol%/g slope and 100 g/gmol for PMMA, the effective global equivalence ratio of the tests is Φglobal = 1.3, fuel rich (19 returned samples; P = 1 atm and T = 300 K as in Eq. 1.3); the summary gives 1.3 as the average, from mass loss and O2 consumption data. [BAS-01 p.10 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.18 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.19 · MODELED]
- The authors conclude that the flames were generally under-ventilated, burning fuel rich under the low-velocity forced flow, and did not burn all the vaporized fuel: some ended as soot, some as CO and some as unburned hydrocarbons. [BAS-01 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Chapter 1 conclusions
- The authors conclude that O2 burned nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, that CO levels appear to depend on geometry and in some cases on the combination of flow velocity and geometry, and that most tests released well below 100 W. [BAS-01 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the one long test that released close to 100 W, the downstream corner of the front window was damaged because a leak steered the heat of this energetic flame to that spot during the prolonged burn (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.19 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The duct leak was repaired on orbit and operations then went on without further incident. [BAS-01 p.15 · MEASURED]

### 6. Crew operations and on-orbit repairs
- On-orbit repairs: Rick Mastracchio repaired the duct door so that its seal integrity and interlock-switch function held for the rest of BASS-II operations; Alex Gerst and Reid Wiseman repaired the video cable, restoring the video overlay data that only that camera gave. [BAS-01 p.19 · MEASURED]
- The crew observed and described transient phenomena during ignition attempts and near extinction that could not be seen from the ground (BASS-II tests, ISS). [BAS-01 p.19 · MEASURED]
- The authors credit the crew with adapting to new flow variations such as blowoff extinctions, which proved very valuable for outlining the U-shaped flammability boundary. [BAS-01 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Objective, samples and apparatus
- RTDFS set out to examine, by varying fuel thickness, how the thermal and species fields can diverge and lead to flame extinguishment in microgravity. [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- RTDFS samples were 1- and 2-cm-wide thin PMMA films 0.1–0.4 mm thick; BASS-II gave 22 test points, listed in Table A.1 as tests B1–B22, and the data are catalogued at http://flame.sdsu.edu (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.111–112 · Table A.1 · MEASURED · ctx]
- In the Section 2.2 description the BASS-II apparatus is a combustion tunnel, a 76-mm square duct, in which PMMA samples 20 mm wide, about 95 mm long and 100–400 µm thick burn in opposed flow; a fan drives an O2–N2 mixture through flow straighteners from right to left, and the sample is lit at its left end. [BAS-01 p.29 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Depending on flow velocity and O2 concentration, a steady flame forms and spreads from the left end of the sample toward the right (opposed flow, BASS-II, ISS). [BAS-01 p.29 · MEASURED]
- The O2 level can be set to 21 % or below and the flow velocity to 0–50 cm/s; a hot-wire anemometer calibrates flow velocity against fan voltage, and the fan voltage then gives the flow velocity. [BAS-01 p.29 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two crew members ran the experiments in the ISS MSG, with operating instructions passed in real time from the NASA Glenn Operations Center. [BAS-01 p.29 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Test procedure: the opposing flow is set by the fan voltage; once it is steady, the igniter is switched on until a flame is visible and then off; a high-resolution digital still camera photographs the flame at 1 frame per second, and the radiometer confirms extinction when the visible flame goes out; in some tests the flow was changed during spread to widen the test matrix without burning more samples. [BAS-01 p.29 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Each test begins with steady spread in a forced flow, after which the flow velocity is lowered gradually (Fig. 2.1). [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 2.6 tunnel schematic: 7.62-cm square duct; 9.5 cm of exposed sample; 4.8 cm from sample end to heat sink; sample card 0.7 cm wide; 2.3 cm from the duct inlet screen to the metal sample card; "74 mm on BASS scale" marked at the igniter end; igniter at the left (downstream) end; opposed-flow velocity Vg from the inlet screen (right) toward the left, absolute spread rate Vf toward the right; anemometer at the inlet screen; tilted radiometer in the top left corner viewing the sample; heat sink and filter at the left exit. [BAS-01 p.29 · Fig. 2.6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Chapter 2 symbols: t, time, s; Vg, opposed-flow velocity. [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Spread-rate measurement from images
- An SDSU MATLAB-based image-processing application extracts flame spread rate and other information from the sequence of top-view photographs. [BAS-01 p.30 · MEASURED · nominal]
- To remove edge propagation, the central flame strip between two white lines parallel to the axis, about 14 mm apart, is isolated; each pixel's RGB values become an intensity, averaged across the strip width to give a 2D picture of the flame (Fig. 2.7b) and the width-averaged intensity along x (Fig. 2.7c). [BAS-01 p.30 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The flame leading edge is located at a fixed threshold intensity, with 30 working well for almost all tests; the bright edge is the maximum of the intensity curve; the spread rate is the slope of a linear regression over consecutive locations, and five consecutive locations were found to balance noise against temporal precision (the uncertainty depends on the number used). [BAS-01 p.30 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Spread rates from tracking the leading edge and the bright edge (Fig. 2.8) were reproducible within 5 % uncertainty whichever way the flame was tracked (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.30 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 2.7a example: top view 10 s after ignition of spread over 100-µm PMMA at 20.7 % O2, 1 atm and an opposed flow of 2.5 cm/s (BASS-II, ISS); the dots along the axis are 6 mm apart, the ignition wire glows red at x = 36 mm, the burnout (black line) is at x = 42 mm, and the leading edge sits at x = 887 pixel for threshold intensity 30. [BAS-01 p.30 · Fig. 2.7 · MEASURED · single-test]

#### ISS results: extinction at low opposed flow
- First test: over a 100-µm sample a steady flame spread at 2.2 mm/s across half the sample length; the flow was then cut off abruptly and the flame went out within 2 s, as the radiometer signal drop shows (Fig. 2.2) (conditions C7; O2, pressure and the flow before cut-off not reported in the pages read for this test). [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Second test, to pin down the extinction flow velocity (conditions C8): the leading-edge spread rate (Figs 2.3, 2.8) shows extinction about 30 s after ignition, when the fan voltage indicates a flow velocity of about 1.1 cm/s. [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Figs 2.1 and 2.9 (same images) show the flame during radiative extinction at t = 27 s, Vg = 3.0 cm/s; t = 28 s, 1.5 cm/s; t = 29 s, 1.1 cm/s; t = 30 s, 1.1 cm/s (conditions C8). [BAS-01 p.22 · Fig. 2.1 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.32 · Fig. 2.9 · MEASURED · single-test]
- On the path to radiative extinction, as the flow is lowered from about t = 27 s, the flame shrinks, its orange colour disappears and it turns completely blue (conditions C8). [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors attribute the all-blue flame most likely to the temperature drop from radiative losses, made stronger by the longer residence time at low flow velocity. [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The radiometer signal (Figs 2.2 and 2.10, legend "B3: Radiometer reading") fits a cooling, shrinking flame: it starts to fall at about t = 27 s; after t = 30 s no flame is visible and the signal slope changes suddenly, the discontinuity at 30 s coinciding with the disappearance of the visible flame (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; BAS-01 p.22 · Fig. 2.2 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; BAS-01 p.32 · Fig. 2.10 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors suggest the slope change after 30 s may occur because the radiation then comes mostly from the sample holder, with the combustion products swept away by the flow. [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Table A.1 row B3 (conditions C9) also prints initial and final CO2 of 0.43 and 0.49 vol% and CO of 12 and 19 ppm, with the observation that the start was probably 20.6 % O2, that lower-flow flames were much bluer overall, and that there was still some soot. [BAS-01 p.112 · Table A.1 · MEASURED · ctx, single-test]

- At every thickness from 100 to 400 µm the maximum spread rate was inversely proportional to fuel thickness (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.21 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED]
- The authors take this inverse proportionality, a hallmark of the thermally thin regime (Ref. 1 in Section 2.1, Ref. 13 in Section 2.2), to mean the fuel can be treated as thermally thin at all these thicknesses. [BAS-01 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Stated limitations of the extinction velocities: significant uncertainty, because the flow calibration at such low velocities has large error bars; the boundary layer formed by the fuel and the tunnel walls affects the velocity the flame sees; and the reduced velocity reaches the flame only after a time lag, which the authors assume acts the same way for every thickness. [BAS-01 p.21–23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A few of these tests were repeated, with very similar results (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.31 · MEASURED]
- The authors conclude that the extinction velocity does not depend on fuel thickness. [BAS-01 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors note that the data at the lower O2 level are insufficient, and state that the extinction velocity rises significantly as O2 falls while staying independent of fuel thickness. [BAS-01 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Normal-gravity companion data at SDSU
- RTDFS took further ground data on downward flame spread over PMMA, from thermally thin to thick, in the SDSU flame stabilizer, and compared them with BASS-II data; that comparison, published in Fire Safety Journal, is reprinted in full as Section 2.3. [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that the flame stabilizer suits downward-spreading flames (Ref. 2) but makes a forced opposed flow hard to create because of the diagnostic probes around it. [BAS-01 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The SDSU flame tower (Ref. 3) creates an opposing or concurrent flow by moving the sample; it has a fixed height of 8 m (1 g, ground). [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Because the tower height is fixed at 8 m, the available test time is inversely proportional to the relative flow created, so the authors state there is not enough time to study blowoff extinction there. [BAS-01 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The SDSU vertical flame tunnel (Fig. 2.4, same dimensions as the Hirano tunnel, Ref. 4) has a 10 × 10 cm test-section cross-section; an array of microcontroller-driven fans creates an opposed flow of up to 100 cm/s; two RTDs below the sample holder, one actively heated and one as reference, monitor the flow velocity and were calibrated in the flame tower by traversing the probe through still air at set velocities; the tunnel can be rotated to any angle to change the effect of buoyancy-induced flow (Fig. 2.5) (1 g, ground lab). [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.24 · Fig. 2.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.24 · Fig. 2.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Data were collected in the SDSU flame tunnel for cellulosic fuels and PMMA sheets (1 g). [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED]
- To establish the boundary-layer effect on flame spread rate, ashless filter paper was burned with the opposing flow velocity as control variable (SDSU, 1 g, ground); the experiments are quite repeatable and gave a correlation for cellulosic fuel (correlation not printed in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.25 · MEASURED]
- The authors state that, although blowoff extinction velocity is assumed to depend only on chemical kinetics, these filter-paper experiments clearly make boundary-layer development an important parameter. [BAS-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Critical flow velocity paper (Section 2.2): background
- Section 2.2 studies how opposing flow affects flame spread over thin solid fuel with scaling theory, a comprehensive computational model and ISS experiments. [BAS-01 p.27 · MEASURED]
- Over thin fuels the spread rate does not depend on opposing-flow velocity in the thermal regime, but in microgravity, where the opposing flow can be very mild or absent without buoyancy, the spread rate is known to fall as the opposed flow is reduced and can, under some conditions, end in extinguishment at a low enough flow. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The paper combines scaling arguments and computations to predict a critical flow velocity for this extinction; the authors state that the results of the recent, limited number of space tests seem to confirm the prediction and validate the closed-form formula. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In opposed-flow spread over thermally thin fuels the flame spreads steadily and the fuel can be taken as uniformly heated through its thickness. [BAS-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Residence time t_res ≈ L_g/V_g ≈ α_g/V_g², the time the oxidizer takes to pass the flame leading-edge length L_g ≈ α_g/V_g (α_g gas thermal diffusivity at Tv, m²/s; V_g opposed-flow velocity); in the thermal regime gas-phase and pyrolysis chemistry are taken as infinitely fast compared with it; scaling relation, fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.28 · MODELED]
- The simplified closed-form thermal limit of spread rate (Refs. 1, 2) does not depend on flow velocity Vg, is inversely proportional to fuel thickness and is directly proportional to the de Ris coefficient F = (T_f − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞), with T_f the adiabatic flame temperature, T_v the fuel vaporization temperature and T_∞ the ambient and virgin-fuel temperature (K); fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.28 · CITED]
- As opposed-flow velocity rises, residence time falls with the square of velocity, so finite-rate gas-phase kinetics matter and finally cause blowoff extinction; this kinetic regime has been studied experimentally (Ref. 3) and computationally (Ref. 4), and the spread rate normalised by its thermal limit has been correlated with the Damköhler number, the ratio of chemical to residence time. [BAS-01 p.28 · CITED]
- Downward spread in a quiescent 1-g environment can be treated as a special case of opposed-flow spread in which buoyancy-induced flow supplies the opposing velocity (Ref. 5). [BAS-01 p.28 · CITED]
- In microgravity the opposing flow can be very mild, and absent altogether in perfectly quiescent zero gravity. [BAS-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Numerical (Refs. 6, 7) and experimental (Refs. 8, 9) studies have established a radiative regime in mild opposed flow, where spread rate falls as the opposed flow is reduced and the flame goes out (Ref. 10) if the flow is low enough; the outcome also depends on other ambient conditions, since steady spread over thin fuels in perfectly quiescent surroundings has been shown at higher O2 levels (Ref. 11). [BAS-01 p.28 · CITED]
- The authors define the critical velocity as the opposed-flow velocity below which steady spread is not observed in microgravity, state that it has been shown to depend on O2 level, and that its dependence on other parameters such as fuel thickness is still not well known, with no experimentally verified closed-form formula available to predict it. [BAS-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The paper reports recent ISS experiments on flame spread over thin PMMA sheets, analyses them for the critical velocity at several fuel thicknesses and ambient O2 levels, compares them with a simplified analysis and a 2D steady flame-spread model, and proposes a predictive formula for the critical velocity. [BAS-01 p.28–29 · MEASURED]
- Section 2.2 symbols: specific heat at constant pressure c (kJ/kg·K); de Ris flame coefficient F; length scale L (m); temperature T (K); time t (s); absolute spread rate Vf; opposed-flow velocity Vg; velocity relative to the flame Vr = Vg + Vf; width W; gas thermal diffusivity αg at Tv (m²/s); surface emissivity ε; gas conductivity λg at Tv (kW/m·K); nondimensional spread rate ηf and flow velocity ηg; gas density ρg at Tv and solid density ρs (kg/m³); fuel half-thickness τ (m); Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ (kW/(m²K⁴)); nondimensional radiation number ℜ0; subscripts: cr critical, f adiabatic flame, g gas phase, res residence, s solid phase, v vaporization, x and y coordinates, ∞ ambient, plus radiative and thermal. [BAS-01 p.27–28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- The model solves the 2D, steady, elliptic gas-phase equations for conservation of energy, species mass, total mass and momentum, with ordinary differential equations for mass and energy in the solid; the two phases are coupled by interface conditions and solved in sequence with the SIMPLER algorithm (Ref. 14). [BAS-01 p.33 · MODELED · nominal]
- Fuel vaporization is modelled with a single-step global gas-phase reaction of second order and first-order pyrolysis kinetics; model details and properties are in Ref. 15; the model has been validated by reproducing analytical solutions (Ref. 4), among them the Emmons problem and the de Ris solution for thin and thick fuels. [BAS-01 p.33 · MODELED · nominal]
- Gas and surface radiation use the global-balance radiation model (Ref. 6): although the CFD is 2D, the Planck-mean absorption coefficient for the radiative source term is found by equating the thin-gas loss from the whole domain to the 3D radiative loss computed with a narrow-band model (Ref. 16), and the radiation calculation (Ref. 17) includes losses due to the sample's finite width. [BAS-01 p.33 · MODELED · nominal]
- At relatively high Vg the computed spread rate Vf is nearly independent of the opposing flow and inversely proportional to fuel thickness, as thermal theory (Ref. 1) predicts (conditions C10). [BAS-01 p.33 · MODELED]
- As Vg falls, Vf drops and the flame goes out, as in the experiments; the computed extinction velocity is the same, 1.5 cm/s, for all four thicknesses, a result checked to be independent of grid density and computational domain (conditions C10). [BAS-01 p.33 · Fig. 2.11 · MODELED]

#### Scale analysis and the closed-form critical velocity (Eqs 2.1–2.5)
- In microgravity the opposing flow can be very mild or absent, raising residence time until gas and surface radiation can become significant next to the other heat-transfer modes. [BAS-01 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Numerical studies (Refs. 6, 7) showed that gas and surface radiation act mainly as losses that depress flame temperature; if N2 in the oxidizer is replaced by a strongly radiating species such as CO2, gas-radiation feedback may become important (Ref. 18). [BAS-01 p.34 · CITED]
- As Vg falls, radiative loss grows and Vf drops below its thermal limit (Figs 2.11, 2.12); surface radiation loss, gas-phase radiation loss and gas-to-surface radiation feedback (Fig. 2.13) all scale the same way with residence time t_res ≈ α_g/V_g², so all become more severe as Vg falls. [BAS-01 p.34 · MODELED]
- Assumptions: radiation feedback is negligible (Ref. 19) and surface radiation loss stands for the radiation term in the surface energy balance; forward conduction through the thin solid (density ρs, heated layer Lsy) is negligible (Ref. 20), so gas-phase conduction minus radiative loss supplies the net forward heat that raises virgin fuel from T∞ to Tv; the gas phase being the only heat source, L_gx ~ L_gy ~ α_g/V_g (convection balanced against x and y conduction at the leading edge, valid for V_g ≫ V_f), and L_sy is replaced by the fuel half-thickness τ, the fuel being uniformly heated through its thickness, which defines a thermally thin fuel. [BAS-01 p.34–35 · MODELED · nominal]
- Eq. 2.1, the surface energy balance (terms reordered, same expression): ρ_s c_s V_f W L_sy (T_v − T_∞) ~ λ_g W L_gx (T_f − T_v)/L_gy − εσ W L_sx (T_v⁴ − T_∞⁴); here W is an arbitrary width, L_sx and L_sy are the solid and L_gx and L_gy the gas length scales, horizontal and vertical (Fig. 2.13), λ_g is the gas conductivity at Tv (kW/m·K), c_s and ρ_s the solid heat capacity and density (kg/m³), ε the surface emissivity, σ the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (kW/(m²K⁴)), V_f the absolute spread rate, and T_f, T_v and T_∞ the adiabatic flame, vaporization and ambient temperatures (K); scaling balance, fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.34–35 · Eq. 2.1 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.2, the thermal limit with radiative loss neglected: V_f,thermal ~ [λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ)] F, with F = (T_f − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞) and τ the fuel half-thickness (m); fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.35 · Eq. 2.2 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.3, Eq. 2.1 made nondimensional with the thermal limit as velocity scale: η_f η_g ~ η_g − ℜ0, so η_f ~ 1 − ℜ0/η_g and V_f,radiative ~ V_f,thermal (1 − ℜ0/η_g); fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.35 · Eq. 2.3 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.4: ℜ0 ≡ (1/F²)(ρ_s c_s/(ρ_g c_g))(εστ/λ_g)[(T_v⁴ − T_∞⁴)/(T_v − T_∞)], η_g ≡ V_g/V_f,thermal, η_f ≡ V_f/V_f,thermal, with c_g gas specific heat and ρ_g gas density at Tv (kg/m³); ℜ0 is the nondimensional radiation number, η_g the nondimensional flow velocity and η_f the nondimensional spread rate. [BAS-01 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.35 · Eq. 2.4 · MODELED]
- Fig. 2.13 shows the heat-transfer modes at the flame leading edge (radiation loss, radiation feedback, solid conduction, gas conduction, surface radiation) and the length scales, with Lsy ≤ τ for a thermally thin fuel, s and g for solid and gas, Vf absolute spread rate, Vg opposed-flow velocity, Vr = Vg + Vf and τ the fuel half-thickness. [BAS-01 p.35 · Fig. 2.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- By Eq. 2.3 the radiative-regime spread rate falls as ℜ0 rises and as ηg falls; fuel thickness does not change ℜ0/ηg, so the inverse dependence of spread rate on thickness typical of the thermal regime carries over to the radiative regime, and the extinction velocity does not depend on fuel thickness, as in the experiments and computations. [BAS-01 p.36 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.5, radiative extinction from η_f = 0 in Eq. 2.3: η_g ≤ ℜ0, so V_g ~ V_g,cr with V_g,cr ≡ [εσ/(c_g ρ_g)](T_v⁴ − T_∞⁴)/(T_f − T_v) (ε surface emissivity, σ Stefan-Boltzmann constant, c_g gas specific heat, ρ_g gas density at T_v, T_v vaporization, T_∞ ambient and T_f adiabatic flame temperature); the conclusions restate it as the closed-form critical velocity of the simplified scale analysis; fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.36 · Eq. 2.5 · MODELED]
- Vg,cr is evaluated at different O2 levels with the property values of the numerical simulation (linearized flame temperature 2,199 K) and a vaporization temperature of 673 K (other property values not printed in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.36 · MODELED · nominal]

#### Chapter 2 conclusions and publications
- The authors conclude that the ISS tests fixed experimentally, for several fuel thicknesses and two O2 levels, a critical flow velocity below which steady spread cannot be sustained; that over four thicknesses the critical velocity does not depend on thickness, even though spread rate is inversely proportional to it, and rises as O2 falls; and that the 2D computation confirms this. [BAS-01 p.36 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors state that RTDFS bore out the theoretical and computational finding that the critical opposed-flow velocity for radiative extinction in microgravity does not depend on fuel thickness. [BAS-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Chapter 2 publication in Fire Safety Journal: "Opposed-Flow Flame Spread: A Comparison of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Experiments to Establish the Thermal Regime", by Bhattacharjee et al., vol. 79 (2016), pp. 111–118, DOI 10.1016/j.firesaf.2015.11.011; reprinted as Section 2.3. [BAS-01 p.23 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.25 · MEASURED]
- Chapter 2 publication in Combustion and Flame: "The Critical Flow Velocity for Radiative Extinction in Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Microgravity Environment: A Comparison of Experimental, Computational, and Theoretical Results", by Bhattacharjee et al., vol. 163 (2016), pp. 472–477, DOI 10.1016/j.combustflame.2015.10.023; reprinted in full as Section 2.2. [BAS-01 p.25 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.27 · MEASURED]

#### Aim of the study
- Section 2.3 reprints Bhattacharjee et al., "Opposed-Flow Flame Spread: A Comparison of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Experiments to Establish the Thermal Regime", Fire Saf. J. 79 (2016) 111–118, DOI 10.1016/j.firesaf.2015.11.011. [BAS-01 p.39 · CITED]
- The authors call the thermal regime of flame spread over solids the reference condition for all other flame spread research, and state that, although its theory is well understood, the well-known closed-form spread formulas do not compare well with available data. [BAS-01 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors add that buoyancy-induced flow makes a thermal regime hard to set up in normal gravity, since it may bring in finite-rate kinetics, so that even the transition thickness at which a fuel becomes thermally thick still lacks a widely accepted formula. [BAS-01 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The study gives opposed-flow spread data over PMMA of several thicknesses from the ISS, where the opposing flow can be lowered at will without interference from gravity-induced flow, plus a larger set of normal-gravity downward spread rates; it presents, for the first time, downward and microgravity data for the same fuel under the same conditions except gravity, with a simplified scale analysis to establish the thermal regime experimentally and to find the thin-to-thick transition thickness for downward spread. [BAS-01 p.39 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.41 · MEASURED]
- The authors state that comparing the two data sets establishes the thermal limit for thin fuel, in which spread rate does not depend on opposing-flow velocity, and that the classical thin-fuel formula fits the data well when the adiabatic flame temperature is used in its flame coefficient. [BAS-01 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The experimentally determined flame coefficient and downward-spread data for thick fuels give a closed-form expression for the thin-to-thick transition thickness in downward spread in the thermal regime. [BAS-01 p.39 · MODELED]

#### Background (introduction)
- Opposed-flow flame spread over solids has been studied for about four decades (Refs. 1–3). [BAS-01 p.40 · CITED]
- The authors describe upward spread as closely tied to fire safety but hard to model, since spread is unsteady and the flame quickly grows very large; in downward spread the flame is 2D, quasi-steady (constant spread rate while the shape may evolve) and quasi-laminar (the trailing edge may fluctuate), with a steady spread rate set by fuel and environment. [BAS-01 p.40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Downward-spread experiments can be cheap (Ref. 4), so quantitative spread theories can be tested and refined on them, and findings can carry over to upward or horizontal spread because much of the physics is shared (Ref. 5). [BAS-01 p.40–41 · CITED]
- Depending on its thickness, a sample may or may not be heated uniformly through its thickness. [BAS-01 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Pyrolysis chemistry for predicting burning rate may not be well known (Ref. 6), and computational models mostly assume one overall gas-phase reaction; a strong enough buoyant flow, a low enough O2 level or both can set combustion time against residence time and bring in chemical-kinetic effects (Ref. 7), lowering spread rate or causing extinction; and too low an opposing flow, as in microgravity, raises residence time so that surface and gas radiation grow in importance (Ref. 8). [BAS-01 p.41 · CITED]
- The authors state that, even with 2D laminar flow, a theory with gas radiation, gas-phase kinetics and pyrolysis kinetics still needs numerical solution. [BAS-01 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- de Ris (Ref. 9) introduced the thermal regime, in which the opposing flow is neither too small nor too large for radiation or chemistry to matter; neglecting radiation and taking infinite-rate kinetics allows an analytical solution, and the closed-form spread formulas of de Ris and Delichatsios (Refs. 9, 10) give a baseline for nondimensionalizing data and for the parametric dependence of spread on fuel and environment. [BAS-01 p.41 · CITED]
- The authors list drawbacks of these formulas: the flame temperature comes from a linearized mass-diffusion theory and can differ widely from the thermodynamic adiabatic flame temperature; constant properties leave much room in how air conductivity, specific heat and so on are evaluated; and when a measured spread rate disagrees with the prediction it is unclear whether property choice or a non-thermal regime is the cause. [BAS-01 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In flow tunnels where the opposing flow is set directly (Refs. 11, 12), high velocities that bring in gas-phase chemistry are easy to reach, but the flow cannot be lowered at will, and even in quiescent surroundings the buoyant flow may not be weak enough for infinite-rate kinetics to hold. [BAS-01 p.41 · CITED]
- The ISS gravity-free environment was used to carry the opposed-flow experiment to its logical end, lowering the opposing flow to any desired value without buoyancy, in search of the thermal regime. [BAS-01 p.41 · MEASURED]
- Only a handful of microgravity flame spread experiments exist; T'ien's book chapter (Ref. 19) reviews them. [BAS-01 p.45 · CITED]

#### Scale analysis (Eqs 2.6–2.10)
- Section 2.3 symbols: a_P, Planck-mean absorption coefficient; c, specific heat, kJ/kg·K; F, flame constant (Eq. 2.12); f, gas-to-preheat-region view factor; g, gravity; g,rad, gas radiation feedback; gy,cond, conduction through gas; L_g, gas diffusion length, m; L_sy, fuel thickness; s,rad, surface radiation; sx,cond, conduction through solid; T, temperature, K; t, time; V_f, absolute spread rate, m/s; V_g, oxidizer velocity, m/s; V_r = V_g + V_f; α_g, gas thermal diffusivity at T_v, m²/s; α_s, solid thermal diffusivity; ε, surface emissivity; λ_g, gas conductivity at T_v, kW/m·K; λ_s, solid conductivity; Ω, ratio (ρc_pλ)_g/(ρc_pλ)_s; ρ_g, gas density at T_v, kg/m³; ρ_s, solid density, kg/m³; σ, Stefan-Boltzmann constant, kW/(m²K⁴); τ, fuel half-thickness, m; ω‴_F, fuel consumption rate. [BAS-01 p.39–40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Section 2.3 subscripts: adb adiabatic; chem chemical; cond conduction; cr critical; de Ris (no meaning printed); eff effective; eql equal; expt experimental; f flame; g gas; lin linear; NC natural convection; rad radiation; res residence; s solid; th thermal; thick, thin and transition (no meaning printed); v vaporization; x, y coordinates; ∞ ambient. [BAS-01 p.40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 2.14 sketches the leading-edge time and length scales (in the thermal regime, fuel preheating and transverse conduction through gas and solid are of the same order); its labels give L_sx = L_g; t_g,res ≈ L_g/V_g and t_s,res ≈ L_g/V_f; t_s,res ≈ t_gy,cond ≈ t_sy,cond; t_g,chem ≪ t_g,res and t_s,chem ≪ t_s,res; t_g,rad ≫ t_g,res; and V_r = V_g + V_f ≈ V_g. [BAS-01 p.41–42 · Fig. 2.14 · MODELED]
- Heat to the virgin fuel, the driver of any flame spread (Ref. 5), comes by gas conduction, solid conduction, surface radiation and gas radiation feedback; forward conduction through the solid has been shown to matter little in theory (Ref. 9) and experiment (Ref. 13), while high lateral conductivity, which can differ from forward conductivity in composites, has been shown experimentally to influence spread strongly (Ref. 14). [BAS-01 p.42 · CITED]
- The analysis is limited to a homogeneous fuel such as PMMA (formula printed as C2H8O2) and neglects radiation, leaving gas-to-solid conduction as the dominant heat-transfer mode. [BAS-01 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Scales: L_g ≈ α_g/V_g from forward conduction against advection at the leading edge; gas residence time t_g,res ≈ L_g/V_g ≈ α_g/V_g²; with gas conduction heating the preheat zone, L_g is also the solid heating length, and fuel residence time t_s,res ≈ L_g/V_f ≈ α_g/(V_g V_f) (L_g in m, V_g and V_f in m/s, α_g in m²/s); scale relations, no fit. [BAS-01 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.42 · MODELED]
- Thermal-regime assumptions: V_f ≪ V_g, so t_s,res ≫ t_g,res; t_g,res ≫ t_g,chem and (as printed) t_s,res ≫ t_g,chem, so finite-rate kinetics drop out and T_f,adb and T_v act as thermodynamic properties; t_g,res large next to t_g,chem but not large enough for radiation to matter; the opposed flow treated as slug flow, neglecting the upstream boundary layer; finite width, humidity and temperature-dependent properties neglected. [BAS-01 p.42–43 · MODELED]
- t_g,chem is the time for combustion at the leading edge to raise the gas to the adiabatic flame temperature T_f,adb, and t_s,chem the time for the fuel to reach its vaporization temperature T_v. [BAS-01 p.42 · MODELED]
- Too large a t_g,res, possible in microgravity where V_g can be very small or absent without buoyancy, makes gas and surface radiation important (Ref. 15); an opposed flow that is not fully developed carries a boundary layer upstream of the leading edge that can change the effective velocity the flame meets (Ref. 12), an effect routinely neglected in theory. [BAS-01 p.43 · CITED]
- In the thermal regime the steady-spread mechanism reduces to heating a fuel layer of thickness L_sy from T_∞ to T_v within t_s,res, while the gas layer L_g that supplies the heat must itself be heated from T_∞ to T_f,adb within t_g,res. [BAS-01 p.43 · MODELED]
- Combustion time t_g,chem ≈ (ρx_F)/ω‴_F, the time to consume fuel vapour of mass fraction x_F in the leading-edge volume L_g², is small next to t_g,res in the thermal regime; lowering O2 lowers ω‴_F, raises t_g,chem and leads to extinction when t_g,chem nears t_g,res, and even with enough O2 a high enough V_g shrinks t_g,res to t_g,chem and causes blowoff extinction. [BAS-01 p.43 · MODELED]
- A heat-transfer timescale is the time to supply or remove the heat ρ_s L_sy L_g c_s (T_v − T_∞) that raises the leading-edge fuel layer from T_∞ to T_v. [BAS-01 p.43 · MODELED]
- Gas radiation timescale, as printed: t_g,rad ≈ [ρ_s L_sy L_g c_s (T_v − T_∞)]/[4 a_P σ (T_f⁴ − T_∞⁴) L_g²], with a_P the Planck-mean absorption coefficient and T_f the flame temperature; it can be shown to be much longer than t_g,res unless V_g is too small, so gas radiation, loss and feedback, plays no significant part in the thermal regime; no fit. [BAS-01 p.43 · MODELED]
- The solid residence time t_s,res ≈ L_g/V_f must allow pyrolysis to start; the characteristic pyrolysis time can be shown to be much shorter, so T_v can be taken as a fuel property (Ref. 16). [BAS-01 p.43 · CITED]
- Surface radiation timescale t_s,rad ≈ [ρ_s L_sy L_g c_s (T_v − T_∞)]/[εσ(T_v⁴ − T_∞⁴) L_g] (ρ_s, c_s and ε constant, L_sy varying) is much longer than t_s,res for large enough V_g; forward solid conduction, t_sx,cond ≈ [ρ_s L_sy L_g c_s (T_v − T_∞)]/[λ_s (T_v − T_∞)(L_sy/L_g)] ≈ L_g²/α_s ≫ t_s,res while L_g ≫ α_s/V_f (true except at very high V_g), is also neglected; no fit. [BAS-01 p.43 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.6: the surviving timescales are of the same order, t_s,res ≈ t_gy,cond ≈ t_sy,cond (Fig. 2.14); no fit. [BAS-01 p.43 · Eq. 2.6 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.7, from the first two timescales: L_g/V_f ≈ ρ_s L_sy L_g c_s (T_v − T_∞)/[λ_g (T_f − T_v) L_g/L_g], so V_f ≈ [λ_g/(ρ_s L_sy c_s)] F with F ≡ (T_f − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞) (λ_g at T_v, kW/m·K; ρ_s, kg/m³; c_s, kJ/kg·K); scale analysis, no fit. [BAS-01 p.39–40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.43 · Eq. 2.7 · MODELED]
- A thermally thin fuel is heated through its thickness, so L_sy ≈ τ (τ the half-thickness; Fig. 2.14 shows the symmetric half), and putting this into Eq. 2.7 gives the familiar thin-limit spread rate (Ref. 10) apart from a factor π/4. [BAS-01 p.44 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.8, for a thick fuel from the last two timescales of Eq. 2.6: L_sy ≈ λ_s L_g/(λ_g F) ≈ λ_s/(ρ_g c_g V_g F); no fit. [BAS-01 p.44 · Eq. 2.8 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.9: V_f,thin ≈ [λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ)] F and the de Ris thick limit (Ref. 9) V_f,thick ≈ [ρ_g c_g λ_g/(ρ_s c_s λ_s)] V_g F² (τ in m, V_g in m/s); spread rate is independent of V_g for thin fuels and proportional to V_g for thick fuels; no fit. [BAS-01 p.39–40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.44 · Eq. 2.9 · MODELED]
- The authors explain that a higher V_g raises the gas-to-solid heat flux (W/m²) but shortens the preheat length, leaving the heat flow (W) unchanged, and this heats a layer equal to the half-thickness of a thin sample; in a thick fuel the heated layer thins to carry the higher flux with a steeper temperature gradient, which brings in the velocity dependence. [BAS-01 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 2.10: a fuel is thermally thin when τ < τ_cr, with τ_cr ≈ λ_s/(ρ_g c_g V_g F); no fit. [BAS-01 p.44 · Eq. 2.10 · MODELED]
- There is no universally accepted way to evaluate the parameters of Eqs 2.9 and 2.10: the temperature for gas properties, the T_f and T_v used in F, and how to include the boundary layer in V_g are all read differently (Refs. 1, 10, 12). [BAS-01 p.44 · CITED]

#### Onset of kinetic effects in 1-g downward spread (Fig. 2.15)
- A major obstacle to thermal-regime data is the onset of gas-phase kinetic effects when t_g,res falls to the combustion time t_g,chem; their ratio, the Damköhler number, falls as opposed-flow velocity rises at a given O2 level, leading to blowoff extinction. [BAS-01 p.44 · MODELED]
- In 1-g downward spread the buoyant flow scales as V_NC ≈ [α_g g (T_g − T_∞)/T_∞]^(1/3) (Ref. 17) and gives a constant opposing flow for a given O2 level (α_g in m²/s, T in K); scaling relation, no fit. [BAS-01 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.44 · CITED]
- The authors state that a superposed forced opposing flow has little effect on spread until forced convection becomes comparable in strength to gravity-driven natural convection. [BAS-01 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In Fig. 2.15 (vertical-tunnel averages, Ref. 18; conditions C14) the spread rate stays roughly independent of the forced opposing flow up to 40 cm/s; filled squares mark blowoff extinction ("Extinction occurred"), open squares "No extinction", and a dashed line is labelled "Thermal limit?"; similar behaviour has been seen over thin cellulosic fuel (Ref. 12). [BAS-01 p.44–45 · Fig. 2.15 · CITED]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C14 | No extinction (open squares) | 0; 40; 60 | ~4.3; ~3.8; ~3.6 | 0 cm/s is the series high; 40 cm/s the velocity the text names; 60 cm/s the highest-velocity point | [BAS-01 p.45 · Fig. 2.15 · CITED · ~fig] |
| C14 | Extinction occurred (filled squares, blowoff) | 70; 100 | ~2.7; ~1.0 | lowest- and highest-velocity points of the series | [BAS-01 p.45 · Fig. 2.15 · CITED · ~fig] |
| C14 | dashed line "Thermal limit?" | drawn 0 to ~68 | ~4.2 | — | [BAS-01 p.45 · Fig. 2.15 · CITED · ~fig] |

- The authors ask whether the constant spread rate up to 40 cm/s in Fig. 2.15 shows a thermal regime, since Eq. 2.9 expects thin-fuel spread in that regime not to depend on opposing flow. [BAS-01 p.44–45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Earlier computations with one-step second-order global kinetics (Ref. 17) concluded that a kinetic effect may exist even at 21 % O2 and read the flow-independent spread rate as a constant kinetic effect set by the buoyant flow. [BAS-01 p.45 · CITED]
- The authors hold that, with so simple a kinetic model, computation alone cannot settle the question; weakening or removing the buoyant flow, as in microgravity, is an experimental test: below 40 cm/s the longer residence time would weaken any kinetic effect, and a kinetically controlled flame would speed up until the thermal limit, whereas a flame already at the thermal limit would keep its spread rate as the flow falls, so comparing downward and microgravity spread can establish the thermal regime for a given O2 level. [BAS-01 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Apparatus, procedure and data analysis
- BASS-II is the only long-duration opposed-flow facility (Ref. 20), on the ISS (Fig. 2.16); the sample, 2 cm wide, is lit at its left end and, depending on flow and O2, a steady flame spreads toward the right end (conditions C12). [BAS-01 p.45 · MEASURED · nominal]
- During each test an O2 sensor tracked the O2 level, which drifted by less than 0.1 %, and the total pressure, which ranged 99.2–99.5 kPa in the tests reported (conditions C12). [BAS-01 p.45–46 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 2.16 setup labels: 7.62-cm square duct; 4.8 cm from sample end to heat sink; 9.5 cm exposed sample; 0.7-cm sample card; 2.3 cm from the duct inlet screen to the metal sample card; "74 mm on BASS scale" near the igniter end; filter, heat sink, tilted radiometer, igniter at the left (downstream) end, anemometer, duct inlet screen, fan at the right (inlet) end, V_g from right to left. [BAS-01 p.46 · Fig. 2.16 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two crew members ran the tests in the ISS MSG with real-time instructions from the NASA Glenn Operations Center; each test set the opposing flow by fan voltage, lit the sample once the flow was steady and switched the igniter off when a flame showed, photographing the top view at 1 frame/s while a video camera recorded the side view; in some tests the flow was changed during spread to stretch the test matrix (conditions C12). [BAS-01 p.46 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Downward tests used the Flame Stabilizer (Ref. 4), with a 2-cm-wide PMMA sample held vertically in a stainless-steel holder, lit at the top and filmed from above; the BASS holder has a built-in igniter, whereas downward tests use piloted ignition (Fig. 2.17 shows both holders), and downward tests ran at atmospheric conditions, 101 kPa and 21 % O2. [BAS-01 p.46 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.47 · Fig. 2.17 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors list the ideally controllable parameters as oxidizer O2 fraction, pressure and velocity, fuel type, thickness, width and length, and external radiation, with fuel thickness the main parameter in these data. [BAS-01 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The per-test Bhattacharjee matrix (Table A.1, B1–B22: opposed, PMMA films 100 µm to 0.4 mm thick and 1 or 2 cm wide, calibrated initial and final O2 per test, observations, details at http://flame.sdsu.edu/) is in Appendix A. [BAS-01 p.111–112 · Table A.1 · MEASURED · ctx]
- BASS still images were turned into videos and posted with the downward-test videos at http://flame.sdsu.edu. [BAS-01 p.47 · MEASURED]
- SDSU's MATLAB-based Flame Analyzer automates finding the instantaneous spread rate from a top-view video; video analysis has long been used in fire research for spread tracking (Ref. 21) and for flame temperature (Ref. 22). [BAS-01 p.47 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 2.18 example: top view 18 s into downward spread over a 75-µm sample, with dots 6 mm apart overlaid for scale; the central slice's RGB values become intensities averaged across the width (Fig. 2.18b) and plotted along x (Fig. 2.18c); a threshold of 70 tracked the leading edge well for this test, and the spread rate is the regression slope over consecutive leading-edge positions. [BAS-01 p.47 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.48 · Fig. 2.18 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Leading-edge tracking has been shown to give spread rates with under 5 % uncertainty except near ignition, when the flame bursts into its spreading form (Ref. 4). [BAS-01 p.47 · CITED]
- Away from the ignition zone, averaging over 5 s of propagation gave spread rates reproducible within 5 %, and the error bar stays at 5 % or less for all Section 2.3 data (conditions C12 and C13). [BAS-01 p.47 · MEASURED]

#### Results: 100-µm PMMA, microgravity against downward (Figs 2.19, 2.20)
- For 100-µm samples, leading-edge positions in microgravity and downward spread are plotted in Fig. 2.19a; conditions were kept similar except that the microgravity opposing flow was 3 cm/s (conditions C15). [BAS-01 p.47 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.48 · Fig. 2.19 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The average normal-gravity spread rate over 100-µm PMMA was 2.0 mm/s (Fig. 2.19b; conditions C13); the instantaneous rate fluctuated slightly, but the average rate and the flame shape stayed fairly steady throughout. [BAS-01 p.48 · MEASURED]
- The authors expect steady spread because buoyancy generates the opposed flow, and attribute any variation probably to surface irregularities and other random factors. [BAS-01 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In microgravity the opposed flow is much lower, and most tests ran at very mild opposed flows; for the same 100-µm PMMA, the highest spread rate was about 2.2 mm/s although the opposing flow was varied from about 40 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s, about the same as the downward spread rate (conditions C12; O2 of these runs not stated beyond the 21 % named in the interpretation). [BAS-01 p.48–49 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.49 · MEASURED]
- At very high flow, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was seen, and at very low flow, about 1 cm/s, radiative extinction (PMMA, conditions C12; O2 not stated for these runs). [BAS-01 p.49 · MEASURED]

#### Thin-fuel spread rate and the flame coefficient (Eqs 2.11–2.12, Fig. 2.21)
- The authors argue that the Damköhler number does not depend on fuel thickness, so downward or microgravity spread over different thicknesses should follow Eq. 2.9. [BAS-01 p.49 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 2.11 evaluates de Ris's limits with the nomenclature properties, the thin one being Eq. 2.9 times π/4: thin, V_f = (π/4)·λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ)·F = 2.34 × 10⁻⁸ F/τ; thick, V_f = ρ_g c_g λ_g/(ρ_s c_s λ_s)·V_g F² = 9.72 × 10⁻⁵ V_g F²; both in m/s, with τ in m and V_g in m/s; the property values behind the two coefficients are not printed in the pages read; fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.39–40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.49 · Eq. 2.11 · MODELED]
- From the measured V_f,thin = 2.2 mm/s at τ = 50 µm (the 100-µm sample), Eq. 2.9 gives a de Ris flame coefficient F = 4.76 (PMMA, conditions C12). [BAS-01 p.40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.48–49 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.50 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.12 sets this against the values used in the literature: F_expt = τV_f,thin/(2.34 × 10⁻⁸) = 4.76; F_de Ris = (T_f,lin − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞) = 5.54 (linearized flame temperature); F_adb = (T_f,adb − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞) = 4.89 (adiabatic); F_eql = (T_f,eql − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞) = 4.41 ("eql" listed as "equal" in the subscripts, called equilibrium in the text); the flame and vaporization temperatures behind them are not printed in the pages read. [BAS-01 p.40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.50 · Eq. 2.12 · MODELED]
- The authors note that de Ris's formula rests on a linearized flame temperature (the theory replaces advection normal to the fuel bed with enhanced linearized diffusion), whereas the adiabatic flame temperature is easier to compute and agrees well with the experimental flame coefficient. [BAS-01 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 2.21 plots spread rates computed with F_adb in Eq. 2.11 for different thicknesses, with the data of all four microgravity thicknesses and of nine downward thicknesses; legend: filled blue circles "21 percent O2, 1 atm: microgravity", open red circles "21 percent O2, 1 atm: downward", red line "Thin behavior: V_f = 223/τ", with the in-plot expression V_f,thin ≈ [λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ)] F_BASS ≈ 223/τ (unit of 223 not printed) (conditions C16). [BAS-01 p.50 · Fig. 2.21 · MEASURED]
- The authors find that the thin-fuel thermal-regime formula, Eq. 2.11, fits the microgravity and downward data quite well (PMMA, 21 % O2, 1 atm per the Fig. 2.21 legend). [BAS-01 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Thick limit, buoyant effective velocity and transition thickness (Eqs 2.13–2.14, Fig. 2.22)
- Further downward tests used progressively thicker fuel: extruded PMMA dripped heavily and spread unsteadily, while cast PMMA dripped less and spread steadily (normal gravity, conditions C13). [BAS-01 p.50 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest extruded PMMA drips more possibly because extrusion breaks the methylmethacrylate chains. [BAS-01 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Data for 2-cm-wide samples were added to Fig. 2.22 to set a thick limit and delineate thermally thin fuel; for thicker fuels the spread rate depends slightly on width, 0.042 mm/s for a 10-cm-wide sample (Ref. 23) against 0.044 mm/s for the 2-cm-wide one (thick PMMA, 1-g downward; O2 and pressure of Ref. 23 not given in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.50 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.50 · CITED]
- 0.044 mm/s was taken as the average thick-limit downward spread rate over PMMA (normal gravity, ambient air, conditions C13). [BAS-01 p.50 · MEASURED]
- F does not depend on fuel thickness, so F_adb also applies in the thick-limit formula of Eq. 2.11, but V_g is unknown in downward spread and is replaced by an effective velocity. [BAS-01 p.50 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.13: from the measured V_f,thick = 0.044 mm/s, the effective natural-convection opposing flow is V_g,eff = V_f,thick,expt/(Ω F_adb²) = 0.019 m/s = 1.9 cm/s (Ω = (ρc_pλ)_g/(ρc_pλ)_s, F_adb = 4.89; 1-g downward spread over thick PMMA in ambient air); fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.50 · Eq. 2.12 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.51 · Eq. 2.13 · MODELED]
- Earlier computations (Ref. 17) gave an effective velocity of 6 cm/s with a more complex flame-coefficient definition (1-g downward spread over PMMA); the present value rests on F defined by the adiabatic flame temperature. [BAS-01 p.51 · CITED]
- Taking T_v as the characteristic gas temperature near the leading edge, the buoyant natural-convection scale V_NC ≈ [α_g g (T_g − T_∞)/T_∞]^(1/3) gives V_NC = 10.2 cm/s, of the same order as the effective velocity (1-g downward spread over PMMA; T_v value not printed in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.51 · MODELED]
- Eq. 2.14: equating the measured thin and thick spread rates gives τ_transition = (π/4) λ_s/(ρ_g c_g V_g,eff F_adb) (m), with λ_s solid conductivity, ρ_g gas density at T_v (kg/m³), c_g gas specific heat, V_g,eff from Eq. 2.13 and F_adb from Eq. 2.12; fitted range not given. [BAS-01 p.39–40 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.51 · Eq. 2.14 · MODELED]
- The thin-to-thick transition thickness 2τ_transition is 5.19 mm for downward spread over PMMA in ambient air (normal gravity, V_g,eff = 1.9 cm/s, F_adb); the conclusions round it to 5.2 mm. [BAS-01 p.51 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.52 · MODELED]
- In a general opposed-flow environment the transition thickness changes with opposing-flow velocity and boundary-layer development length through V_g,eff, with pressure through ρ_g, and with O2 level through F_adb. [BAS-01 p.51 · MODELED]
- Fig. 2.22 compares microgravity, downward and Fernandez-Pello and Williams data over a range of PMMA thicknesses with the theoretical thin and thick thermal limits; legend: open circles "MRC" (red), "VCF" (green), "Astra" (blue), "NASA" (black); filled red circles "BASS"; filled triangles "Ridout" (red) and "Fernandez-Pello and Williams" (blue); solid red "Thermally thin limit", blue dashed "Thermally thick limit" (conditions C17). [BAS-01 p.51 · Fig. 2.22 · MEASURED]

#### Section 2.3 conclusions
- The paper compares flame spread over thin PMMA sheets in quiescent downward spread and in opposed flow in microgravity. [BAS-01 p.51 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A curve fit of maximum spread rate against fuel thickness with de Ris's thermal-regime formula gives F = 4.76 for 21 % O2 and 79 % N2, and the adiabatic-flame-temperature F is only about 3 % higher (printed as 4.89 in Eq. 2.12) (PMMA, microgravity and 1-g downward data). [BAS-01 p.50 · Eq. 2.12 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.51–52 · MODELED]
- The authors conclude that downward spread in ambient air correlates with the microgravity data within experimental uncertainty, extending the thermal limit to downward spread in atmospheric conditions on Earth (PMMA, 21 % O2). [BAS-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With F known, thick-PMMA data give a buoyancy-induced effective velocity of 1.9 cm/s (1-g downward, ambient air). [BAS-01 p.52 · MODELED]

#### Objective, samples and test matrix
- The task aimed to understand better what controls flame spread over solid combustibles, especially in spacecraft, by testing on the ISS the effect of microgravity on spread over PMMA rods of several diameters at different O2 concentrations and low flow velocities. [BAS-01 p.55 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that low O2 and low flow, along with low pressure, are expected in spacecraft, and expect that comparing the ISS results with ground data will clarify the mechanisms of microgravity flame spread, while cylindrical samples show the effect of geometry such as transverse surface curvature. [BAS-01 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The BASS-II hardware for this task, in the MSG in the ISS Destiny Lab, consists of the flow duct, still camera, video camera, external control box, plumbing and mounting systems, and the fuel samples (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.55 · MEASURED · nominal]
- All rods started with rounded (hemispherical) ends to limit the flow disturbance of an abrupt bluff-body edge at the downstream end, and a hot wire heated the PMMA surface at the downstream edge for ignition (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.55 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Most tests used black PMMA, because black PMMA rods are also used in the Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) project to reduce in-depth absorption of thermal radiation; Tables 4.1 and 4.2 give the test conditions. [BAS-01 p.55 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Results are therefore given for black PMMA only; a few clear-PMMA tests were run for comparison, but the authors judge those data too limited to present. [BAS-01 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- From standard Grashof-number arguments (Ref. 1), the buoyant velocity a heated sample induces at ignition is about 0.50 m/s, an order of magnitude above the largest forced flow tested in BASS-II (Table 4.2) (1 g, heated PMMA rod; diameter, O2 and pressure not given for this estimate). [BAS-01 p.56 · MODELED]

#### Spread rate against opposed flow and O2 (Figs 4.1, 4.2)
- The chapter reports the effects of O2 concentration and flow velocity on microgravity opposed-flow spread over black PMMA rods: Fig. 4.1a gives spread rate against flow for the 0.00635-, 0.009525- and 0.0127-m rods, Fig. 4.1b against O2 at different flows (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.56 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.57 · Fig. 4.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Average spread rate rises with opposed-flow velocity even within the narrow flow range tested (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.56 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute part of the scatter in Fig. 4.1a to the points being at different O2 concentrations. [BAS-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No sustained flame spread was seen below an opposed flow of about 4 mm/s for the 6.35- and 9.525-mm rods (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.56 · MEASURED]
- At very low flow the flames looked very small, blue, faint and open at their downstream ends; as the flow rose toward 20 mm/s and above they became much more luminous, bright yellow, with a closed downstream tip (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.56 · MEASURED]
- In Fig. 4.1b spread rate trends upward with O2, most markedly for the 6.35-mm rods (conditions C19, at different flows). [BAS-01 p.56 · MEASURED]
- The authors find both sets of observations similar to earlier microgravity flame-spread work. [BAS-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Near the quenching limit diffusion supplies more of the oxidizer to the flame, the flame becomes very faint, and re-radiation from the sample surface grows in importance (Refs. 2, 3). [BAS-01 p.56 · CITED]
