- The authors note complications in comparing ground and ISS results: above all, buoyancy makes the effective opposed flow in 1 g an order of magnitude larger than the microgravity test velocities. [BAS-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In 1 g, spread rates under natural convection and under a 0.25 m/s opposed flow have been shown to differ negligibly (no reference given). [BAS-01 p.57 · CITED]
- The microgravity flows studied lie near the quenching limit, below what the ISS air supply and recirculation systems normally provide (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In microgravity only the two larger rods were tested near 21 % O2; the 6.35-mm rods reached at most about 19 %, and about 17.5 % O2 was the only level at which all three diameters were tested (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.57 · MEASURED]
- In 1 g the lowest O2 at which all four tested rod diameters burned without an external radiant heat source was 19 % (black cast PMMA, 1-g ground tests, opposed flow; 1-g diameters not printed in the text; total pressure not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.57 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.59 · Fig. 4.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors accept compromises in the comparison, since the O2 and diameter ranges of the two data sets do not fully overlap (Fig. 4.3), but find the trends with O2 and diameter clear even allowing that the flows are not strictly comparable. [BAS-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Main result: flame spread was seen at O2 as low as 17.5 % in microgravity but not below 19 % in normal gravity (black cast PMMA rods, opposed flow; microgravity at low forced opposed flow, conditions C19; 1 g ground tests without external radiant heating; total pressure not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.57 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.58 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.59 · Fig. 4.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors attribute this probably to the lower opposed flow in the microgravity tests than the buoyancy-induced flow in normal gravity. [BAS-01 p.58 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A smaller rod diameter gives a faster spread rate in both 1 g and microgravity, and spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1 g for PMMA rods (conditions C20). [BAS-01 p.59 · Fig. 4.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- These results agree well with similar 1-g against microgravity comparisons for opposed-flow spread over wire insulation (Refs. 4, 5) and with theory (Ref. 6). [BAS-01 p.59 · CITED]
- Fig. 4.3 caption: spread rates of black cast PMMA rods against gravity, O2 and diameter, all without external radiant heating, with microgravity O2 and flow averaged over the associated test conditions (conditions C20). [BAS-01 p.59 · Fig. 4.3 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Flame shape: spread with an open tail against regression (Fig. 4.4)
- The rods were lit at the downstream end and the flame was left to spread along the rod for a while at each velocity (conditions C19). [BAS-01 p.59 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In a typical test (Fig. 4.4a–e: black PMMA rod printed 4.76 mm, 18.5 % O2, flow lowered 1.9, 1.7, 1.6, 1.5 cm/s; microgravity, ISS; total pressure not reported in the pages read) the flame starts sooty, the soot fades and disappears as the flow falls, the flame tail opens as spread continues, and the rod reaches past the end of the flame; the post-test rod (e) shows a generally conical burn with a blunt melted tip. [BAS-01 p.59 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.60 · Fig. 4.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors state that this wide-open flame tail, with rod left behind it, is unique to microgravity. [BAS-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In normal gravity the flame burns the rod away in a conical regression with the rod tip always inside the flame, and the cone's regression angle grows with forced-flow velocity (Ref. 6); at relatively high flows, 120 cm/s and above (Refs. 6, 7), the flame is small and flat behind a flat rod tip (regression angle 90°), stabilized in the recirculation zone behind the rod. [BAS-01 p.59 · CITED]
- This flame is quite hard to blow off, as predicted (Ref. 8). [BAS-01 p.59 · CITED]
- The authors stress the spread-versus-regression distinction for the classic limiting O2 index test (Ref. 9), in which a small sample burns like a candle in a 4-cm/s oxidizer flow while O2 is lowered until extinction, and in which the small 1-g flames near the limit sit on top of the sample instead of spreading down it. [BAS-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A similar flame appeared at very low O2 in space (Fig. 4.4f: black PMMA rod printed 3.18 mm, 16.3 % O2, 5 cm/s; microgravity, ISS; total pressure not reported in the pages read): a cap-shaped flame survived until the initially hemispherical tip regressed to a flat surface, then went out, never spreading along the rod's outer surface. [BAS-01 p.59 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.60 · Fig. 4.4f · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors hypothesize that this flame quenched because the local flow in the flame zone fell as it turned into a wake flame, and the thickness needing heating exceeded what the weakened flame could heat. [BAS-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Bubble layers in burned rods and fuel release after extinction (Fig. 4.5)
- Burned rods preserve bubble layers (Fig. 4.5): the opposed-flow rod has a dense white bubble layer that starts abruptly near the flame leading edge and runs downstream as the rod regresses symmetrically, until the full thickness is heated and the molten tip forms a sphere to minimize surface tension (PMMA rods, microgravity, ISS, BASS-II). [BAS-01 p.60 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.61 · Fig. 4.5 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that at the flame leading edge the upstream solid preheat length is relatively short, so the flame must supply enough heat flux to preheat the upstream rod. [BAS-01 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the concurrent-flow PMMA rods (Olson tests) the molten tip is upstream, the dense bubble layer varies with flame length, and convective heating of the downstream rod forms large, widely spaced internal bubbles well downstream of the flame (microgravity, ISS, BASS-II). [BAS-01 p.60 · MEASURED]
- The authors state that these bubbles hold methylmethacrylate vapour under pressure from polymer chain scission, rupture at the surface into vapour jets that ignite near a flame, and that after extinction the hot material can keep producing fuel until it cools. [BAS-01 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Premixed flame oscillations along the rod were seen in the concurrent rod geometry and last much longer in microgravity than in normal gravity, because the rod is cooled less by convection (PMMA rod, concurrent flow). [BAS-01 p.60 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors take this to suggest that spacecraft fire suppression should continue until the burning material has cooled and stopped giving off vapours. [BAS-01 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### 12. BASS SIBAL concurrent tests in the SAF-06 thin-fuel matrix (second report)
- SAF-06 Table 1, the thin-fuel concurrent-flow test matrix with flame measurements, has 8 rows, one per test: Saffire I sample 1, Saffire II samples 5 and 6, Saffire III sample 1, Saffire IV sample 4, Saffire V sample 5, and two BASS rows, sample 11 (printed on two lines, "1" / "1") and sample 4 (tests-table keys BASS:65 and BASS:12, the latter a fallback key not merged); every row is thin cellulosic fuel (SIBAL, except cotton in Saffire V) in concurrent forced flow in microgravity in a habitable spacecraft (Saffire flights, and BASS, Ref. 30). [SAF-06 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.8 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Table 1 columns: flight, sample, flow (cm/s), sample length × width (cm, with holder dimensions), duct L × W × H (cm), O2 (% by volume), P (kPa), Vf (cm/s), Lf (cm), Lp (cm), Hf (cm) and surface thermocouple locations (cm). [SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Table 1 footnotes: the Cygnus vehicle was first filled with ISS atmosphere, whose values at hatch closing are listed for Saffire I–IV; Hf values marked * (Saffire I, II and III rows) are estimates, as no side view was recorded, used only in SAF-06 section 5.0 to estimate the flow effect of flame thermal expansion. [SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]

## Findings

### 1. Chapter 5 context: Earth screening test and BASS-II sample types
- In microgravity, flames are driven by diffusion and by weak advection from ventilation and crew movement, whereas NASA's material selection method, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, is driven by buoyancy because gravity is present. [BAS-01 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors intend BASS-II results for comparison with ground test setups meant to replace NASA's current screening method for spacecraft materials, and for better understanding of fire behaviour in space. [BAS-01 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BASS-II gave an extensive microgravity database for thick fuels that had not existed before; the chapter 5 conclusions call BASS some of the first data on thick-fuel combustion in microgravity. [BAS-01 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.71 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Earlier true-microgravity thick-fuel data came from sounding-rocket experiments by Olson and others on PMMA in very low-speed opposed flow with an external radiant flux (Ref. 2). [BAS-01 p.63 · CITED]
- BASS-II used three sample categories: flat samples (acrylic films and sheets of several thicknesses, and SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric), rods of black or clear acrylic (solid regression rates and extinction limits in opposed and concurrent flow) and a section of a large solid acrylic sphere (ignition of, and flame growth over, thick material). [BAS-01 p.63 · MEASURED]

### 2. Flat PMMA slabs in opposed flow (Miller and Wichman)

#### Hardware and procedure
- The BASS-II hardware is a small flow duct with an igniter, a small nozzle and exchangeable fuel samples, placed inside the MSG (255 L) aboard the ISS; a radiometer at the top reads flame intensity, a fan forces air through the duct and an anemometer measures the velocity of the incoming air. [BAS-01 p.64 · Fig. 5.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 5.1 layout: 7.62-cm square duct; 2.3 cm from the inlet screen to the metal sample card; 9.5 cm of exposed sample; sample card 0.7 cm wide; 4.8 cm from the sample end to the heat sink; igniter at the downstream sample end beside the heat sink; fan upstream, honeycomb flow straightener and anemometer at the inlet, filter at the exit, radiometer tilted at the top downstream corner; the drawing also prints "74 mm" on a BASS scale. [BAS-01 p.64 · Fig. 5.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In Fig. 5.1, V_f is the absolute spread rate and V_g the opposed-flow velocity. [BAS-01 p.64 · Fig. 5.1 · MEASURED]
- Procedure: before each session a crew member installs the hardware in the MSG and the fan calibration is set; after ignition the flame is left to stabilise, then the airflow is changed through the test while fan speed, radiometer reading and time are monitored, and the airflow is switched off at the end. [BAS-01 p.64 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two cameras recorded the flames; video and data were downlinked, the flame was tracked in stills and video with Spotlight-16 (NASA image-tracking software) and spread rates were computed in Excel. [BAS-01 p.63–64 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Test matrix
- 20 flat PMMA samples were burned (Table 5.1), 1–5 mm thick, 1 or 2 cm wide, one- or two-sided, always in opposed flow of 3–20 cm/s (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.64 · MEASURED]
- The flight study covered five slab thicknesses (1–5 mm), two widths (1.2 and 2.2 cm) and one- vs two-sided burning at various O2 levels, varying the flow to get spread rates at several flows; some tests lasted more than 30 min (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.66 · MEASURED]
- Table 5.1 lists tests M1–M20 (keys BASS-II:M1 to BASS-II:M20) with thickness (mm), width (cm), one or two sides burning, velocity (cm/s), spread rate (mm/s), burn time (min) and initial and final O2 (vol%); one cell can hold several successive velocities with their spread rates, and some spread-rate cells read "Not tracked" (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.65 · Table 5.1 · MEASURED]
- Table A.4 prints both calibrated and uncalibrated initial and final O2; for M1 (1-mm PMMA, one-sided, 2 cm) they are 22.2 and 21.9 vol% calibrated and 20.6 and 20.3 vol% uncalibrated (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.116 · Table A.4 · MEASURED · ctx]

#### Link to the narrow channel apparatus (NCA)
- Flat PMMA samples have been burned in the narrow channel apparatus (NCA) to simulate microgravity (Refs. 7 and 8). [BAS-01 p.66 · CITED]
- The flight tests aimed to start gathering data on finite-thickness samples, where regression and consumption of the sample matter more than for an extremely thin sample. [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The objective was microgravity flame-spread data over a thick fuel, to compare with the normal-gravity NCA, whose low-height flow duct suppresses buoyant flow; quenching extinction data at finite flow were also obtained in most tests, and preliminary comparisons are published (Refs. 7 and 10). [BAS-01 p.66 · MEASURED]

#### Spread versus burn-through (Fig. 5.4)
- At near-air O2, flames spread over the fuel surface without burning through, on one- and two-sided samples (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.66 · MEASURED]
- When O2 fell to about 19 %, flames on two-sided 2-mm-thick, 2.2-cm-wide samples no longer spread over the surface but consumed the fuel from the trailing edge (Fig. 5.4; conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.66–67 · Fig. 5.4 · MEASURED]

| Fig. 5.4 panels (2-mm × 2.2-cm PMMA slab, conditions C1; velocities are quenching velocities) | Caption conditions | Observation | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) pre-extinction flame, (b) burned sample | two sided, 18.8 % O2, 3 cm/s | regression like that of normal-gravity downward spread; fuel fully consumed a few millimetres downstream of the flame leading edge | [BAS-01 p.66–67 · Fig. 5.4 · MEASURED · single-test] |
| (c) pre-extinction flame, (d) burned sample | two sided, 21.7 % O2, <1 cm/s | flame spread across the material and left a very long bubbled sample; the flames on the two sides went out separately, within a few seconds of each other | [BAS-01 p.66–67 · Fig. 5.4 · MEASURED · single-test] |
| (e) pre-extinction flame, (f) burned sample | caption: two sided, 22.2 % O2, 11 cm/s; text: a single-sided sample | flame quite weak despite the high flow and high O2; long bubbled sample left | [BAS-01 p.66–67 · Fig. 5.4 · MEASURED · single-test] |

- The authors attribute the curved melt layer to heat loss to the holder sides and liken it, down to the ring-shaped tail, to the last image of Fig. 5.3 for a much thinner material. [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They attribute the curvature of the flame in Fig. 5.4 to heat loss to the sample holder, growing as the forced flow decreases. [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They name heat loss to the metal substrate as what weakened the single-sided flame of panels (e)–(f). [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Extinction limits (Fig. 5.5)
- Spread rates decrease as thickness increases and as forced flow decreases (Ref. 10; conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.66 · CITED]
- One-sided samples (1.2 cm wide per the Fig. 5.5 legend): as thickness increased, the O2 at extinction fell while the forced-flow velocity at extinction rose (conditions C2). [BAS-01 p.66–67 · Fig. 5.5 · MEASURED]
- Two-sided samples that spread over the surface showed no clear trend with thickness, and their extinction velocities were much lower than those of the one-sided samples (conditions C2). [BAS-01 p.66 · MEASURED]
- The authors read the lower two-sided extinction velocities as a much larger substrate heat loss for the one-sided flame than for the two-sided flame, which has no substrate. [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Two-sided regressing samples showed no clear thickness dependence of the extinction limits at either width (printed as "1- and 2.2-cm-wide"); the 1.2-cm-wide samples went out at about 1 % O2 higher than the 2.2-cm-wide ones (conditions C2). [BAS-01 p.66 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the higher limit of the narrower samples most likely to larger relative heat loss to the sample holder. [BAS-01 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### O2 analysis method
- The BASS hardware has no means to measure O2 through the whole test; O2 is known only at its start and end. [BAS-01 p.68 · MEASURED]
- Miller and Wichman assumed a linear O2 change between those two values to draw an O2-vs-time curve for each test (Fig. 5.2 example), estimate O2 at any moment and average O2 for each flow speed. [BAS-01 p.63 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.68 · MODELED · nominal]
- Summary plots of average O2 (vol%) against opposed-flow speed (cm/s), one- and two-sided tests apart, class each point by spread rate and add the extinction points, giving flammability maps of flame behaviour against O2 and flow; the analysis is meant as a reference for later BASS operations. [BAS-01 p.63 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.68 · MODELED · nominal]
- An extinction analysis plots O2 against flow velocity at the moment of extinction, by one- or two-sided test. [BAS-01 p.63 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Spread rate against opposed flow (Figs. 5.8, 5.9)
- Fig. 5.8 (two-sided burns; samples 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 mm thick at 1 cm width (open diamonds) and at 2 cm (filled), model triangles at 1 and 3 mm; axes opposed flow, cm/s, and spread rate, mm/s): the higher the flow or the thinner the sample, the higher the spread rate; the conclusions add that the tested thicknesses clearly show slower spread for thicker fuel (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.69–70 · Fig. 5.8 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.71 · MEASURED]
- Width effect in Fig. 5.8: especially for 1-mm-thick fuel, 2-cm-wide samples spread faster than 1-cm-wide ones; the conclusions state that sample width affects spread rate for thin fuels (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.69 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.71 · MEASURED]
- The authors expect these trends to help choose sample sizes for later ISS experiments. [BAS-01 p.69 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 5.9 (one-sided; legend 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 mm thick, all 2 cm wide): one-sided samples burned more slowly than two-sided ones and needed a higher opposed flow to keep burning; overall, two-sided burns spread faster (conditions C1). [BAS-01 p.69–70 · Fig. 5.9 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.71 · MEASURED]
- In Fig. 5.9, symbol size is the O2 estimated at that velocity from an assumed linear O2 decay during the test. [BAS-01 p.69 · MODELED]

#### FDS model (conditions C3)
- The model is FDS v5.5.3 (NIST), a CFD model of fire-driven flow, run in DNS mode because the flow is laminar and the domain small, with the experiment's sample and an approximation of the BASS flow duct geometry. [BAS-01 p.63 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.68 · MODELED · nominal]
- The inlet profile was built in MATLAB from anemometer readings at several upstream points and input to the model; the measured BASS-II duct profile is quite irregular. [BAS-01 p.68 · MODELED · nominal]
- Fig. 5.6 two-dimensional geometry: x = 17.5 cm, z = 7.51 cm; 9-mm quartz window on top, 5-mm aluminium bottom, inlet on the right, igniter (1,300 °C) at the downstream sample end, PMMA sample labelled 1 mm thick, 8.8-cm sample span and a 0.78-cm holder segment at the upstream end. [BAS-01 p.68 · Fig. 5.6 · MODELED · nominal]
- The case run used a 3-mm-thick sample, averaged opposed flow of 10 cm/s and a grid of 0.389 mm (x) by 0.376 mm (z); cold flow ran for 1 s of simulated time, then the igniter was on for about 5 s, ramped down and switched off. [BAS-01 p.69 · MODELED · nominal]
- The peak heat release rate per unit area in the two-dimensional run was 225 kW/m² (conditions C3; Fig. 5.7 Smokeview colour bar 0.0–225.0 kW/m²). [BAS-01 p.69 · Fig. 5.7 · MODELED]
- The two model points of Fig. 5.8 lie far above the experiments: ~0.51 mm/s for 1-mm and ~0.27 mm/s for 3-mm PMMA, both at ~10 cm/s opposed flow (two-sided; read within ±1.25 cm/s and ±0.05 mm/s, linear axes 0–25 cm/s and 0–0.60 mm/s; Refs. 9 and 10). [BAS-01 p.69–70 · Fig. 5.8 · MODELED · ~fig]
- The model predicts higher spread rates than measured ("much higher" in the conclusions); revised chemical kinetics and material properties, a domain study and a grid sensitivity analysis are planned. [BAS-01 p.63 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.71 · MODELED]

#### Study, hardware and procedure
- This was the first series of concurrent-flow rod flammability tests in microgravity, aboard the ISS (conditions C4); its objective was the lower part of the concurrent microgravity flammability map as a function of ventilation flow and ambient O2. [BAS-01 p.72 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- The stagnation geometry was chosen to study material flammability in microgravity: an axisymmetric cylindrical PMMA rod with low heat loss to its downstream support pin; the other intrinsic losses (surface radiation, conduction along the axis) are estimated in Section 6.1.5.5. [BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The three primary variables were flow velocity through the duct, rod radius and working-volume O2. [BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED]
- Hardware (detailed in Ref. 14): the black-anodised duct is a low-reflection backdrop for a colour video camera at 30 frames/s and an orthogonal digital still camera (4,320 × 2,968 pixels) at ~1 frame/s; the front window opens for samples and igniters, a top window serves the still camera, and a non-calibrated radiometer in the downstream top back corner gives a relative flame-strength reading at 5 Hz; Fig. 6.1 labels the PMMA rod, still camera, N2 supply, MSG working volume, flow duct, front window, control box and the video camera with turning mirror and digital overlay (gas sensors not shown). [BAS-01 p.74–75 · Fig. 6.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Flow: a small variable-speed fan at the upstream end, with its voltage shown and settable; up to two restrictors at the fan inlet raise the pressure drop to change the flow range (maximum ~55 cm/s without restrictors, ~35 cm/s with two); a honeycomb straightener and an inlet screen reduce swirl. [BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Flow measurement: an omnidirectional spherical air velocity transducer (TSI 8475) between the honeycomb and the screen measured the steady flow; its response time was about 1 min and its display showed whole units only, an effective resolution of ±0.5 cm/s; the fan voltage was calibrated against flow velocity for each restrictor at the end of each operations day, after fan warm-up (p.13 gives the same daily calibration of fan voltage against the airspeed transducer). [BAS-01 p.13 · MEASURED · ctx; BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED]
- Gas readings: O2, CO2 and CO sensors gave initial and final values for each test; the O2 readings, calibrated with the onboard mass spectrometer, verified the CSTR model and measured the O2 consumed, the CSA-CP readings being corrected each day for their offset from the MCA (Appendix B); the CO and CO2 readings were used to evaluate average burning efficiency per test. [BAS-01 p.72 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.75 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.124 · MEASURED · ctx]
- Table A.5 names the rods 6.35-mm clear, 6.35-mm black (rows O11 and O14), 9.525-mm clear and 12.7-mm clear PMMA rod. [BAS-01 p.118–119 · Table A.5 · MEASURED · ctx]
- The two black rods showed no obvious difference in flammability from the clear rods (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.75 · MEASURED]
- Operations: from a control box outside the MSG (Fig. 6.1, lower right) the astronaut changed the fan voltage, set the N2 flow, switched the igniter and adjusted the radiometer gain, while the ground team watched live video and talked directly with the astronaut, calling for flow changes, still-camera adjustments and ignition steps. [BAS-01 p.75 · MEASURED · nominal]
- After ignition the flow was lowered stepwise until the flame quenched; in blowoff tests it was raised until blowoff; each test was followed by at least 9 min of cool-down to a safe touch temperature before the next setup. [BAS-01 p.75–76 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Complementary blowoff drop tests (5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility, microgravity wind-tunnel drop rig, Ref. 15) ignited the rod in 1 g at a flammable O2 flow, then switched the gas to a lower O2 and released the package as this flow reached the flame. [BAS-01 p.76 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Blowoff extinction could be seen in these drops because its characteristic time was shorter than the drop; quenching could not, its characteristic time being much longer than the drop. [BAS-01 p.76 · MEASURED]

#### Background cited in the report
- A hemispherical stagnation flow geometry was shown by early work (Ref. 2) to be a good way to get flammability limits of fuels against upward-flowing oxidiser, and many heavier hydrocarbons show similar limiting O2 (13 to 14 %) and flame temperatures (1,450 to 1,500 °C) (gravity, pressure and flow speed not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.73–74 · CITED]
- Radiative heat loss was found mainly to lower the flame temperature (Refs. 4 and 5), and the flammability map in O2 and stretch rate a (Ref. 5) has a blowoff branch plus a new quenching branch where the low-power flame is too weak to offset surface radiative loss, a branch said to be likely observable only in microgravity (Ref. 5). [BAS-01 p.74 · CITED]
- The first solid-fuel quenching extinction limits were observed in microgravity opposed-flow spread tests over thermally thin cellulose (Ref. 12). [BAS-01 p.74 · CITED]
- The authors note that very few solid-fuel stagnation-flow extinction studies have been run in reduced gravity, free of buoyant flow. [BAS-01 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mir Skorost tests (Ref. 13) of concurrent spread on extruded PMMA, POM and HDPE rods: all melted under the flame into growing molten balls on the stagnation end, wrapped by the flame; at low flow the small hemispherical tip flame advanced by rod regression (bulk burning) rather than by concurrent spread along the rod; flames survived airflow below 1 cm/s (O2, pressure and rod size not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.74 · CITED]

#### Symbols and model constants (Olson list)
- Olson symbol list, p.72 (meaning first, then symbol and value): stretch rate a = (3/2)(U/r)(r/r_o)^½ in s⁻¹; PMMA-surface absorptivity a_s; area A in cm², with A_r the rod cross-section and A_h = 2 A_r the hemispherical tip area; Biot number Bi = h r/λ_s; diameter D; Damköhler number Da of Eq. (6.2), normalised by 7.35×10⁷ (Ref. 1); activation energy E = 1.45×10⁵ J/mol; surface-to-flame hemispherical radiative view factor F = 0.93; heat-transfer coefficient h; flame length L, cm, from the stagnation standoff to the flame tails (L also used for the rod initial length); rod initial length L_o = 5.9 cm; latent heat of vaporisation L_v = 1700 J/g; average burning rate over the hemispherical surface m'' = V_r ρ_s A_r/A_h, g/cm² s; Nusselt number Nu of Eq. (6.3) (convective vs conductive heat flux); Péclet number Pe = L_o V/α_s; Prandtl number of air at T_m, Pr = 0.69; heat flux q'' of Eq. (6.4), W/cm². [BAS-01 p.72 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Olson symbol list, p.73: heating rate q of Eq. (6.4), W; radius r, cm; ideal gas constant R = 8.314 J/(gmol K); Reynolds number Re = UD/ν; flame standoff distance s in cm, taken to the outer bright cyan zone of the flame; temperature T, with T_m = 800 °C (as printed); time t in s and solid-phase response time t_s = 0.7 r²/α_s in s; ΔT = T_crit − T_s; forced-flow velocity U, cm/s; diffusion velocity U_D = 2 cm/s; measured rod-tip regression velocity V_r, cm/s; X = percent by volume (mole percent); y = distance along the rod (cm) and Y = y/L; thermal diffusivity α, 1.19 cm²/s for air at T_m and 1.2×10⁻³ cm²/s for PMMA; pre-exponential constant β = 1.3×10¹⁶ cm³/(gmol s); emissivity ε, 0.8 for the surface and 0.02 for the gas, the surface absorptivity following by Kirchhoff's law; thermal conductivity λ, 0.000577 W/cm K for air at T_m and 2.09×10⁻³ W/cm K for the solid at T_∞; kinematic viscosity ν = 0.822 cm²/s at T_m; density ρ, 0.0441 g/cc for air at T_m and 1.19 g/cc for the solid; nondimensional temperature θ; Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.729×10⁻¹² W/cm² K⁴ (experimental value); thermal length scale ℓ = (α_g/a)^½, cm; nondimensional solid-phase response time τ = t/t_s. [BAS-01 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Olson subscripts, p.73: convective (conv); flame extinction condition (crit); diffusion (D); fuel (f), taken as unity at the fuel surface; gas (g); ignition (ign); mean (m), at 800 K as printed; base rod size (o), 0.318 cm; oxygen (O2); radiative (rad); surface at 675 K, or solid (s); total feedback to the surface (tot); vaporisation (vap); ambient at 300 K (∞). [BAS-01 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Ignition (Fig. 6.2)
- Procedure: the astronaut placed the igniter within a millimetre of the rod tip and powered it until a stable flame formed; because the igniter glare hid the flame, the igniter was switched off to judge the flame and back on for a few seconds if the flame seemed to be dying, a cycle that could repeat several times in one test. [BAS-01 p.76 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Ignition delay t_ign is the time from the first igniter switch-on to the last switch-off after which a stable flame persisted; the right axis of Fig. 6.2 gives τ = t_ign/t_s, with t_s = 0.7 r²/α_s (α_s = solid thermal diffusivity) and the empirical 0.7 chosen so that τ = 1 at the ignition limit. [BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6.2 legend: green-filled circles t_ign; black circles unsustained ignition; open red circles τ; grey circles with red rim unsustained-ignition τ; dashed blue box "Observed O2 ignition limit"; red dashed line with "Ignitable τ region" below it; green band at the bottom "NASA Test 1 t_ign". [BAS-01 p.77 · Fig. 6.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors note inherent scatter in ignition time from manual positioning and activation of the igniter, with some clear trends. [BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Times to a sustained flame varied, up to 230 s; at higher O2 ignition came within about 40 s; below 16 % initial O2 the delay rose markedly; larger rods took longer, most of all at lower O2 (up to 230 s) (conditions C8). [BAS-01 p.75–76 · MEASURED]
- Below ~14.5 % initial O2 no sustained ignition was obtained, although flames were seen while the igniter was on and briefly after it was switched off; at very low O2 even ignition times up to 500 s gave no sustained flame with the initial flow varied between 2 and 10 cm/s; every τ ≥ ~1 lies below this ~14.5 % ignition limit, so a sample not ignited within τ ≈ 1 is likely not flammable (conditions C8; test key BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-SUSTAINED-IGNITION-LIMIT:577ceb4b). [BAS-01 p.75–76 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flames ignited at higher O2 survived to final O2 as low as 13.6 % (conditions C4; test key BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-LOWEST-FINAL-O2-SUSTAINED:23bb3421). [BAS-01 p.76 · MEASURED]
- The conclusions state that ignition delay rises sharply as the limiting O2 is approached and that ignition limits lie at higher O2 than flammability limits, owing to the added heat loss into the initially cold rod (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors explain that weak low-O2 flames cannot be sustained on a cold rod because too much flame heat is conducted into the fuel; only after a long ignition time is the rod warm enough for the flame to persist (conductive loss examined in Section 6.1.5.5). [BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They read the ignition-vs-extinction gap the same way: high heat loss into the initially cold rod quenches a post-ignition flame, while a developed solid temperature profile sustains a flame down to these low O2 levels, and this gap between O2 ignition and extinction limits matters for a flammability test. [BAS-01 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA's Test 1 (Ref. 16, NASA-STD-6001B, 2011) is an upward flame spread test with a fixed ignition time of ~25 s, drawn as the bottom shaded band of Fig. 6.2; a material not ignited by then passes. [BAS-01 p.76–77 · CITED; BAS-01 p.99 · CITED]
- The authors argue from Fig. 6.2 that a longer ignition time can ignite the material, especially at lower O2; the caption says ignitions succeed in the nondimensional ignitable region with delays up to 230 s, so the 25-s Test 1 ignition time may be too short for a flammability test and may make it an ignition test. [BAS-01 p.77 · Fig. 6.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The conclusions put the ignition delay at up to almost 10 times the NASA-STD-6001 standard igniter on-time (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]

#### Quenching extinction (Figs. 6.3–6.6)
- Products leave the duct and mix into the 250-L MSG working volume, so O2 falls very slowly during a test (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.77 · MEASURED · nominal]
- To find the quenching limit the flow was lowered in steps, holding each flow for at least 100 s so the solid temperature could settle to the new flame and the flame was steady; quench tests lasted up to 28 min. [BAS-01 p.77 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flow: the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with growing amplitude just before going out; the conclusions add 1.1-Hz pre-quench oscillations seen by the radiometer, similar to reported quiescent candle-flame oscillations in microgravity, and a standoff trend with O2 and a (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.72 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 6.3(a)–(c) show near-quenching flames for r = 0.318, 0.476 and 0.635 cm, each the lowest-O2 test for its size (flow and O2 differ and are not given per image): all blue and roughly hemispherical; panels (d)–(f) show blowoff after the stagnation tip opens, for the same three radii (conditions C4; panel (e): 5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility drop test). [BAS-01 p.77–78 · Fig. 6.3 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 6.4 gives the time history (flame length, width, standoff distance, aspect ratio, rod tip position, radiometer; left axis mm, right axis aspect ratio, radiometer and flow, a yellow band marking ignition) of the lowest-O2 quenching test, with the flow lowered in steps (red stepped line) (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.77 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.79 · Fig. 6.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In that test the flame length stopped growing at the 2 → 1.5 cm/s change, and shortly after the rod reached an apparently steady regression rate V_r = 0.0385 mm/s (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.77 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.79 · Fig. 6.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Standoff distance stayed nearly constant; flame length settled to a nearly constant value at each later flow until the last step before extinction and tracked the radiometer signal closely; flame width rose smoothly up to the 2 → 1.5 cm/s change, then fell slowly, and faster after the last change; the aspect ratio L/W fell stepwise to 0.5 at extinction, a hemispherical flame at the quenching limit (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.77–78 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Quenching came more than 100 s after the last flow change, of the order of the solid-phase response time t_s (cause examined in Section 6.1.5.3; conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.78 · MEASURED · single-test]

- Fig. 6.5 compares the flame length (minus standoff, circles) with the clear bubble layer length (diamonds) and the flow (line), from the same test, with an inset image showing the bubble layer (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.79 · Fig. 6.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Flame length minus standoff equals the clear bubble layer length just before each flow change; the dense small bubble layer tracks the length closely except just after a turn-down, since the flame adjusts at once while the bubble layer can shrink only as fast as the tip regresses; at quenching the bubble layer has shrunk to about the rod diameter (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.80 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors read this as bubble-layer formation driven by the flame heat flux (inset of Fig. 6.5 at 1,100 s) and as further evidence of a hemispherical flame before quenching. [BAS-01 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- After the last flow change the flame length did not settle but shrank and began to oscillate; the radiometer gave the best timing of these oscillations, shown for the last 30 s in Fig. 6.6 (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.80 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The radiometer signal oscillated at about 1.1 Hz, dropped to 1.05 over a few seconds and then made a large oscillation; the flame seemed to recover to smaller oscillations, a few seconds later the signal again dropped to 1.05, another large oscillation followed and the flame went out (non-calibrated, relative signal; conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.80 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.74 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 6.6 (radiometer signal vs time from ignition start, 1,190–1,220 s; same test) annotates oscillations no. 1 to 30, a "Large oscillation", "Restabilized", "Shrinking", "~1.1 Hz oscillations" and "Flame quenched"; the inset fits oscillation number y against time x (s) as y = 1.1071x − 1319.2, R² = 0.9987, over oscillations 1–30 (~1,190 to ~1,220 s), a steady 1.1 Hz (conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.80 · Fig. 6.6 · MODELED · single-test]
- The "Flame quenched" point sits at ~1,219.6 s from ignition start, radiometer signal 1.00 (read within ±0.5 s, low confidence; conditions C5). [BAS-01 p.80 · Fig. 6.6 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test]
- A still image inset in Fig. 6.6, from a similar test (its rod size and O2 not given), shows the flame shrinking forward to about the standoff distance on its way to quenching (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.80 · Fig. 6.6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- These oscillations closely resemble those of candle flames in a quiescent environment (Ref. 17), the ~1-cm/s convective flow being at the level of diffusive flows. [BAS-01 p.80 · CITED]
- Proposed mechanism: fuel vapour escapes downstream through the open tail of the small hemispherical flame, mixes with O2 into a flammable mixture, and the flame flashes downstream through it; this larger flame depletes O2 locally and briefly weakens the flame, and in a large-amplitude oscillation the depletion destabilises the stagnation-region anchor and the flame goes out entirely. [BAS-01 p.80–81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The oscillation frequency is set by diffusive mixing rates of the reactants and inherent heat losses (Ref. 17); radiative loss acts like a change in reactant thermal diffusivity (Ref. 18), giving thermodiffusive oscillations even at unity Lewis number. [BAS-01 p.81 · CITED]

#### Blowoff extinction (Figs. 6.3, 6.7, 6.8)
- Blowoff limits were usually found after stable rod regression was established at a modest flow; the astronaut then raised the flow until blowoff. [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Blowoff was defined as the instant a hole formed in the stagnation region (Ref. 19), as in the lower row of Fig. 6.3. [BAS-01 p.81 · CITED]
- As flow rises, blowoff extinction starts with a hole in the flame sheet at the stagnation region; the conclusions add that once the stagnation region is blown more than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ downstream, the flame cannot propagate back upstream even if the flow is lowered (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.72 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No ISS blowoff tests were obtained with the intermediate rod (r = 0.476 cm), so the centre blowoff image, Fig. 6.3(e), comes from a 5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility drop test, with the rod lit by a green LED. [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.78 · Fig. 6.3 · MEASURED]
- Drop-tower blowoff flames are much smaller than the ISS flames in Fig. 6.3 (O2 and flow not given for these images). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the smaller drop-tower flames to less fuel preheating in the short burn before blowoff. [BAS-01 p.81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Earlier research (Refs. 6, 7, 20 and 21) and Section 6.1.5.5 indicate that blowoff extinction is insensitive to heat losses. [BAS-01 p.81 · CITED]
- After the stagnation region blows off, the remaining annular flame leading edge oscillates upstream and downstream several times before the flame blows off completely (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED]
- In one test the envelope flame was re-established once after a local blowoff, by quickly cutting the flow below the blowoff velocity; a second attempt failed (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED · single-test]
- In each blowoff the astronaut quickly raised the flow from a low to a high a, the flame blew downstream, and the flow was quickly lowered to an a near the minimum flammability (Section 6.1.4.4); Fig. 6.7 (stretch rate a, solid line, left axis s⁻¹; radiometer, dashed line, right axis; annotations Blowoff 1, Blowoff 2, Flame extinction) shows the two attempts were alike but their outcomes were not (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.81–82 · Fig. 6.7 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]
- Blowoff 1: the flame hole, about 9 mm across at first, moved back ahead of the rod tip position within 2 s (yellow line in Fig. 6.8) and closed 7 s after the flow was lowered (Fig. 6.8a); the radiometer signal was then higher, the flow being slightly higher and the flame visibly longer than before blowoff (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Blowoff 2, 55 s later: a slightly larger initial hole of 10 mm could not move ahead of the flame tip to re-establish the stagnation region (Fig. 6.8b) and persisted for over a minute, even after the flow was returned to its initial value, before the flame destabilised and blew off completely (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The flow profile was much the same for both blowoffs, but O2 had dropped further by the second, visible as less soot on the second pre-blowoff flame (conditions C6). [BAS-01 p.81 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors interpret the second blowoff as showing that once the flame is held farther than the thermal length (ℓ = 2 mm) downstream of the stagnation region, it cannot propagate back upstream at the low O2 tested (final X_O2 14.5 %), even with preheated fuel. [BAS-01 p.81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In BASS-II opposed-flow spread tests over rods (Ref. 14), no opposed-flow spread was seen below 16.4 % O2 at any flow (pressure not reported in the pages read; test key BAS-01:nodate:RODS-OPPOSED-FLOW-SPREAD-LIMIT:80f34ec0). [BAS-01 p.81 · CITED]
- The conclusions call this consistent with the observation that an opposed-flow flame cannot be established at the low O2 levels of interest. [BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6.8 shows still images 1 s apart for (a) Blowoff 1 and (b) Blowoff 2, with yellow horizontal lines at the rod tip position. [BAS-01 p.82 · Fig. 6.8 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Flammability boundary: final O2 against stretch rate (Figs. 6.9, 6.10, Eq. 6.1)
- Fig. 6.9 (linear axes) plots final X_O2 (vol%) against a with symbols ISS blowoff (×), ISS stable flame (◇), ISS quench (✱), drop-tower blowoff (+) and drop-tower stable flame (△); error bars give the O2 and flow uncertainties and are mostly smaller than the symbols (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.83 · Fig. 6.9 · MEASURED]
- The gas-phase length scale ℓ = (α/a)^½ (Ref. 7) scales with r^½ at a given velocity, and all a are normalised to the base rod radius r_o = 0.318 cm through the ratio of these ℓ. [BAS-01 p.83 · CITED]
- The thick grey boundary of Fig. 6.9 is the border between stable and extinguished flames. [BAS-01 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Along this boundary the flame is sensitive to stochastic perturbations that can put it out (Ref. 22). [BAS-01 p.83 · CITED]
- Eq. 6.1, the empirical boundary: X_O2 = 6 exp(−0.5a) + 0.0167a + 13.4 (X_O2 = final O2, vol%; a = forced stretch rate, s⁻¹, normalised to r_o = 0.318 cm), combining the quenching branch 6 exp(−0.5a) + 13.4 (red dashed) and the blowoff branch 0.0167a + 13.4 (black dashed) into the thick grey boundary; a purple dashed "Linear (Drop Tower blowoff)" line has no printed equation; fitted range not stated (data span a ~0 to ~150 s⁻¹, X_O2 ~13.5 to ~18 vol%; conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.83 · Eq. 6.1 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.83 · Fig. 6.9 · MODELED · ~fig]
- The boundary minimum lies at a = 8 to 12 s⁻¹ and about 13.5 % final O2; the conclusions describe the lower boundary as a stochastic region between stable and extinguished flames, fitted with an exponential plus a linear term, with a adjusted for rod size through ℓ (conditions C7; test key BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-BOUNDARY-MINIMUM:df589e15). [BAS-01 p.83 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- This minimum agrees well with the a predicted at the minima of the flammability boundary (Refs. 6, 7, 20 and 21). [BAS-01 p.83 · CITED]
- The drop-tower blowoff data (purple dashed line) agree very well with the flight data, and the conclusions state that ISS blowoff limits agree well with the 5.18-s drop-test limits (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.83 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- The authors fit the quenching branch with an exponential decay: there, heat losses cool the flame to extinction through the strong Arrhenius dependence of reaction rate (as modelled in Refs. 6, 7, 20 and 21; evaluated in Section 6.1.4.3), and the branch is very steep at small a on a linear axis. [BAS-01 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6.10 replots the same data with a logarithmic a axis (same legend and lines; horizontal error bars on the low-a points): the classic U-shaped boundary appears, the quenching branch is expanded and the linear blowoff branch looks curved; it also stresses the flow uncertainty at very low velocities (<1 cm/s) along the quenching branch (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.84 · Fig. 6.10 · MEASURED]

#### Comparison with the normal-gravity upward limit (Fig. 6.22)
- The normal-gravity upward flame spread limit used for comparison is 15.4 % O2, with an extra 4-cm/s forced flow (Ref. 23: Hirsch et al., ASTM STP1454, 2003); Fig. 6.22 places it by assuming linear superposition of the buoyant velocity at the flame base (20 cm/s, Ref. 32: Hirano, Noreikis and Waterman, Combust. Flame 23, 1974) and the 4-cm/s forced flow (material, sample form and pressure of Ref. 23 not reported in the pages read; test key BAS-01:nodate:REF23-1G-UPWARD-LIMIT:a592501e). [BAS-01 p.84 · CITED; BAS-01 p.96 · Fig. 6.22 · CITED; BAS-01 p.97 · CITED; BAS-01 p.99–100 · CITED]
- The microgravity boundary minimum of 13.5 % O2 at a = 8 to 12 s⁻¹ is significantly lower than that 15.4 % normal-gravity upward limit (conditions C7). [BAS-01 p.83 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.84 · MEASURED]
- The authors conclude that the material stays flammable under the weak ventilation that only microgravity provides, a "Goldilocks" flow range that is typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces. [BAS-01 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6.22 replots the boundary (Eq. 6.1) against U/U_D, the forced-flow velocity over a diffusive velocity U_D = 2 cm/s (axes X_O2 13.0–16.0 vol%, U/U_D 0–20; legend: Hirsch 1g limit ×, BASS-II boundary as a thick green band with a dashed line along the blowoff branch); the blowoff-to-quenching transition falls where U is of the order of U_D (U/U_D = 1) for this geometry (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.96 · Fig. 6.22 · MEASURED]
- The Hirsch 1-g point sits at U/U_D ~12 (read within ±0.5) and X_O2 15.4 %, inside the stochastic BASS-II boundary. [BAS-01 p.96 · Fig. 6.22 · MEASURED · ~fig; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- Extrapolation proposals (authors): because the blowoff boundary is linear in flow, blowoff data can be extrapolated to zero a, the O2 found there being an accurate but conservative estimate of the minimum O2 for material flammability in space, which may give a consistent way to derate materials from normal-gravity tests that include buoyant flow; Earth tests need a reliable way to account for this extended flammability in microgravity, and extrapolating the normal-gravity blowoff boundary to zero stretch may work if a buoyant stretch is included; several limits at different forced plus buoyant flows along the blowoff boundary could be extrapolated linearly to zero flow for a reasonable yet conservative minimum. [BAS-01 p.83–84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On the quenching branch, as U falls the ambient O2 at the limit must rise to keep an O2 gradient large enough for diffusion to the flame, 3D diffusive transport becomes significant, and the limiting time shifts from residence time to diffusion time; the abstract places this blowoff-to-quenching transition at the bottom of the map, where convective flows reach the order of diffusive flows and the critical Damköhler number moves from a residence-time to a diffusive-time limit. [BAS-01 p.72 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors describe near-quench flames as O2-starved (O2 is the limiting reactant), with fuel leaking from the open tail, oscillations and mixing layers through which the flame flashes, locally depleting the already low O2, until the lower reaction rate cools the flame to quenching. [BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Combustion products and global stoichiometry (Figs. 6.13–6.16)
- Initial and final O2, CO2 and CO were recorded for each test; flow and O2 change within a test, but the averages still show the overall processes (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.87 · MEASURED]
- O2 consumed against CO2 generated (Fig. 6.13: stoichiometric ratio solid line, sensor data circles, linear fit dashed) scatters, but its linear trend agrees very well with the PMMA stoichiometric ratio of 6 O2 to 5 CO2 (initial-to-final sensor differences per test in the 250-L MSG volume; conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.86–87 · Fig. 6.13 · MEASURED]
- The authors take this to mean the O2 burned mainly to the expected CO2 and water. [BAS-01 p.87 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CO produced is fairly linear in CO2 produced, about 600 ppm CO for every 1 vol% CO2 (Fig. 6.14, circles with a dashed linear trend; conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.87 · Fig. 6.14 · MEASURED]
- The CO to CO2 ratio rises as O2 falls; the text plots it against initial O2 while the Fig. 6.15 caption labels the axis final O2 (legend: CO/CO2 ratio circles, exponential fit dashed, R² = 0.8652; conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.87–88 · Fig. 6.15 · MEASURED]
- These ratios are an order of magnitude above the 1-g cone-calorimeter values for PMMA (Ref. 24; cone conditions not reported in the pages read). [BAS-01 p.87 · CITED]
- The authors read this as very inefficient burning at low ambient O2 in microgravity. [BAS-01 p.87 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Global stoichiometry per test: the rod length burned away was measured on the stills, the O2 consumed came from the 250-L MSG free volume (Ref. 14) and the ideal gas law, and the fuel-to-oxidiser molar ratio was divided by the stoichiometric ratio (1 monomer unit per 6 O2). [BAS-01 p.87 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that the effect of the bubble layer on density was not included, the most likely cause of the scatter. [BAS-01 p.87 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flames are nearly stoichiometric (globally) at higher O2 and the global equivalence ratio rises at lower O2 (Fig. 6.16, against initial O2, annotated "Fuel rich" and "Stoichiometric burning"); the conclusions, from gas data and rod mass loss, call the flames globally stoichiometric at higher O2 and increasingly fuel-rich towards the minimum O2, with CO production and the CO/CO2 ratio both rising markedly at low O2 (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.72 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.87–88 · Fig. 6.16 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.97 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that O2, not fuel, is the limiting reactant at the lowest O2, with marked fuel leakage from the open back of the flame at low O2 and low flow, the abstract attributing the fuel-rich trend to this excess pyrolysate leakage; they find this consistent with the near-extinction oscillation mechanism (leakage, mixing, flashback through the premixed region) and with the inefficient burning shown by the CO/CO2 trend. [BAS-01 p.72 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.87 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.97 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Analyses: critical Damköhler number, flame temperature and convective heating (Eqs. 6.2–6.4, Fig. 6.17)
- Analysis chain: the experimental boundary (Eq. 6.1) is put into a constant critical Damköhler number formulation (Section 6.1.5.1) to estimate critical flame temperatures along the extinction boundary; these and the measured standoff distances feed a Nusselt correlation (Section 6.1.5.2) for the convective heat flux from the flame to the rod; a surface energy balance (Section 6.1.5.3) then uses that flux to weigh radiative exchange and heat losses on the blowoff and quenching sides and gives the mass burning rate along the boundary; measured and predicted regression rates are compared (Section 6.1.5.4), and relative losses across the boundary are examined for the blowoff-to-quenching transition; a constant base rod size is used throughout, so the radius factor in a is unity. [BAS-01 p.72 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.89 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.97–98 · MODELED]
- The authors apply the Da_crit analysis to both sides of the boundary because finite-rate chemistry holds along all of it: Da_crit becomes too small in both cases, at blowoff because the flow is too fast for the relatively fast reactions and at quenching because slow mixing of the reactants cuts the reaction rate. [BAS-01 p.89 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 6.2: Da_crit = flow time/reaction time ~ reaction rate/flow rate = β ρ X_f X_O2 exp(−E/(R T_crit))/a, with β = 1.3×10¹⁶ cm³/(gmol s), ρ = gas density at the mean temperature (air at T_m, 0.0441 g/cc), X_f and X_O2 the fuel and oxidiser concentrations, E = 1.45×10⁵ J/mol, R = 8.314 J/(gmol K), T_crit the critical temperature and a the stretch rate (s⁻¹); applied along Eq. 6.1, fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.89 · Eq. 6.2 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.72–73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Assumptions: Da_crit is constant along the whole boundary (Ref. 1) and set to unity, a critical balance of flow and reaction times; the reaction constants are close to the extinction values of Ref. 8, with β normalised by a blowoff Da reported in Ref. 1 to give unity; fuel concentration is unity at the fuel surface; Eq. 6.2 is solved for T_crit (not a constant) along the boundary using the O2 and stretch dependence of Eq. 6.1. [BAS-01 p.89 · MODELED · nominal]
- Predicted T_crit (Fig. 6.17) falls as a decreases, and falls more steeply in the quenching region (a < ~10 s⁻¹) (model, base rod radius 0.318 cm, along the Eq. 6.1 boundary). [BAS-01 p.89 · MODELED]
- The authors attribute the steeper fall to the lower flame heat flux relative to intrinsic heat losses (Section 6.1.5.3); T_crit is then used to estimate the flame-to-fuel heat flux. [BAS-01 p.89 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6.17 plots T_crit (dashed), T_crit − T_s (dash-dot), Nu (solid green), convective heating rate in W (dotted), radiative watts (red dashed) and total watts (solid black) against a (left axis temperature, K; right axis Nu or heating rate, W; a vertical dashed line separating "Quenching extinction", left, from "Blowoff extinction", right), with printed fits q_tot = 0.13α + 0.27 (W; printed with α though plotted against a), (T_crit − T_s) = 578 a^0.16 (K) and q_rad = 0.12 a^0.36 (W); fitted ranges not stated (curves drawn from a ~2 to 150 s⁻¹; model, base rod radius 0.318 cm). [BAS-01 p.90 · Fig. 6.17 · MODELED · ~fig]

- Heat transfer to the stagnation region uses Sibulkin's correlation (Ref. 25) for the forward stagnation point of a hemispherically tipped body of revolution, Eq. 6.3: Nu = 1.32 Re^0.5 Pr^0.4, with Re = UD/ν based on the diameter and Pr = 0.69 for air at T_m; fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.90 · Eq. 6.3 · CITED; BAS-01 p.72–73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors note that the correlation neglects dissociation (thermochemical heat release), given the low temperatures and strong N2 dilution along the boundary (Ref. 26), and gas radiation for these non-luminous flames (Ref. 27). [BAS-01 p.90 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 6.4 gives the convective heat flux to the stagnation region, in W/cm², as q''_conv = Nu λ (T_crit − T_s)/s, and the convective heating rate, in W, as q_conv = q''_conv A_h = h (T_crit − T_s) A_h, where T_s is 675 K, s the standoff and A_h = 2 A_r; on p.90 the text describes λ as a diffusivity evaluated at the mean gas temperature, whereas the symbol list defines λ as the thermal conductivity of air at T_m, 0.000577 W/cm K; fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.90 · Eq. 6.4 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.72–73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- T_crit from Fig. 6.17 and the measured standoff power law of Fig. 6.12 give q_conv to the stagnation region. [BAS-01 p.91 · MODELED · nominal]
- q_conv comes out linear in a, since the a powers in Eq. 6.4 add up: 0.5 from Nu (Eq. 6.3), about 0.33 from the approximately minus-cube-root standoff dependence (0.334 power, Fig. 6.12) and about 0.16 from T_crit − T_s (Fig. 6.17), total 0.99 ≈ 1 (model, base rod radius 0.318 cm). [BAS-01 p.91 · MODELED]

#### Two-zone surface energy balance and solid conduction (Eqs. 6.5–6.8, Fig. 6.18)
- To weigh radiative and solid-conduction losses, a two-zone balance (Fig. 6.18: PMMA rod, Zone 1 hemispherical tip, Zone 2 cylindrical rod, flame as a hemispherical shell around the tip, y along the rod away from the tip, flow U toward the tip) treats the 3D flame over the nearly spherical tip; Zone 1 is assumed wholly at the pyrolysis temperature T_s, consistent with the bubble layer length of Fig. 6.5 and with Bi << 1 at the Eq. 6.4 heat-flux levels; only solid conduction from Zone 1 into Zone 2 is counted, through the rod cross-section, while the other terms use the tip hemispherical area, twice as large. [BAS-01 p.91 · Fig. 6.18 · MODELED · nominal]
- Eq. 6.5: q_tot = q''_conv A_h + ε_g a_s σ F T_crit⁴ A_h = m'' L_vap A_h + ε_s σ (T_s⁴ − T_∞⁴) A_h + λ_s (∂T_solid/∂y)|₀ A_r, with ε_g = 0.02, ε_s = 0.8, σ = 5.729×10⁻¹² W/cm² K⁴ (experimental), F = 0.93, L_vap = 1700 J/g, T_s = 675 K, T_∞ = 300 K; λ_s is printed as the solid-phase "thermal diffusivity" while the symbol list gives the solid thermal conductivity, 2.09×10⁻³ W/cm K; fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.92 · Eq. 6.5 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.72–73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- q_tot is the Eq. 6.4 convection plus an estimate of gas-phase radiative feedback, included because it becomes an important energy source in the quenching region; Kirchhoff's law sets a_s = ε_s at the surface, and ε_g ≈ 0.02 comes mainly from CO2 and H2O; the energy reaching the surface goes into fuel vaporisation (burning rate m'', latent heat L_vap), surface radiative loss (from T_s and T_∞) and conduction into Zone 2 through the rod cross-section A_r. [BAS-01 p.92 · MODELED · nominal]
- The surface radiative loss assumes a constant pyrolysis temperature, which may fail very near quenching. [BAS-01 p.92 · MODELED]
- For the conductive loss, the solid profile is taken as roughly steady for long burns in slow flow and one-dimensional along the axis, with no vaporisation in Zone 2 and surface radiative loss offset by convection from the slowly passing hot gases; conduction balances the convective term from the measured steady regression V_r, assumed small enough that ΔL << L over t_s. [BAS-01 p.92 · MODELED · nominal]
- With the regression rate of Fig. 6.4 for the 0.476-cm rod (V_r = 0.0385 mm/s, conditions as the lowest-O2 quenching test), t_s = 132 s and ΔL = V_r t_s = 0.5 cm << L_o = 5.9 cm, so the temperature profiles are quasi-steady; the assumption fails once the rod has shortened a lot. [BAS-01 p.92 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.77 · MEASURED]
- Nondimensional form: Y = y/L, θ = (T − T_∞)/(T_s − T_∞), Pe = L V_r/α_s (α_s = 1.2×10⁻³ cm²/s for PMMA); Eq. 6.6: 0 = Pe ∂θ_s/∂Y + ∂²θ_s/∂Y², with θ(0) = 1 at the Zone 1–Zone 2 interface and θ(1) = 0 at y = L (roots 0 and −Pe); Eq. 6.7: θ(Y) = [exp(−PeY) − exp(−Pe)]/[1 − exp(−Pe)]; Eq. 6.8: dT_s/dy|_(y=0) = [Pe/(exp(−Pe) − 1)] (T_s − T_∞)/L_o (L_o = 5.9 cm), the surface gradient used for conduction loss in Eq. 6.5; fitted ranges not stated. [BAS-01 p.92–93 · Eq. 6.6 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.72–73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For Pe >> 1 the gradient at the pyrolysis interface is steep, as heat conducted along the rod is carried back toward the tip by regression; for Pe ≤ 1 conduction dominates and the profiles are nearly linear. [BAS-01 p.93 · MODELED]
- The authors call it counterintuitive that, in this steady state, the slowest-burning samples lose the least heat into the solid. [BAS-01 p.93 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With Eqs. 6.4 and 6.8, Eq. 6.5 is solved for m'' as a function of a, the tip mass flux being its only unknown; Eq. 6.5 gives vaporisation from the hemispherical surface while the experiments measure the average rod regression rate, a factor of 2 apart because of the areas. [BAS-01 p.93 · MODELED · nominal]

#### Regression rates: models against measurements (Fig. 6.19)
- Two-zone (3D) predicted average regression rates are compared with measured averages; the measurements scatter strongly because flow and O2 varied within each test but are of the right magnitude, and the abstract and conclusions say the computed regression rates compare favourably with the measurements (conditions C4). [BAS-01 p.72 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.93 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.97–98 · MODELED]
- The 1D solution of Eq. 6.5 (all heat-transfer areas equal, solved for V_r, stretch defined as U/D with the base rod size) agrees quite well with earlier pseudo-1D flat-flame data (Refs. 28 to 30), whose flames are much wider than their standoff distance; the two-zone burning rates are much higher than the 1D ones at a given a, from the larger heat-flux and vaporisation area of the 3D geometry. [BAS-01 p.93 · MODELED]
- Fig. 6.19 axes: rod-tip V_r or surface regression rate, cm/s (log, 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹), against a(r/r_o)^½, s⁻¹ (log, 10⁻¹ to 10³); legend 0.318 cm, 0.476 cm, 0.636 cm (as printed), black 0.318 cm, Olson and T'ien 2001, T'ien et al. 1978, Ohtani et al. 1983, two-zone model (dashed), 1D model (solid). [BAS-01 p.94 · Fig. 6.19 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The pseudo-1D sources in the reference list are Olson and T'ien (Combust. Flame 121, 2000), Ohtani, Akita and Hirano (Combust. Flame 53, 1983) and T'ien et al. (Combust. Flame 33, 1978). [BAS-01 p.99 · CITED]

#### Heat losses along the boundary (Figs. 6.20, 6.21)
- Energy-balance summary: on the blowoff branch heat losses are negligible; in the quenching region surface radiative loss dominates; solid conduction down the rod is smaller and falls with decreasing stretch because of the low Péclet number; gas-phase radiative feedback becomes an important heat input that extends the flammability limit to lower a (model along the microgravity boundary). [BAS-01 p.72 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.98 · MODELED]
- Fig. 6.20 plots the Eq. 6.5 terms against a on log axes (watts 10⁻² to above 10¹; a 10⁰ to ~50 s⁻¹) to expand the quenching region (a < 10 s⁻¹, shaded) where losses matter, using Eq. 6.4 convection and Eq. 6.8 conduction as inputs; legend: total flame-surface feedback, convective watts to surface, flame radiative feedback to surface, fuel vaporisation, solid conduction from surface, surface radiative loss. [BAS-01 p.94–95 · Fig. 6.20 · MODELED · nominal]
- The total flame heating rate to the surface falls linearly as a decreases (Fig. 6.17); the minimum heat flux, at a = 1, is 1 W/A_h = 1.57 W/cm² (model, base rod radius 0.318 cm). [BAS-01 p.94 · MODELED]
- 1.57 W/cm² lies within the literature range of the critical heat flux for ignition of PMMA (Ref. 31: Lyon and Quintiere, Criteria for Piloted Ignition of Combustible Solids, Combust. Flame 151, 2007). [BAS-01 p.94 · CITED; BAS-01 p.99 · CITED]
- On the blowoff branch (a > 10 s⁻¹) fuel vaporisation follows the total flame-to-surface heat flux and losses are small, in-depth solid conduction being the largest but falling with a as the Péclet number does; flame radiative feedback matches surface radiative loss at high a but falls with a as the flame cools; on the quenching branch vaporisation drops sharply with the total heat flux and losses become a large fraction of it. [BAS-01 p.94 · MODELED]
- In ratio form (Fig. 6.21, each term over convective plus gas-radiative input), vaporisation is ~70 % across the blowoff branch and drops sharply to 20 % at low a on the quenching branch. [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED]
- As a falls, the solid conductive loss ratio surprisingly decreases for this geometry, matching the observation that the slowest-burning rods lose least by conduction, while the surface radiative loss ratio grows, not from a larger surface loss but from the smaller total energy from the flame (consistent with Ref. 6). [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED]
- Above a ~10 s⁻¹ (the blowoff side of Figs. 6.9 and 6.10), surface radiative loss is comparable to flame radiative feedback, so radiative exchange as a whole can be neglected. [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED]
- Flame radiative feedback grows from an insignificant 1 % of the total flame-to-surface feedback (agreeing with Ref. 26) to over 13 % at low a, in general agreement with the more rigorous radiation analysis of Rhatigan et al. (Ref. 20). [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED]
- The authors state that this extra energy source extends flammability to lower a. [BAS-01 p.96 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Surface radiative loss becomes a significant fraction of the flame-to-surface heat only in the quenching region; at the lowest a the total loss fraction exceeds 60 % of the flame-to-surface feedback. [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED]
- At the bottom of the map (a ~10 s⁻¹) losses are only ~30 % of the flame-to-surface feedback, yet the blowoff-to-quenching transition begins there; the conclusions attribute the transition to convective flows becoming of the same order as diffusive flows, shifting the critical Damköhler number from residence-time to diffusive-time limits, with O2 transport limited by concentration gradients so that the needed ambient O2 rises as a falls. [BAS-01 p.96 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.98 · MODELED]
- Fig. 6.21 legend: convection/total, flame radiative feedback/total, vaporisation/total, (conduction + surface radiative loss)/total, surface radiative loss/total, conduction/total; quenching region (a < 10 s⁻¹) shaded; y axis 0.0–1.0 linear, a axis log. [BAS-01 p.95 · Fig. 6.21 · MODELED · nominal]

### 4. SIBAL fabric in low-speed concurrent flow (T'ien, chapter 7)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity and platform | Atmosphere | Flow | Ignition and enclosure | Reading | Not reported (pages read) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C9 | SIBAL fabric: flat cotton-fiberglass blend (75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass), about 0.32 mm thick, 18.2 mg/cm², 1.2 or 2.2 cm wide, 10 cm exposed length, stainless-steel holder | microgravity, ISS, BASS and BASS-II small flow duct (7.6 × 7.6 cm cross-section) inside the MSG | ambient O2 16–21 % (molar), fixed during each test (BASS-II lowers MSG O2 to a preset value by N2 dilution, Ref. 7); 1 atm | concurrent forced flow, available 1–55 cm/s, tested from 40 down to 1 cm/s, in some tests reduced during the run | Kanthal hot wire at the sample leading edge | — | ambient temperature | [BAS-01 p.101–102 · MEASURED · nominal] |

#### Study and setup
- Chapter 7 is a version of work published as Zhao and T'ien, A Three-Dimensional Transient Model for Flame Growth and Extinction in Concurrent Flows, Combust. Flame 162 (2015) 1829–1839 (chapter-title footnote). [BAS-01 p.101 · CITED]
- BASS and BASS-II studied flame growth, spread and extinction of SIBAL fabric in low-speed concurrent forced flow in a small duct inside the MSG; this chapter reports growth, spread and quenching extinction of this thin fabric at various O2 levels and flow speeds (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.101–102 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Background: microgravity spread and extinction over condensed fuels has been studied widely because of fire safety in human missions (Refs. 1 to 4); without buoyancy-induced flow, microgravity diffusion flames allow study of the basic mechanisms of low-speed quenching (Ref. 5); the transition from spread to quenching extinction is a slow heat-loss process in which radiative and conductive losses grow relative to heat generation (Ref. 3). [BAS-01 p.101 · CITED]
- The authors note that such studies need long microgravity times that ground facilities generally cannot give, so these long-duration ISS experiments are a rare opportunity for solid-fuel combustion. [BAS-01 p.101 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BASS and BASS-II burned various thermally thin and thick solid fuels in concurrent, opposed or stagnation flow in a small duct on the ISS, each run lasting tens of seconds to minutes depending on sample type and flow. [BAS-01 p.101 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors note that thin samples in concurrent flow spread much faster and can grow long flames, so the short sample (size limits) may not reach fully steady spread, but the transient ignition and growth history is useful for developing transient flame models (Ref. 6); the BASS-II N2 dilution, by adding O2 as a variable, helps determine a material's O2–flow-velocity flammability boundary. [BAS-01 p.101–102 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The fabric was custom-made for the earlier Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speeds (SIBAL) project (Ref. 8), hence the name SIBAL fabric (Table 7.1 footnote a repeats the expansion). [BAS-01 p.102 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.104 · Table 7.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors cite as an advantage that the fiberglass mesh keeps the sample intact after the cotton cellulose has burned, without the cracking or curled ash of pure cellulose samples such as paper or cloth. [BAS-01 p.102 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Other studies with SIBAL fabric are Refs. 8, 9 and 10. [BAS-01 p.102 · CITED]
- Imaging: a side-view video camera gave edge-on images at 29.97 frames/s and a top-view digital camera gave high-resolution stills about every 1.2 s; at low flow and low O2 the flame turned very dim blue and was hard to see on the side video, but the top-view exposures (1/8 to 1/4 s) caught even dim flames just before quenching, giving a quenching time history for comparison with transient models; Fig. 7.1 shows the duct (fan section with inlet, top window, side window, flow exit) and the sample, holder and igniter (2.2-cm sample). [BAS-01 p.102–103 · Fig. 7.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At low flow the flame was small, so its whole history could be followed: ignition, growth, steady spread (in some cases) and decay at the end of the sample (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.101 · MEASURED]

#### Test matrix (Table 7.1)
- BASS-II made 27 fabric tests, including six quenching tests, three non-ignited tests and one blowoff test; four BASS tests are added at the bottom of Table 7.1, all at 21 % O2 with a fixed flow in each test (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED]
- Table 7.1 (flat SIBAL fabrics in concurrent flow, BASS and BASS-II) has 31 rows: 27 BASS-II tests, GMT45-T1 to GMT216-T29 (keys BASS-II:T1 to BASS-II:T29 in the tests table), then 4 BASS tests, GMT96-T8, GMT96-T7, GMT131-T10 and GMT222-T11 (keys BASS:5, BASS:4, BASS:13, BASS:65); columns test number, sample width (2.2 or 1.2 cm), flow (cm/s), O2 (vol%) and comments (Quenched, No blowoff, Blow-off, No ignition, Reused with did not ignite, one-sided flame or ignited, BASS, or a dash) (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.104 · Table 7.1 · MEASURED]
- In the flow column, tests with a velocity change show the start and final velocities ("<start> to <final>"); GMT is Greenwich Mean Time, the standard time on the ISS. [BAS-01 p.103 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- Table 7.1 footnote b flags the O2 readings (18.5 vol%) of GMT45-T1 and GMT45-T2 (BASS-II:T1, BASS-II:T2) as possibly inaccurate. [BAS-01 p.104 · Table 7.1 · MEASURED]
- The rate of flow change varied with astronaut–ground communication and the crew's manual adjustment time; many tests served to find low-speed quenching limits against O2; samples whose flame quenched quickly or did not ignite were reused (Table 7.1), relit by a retractable igniter on one side at the burnout position. [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The reused samples generally had a short unburned length and gave less quantitative data, so the report leaves them out. [BAS-01 p.103 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Flame development at 21 % O2 (Figs. 7.2, 7.3)
- Fig. 7.2 (2.2-cm sample, 10 cm/s, 21 % O2; conditions C9) gives side-view tracking of flame tip, flame base and flame length (a) and edge-view video stills (b) at t = 0.52, 1.03, 3.62, 5.69, 10.86, 20.17, 24.83 and 36.20 s, flow from right to left. [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.105 · Fig. 7.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In that run the igniter started a strong flame on both sides of the fuel, which stabilised, grew and moved downstream; at about 19 s it reached a limiting constant length and steady spread relative to the laboratory (Ref. 11), held for around 9 s with almost identical images (20.17 and 24.83 s); then the flame tip (more precisely the preheating front) neared the end of the sample and the flame decayed to burnout; the whole process took about 40 s (2.2 cm, 10 cm/s, 21 % O2, two-sided; conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Fig. 7.3 (2.2-cm sample, 5 cm/s, 21 % O2; conditions C9) uses top-view tracking (a) and images (b) at t = 6, 14.6, 35.59, 45.59 and 59.842 s, flow from right to left, because the side-view flame was very dim, unlike the 10-cm/s flame. [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.105 · Fig. 7.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At 5 cm/s the whole sample took more than 60 s to burn; steady spread lasted about 21 s, much longer than at 10 cm/s, with virtually identical images at 35.59 and 45.59 s; bright spots appeared behind the flame base as the flame passed; compared with 10 cm/s the flame was shorter and spread more slowly (2.2 cm, 21 % O2; conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors attribute the bright spots to smouldering of a little fuel not fully consumed by the flame. [BAS-01 p.103 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Steady spread rate (Fig. 7.4)
- Steady flame spread means a constant spread rate held for more than 20 s. [BAS-01 p.103 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 7.4 plots steady spread rate V_f (mm/s, linear 0.0–3.5) against flow U0 (cm/s, log 2–20) for 2.2- and 1.2-cm samples (legend width, O2: 2.2 cm at 21, 18.8, 17.6, 17.1 and 16.9 %; 1.2 cm at 21 and 17.2 %), the flow being varied in some tests; flames spread more slowly on the narrower samples, at lower flow and at lower O2 (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.103 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.106 · Fig. 7.4 · MEASURED]
- The authors find these trends consistent with physical intuition. [BAS-01 p.103 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Quenching sequence (Figs. 7.5, 7.6)
- In a typical BASS-II quenching sequence a 2.2-cm sample in 18.7 % O2 was lit at 10 cm/s and the flow lowered in steps, reaching 2.2 cm/s after 25 s and held there; flame length and width first grew, then fell with the flow, and kept shrinking toward a circular blue flame (top view) until extinction; the conclusions add that at quenching the flame shrinks in both length and width and goes out in a three-dimensional way (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.106 · MEASURED · single-test; BAS-01 p.109 · MEASURED]
- The post-burn photo shows the burnt region narrowing as the flame shrank toward extinction, with much fuel left unburnt along both sides of the holder (same run). [BAS-01 p.106 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors call this typical of quenching extinction: as the limit is approached (here by lowering the flow), fuel pyrolysis and heat release rate (HRR, W) fall, radiation loss becomes a large fraction of the HRR of the shrinking flame, and once the flame is small enough conduction adds a further loss; though the spread is concurrent, the sequence resembles opposed flow (Ref. 2), the circular flame pointing to the importance of three-dimensional (3D) heat and mass transfer near the limit. [BAS-01 p.106 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- Fig. 7.5 (top view, flow right to left) panels: (a) t = 6.7 s, V = 8 cm/s; (b) 32.6 s, 2.2 cm/s; (c) 15.7 s, 4 cm/s; (d) 45.0 s, 2.2 cm/s; (e) 25.8 s, 2.2 cm/s; (f) 54.0 s, 2.2 cm/s; (g) 29.2 s, 2.2 cm/s; (h) post-burn; Fig. 7.6 plots top-view flame tip, flame base and flame length (mm, left axis) and U0 (cm/s, right axis) against time (s) (same run). #### Low-speed quenching boundary (Fig. 7.7)
- The authors explain that this thin fabric spreads fast in concurrent flow and the sample is too short to fine-tune the flow during the 1 to 2 min of a run, so the near-quenching state is hard to reach every time. [BAS-01 p.108 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Lowering the flow during some tests gave low-speed quenching limits as a function of O2; BASS-II achieved six quenching cases with SIBAL, four on 2.2-cm samples, which with the near-limit stable flames outline part of the quenching branch for the 2.2-cm fabric (Fig. 7.7; conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.101 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-01 p.108 · MEASURED]
- Quenching velocities lie between 1 and 5 cm/s, higher at lower O2 (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.101 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.108 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.109 · MEASURED]
- This trend of the quenching boundary supports earlier theoretical predictions (Refs. 1 and 8). [BAS-01 p.108 · CITED]
- The authors state that the shape of the boundary supports earlier theoretical models, at least qualitatively, of solid flammability limits at low flow due to radiative and conductive losses; that flow reduction gave accurate quenching limits, accuracy being needed to resolve the slope of the boundary; and that this is the first clean, unambiguous determination of a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread. [BAS-01 p.101 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A recent 3D transient numerical model (Ref. 6) suits this experiment and includes many material properties, kinetic rate constants among them. [BAS-01 p.108 · CITED]
- The authors report that pyrolysis rate constants of the SIBAL fabric are being measured and deduced for quantitative model–experiment comparison. [BAS-01 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Very near the boundary, ignition of the sample was sporadic (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.108 · MEASURED]
- The authors expect the bottom (lowest-O2) part of the boundary to be flat in Fig. 7.7, but it cannot be found accurately by varying velocity; a procedure with slowly decreasing O2 is needed. [BAS-01 p.108 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With few tests, the quenching limit of the 1.2-cm sample was not resolved (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.108 · MEASURED]
- The authors see in Fig. 7.7 that the narrower sample has a smaller flammable domain, as expected. [BAS-01 p.108 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 7.7 (flammability map for SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow in microgravity; O2, vol%, linear 16.2–19.0, against U0, cm/s, log 1–100) marks the experimental 2.2-cm quenching boundary with a dotted line; legend: 2.2 cm spread (black filled circle), quench (red filled circle), not ignited (red cross); 1.2 cm spread (purple filled triangle), quench (orange open triangle), blowoff (olive crossed triangle) (conditions C9). [BAS-01 p.108 · Fig. 7.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors call the ignition-to-decay sequences recorded over whole samples in low-speed purely forced flow precious data for understanding flame development in microgravity and a basis for checking theoretical models. [BAS-01 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
