# FILE: BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_3
# BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_3 — BASS-II appendices, BASS 2013 results deck and BASS-II concurrent PMMA rod limits

## Scope
Covers: three documents. BAS-01 Appendices A (Tables A.5 Olson and A.6 T'ien), B (setting test O2 by nitrogen dilution of the MSG), C (in-flight anomalies) and D (worst-case heat release estimate, BASS slab and sphere data). BAS-03, the 2013 BASS slide deck (hardware, thin fabric, Ultem and Nomex, PMMA spheres and their model, flat PMMA, nitrogen suppression, conclusions). BAS-04, the BASS-II concurrent-flow PMMA rod campaign (procedures, Fig. 4 flammability boundary, drop-tower comparison, Damkohler and energy-balance interpretation).
Not here: the main chapters and other appendices of BAS-01 (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 and BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_2); BAS-05, BAS-07, the OVR-13 BASS item and the PSI records and as-run matrices PSC-01, PSD-01, PSD-02, PSD-03 (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4); normal-gravity studies built to predict the BASS-II limit and general Test 1-vs-space statements (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2); Saffire (see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1, LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2); SoFIE and Confined Combustion (see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1, NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2).

### Setting test O2 by nitrogen dilution of the MSG working volume
Model: a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) mole balance on O2, with the working volume of the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG, an ISS facility) as control volume, an N2 inflow and a leak of well-mixed gas. [BAS-01 p.123 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
Symbols: C_in = O2 concentration entering the work volume, 0 (pure N2); C_o = initial O2 in the work volume; C_out = O2 leaving, = c(t) (CSTR property); c(t) = O2 in the work volume over time; r = N2 flow rate, 0.0005 m3/min maximum, adjustable; T = temperature; V = MSG working volume, 0.25 m3. [BAS-01 p.123 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
With C_in = 0, C_out = c(t) and C(0) = C_o, Eq. B.1 is V dc/dt = r(C_in − C_out) = −r c(t), and its integral Eq. B.2 is c(t) = C_o exp(−r t / V); the concentration unit is not given and no fitted range is stated. [BAS-01 p.123 · Eq. B.1 · MODELED; BAS-01 p.123 · Eq. B.2 · MODELED]
BAS-04 describes the same vitiation model (its ref. [16]) as CSTR-based and valid while the residence time (V/r = 500 min) is 5 to 10 times the mixing time, which holds at the 100 LPM fan mixing rate (250 L / 100 LPM = 2.5 min). [BAS-04 p.4 · MODELED]
Hardware: the MSG working volume was diluted with ISS nitrogen through a hose from the BASS-II duct to the MSG back wall; a small (< 0.5 LPM) MKS 179A mass flow meter regulated the N2, which entered through a small nozzle just downstream of the fan; the duct fan ran at maximum (> 100 LPM) to mix and circulate the gas through the hours-long vitiation. [BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]

The authors attribute the minimal curvature to the slow N2 flow into the large volume, and judge that the model agrees very well with the CSA-CP readings, both direct and offset-corrected, giving a calibrated O2 level over time. [BAS-01 p.124 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
For BASS-II operations the model set the N2 flow rate and flow time needed to reach each test's target O2 from the initial reading, within crew-time limits. [BAS-01 p.124 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.4 · MODELED · nominal]
BAS-04 states the model was verified with intermittent on-board O2 sensor readings during an initial vitiation. [BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
The CSA-CP O2 sensor is not recalibrated on orbit, so the daily offset against the MCA data (BAS-04 writes "Mass Constituents Analyzer") corrected each CSA-CP reading to a calibrated O2 per test; the sensor's O2 resolution was 0.1 % (BAS-04 prints the sensor name as "CSA-CO"). [BAS-01 p.124 · MEASURED; BAS-01 p.14 · MEASURED · ctx, nominal; BAS-04 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
The authors report that the model worked very well, post-dilution CSA-CP readings agreeing extremely well with predictions over a range of dilution rates, and that controlling both flow rate and dilution time let them fit crew schedules while reaching the wanted O2. BAS-04 sensors: two portable battery-powered instruments in the working volume, CDM and CSA-CP, measured O2 depletion and combustion completeness (CO, CO2) to rate combustion-product levels; the CO sensor is zero-calibrated every 60 days (range 0–1000 ppm, resolution 1 ppm) and the CO2 sensor was within its calibration window (range 0–5 %, resolution 0.1 % by volume). [BAS-04 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
The sensor data gave initial and final conditions for repeated tests in the sealed working volume and showed when it needed purging. [BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]


### Flow duct, sensors and procedure
BASS-II hardware (BAS-04): a flow duct, still camera, video camera, external control box and plumbing and mounting, shown inside the MSG working volume in Fig. 1. [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
Duct: black anodized, 7.6 cm × 7.6 cm × 17 cm, rectangular with rounded corners, first built for gas-jet diffusion flame studies (BAS-04 ref. [15]) and modified for BASS solid samples; the 17-cm test section holds a nitrogen nozzle for vitiating the working volume and a moveable scale for reference at the sample plane; of its two orthogonal windows the top one was replaced by a sample mounting rail, and the front window opens for sample and igniter change-out. [BAS-04 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal]
Flow: a small fan at the upstream end, its voltage varied to change the flow; up to two extra flow restrictors at the fan inlet raise the pressure drop to lower the flow; a honeycomb straightener and inlet screen reduce swirl. [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
An omnidirectional spherical air velocity transducer (TSI 8475) between honeycomb and screen measured the steady duct velocity, and the fan voltage was calibrated against it at the end of every operations day for that day's restrictor configuration(s). [BAS-04 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal]
The velocity probe's response time was about one minute. [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED]
Exit: a perforated copper plate then a brass screen reject heat and give a cold surface for soot deposition; the flow turns 90° to leave the duct, mixing the hot products with cool ambient gas, and the products mix into the work-volume gas. [BAS-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
Diagnostics: an Oriel 71768 thermopile detector (calcium fluoride window, 0.13 to 11 µm) in the downstream top back corner; a Nikon D300 12.3-megapixel still camera with a 60-mm lens (4320 × 2968 pixel images) through the top window; a Panasonic WV-CP654 video camera (760 × 480 pixels) through the front window by a turning mirror; a control box for fan voltage, nitrogen flow level, igniter and nitrogen enable switches and radiometer gain. [BAS-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
The video overlay showed nitrogen flow rate (cm3/min), fan voltage (10×V), hot-wire anemometer reading (cm/s) and the radiometer signal; the radiometer was not calibrated but gave a measure of flame dynamics and steadiness. [BAS-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
BAS-03 is titled "Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment"; its mission patch reads "Burning and Suppression of Solids" around "BASS", rim "NASA GRC • NCSER • CWRU • ZIN". [BAS-03 p.1 · MEASURED · slide]
BAS-03 lists BASS science applications as aims: understanding long-duration microgravity burning and extinction of solid materials; better NASA spacecraft materials selection, linking actual microgravity burn behaviour to Earth-based selection methods; better combustion models for designing fire detection and suppression in microgravity and on Earth; detailed models validated in the simpler microgravity flow environment building the more complex models needed for normal-gravity flames; and wide applicability of such models to terrestrial combustion problems. [BAS-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
Uncaptioned model figures on the same slide: left, a 3-D computational domain (centerline plane of symmetry; U∞ in cm/s entering at the negative-X end; V_F in cm/s pointing toward negative X; an inert strip and fresh solid fuel along the bottom with a flame drawn over the fuel; axes X −5 to 15 cm, Y 0 to 5 cm, Z 0 to 4 cm); right, the plane Y = 0.23 cm (X −3 to 6 cm, Z 0 to 4 cm) with O2 mass-flux vectors (reference 1.375 × 10^-3 g/cm^2/s), velocity vectors (reference 5 cm/s), stream-function lines ψ = 0 to 10, T contours labelled 2 to 4.2 (no unit) and a dashed contour labelled 10^-5 g/cm^3/s (quantity not named); model O2, U∞, fuel, thickness, gravity level and pressure not reported by this source. [BAS-03 p.4 · MODELED · slide, nominal]
BASS (BAS-03): tests aboard the ISS used the on-orbit SPICE hardware with minor changes for solid samples, a small wind tunnel imposing airflow up to 40 cm/s, installed in the MSG, which supplied power, imaging and a level of containment; the MSG working volume is labelled 255 liters. [BAS-03 p.2 · MEASURED · slide, nominal; BAS-03 p.5 · MEASURED · slide, nominal; BAS-03 p.8 · MEASURED · slide, nominal]
Other MSG diagram labels: International Standard Payload Rack, Control and Monitoring Panel, Stowage Drawer, Video drawer, Utility Interface Panel, Remote Power Distribution Assembly, Foot restraint. [BAS-03 p.5 · MEASURED · slide, nominal]

### Worst-case heat release and hardware temperature (BAS-01 Appendix D, pre-flight estimate)
Appendix D estimates the heat release rate and hardware temperature rise for the BASS-II thick PMMA slab samples. [BAS-01 p.129 · MODELED · nominal]
The principal investigator, Sandra L. Olson, wrote it on January 10, 2014, and notes that no test like this was planned. [BAS-01 p.129 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
Purpose: BASS-II samples are larger than earlier flown samples, raising concern that burning them could overheat and damage the hardware, so the analysis gauges how hot the BASS experiment assembly could get under a worst-case flame on this large, thick sample. [BAS-01 p.129 · MODELED · nominal]

| Set | Material and form | Platform | Atmosphere and flow | Flame and burn assumptions | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | 0.5-cm-thick, 8.5-cm-long, 2-cm-wide PMMA slab (the worst-case, largest sample) | BASS-II, in the MSG aboard ISS | air at 30 cm/s, three times the highest flow in these samples' test matrix | concurrent flame (expected larger than opposed; the samples were meant for opposed flow only, but the larger flame is assumed so as not to limit the plan); two-sided, symmetric; stoichiometric; grows to a steady size; maximum burn time = time to burn the whole sample; duct exit air in temperature equilibrium with the exhaust hardware | total pressure, ambient temperature | [BAS-01 p.129 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.10 · MEASURED · ctx, nominal]

Symbols (D.1): Q̇ = steady total heat release; Q̇air = energy carried out of the BASS duct, kJ/min; ρ = air density, 1.2 kg/m3; cp = air heat capacity, 1 kJ/kg K; H, W = duct height and width, 7.5 cm (0.075 m) each; m = mass; r0 = initial and rmax = peak regression rate; t = time; ΔT = temperature change; U = flow velocity, 30 cm/s = 0.3 m/s = 18 m/min; BASS-II = Burning and Suppression of Solids—II experiment in the MSG aboard ISS. [BAS-01 p.129 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-01 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
Basis (C3): the burning-rate estimates rest on a computational study of boundary-layer combustion of a PMMA plate in forced flow (ref. 1, Fig. D.1) and on a BASS 1-cm PMMA sphere burning in stagnation flow, which captures the burning of the exposed sample base. [BAS-01 p.130 · MODELED · nominal]
Fig. D.1, from ref. 1 (Ananth, Ndubizu and Tatem, Combust. Flame vol. 135, 2003): predicted flame temperature for a PMMA plate between inert plates in forced flow U = 60 cm/s, plotted as flame height (cm) against position (no unit); contour legend values, no unit printed: 1,837.310; 1,734.630; 1,631.940; 1,529.250; 1,426.560; 1,323.880; 1,221.190; 1,118.500; 1,105.810; 913.125; 810.438; 707.750; 605.063; the PMMA segment spans ~1.7 to ~8.4 axis units (±0.5, read from figure); O2 and pressure not reported in the pages read. [BAS-01 p.130 · Fig. D.1 · CITED · ~fig]
The authors note that a thick PMMA slab takes time to ignite and grow to a steady size, and that the burning-rate distribution sets how much heat the flame generates; Fig. D.2 shows the flame base (x = 0) with the highest burning rate and an exponential decay of regression rate away from it, and the exposed, most upstream base is expected to be the strongest part of the flame with the maximum burning rate. [BAS-01 p.130 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
Method (C3): the peak regression rates rmax of the four ref. 1 flow profiles are extrapolated down to 30 cm/s by a curve fit with the square-root trend expected as flow falls (ref. 2); Fig. D.2 plots peak regression rate (mm/min) against flow (cm/s) for the ref. 1 data, the extrapolated values and the BASS 1-cm sphere. [BAS-01 p.130–131 · Fig. D.2 · MODELED · nominal]

| Set | Fig. D.2 series | Flow, cm/s | Peak regression rate, mm/min | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | Data from ref. 1 (PMMA plate, computed) | ~60, ~84, ~120, ~169 | ~3.6, ~4.0, ~4.5, ~4.8 (read tolerance ±5 cm/s, ±0.25 mm/min) | [BAS-01 p.131 · Fig. D.2 · CITED · ~fig]
| C3 | Extrapolated values (series spans ~5 to ~30 cm/s), lowest-flow point | ~5 | ~2.4 (±5 cm/s, ±0.25 mm/min) | [BAS-01 p.131 · Fig. D.2 · MODELED · ~fig]
| C3 | Extrapolated value at the flow of interest | 30 | 3.13 | [BAS-01 p.131 · Fig. D.2 · MODELED]
| C3 | BASS 1-cm sphere (single point, plotted just below the extrapolated value) | ~30 (±5) | 3.05, estimated from the D.7 sphere data and in keeping with Fig. D.2 (Fig. D.3) | [BAS-01 p.130–131 · Fig. D.2 · MODELED · ~fig]

Downstream of the base, regression rates are predicted to decay exponentially (C3, Fig. D.2). [BAS-01 p.130 · MODELED]
Flame growth (C3): with an expected power-law growth rate (ref. 3) the flame reaches steady size in about 2.5 min (Fig. D.3); the Fig. D.3 trend line is y = 0.5x^2, R^2 = 1 (y = peak regression rate, mm/min; x = time, min; fitted range not stated), its points spanning ~0.5 to ~2.5 min, the first at ~0.1 mm/min at ~0.5 min and the steady state at ~3.1 mm/min at ~2.5 and ~3 min (read tolerance ±0.25 min, ±0.25 mm/min). [BAS-01 p.131 · Fig. D.3 · MODELED · ~fig]
The authors call this growth rate reasonable because an earlier BASS PMMA slab took over 3 min to reach steady size (Appendix D.7). [BAS-01 p.131 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
At 3.05 mm/min the flame base needs ~28 min to regress the whole 8.5-cm sample (C3). [BAS-01 p.131 · MODELED]
That is far beyond the 7-min limit of the still camera card. [BAS-01 p.131 · MEASURED · nominal]
Fuel consumption method (C3): regression-rate profiles over time come from the growth history and the peak rates; the profiles, on both sides of the sample, are summed along x (the area under the curves) and multiplied by the 2-cm width to give the fuel consumed per minute. [BAS-01 p.131 · MODELED · nominal]
The authors note that these profiles come from steady slab burning, in which a significant part of the heat release goes back into the fuel as preheating or is reradiated to the surroundings. [BAS-01 p.131 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| Set | Fig. D.4 quantity (30-cm/s flame) | Values read from figure | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | regression rate at the leading edge (0 cm) for the 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 min and steady-state profiles | ~0.1, ~0.5, ~1.1, ~2.0, ~3.15 mm/min (±0.05 mm/min) | [BAS-01 p.132 · Fig. D.4a · MODELED · ~fig]
| C3 | distance from the leading edge where all five profiles reach ~0 mm/min | ~6 cm (±0.25 cm) | [BAS-01 p.132 · Fig. D.4a · MODELED · ~fig]

Heat release method (C3): the fuel volume per minute is converted to heat release rate assuming stoichiometric burning on both sides and O2-consumption calorimetry at 13.1 kJ/g O2, with C5H8O2 + 6 O2 → 5 CO2 + 4 H2O and the unit chain (mm3 per side per minute) × (2 sides) × (g fuel/mm3) × (gmol fuel/g fuel) × (gmol O2/gmol fuel) × (g O2/gmol O2) × (13.1 kJ/g O2) × (1,000 J/kJ) = Q̇comb (J/min) (the chain prints "minimum side"; Q̇comb is not in the symbol list); inputs: fuel density 1.19 g/cc (1.19 mg/mm3), 100 g/gmol fuel, 32 g/gmol O2, 6 gmol O2 per gmol fuel. [BAS-01 p.132 · MODELED · nominal; BAS-01 p.129 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The steady total heat release rate Q̇ is 72 W (C3). [BAS-01 p.132 · MODELED]
Ignition energy is taken as 4 A through a 1-Ω igniter, 16 W; the heat passes through the duct into the MSG, and the experiment housing absorbs part of it. [BAS-01 p.132 · MODELED · nominal]
Air heat removal (C3): Q̇air/ΔT (kJ/(min·°C)) = ρ cp U H W, with ρ = 1.2 kg/m3, cp = 1 kJ/kg K, U = 30 cm/s (18 m/min) and H = W = 7.5 cm, gives 121.5 J/min Δ°C; fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.132–133 · MODELED]
The exhaust passes heat-exchanger parts (Table D.1) joined to the main housing of the experiment assembly, about 1,580 g of aluminum; the whole experiment assembly is 6.94 kg. [BAS-01 p.133 · MODELED · nominal]

Temperature over time: Q̇t = [(ρ cp U H W)air + Σ m cp] ΔTexhaust, with Q̇ the total heat release rate in watts and Texhaust the exhaust-gas temperature after each component, solved for ΔT; fitted range not stated. [BAS-01 p.133 · MODELED]
Fig. D.5 plots heat release rate (W) and temperature (°C) against time from ignition start (min) for the exhaust hardware, the main housing and the whole experiment assembly (series: ignition watts, combustion watts, total heat release rate, exhaust heat sink, main housing and experiment assembly temperatures); the maximum burn time is the 2.5-min growth phase plus the 28-min regression phase, 30.5 min, and the maxima below are for that time. [BAS-01 p.133–134 · Fig. D.5 · MODELED · nominal]
Early heat release is dominated by ignition energy; the igniter is switched off once combustion heat release nears steady state and the flame sustains itself; read from Fig. D.5, ignition holds ~16 W from 0 to ~2 min and falls to ~0 W at ~2.5 min, total heat release reaches its 72-W plateau at ~2.5 min and holds to the end (~30.5 min), and all three temperatures start at ~25 °C (±1.25 min, ±2.5 W, ±5 °C). [BAS-01 p.134 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

Model domain read from the mesh figure: bottom edge Y = 0 from X ~0 to ~0.72 m; top edge Y ~0.2 m from X ~0.07 m (rounded upper-left corner) to ~0.74 m; the right end narrows to a section between Y ~0.06 and ~0.09 m reaching X ~0.82 m (±0.025 m in X, ±0.01 m in Y); densest mesh near Y = 0 around the sphere at X ~0.40 to ~0.44 m; in the zoom the sphere surface spans X ~0.400 to ~0.440 m and reaches Y ~0.020 m at X ~0.420 m (±0.001 m), with coarser cells inside the solid and the finest just outside the surface; sphere diameter not printed. [BAS-03 p.32 · MODELED · slide, ~fig]
Interface energy balance: λg(∂T/∂n)g = λs(∂T/∂n)s + ṁL + εσTs^4 (g and s are the gas and solid sides; ṁ, L, ε, σ, Ts and n are not defined on the slide; units not given); Φ = (λs ∂T/∂n|s)/(λg ∂T/∂n|g), heat flux into the solid over heat flux from the gas, dimensionless, no value printed; Φ closes the quasi-steady gas-phase description, is taken as uniform (independent of angle) and is treated as a parameter for successive quasi-static gas-phase flames; boundaries: uniform inlet upstream (left), symmetry on the top edge (the bottom edge either side of the half-sphere drawn in the same colour), zero gradient at the outlet (right). [BAS-03 p.46 · MODELED · slide, nominal]
A large Φ means more heat loss from the gas phase to the solid. [BAS-03 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

[BAS-03 p.53 · MEASURED · slide, ~fig]

[BAS-03 p.53 · MEASURED · slide, ~fig, single-test]
PMMA sphere burning in 17 % O2 with occasional vapor jetting (closing photo; diluent, pressure, diameter, flow, ignition and duration not stated, nor whether it is the p.52 burn). [BAS-03 p.58 · MEASURED · slide]
In the summary, as flow speed changes the flame responds with almost no delay; at the lowest speeds examined (below 1 cm/s) all flames tended to become dim blue and very stable; at moderate speeds (about 1 to 5 cm/s) the flame grows stronger and more luminous as time goes on (C12; materials, O2 and pressure not given in these bullets). [BAS-03 p.54–55 · MEASURED · slide]
The authors find microgravity flames especially sensitive to air flow speed between 0 and 5 cm/s and explain the quick response by a gas phase much faster than the solid; below 1 cm/s heat loss at these very low convective rates is small, so the flames can burn a long time; at about 1 to 5 cm/s the flame keeps heating the solid, raising its temperature and vaporization rate. [BAS-03 p.54–55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
Extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible at the given flow rate (rate not printed; sample, O2, pressure and air speed not given in this bullet). [BAS-03 p.55 · MEASURED · slide]
The smallest flames burning acrylic slabs still burned for over 5 min before self-extinguishing (slab size and thickness, O2, pressure and air speed not given). [BAS-03 p.55 · MEASURED · slide]
The authors conclude that thicker solids can store much heat even with a small flame, and that only the smallest flames on acrylic slabs appeared hindered by solid conductive heat loss. [BAS-03 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
They draw a spacecraft fire-safety implication: a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time, and although not very hazardous while small, it might flare up if air convection suddenly increases or it spreads into another fuel. [BAS-03 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]


### BASS-II concurrent PMMA rods: campaign and procedures (BAS-04)
| Set | Material and form | Platform | Atmosphere | Flow | Ignition | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C13 | cast PMMA cylindrical rods, radius 0.318, 0.476 or 0.635 cm | BASS-II flow duct in the MSG aboard ISS | O2 lowered by diluting the MSG working volume with ISS nitrogen; plotted O2 is the post-burn (final) reading | concurrent, axial along the rod, set by a fan at the duct entrance | hot wire at the initially hemispherical stagnation tip | total pressure, ambient temperature | [BAS-04 p.1–4 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.6 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · nominal]

Twenty-four concurrent axial-flow flammability tests with cast PMMA rods of three diameters were run in the MSG in the ISS Destiny Lab, aimed at flammability limits as a function of oxygen and flow speed (C13). [BAS-04 p.1–2 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.9 · MEASURED]
Of these rods 22 were clear and 2 black (C13). [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
No obvious difference between clear and black rods had been noted to date (C13). [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED]
The rod tests aimed to map the lower part of the concurrent microgravity flammability map against ventilation flow and ambient O2; the three primary variables were working-volume O2, duct flow velocity and rod diameter. [BAS-04 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
Seventeen clear cast PMMA rods were burned in concurrent flow: 11 of 1/4", 4 of 3/8" and 2 of 1/2" diameter. [BAS-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
Radii tested: R = 1/8" (0.318 cm), 3/16" (0.476 cm) and 1/4" (0.635 cm) (Fig. 2 caption). [BAS-04 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal]
Ignition (C13): the astronaut ignited each rod by hand at the initially hemispherical stagnation tip with a Kanthal A-1 29-gauge hot wire (nominal resistance 0.8–1 Ω, about 3.5–3.8 A), and the flame was left to develop and heat the rod axially at a flow high enough to sustain burning. [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
Working-volume O2 ran from ambient ISS levels (~21 %) down to ~14 % for very near-limit flames and was measured before and after each test with the on-board CSA-CP; duct flow was varied by fan voltage and measured with a hot-wire anemometer (C13). [BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.9 · MEASURED]
The time to develop the solid thermal profile is estimated from a Fourier number Fo = αt/R² ~ 0.3 (BAS-04 ref. [17]), with α = thermal diffusivity (PMMA 1.2 × 10^-3 cm2/s), t = time (s), R = rod radius (cm); fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.4 · MODELED]
For the radii tested this gives 25 s to 100 s (C13). [BAS-04 p.4 · MODELED]
Quenching tests (C13): the flow was turned down in steps, the flame being left to stabilise at each new flow for at least the solid-phase response time. [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]
Quenching occurred once forced flow and/or O2 were weak enough that the flame could no longer supply enough heat flux to offset the losses by conduction into the rod and by radiation (C13). [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
Quench-test burns lasted up to 28 min (C13). [BAS-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
Fig. 2 shows one near-quench flame per rod size, each the lowest-O2 test for that size; their flows and O2 differ and are not given. [BAS-04 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED]
Blowoff tests (C13): the astronaut quickly turned the flow up until the flame went out. [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]
The blowoff flow is defined as the fan-voltage reading at the moment the stagnation region opened and the flame moved downstream. [BAS-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The annular flame oscillated upstream and downstream several times before blowing off completely (C13). [BAS-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
Later in the programme the crew tried to re-establish the stagnation flame after a local blowoff by quickly cutting the flow below the blowoff velocity (C13). [BAS-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
It worked once, perhaps because the stagnation region had not fully blown off (opening less than a thermal length, perhaps) thanks to the astronaut's quick response; the O2, flow and rod size of that case are not given; an attempt shortly after failed (C13). [BAS-04 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
The authors infer that once blown downstream of the stagnation region the flame cannot propagate upstream at the low O2 levels tested (16.1 % O2 and lower) (C13). [BAS-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
They call this consistent with BASS-II opposed-flow flame spread tests on rods (BAS-04 ref. [18], Link, Fernandez-Pello, Olson and Ferkul, ASGSR 2014), where no spread was seen below 16.4 % O2 (rod material and size, pressure and flow not given). [BAS-04 p.5 · CITED; BAS-04 p.10 · CITED]
Fig. 3 shows blowoff images for the three rod sizes, each the lowest-O2 test for that size (flows and O2 not given); the tip starts hemispherical and becomes slightly tapered and round-nosed as it burns (Figs. 2 and 3). [BAS-04 p.5 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.7 · MEASURED]
No ISS blowoff test was obtained with the 0.476-cm rod; the centre image of Fig. 3 is a 5.18-s drop test ("Zero Gravity Research Center" in the caption) in which the flame blew off during the drop, the rod lit by a green LED. [BAS-04 p.5 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
Drop tests: complementary 5.18-s Zero Gravity Facility drops with the microgravity wind tunnel drop rig (BAS-04 ref. [19]) compared blowoff limits in short- and long-duration microgravity; the rod was lit in normal gravity and burned briefly at a flammable O2 flow to preheat, then the gas was switched to the test atmosphere and the package released according to the gas's travel time to the flame zone. [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-04 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]
Drop-tower blowoff flames were significantly smaller than the ISS flames (Fig. 3). [BAS-04 p.5 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
The authors attribute this most likely to the short burn before blowoff, which left the rod little preheated. [BAS-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The authors see bulk burning by tip regression as the likely near-limit flame geometry for axial concurrent flow along any rod, and proposed it as a simple axisymmetric geometry with minimal heat losses (surface radiation, axial conduction, no holder losses) for studying material flammability, the heat loss being varied through rod diameter, which changes the in-depth conduction term of the surface energy balance. [BAS-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
Earlier rod work cited by BAS-04: Tarifa and colleagues [9], in parabolic-flight and sounding-rocket opposed-flow spread tests on hollow rods, found extinction strongly dependent on both O2 and flow velocity, with quenching at low flows of the order of diffusive velocities; on the Mir station's Skorost hardware [14], extruded PMMA, Delrin and high-density polyethylene rods in concurrent flow all melted beneath the flame into growing molten balls at the stagnation end, wrapped by the flame, and at low flow the small tip flame advanced by rod regression (bulk burning) rather than by spread along the rod (material, O2, pressure, flow and diameter values not given). [BAS-04 p.2 · CITED]

### Interpretation: Damkohler number, the two branches and flame stretch (BAS-04)
Da_crit = [flow time/reaction time]_crit ~ [reaction rate/flow rate]_crit ~ [A_g (ρ_g Y_f)(ρ_g Y_ox) e^(−E_g/RT_g) / a]_crit, with Y_f fuel concentration, Y_ox oxygen concentration and a stretch rate (s-1, a = af + acurv on p.7); A_g, ρ_g, E_g, R and T_g are not defined; units not stated; fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.6–7 · MODELED]
The authors show the boundary as a critical Damkohler number, reaction rate divided by stretch rate, and say its distinctive shape in O2 and forced stretch rate correlates well with it. [BAS-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-04 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The blowoff branch of Fig. 4 is linear (Yox ~ a). [BAS-04 p.6 · Fig. 4 · MODELED]
The authors read the linear blowoff branch as showing a fairly constant critical temperature at blowoff: the dominant blowoff parameters are those in the Da_crit equation, so fuel concentration and critical temperature stay fairly constant in the flame zone, where reactants pass too fast to react; treating fuel and oxidizer as in continual ignition, the flame blows off once the flame-zone temperature falls below the critical ignition temperature; and the drop-tower agreement implies that the different rod preheat levels do not affect blowoff extinction. [BAS-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-04 p.6–7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-04 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The authors propose that blowoff data might be extrapolated linearly to zero stretch, the O2 there serving as a conservative estimate of the minimum O2 at which the material burns, so that materials rated by normal-gravity flammability tests could be de-rated to ensure they will not burn in space; using the 13.3 % intercept instead of the 13.6 % minimum test point adds a slight margin of conservatism. [BAS-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
The quenching branch is fitted by the red dashed exponential (Quench: 7 exp(-0.8x) + 13.3). [BAS-04 p.6–7 · Fig. 4 · MODELED]
On the linear stretch axis of Fig. 4 the quenching branch is very steep (BASS-II ISS concurrent cast PMMA rods, final O2). [BAS-04 p.7 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.6 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED; BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED]
The authors read the exponential quench branch as dominance of the Arrhenius temperature term, expected at quenching where temperature falls sharply while flow time is plentiful: heat losses lower the flame temperature until the reaction rate slows to the critical Damkohler number. [BAS-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-04 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
Heat losses dominate in cooling the flame to extinction, as modelled in BAS-04 refs. [20, 21]. [BAS-04 p.7 · CITED]
The authors take flame stretch, a = af + acurv (flow-induced plus curvature-induced), as the flow parameter for comparing rod sizes; curvature-induced stretch is not negligible for these small rods at low flow, and the two are combined following an example for mixed convection (BAS-04 ref. [21]). [BAS-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
af = 3/2 U/R is the flow-induced stretch around the roughly spherical tip and acurv = [3U/R] × [(Rflame − R)/R] the curvature-induced stretch around the hemispherical flames, estimated for the small samples (U flow velocity, R rod radius in cm, Rflame flame radius; both in s-1); fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.7 · Table 1 · MODELED]
The flame-radius analysis at each limit is not complete, so Fig. 4 plots forced stretch rate with points marked by rod size, and the authors expect the points to shift right once curvature-induced stretch is included. [BAS-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
Table 1 estimates curvature-induced stretch from flame radii measured on Fig. 2, to show the size of the shift. [BAS-04 p.7 · Table 1 · MEASURED]

### Rod heat-conduction and surface energy-balance model (BAS-04)
For long burns the solid thermal profile away from the tip is taken as roughly steady, allowing a 1D axial profile: 0 = ρs cs Vr ∂Ts/∂y + λs ∂²Ts/∂y², conduction balanced by convection from the steady surface regression rate Vr, measured in the experiment (ρs, cs, λs solid density, specific heat and conductivity; Ts solid temperature; y axial coordinate); Vr is assumed so small that ΔL << L over the timeframe τ (L the characteristic rod length), so the profiles are quasi-steady; boundary conditions are Ts at y = 0 (a constant pyrolysis temperature) and T∞ at y = L; fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.7–8 · MODELED]
Non-dimensional form 0 = Pe ∂θs/∂Y + ∂²θs/∂Y², with Y = y/L, θ = (T − T∞)/(Ts − T∞), Pe = L Vr/αs, θ(0) = 1, θ(1) = 0; general solution C_1 e^(−PeY) + C_2 (roots 0 and −Pe), giving θ(Y) = [exp(−PeY) − exp(−Pe)]/[1 − exp(−Pe)] and the surface gradient dθ/dY at Y = 0 = Pe/(exp(−Pe) − 1), used to get the conductive loss down the rod and the flame heat flux as functions of Pe; fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.8 · MODELED]
Pe is a solid-phase Peclet number, the ratio of heat convected as the fuel regresses to heat conducted from the hot surface; for Pe > 1 the profile is strongly exponential, heat conducted along the rod being carried back toward the burning tip so it cannot penetrate deeply, while for Pe ≤ 1 conduction dominates and the profiles are nearly linear. [BAS-04 p.8 · MODELED]
Counter-intuitively, in this steady state the slowest-burning samples lose the least heat into the solid, as noted before (BAS-04 ref. [23]). [BAS-04 p.8 · CITED]
Tip energy balance: q"flame = λg ∂Tg/∂x|s + q"rad = λs ∂Tsolid/∂x|s + ṁ" Lvap + εσ(Ts⁴ − T∞⁴), the left side being the net flame heat flux including gas-phase conduction and gas radiation; inputs Lvap = 1700 J/g, ṁ" = Vr ρ, ε = 0.85, Ts = 300 °C, λs = 2.09 × 10^-3 W/cm K at 300 K, λg = 5.77 × 10^-4 W/cm K at 800 K, ρ = 1.19 g/cc, L = 5.9 cm, σ = 5.729 × 10^-12 W/cm2 K4 (as printed); each term is evaluated against Pe in Fig. 5, the surface radiative loss being held constant; fitted range not stated. [BAS-04 p.8–9 · MODELED · nominal]
Burning rate has been shown to fall nearly linearly with stretch rate until very near the quench or blowoff limit (BAS-04 ref. [17]), so Pe ~ a. [BAS-04 p.8 · CITED]
Model trends: as Pe falls (the regression rate falls as forced stretch falls), solid conduction falls, the energy left for vaporization falls and the net flame heat flux drops precipitously; normalised by the net flame heat flux (right axis of Fig. 5), the radiative loss ratio rises steeply because surface radiation stays constant while flame heat flux falls linearly with Pe, the conduction ratio falls and the combined loss ratio rises at low Pe. [BAS-04 p.8–9 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]
Fig. 5 axes and series: Peclet number 0 to 20; heat flux 0 to 12 W/cm2 (left) and ratios 0.0 to 0.9 (right); net flame heat flux, energy to vaporize fuel, solid conduction, surface radiative loss, (Cond+Rad)/Net Flux, Vaporization/Net Flux, Conduction/Net Flux, Rad/Net Flux. [BAS-04 p.9 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]

A flame is expected to quench when the combined losses exceed about 70 % of the net flame heat flux (BAS-04 refs. [24, 25]). [BAS-04 p.9 · CITED]
Model conclusion: as regression rate falls (Pe and a fall) the losses grow in relative importance until the flame quenches; near the limit the surface radiative loss exceeds the conductive loss into the rod, and the drop in net flame heat flux at low stretch drives quenching even though the losses themselves decrease slightly. [BAS-04 p.1 · MODELED; BAS-04 p.9–10 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]
The authors name the main cause of quenching as the reduced net heat flux from the flame compared with the ongoing losses. [BAS-04 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4
# BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4 — SIBAL fabric flames on ISS (BASS / BASS-II), PSI BASS records and as-run test matrices

## Scope
Covers: seven documents. BAS-05, the BASS / BASS-II concurrent-flow paper on SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric (flame development, steady spread, quenching sequence, flammability map, Appendix test summary). BAS-07, the 2012 BASS slide deck on the same fabric in opposed and concurrent flow (hardware, runs, spread rate vs flow, 0-g vs 1-g flames, model backup). OVR-13 p.19 only, its cited ISS SIBAL quenching-boundary plot. PSC-01, the PSI records PSI-25 (BASS-II), PSI-26 (BASS) and PSI-62 (ground modelling on BASS imagery). PSD-01, the BASS as-run test matrix spreadsheet; PSD-02, the BASS-II test matrix by PI; PSD-03, the BASS-II data FAQ. The per-test rows of the BAS-05 Appendix and of the PSD-01 / PSD-02 matrices are in the tests table (tables/tests.csv); this file holds what the spans say about them.
Not here: the BAS-01 summary report (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1, BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_2 and, for its appendices, BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_3); BAS-03 and BAS-04 (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_3); the rest of OVR-13 and general Test 1-vs-space statements (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2); identity and conditions of the other PSI records (see PSI_CATALOGUE); Saffire (see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1, LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2); SoFIE and Confined Combustion (see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1, NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2).

## Findings
### SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow on ISS: BASS and BASS-II (BAS-05; OVR-13 cited plot)

#### Campaign and sample
- BASS and BASS-II burned thermally thin and thermally thick solid fuels aboard ISS in concurrent, opposed or stagnation flow in a small flow duct. [BAS-05 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
- BAS-05 covers flame growth, steady spread and quenching extinction of the thin SIBAL fabric at several O2 levels and concurrent flow speeds (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.1–2 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-05 p.8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The fabric takes its name from the earlier project SIBAL, for which it was custom-made. [BAS-05 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Other SIBAL fabric studies are the paper's refs. [8], [9] and [10]. [BAS-05 p.2 · CITED]
- The fiberglass mesh keeps the sample intact after the cotton cellulose has burned: it neither cracks nor leaves the curly ash typical of pure cellulose samples such as paper or cloth. [BAS-05 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 1 shows the small flow duct (fan section at the flow inlet, top window, side window, flow exit) and the cotton-fiberglass sample, labelled 2.2 cm wide, on its holder with the igniter at the leading edge. [BAS-05 p.2 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two cameras recorded flame growth: a side-view video camera giving edge-on images at 29.97 frames per second, and a top-view digital still camera at about one image every 1.2 s with exposures of 1/8 s–1/4 s, long enough for dim flames right before quenching. [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At low flow speed and low O2 the flame turned very dim blue and was hard to see on the side-view camera (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that the stills give a time history of quenching that can be compared with transient model results. [BAS-05 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BASS-II ran 27 fabric tests (6 quenching, 3 not ignited, 1 blow-off), listed in the paper's Appendix table; four BASS tests, all at 21 % O2 with a fixed flow during each test, are listed at its bottom. [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED]
- For tests with flow changes, the Appendix velocity column gives the starting and final velocities. [BAS-05 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The rate of flow change varied from test to test, set by crew–ground communication and the crew's manual adjustment time; many of these tests served to find the low-speed quenching limits versus O2 (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Samples whose flame quenched quickly or that did not ignite were reused in further tests, re-ignited by a retractable igniter on one side of the sample at the burnout position. [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors leave these reused samples out of the discussion: their unburned length was generally short and they gave less quantitative data. [BAS-05 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The Appendix table, "Test summary of flat SIBAL fabrics in concurrent flow in BASS and BASS II", has 31 test rows in three groups: 19 rows (GMT45-T1 to GMT190-T22), 8 rows whose comments begin "Reused" (GMT190-T23 to GMT216-T29) and 4 rows commented "BASS" (GMT96-T8, GMT96-T7, GMT131-T10, GMT222-T11); columns Test No., Sample width (cm) (2.2 or 1.2), Flow (cm/s) (one value, or start→final), O2 % by Vol. and Comments (Quenched; No Blow-off; No ignition; Blow-off; Reused, did not ignite; Reused, one sided flame; Reused, ignited; BASS; or blank); conditions C1. [BAS-05 p.9 · MEASURED]
- A footnote marks the O2 reading "18.5*" of tests GMT45-T1 (2.2 cm, 10 cm/s) and GMT45-T2 (2.2 cm, 10→5 cm/s) as possibly inaccurate (conditions C1; tests table BASS-II:T1, BASS-II:T2). [BAS-05 p.9 · MEASURED]

#### Background stated in the paper
- Flame spread and extinction over condensed fuels in microgravity have been studied widely for crew fire safety (refs. [1–4]); without buoyancy-induced flow, microgravity diffusion flames allow the mechanisms of low-speed quenching to be studied (ref. [5]); the move from spreading to quenching extinction is a slow heat-loss process in which radiative and conductive losses grow relative to heat generation (ref. [3]). [BAS-05 p.1 · CITED]
- The authors call these long-duration ISS tests a rare opportunity for solid-fuel combustion, since ground facilities generally cannot give enough microgravity time. [BAS-05 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-05 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In concurrent flow a thin sample's flame spreads much faster and can grow quite long, so on a short sample it may not reach fully steady spread; the transient ignition and growth history is still useful for transient flame models (ref. [6]). [BAS-05 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors note that setting O2 by N2 dilution helps determine a material's O2–flow velocity flammability boundary. [BAS-05 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Flame development at 21 % O2 (Figs. 2 and 3)
- A small flame at low flow let the whole history be seen: ignition, growth, steady spread (in some cases) and decay at the sample end (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.1 · MEASURED]
- After the igniter came on, a strong flame formed on both sides of the fuel, stabilized, grew and moved downstream (conditions C1; 2.2 cm wide, 21 % O2, 10 cm/s). [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- During steady spread the images look almost identical (20.17 s and 24.83 s in Fig. 2b); the flame then decays in size as its tip, more precisely its preheating front, nears the sample end, until complete burnout (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 21 % O2, 10 cm/s). [BAS-05 p.3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Fig. 2 (flow right to left) gives side-view tracking of flame tip, flame base and flame length (2a: flame position, mm, linear 0–110, vs time, s, linear 0–40, with stage lines "ignition", "growth", "steady spread", "decay") and edge-view frames at t = 0.52, 1.03, 3.62, 5.69, 10.86, 20.17, 24.83 and 36.20 s: flame on both sides of the edge-on sample early, then an elongated flame moving downstream (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 21 % O2, 10 cm/s). [BAS-05 p.3–4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · single-test]
- At 5 cm/s the side-view flame is very dim, so Fig. 3 tracks it from top-view images (3a: same axes and stages, time 0–60 s); frames at t = 6, 14.6, 35.59, 45.59 and 59.842 s show a rounded flame moving right to left, the 35.59 s and 45.59 s images are virtually identical, and bright spots appear behind the flame base as it passes (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 21 % O2, 5 cm/s). [BAS-05 p.4–5 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors attribute the bright spots to smouldering of a small amount of fuel that the flame did not fully consume. [BAS-05 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Compared with 10 cm/s, the 5 cm/s flame is shorter and spreads more slowly (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 21 % O2). [BAS-05 p.4 · MEASURED]
- The authors relate the longer total burn at 5 cm/s to the lower flow speed. [BAS-05 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Steady spread rate versus flow, O2 and width (Fig. 4)
- Steady flame spread here means the flame held a constant spread rate for more than 20 s. [BAS-05 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 4 ("Steady flame spread rate for both 2.2-cm and 1.2-cm wide samples") plots Vf (mm/s, linear 0.0–3.5) against U0 (cm/s, log, labelled 2 to 20), one series per width and O2, each point labelled with its O2; in some tests the flow was varied during the test (conditions C1). Reads below carry ±0.125 mm/s in Vf and ±0.25 cm/s in U0. [BAS-05 p.5 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED]
- Flames spread more slowly over the narrower samples, at lower flow velocity and at lower O2 (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.5 · MEASURED]

#### Quenching sequence by flow reduction at 18.7 % O2 (Figs. 5 and 6)
- In this typical BASS-II quenching sequence a 2.2 cm sample in 18.7 % O2 was ignited at 10 cm/s, the flow was lowered in steps after ignition, and after 25 s it was held at 2.2 cm/s for the rest of the test (conditions C1; tests table BASS-II:T4). [BAS-05 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]
- As the flow fell, flame length and width fell with it; at 2.2 cm/s both kept shrinking toward a circular blue flame seen from the top, until extinction (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 18.7 % O2). [BAS-05 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors call this typical of quenching extinction: as the limit nears, pyrolysis rate and heat release rate (HRR) drop, radiation loss becomes a significant fraction of the shrinking flame's HRR, and once the flame is small enough conduction adds to the loss. [BAS-05 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The post-burn photo shows the burnt region narrowing as the flame shrank toward extinction, with much of the fuel left unburnt along both sides of the holder (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 18.7 % O2). [BAS-05 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Fig. 5 top-view frames (flow right to left): t = 6.7 s at 8 cm/s, 15.7 s at 4 cm/s, then 25.8, 29.2, 32.6, 45.0 and 54.0 s at 2.2 cm/s; the flame goes from large and rounded to small and circular and shrinks frame by frame, and the post-burn photo shows the burnt region narrowing toward the downstream end (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 18.7 % O2, ignited at 10 cm/s). [BAS-05 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Fig. 6 plots top-view flame tracking (mm, linear, labelled 0–50; series Flame Tip, Flame Base, Flame Length) and U0 (cm/s, right axis, labelled 1–11) against time (s, 0–60); reads, ±2.5 s and ±2.5 mm: U0 at 10 cm/s until ~4 s, then lowered stepwise; flame length peak ~14 mm at ~10 s; flame base minimum ~-3.5 mm at ~2 s (10 cm/s); tracking ends at ~54 s with tip ~43.5 mm, base ~37 mm and length ~7 mm (2.2 cm/s), while U0 continues at its final value to 60 s (conditions C1; 2.2 cm, 18.7 % O2). [BAS-05 p.6 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test]
- The quenching sequence resembles that in opposed flow, where the flame also becomes circular (ref. [2]). [BAS-05 p.5–6 · CITED]
- The authors take the circular shape to show that three-dimensional heat and mass transfer matter near the limit. [BAS-05 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Quenching boundary and flammability map (Fig. 7; OVR-13 p.19)
- Low-speed quenching extinction limits versus O2 were found by lowering the flow during some tests (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Quenching speeds were between 1 and 5 cm/s, higher at lower O2 (conditions C1; tested O2 range 21 % to 16 %). [BAS-05 p.1 · MEASURED; BAS-05 p.7 · MEASURED; BAS-05 p.8 · MEASURED]
- BASS-II achieved six SIBAL quenching cases, four of them on 2.2 cm samples; with the near-limit stable flames they trace part of the quenching branch of the 2.2 cm flammability boundary in Fig. 7 (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors note that, for this thin fabric in concurrent flow, spread is relatively fast and the sample is too short to fine-tune the flow during the one to two minutes of a run. [BAS-05 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Reaching the near-quenching-limit state every time was difficult (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Very near the boundary, ignition of the sample is sporadic (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.7 · MEASURED]
- With few tests, the quenching limit of the 1.2 cm sample was not resolved, but the narrow sample has a smaller flammable domain, as expected (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors expect the lowest-O2 part of the boundary to be flat in Fig. 7, but say the velocity-varying procedure cannot fix it accurately and a procedure with gradually decreasing O2 is needed. [BAS-05 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the authors' view the shape and trend of the quenching boundary support the predictions of earlier theoretical models (refs. [1, 8]). [BAS-05 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-05 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BAS-05 calls this the first clean and unambiguous determination of a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread. [BAS-05 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 7 (caption: flammability map for SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow in microgravity; the dotted line marks the experimental quenching boundary of the 2.2 cm sample) plots O2 % by volume (linear, labelled 16.2 to 19.0 every 0.2) against U0 (cm/s, log, 1 to 100) with the markers "2.2cm spread", "2.2cm quench", "2.2cm not ignited", "1.2cm spread", "1.2cm quench" and "1.2cm blowoff"; the boundary is drawn as a dashed dark-blue line (conditions C1). Reads carry ±0.1 % O2 and ±0.5 cm/s below 10 cm/s, ±5 cm/s above. [BAS-05 p.7 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED]
- OVR-13 shows the flammability boundary of SIBAL fabric from the ISS experiments, taken from Zhao, Liao, Johnston, T'ien, Ferkul and Olson, Proc. Comb. Inst. 36 (2017): O2 % by volume (linear, 16.0 to 19.5) against U0 (cm/s, log, 1 to about 60), the same six experimental series plus "2.2cm spread (model)" and "2.2cm quench (model)", with the 2.2 cm quenching boundary drawn solid for the experiment and dashed for the computation (conditions C2). Reads carry ±0.25 % O2 and a factor 1.1 in U0. [OVR-13 p.19 · CITED · slide]

#### Conclusions of BAS-05
- Lowering the flow during tests gave accurate quenching extinction limits; an accurate determination of the quenching velocities is needed to resolve the slope of the boundary; and the data support, at least qualitatively, earlier predictions of low-flow solid flammability limits caused by radiative and conductive losses. [BAS-05 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At quenching the flame shrinks in both length and width and goes out in a three-dimensional manner (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.8 · MEASURED]
- Besides the quenching limits, the full sequence of ignition, flame growth, steady spread and final decay across the whole sample in low-speed purely forced flow was recorded (conditions C1). [BAS-05 p.8 · MEASURED]
- The authors see these records as precious data for understanding flame development in microgravity and as a basis to check theoretical model development. [BAS-05 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A recently published three-dimensional transient numerical model (ref. [6]), containing many material properties including kinetic rate constants, is suited to simulate this experiment. [BAS-05 p.8 · CITED]
- The authors were measuring and deducing SIBAL pyrolysis rate constants to compare model and experiment quantitatively. [BAS-05 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### SIBAL fabric in opposed and concurrent flow on ISS, and 0-g vs 1-g flames (BAS-07, 2012 BASS slides)
| Set | Material and form | Platform, gravity | Flow | Ignition, enclosure | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | "SIBAL" fabric: 25 % fiberglass / 75 % cotton blend, cotton and fiberglass fibres intermingled, simple weave of 60 × 40 threads per inch, overall area density 18 mg/cm2; flat samples 8.5 cm long, 1 or 2 cm wide (bagged holders labelled "1 cm Flat Sample", P/N S1183MFA1025, and "2 cm Flat Sample", P/N S1183MFA1020, as read from the photo) | ISS, microgravity; BASS hardware, i.e. the on-orbit SPICE hardware with minor modifications for solids, its small wind tunnel installed in the MSG, which supplied power, imaging and a level of containment | small wind tunnel imposing airflow up to 40 cm/s | igniter coil | O2, diluent, total pressure, ambient temperature (in the pages read) | [BAS-07 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal, slide; BAS-07 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal, slide; BAS-07 p.17–18 · MEASURED · nominal, slide] |

#### Background and hypothesis
- Numerical models predict that 1-g buoyant flows profoundly affect fuel flammability, microgravity tests on thin fuels have verified this, and ground facilities are too short for thicker fuels (no references on the slide). [BAS-07 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Flow below 30 cm/s is the range of interest. [BAS-07 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]
- A schematic "Typical Flammability Boundary for a Solid Fuel" (no material, thickness, pressure, diluent or data source stated) plots O2 mole fraction (0.15 to 0.23) against flow speed (cm/s, log, 1 to 300): a U-shaped boundary with "Flammable" inside and above it and "Not Flammable" below, and a red vertical "1-g buoyant flow limit" line with a hatched band on its low-flow side. [BAS-07 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Reads from that schematic (±0.005 in O2 mole fraction, a factor ~3.2 in flow; conditions not stated): boundary minimum ~0.171 at ~6.5 cm/s; "1-g buoyant flow limit" line at ~50 cm/s, its hatched band starting at ~38 cm/s; the line crosses the high-flow branch at ~0.205; the low-flow branch reaches 0.21 at ~1.7 cm/s. [BAS-07 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ~fig, slide]
- Hypothesis: with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity may burn more readily than in normal gravity, other conditions (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature) being identical. [BAS-07 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Testing at constant O2 mole fraction, drawn as a dashed line at 0.21 across the same schematic (flow 1 to 100 cm/s, log), allows flame spread and extinction to be studied at low and high flow speed. [BAS-07 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]

#### Approach, applications and model
- Airflow effects on flame appearance, flame growth and spread rate were determined in both opposed and concurrent flow (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.4 · MEASURED · slide]
- Stated science applications: understanding long-duration microgravity burning and extinction of solids; better NASA spacecraft materials selection, linking actual microgravity burning to Earth-based selection methods; better computational models for designing fire detection and suppression in microgravity and on Earth; and models validated in the simpler flow of microgravity as the base for the more complex models that normal-gravity flames need, widely applicable to terrestrial combustion problems. [BAS-07 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Flame-spread model domain (no caption, also shown on p.39): a computational box with a centerline plane of symmetry, an inert strip beside the fresh solid fuel, incoming flow U∞ and flame spread velocity VF (both cm/s), X about -5 to 15 cm, Y 0 to 5 cm, Z 0 to 4 cm; model flow speed, O2, pressure and fuel not reported in the pages read. [BAS-07 p.5 · MODELED · nominal, slide; BAS-07 p.39 · MODELED · nominal, slide]
- Model field in the plane Y = 0.23 cm (X -3 to 6 cm, Z 0 to 4 cm; also on p.39): velocity vectors (reference 5 cm/s), O2 mass flux vectors (reference 1.375 x 10^-3 g/cm^2/s), a dashed reaction contour at 10^-5 g/cm^3/s, streamlines ψ = 0 to 10 and temperature contours T = 2, 2.5, 2.8, 3, 4, 4.2 (T units not printed; model conditions not reported in the pages read). [BAS-07 p.5 · MODELED · slide; BAS-07 p.39 · MODELED · slide]
- Model centerline temperature contours T = 2, 3, 4, 5 with "Tmax = 5.06" (units not printed); the T = 2 contour reaches ~9.4 cm in X and ~1.95 cm in Y, read ±0.5 cm (model flow speed, O2, pressure and fuel not reported in the pages read). [BAS-07 p.39 · MODELED · ~fig, slide]

#### Hardware and operation
- Photos: the ISS, a crew member at the glovebox, the flow-duct hardware with a sample and a flame; the MSG with labelled International Standard Payload Rack, Control and Monitoring Panel, working volume (255 liters), Stowage Drawer, Video drawer, Utility Interface Panel, Remote Power Distribution Assembly and Foot restraint, and a "BASS flame visible through viewport"; and a fish-eye view inside the MSG showing the flow duct and a camera. [BAS-07 p.6–8 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Samples mounted through the duct's top window, with counts as printed (not to scale; can be flipped 180 degrees): thin flat (17), spheres (12), thick flat (4), candles (8). [BAS-07 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Operation schematic: airflow enters one end of the duct; the flat sample hangs from the top window inside the duct, parallel to the airflow; the igniter coil sits at the sample end facing the incoming airflow. [BAS-07 p.10–12 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Operation schematic, continued: a flame forms at the upstream end, spreads downstream leaving burnt fuel, grows when the flow is raised, and goes out when the flow is reduced too far or the fuel is consumed. [BAS-07 p.13–16 · MEASURED · slide]
- Solid samples were installed, ignited, extinguished and recorded; video and a digital still camera gave most of the data (flame appearance, behaviour, spread rate, extinction dynamics); airflow speed was the main variable. [BAS-07 p.17 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Sample images, airflow upward: the still shows a bright orange flame with glowing particles at its base, the video frame a dim flame, with overlay "FUEL -2 AIR 10 FAN 66 RAD 4.1[last digit cut off] 03/31/12 11:19:16" (overlay fields not defined; material, width and O2 not stated on this slide). [BAS-07 p.17 · MEASURED · slide, single-test]

- Edge-view video of a 2 cm wide sample in concurrent flow, ignited at 10 cm/s with the flow then reduced to 5 cm/s; overlay "FUEL -1 AIR 10 FAN 66 RAD 0.0[6 or 8] 03/31/12 11:18:56" (conditions C3; tests table BASS:1). [BAS-07 p.19–20 · MEASURED · nominal, slide, single-test]
- Top views of the 2 cm sample in concurrent flow: at 10 cm/s the flame reaches further downstream and is brighter orange; at 5 cm/s it is shorter, with more blue-violet at its edges; glowing spots sit on the burnt fabric upstream of both flames (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.21 · MEASURED · slide]
- 1 cm wide sample, concurrent airflow 10 cm/s: stills every 1.125 s (scale bar 1 cm) show the flame steady after about 10 s; in the last images the flame is gone and only small glowing spots remain (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.22 · MEASURED · nominal, slide, single-test]
- Linear fits printed on the p.23 plot (1 cm wide, 10 cm/s concurrent, conditions C3): x_tip = 1.71 t + 2.25 and x_base = 1.68 t - 13.81 (x in mm, t in s, from the axis labels); fitted range not stated, the fit lines drawn over ~12 to ~45 s and ~18 to ~45 s. #### Opposed-flow runs (slides 25 to 27)
- 2 cm wide sample, opposed airflow 10 cm/s: stills every 1.25 s (scale bar 2 cm; the first frame bright orange, the second a glowing wavy line at the sample's top end) show the flame quickly reaching steady state and going out when it runs out of fuel (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.24–25 · MEASURED · slide, single-test]
- 2 cm wide sample, opposed flow cut in discrete steps of 10, 6, 4, 2, 1.5 and 1 cm/s (labels at frame 1 and ~18 of row 1, ~9 and ~20 of row 2, ~9 and ~19 of row 3; three rows of ~23 frames, stills every 1.25 s): the flame responds very rapidly, the flow effects on flame and spread rate are dramatic, and the total burn time is 90 s (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.26 · MEASURED · nominal, slide, single-test]
- In that stepped sequence the flame gets smaller and bluer as the flow drops, and the last frames after the 1 cm/s label show a small red, then orange, spot; the slide does not state how the flame ended (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.26 · MEASURED · slide, single-test]
- Video of a 2 cm wide sample in opposed flow with blowoff attempted at high flow (~44 cm/s); overlay "FUEL -2 AIR 10 FAN 51 RAD 0.12 07/20/12 09:16:53"; the outcome is not stated on the slide (conditions C3; tests table BASS:55). [BAS-07 p.27 · MEASURED · nominal, slide, single-test]

#### Summary slide (p.33)
- Opposed flow: the flame quickly reached steady spread at each flow speed, and spread was fastest at an intermediate flow speed (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.33 · MEASURED · slide]
- Concurrent flow: a limiting length and steady spread rate were reached only at low flow speeds (not quantified on the slide), where spread rate rose linearly with flow (conditions C3). [BAS-07 p.33 · MEASURED · slide]
- Lowering the concurrent flow to a very low value, around 1 cm/s, gave quenching extinction (conditions C3; width not stated on this slide). [BAS-07 p.33 · MEASURED · slide]
- The authors: these tests show enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry; they are the first detailed transient flame-growth data in purely forced flow in microgravity; and the long-duration results validate a number of theoretical predictions (not named) and supply data for a transient flame-growth model under development. [BAS-07 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

#### Shared hypothesis (PSI-25 and PSI-26)
- Both records state the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well as, if not better than, the same material in normal gravity, other conditions (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature) being identical; no values and no material are given for it. [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### PSI-25 BASS-II: objectives, hypothesis notes, approach, impacts
- BASS-II results contribute to the combustion models used to design fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. [PSC-01 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Objectives: (1) study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity; (2) begin to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity; (3) give SoFIE PIs preliminary data to refine science requirements; (4) examine practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries, including slabs, cylinders and spherical sections. [PSC-01 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Primary variables: forced flow velocity (speed and direction), ambient O2 (by N2 vitiation of the working volume) and sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films and fabric sheets). [PSC-01 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The record adds that NASA tests and controls materials with an upward-burning test in normal gravity, considered the worst-case geometry for flammability on Earth, which may not be conservative in space. [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Testing at constant O2 mole fractions allows spread and extinction to be studied at low and high flow speed, with the aim of finding the fundamental limit for a given material. [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Approach: microgravity combustion tests aboard ISS with active crew support for real-time "lab partner" operations; the wind tunnel was installed in the MSG, which supplied power, imaging and a level of containment; fuel samples were mounted in a small wind tunnel imposing airflow up to 40 cm/s; the main variables were airflow speed and O2 (varied below 21 % by adding N2); flame appearance, growth and spread rates were determined in both opposed and concurrent flow. [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Stated impacts: improved spacecraft fire safety and understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it, since a fire far from Earth can be catastrophic; helping engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods; and a simpler combustion process in space that lets researchers evaluate computer models of fuel burning, which can then be used to study flames on Earth more accurately, such as in wildfires, building fires and energy recapture from waste recycling. [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The record states that in space fuels burn as oval balls rather than with the upward-pointed cone flame seen on Earth (material, O2, pressure, flow and other conditions not stated for this statement). [PSC-01 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### PSI-26 BASS: objectives, approach, impacts
- Objective 1: begin to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual flammability in microgravity, by observing flames over the longer times available in flight and examining practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries, including wake flames that resemble a fire burning behind another object in a tight, hard-to-reach area. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Objective 2: assess how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent, similar to that used on ISS, puts out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Testing the hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials needs extended microgravity time, longer than drop towers or parabolic aircraft provide. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Approach: run aboard ISS inside the "Microgravity Glove Box" (MSG); custom-made fabric of 75 % cotton and 25 % fiberglass by mass (the word "measuring" is followed by no size), Nomex fabric and Ultem, plus spheres and cylinders; a 29-gage Kanthal wire igniter at one end of the fabric; airflow from a variable-speed fan up to 40 cm/s along the fuel surface, concurrent or opposed, in a small flow duct of 76 mm × 76 mm cross-section; flames watched in top and edge views for size, shape, colour, spread rate and possible quenching. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In concurrent flow the air moves in the direction of flame spread, in opposed flow against it. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Current NASA spacecraft materials selection rests on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which sorts materials by their 1-g behaviour without considering low-gravity effects. [PSC-01 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Further stated impacts: radiative heat emission from the flame is a critical element of this understanding; the results feed first-order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and a way to extend heat-release data from tests such as the NASA cone calorimeter (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2) to performance-based material selection; N2 as a flame suppressant in microgravity links directly to current and planned extinguishment; BASS results guide ground-based microgravity combustion research; and detailed combustion models validated in the simpler microgravity flow environment can then be used to build the more complex models needed for flames in normal gravity, with wide terrestrial use, guidance for novel spacecraft design and crew safety. [PSC-01 p.28–29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### PSI-62: UFGM modelling benchmarked on BASS and BASS-II
- Objective: develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modelling of concurrent flame spread in microgravity, through an unsteady FGM (UFGM) framework that reduces reacting systems to lower-dimensional manifolds, using BASS and BASS-II as benchmarks; long-term, accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and a subgrid-scale model for large-eddy simulation of fires. [PSC-01 p.37–38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The record calls concurrent flame spread one of the greatest modelling challenges in combustion science, because heat transfer, mass transport and chemical kinetics couple near the solid–vapour interface, and says traditional hybrid turbulence–chemistry models were not fully consistent and missed important intermediate reaction pathways. [PSC-01 p.37–38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Hypothesis: UFGM could reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including the "Goldilocks" flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass-transport and chemical processes with far-field flow (BASS geometries per the approach; O2, pressure, flow speed, ignition, thickness, ambient temperature and duration not reported in the pages read). [PSC-01 p.38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Approach: high-resolution modelling with experimental validation; an existing framework for fully coupled fluid–solid simulations of charring and ablating materials, with UFGM implemented and tested on BASS geometries (flat sheets, spheres and rods of PMMA, and wax cylinders); BASS and BASS-II imagery from PSI post-processed with new two-colour tomography from DSLR cameras into 3-D soot and temperature fields; metrics flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction and spread rate, with emphasis on the "Goldilocks" zone reported by Olson and Ferkul; and comparisons with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame-spread project across microgravity and normal gravity. [PSC-01 p.38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Stated impacts: predictive tools to screen new materials' flammability limits for safer spacecraft; large-eddy-simulation subgrid models expected to improve hazard assessment for long missions and confined habitats; better combustion modelling, fire-safety standards, prevention, mitigation, diagnostics and simulation on Earth; and safer human space exploration overall. [PSC-01 p.38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1
# CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1 — Cabin atmospheres and ISS hardware in the Exploration Atmospheres (NESC assessment, part 1)

## Scope
Covers: maximum and nominal cabin atmospheres of past, present and planned crewed vehicles (CAB-01 Table 1; CAB-02 Table 1 and the ISS control bands), why exploration cabins move to 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2 and 8.2 psia/34 % O2, and the first part of the NESC assessment of ISS crew-system hardware in those Exploration Atmospheres (CAB-02 sections 1–7.4.4, pages 10–79: scope and method, depth and confidence, impact ratings, cross-cutting effects on fans, heat rejection, acoustics, offgassing and material flammability, then each ECLSS, CHeCS and crew-system subsystem up to the ISS food warmer).
Not here: the rest of CAB-02 (sleeping bags, the Table 9 impact summary, findings, observations, NESC recommendations and the appendices with Table A-1 and the meeting notes), fire-resistant textiles for 37 % O2/8.2 psia (CAB-03), surface-vehicle atmospheres (CAB-04) and the OVR-03/OVR-13 cabin blocks (see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2); the Test 1 method and acceptance rules (see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1, MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2); how gravity shifts flammability limits (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2).

## Findings

### Cabin atmospheres of past, present and planned crewed vehicles
- CAB-01 (JSC 29353B) starts every flammability assessment by defining the maximum O2 concentration and its associated pressure in the use environment; its Table 1 gives these for crewed spacecraft in current NASA programs. [CAB-01 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

- Many of the CAB-01 test examples were tested at high O2 concentrations (levels not given in this statement). [CAB-01 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- CAB-01 expects O2 as high as 35 % (nominally 34 % at 8.2 psia) for the high-frequency EVA phases of future exploration missions and concludes that material flammability has to be evaluated at that higher concentration. [CAB-01 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
