[CAB-02 p.17 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On the ISS, where research into the physiological effects of microgravity is a primary objective, a cabin close to normal sea-level conditions is desirable so those effects are not mixed with atmospheric effects. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS was designed and is operated to approximate an Earth-equivalent 14.7 psia with 21 % O2; because EVA is infrequent there, the time-consuming prebreathe protocols are accepted as a consequence of serving its research objectives. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The ISS environmental control system holds the cabin within 13.9–15.2 psia and an O2 partial pressure of 2.83–3.35 psia, with a maximum allowable 24.1 vol% O2 (ref. 5: SSP 41000, System Specification for the ISS, Rev CD, 2014). [CAB-02 p.18 · CITED · nominal; CAB-02 p.91 · CITED · ctx]
- All other ISS on-board equipment was designed and certified to operate safely and meet its performance requirements within these ranges. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Why exploration cabins move to lower pressure and higher O2
- CAB-02 treats the cabin atmosphere as a choice made within human-physiology limits that carries substantial development, design and operational consequences; the two conditions most relevant to its assessment are total pressure and O2 content. [CAB-02 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O2 transfer in the lungs is driven by the alveolar O2 partial pressure, so a lower cabin total pressure must hold a higher O2 percentage to sustain a given O2 partial pressure (discussion in NASA/TP-2013-217377, ref. 3). [CAB-02 p.16 · CITED]
- Low cabin pressure helps EVA: suits must contain pressure yet stay mobile and dexterous, so they are designed and operated at low internal pressure (~4.3 psia) with high O2, historically 100 %, to avoid mixed-gas control in small volumes. [CAB-02 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Moving from a cabin of O2 plus a diluent such as N2 into a low-pressure suit risks decompression sickness: a large cabin-to-suit pressure difference needs complex, time-consuming prebreathe protocols to purge N2 from the lungs, while a small difference lets prebreathe be reduced and potentially eliminated. [CAB-02 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Raising O2 concentration to sustain O2 partial pressure at low total pressure increases material flammability, and the resulting shrinkage of the candidate-material list is described as a significant challenge for designing and operating a spacecraft. [CAB-02 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Lower cabin pressure lowers air density, which reduces the heat-carrying capacity of air and the efficiency of convective heat transfer, so air-cooling equipment gets harder; matching convective cooling needs higher air velocities from higher fan speeds, aerodynamic optimisation for low pressure, multiple fans, or a combination. [CAB-02 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Pressures referenced to the cabin through regulators, tank bellows or gauge sensors may shift, and leakage rates between systems and cabin may change enough to affect hazard potentials and controls, requiring design or operational changes; a lower internal operating pressure driven by the cabin may also change baseline performance (e.g. gas/liquid separators, the Sabatier Carbon Dioxide Reduction Assembly). [CAB-02 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Planned Exploration missions are not primarily about microgravity physiology research (it will likely continue as a secondary focus); transit missions are to carry crew safely and reliably to and from lunar and Martian vicinities, working in tandem with Gateway. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Lunar and Martian surface missions will by necessity involve frequent EVA, where prebreathe protocols are less acceptable operationally than on the ISS (ref. 3). [CAB-02 p.18 · CITED]
- Designing surface habitats to operate at cabin pressures low enough to reduce or eliminate prebreathe is named one of the most enabling means of frequent EVA. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For planning and for this assessment the atmospheres considered are 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2 and 8.2 psia/34 % O2; the ability of available hardware to control within these limits may force Exploration systems to be designed and certified at higher O2 concentrations. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### The NESC assessment: Exploration Atmospheres, scope and method
- The assessment (NESC-RP-20-01610) was requested by the project manager of the HEOMD Advanced Exploration Systems NextSTEP (Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships) Habitat Project to evaluate the safety, engineering, operational and programmatic risks of operating state-of-the-art (SOA) ECLSS hardware at reduced pressure and increased O2 in Exploration habitats and to propose mitigating recommendations; Gateway and Human Landing System (HLS) ECLSS system managers joined as liaisons to commercial providers (p.10 prints ECLSS as "Environmental Control and Life Systems"). [CAB-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Goal: identify and qualitatively characterise impacts on the performance, thermal control and material selection of ISS ECLS hardware used in cabin atmospheres with lower total pressure and higher O2 than those it was designed and certified for. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Nominal cabin atmospheres of 10.2 psia with 26.5 % O2 and 8.2 psia with 34 % O2 are together called "Exploration Atmospheres", to set them apart from the ISS nominal atmosphere. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because cabin O2 control is expected to be harder at the lower pressures, O2 concentrations up to 40 % were considered at 8.2 psia when assessing flammability. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, ctx]
- The two environments evaluated: 8.2 +0.2 psia with 34 +2 % O2 by volume (each "+" printed underlined, ±-like), based on NASA direction for Exploration (ref. 1, Gerstenmeier memo "Exploration Atmospheres", February 2013) and earlier high-EVA mission studies (ref. 2, NASA-TP-2010-216134, October 2010; ref. 3, Norcross et al., NASA-TM-2013-217377, June 2013, on the 8 psia/32 % O2 atmosphere); and 10.2 psia with 26.5 % O2 by volume, based on the Space Shuttle orbiter practice of moving the cabin from 14.7 psia/21.7 % O2 before EVA (ref. 4, Wieland, NASA-TM-2005-214007, July 2005). [CAB-02 p.15 · CITED · nominal; CAB-02 p.91 · CITED · ctx]
- The assessment sought the effects of Exploration cabin environments on ISS crew-serving hardware and how they change mass, power, volume and schedule planning for the NextSTEP Lunar Surface Habitat (LSH) and Exploration Command Module (ECM); Gateway, Mars transit and Mars surface missions are expected to benefit too. [CAB-02 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Reusing long-flown ISS systems in Exploration habitats limits reliability uncertainty, which can drive logistics costs (ref. 6), and avoids the high cost of bringing developmental systems to certifiable states. [CAB-02 p.18 · CITED]
- The complication is that ISS systems would have to operate in atmospheres they were not designed or certified for. [CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The assessment is therefore a first-order evaluation of reduced-pressure/increased-O2 impacts on ISS crew-supporting hardware from the ECLSS, the Crew Health Care System (CHeCS) and the habitation system: 33 subsystems and/or components, including emergency systems, evaluated from available design data and historical literature (list in Table 2). [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Six crew-serving systems were first identified (ECLS, intravehicular activity (IVA) and EVA hardware, crew health care hardware, crew habitation systems, shortened to "crew systems", and emergency equipment); ISS IVA/EVA hardware was left out because Exploration IVA and EVA hardware will be new designs with Exploration-compatibility requirements. [CAB-02 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Each item was evaluated in three impact categories: thermal (active and passive thermal control at lower pressure), performance (functional capability in the Exploration environments) and materials (increased flammability and offgassing of state-of-the-art (SOA) materials at the higher O2). [CAB-02 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.91 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- Excluded: effects on crew health, avionics, power systems, existing ISS science payloads, international partner hardware, vehicle structure, other hardware not directly supporting crew survivability, and developmental technologies not yet flown as flight experiments (ISS upgrades excepted). [CAB-02 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Five tasks: (1) compile the in-scope hardware list on ISS and the MPCV crew module (CM) with the ISS subsystem managers, prioritised by likely use in LSH or ECM missions and by impact; (2) gather specifications, schematics, hazard reports, critical-design-review, verification-and-validation and design-certification data; (3) review the documents by priority and availability; (4) analyse impacts with LSH/ECM consultants and estimate mass, volume, power and schedule effects; (5) write findings, observations and NESC recommendations. [CAB-02 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Impacts are expressed qualitatively on purpose: weight, power, volume or schedule numbers would need mission- and vehicle-specific trades that providers are still developing, and providers weigh mass, volume, development time and cost differently, so no single "best" mitigation exists; the report names the affected hardware, how and how far it is affected, and qualitative mitigation options, leaving the choice to the Exploration system developers. [CAB-02 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Executive-summary outcomes
- Seven considerations recur across subsystems: (1) lower fan, blower and air-mover performance from lower air density; (2) packed-bed performance changes from combined kinetics and heat-transfer effects; (3) changes in ambient-referenced hardware (valves, regulators, sensors, bellows); (4) possible simplification of gas-liquid separation in partial gravity; (5) lower heat rejection of hardware in cabin air; (6) increased material flammability; (7) higher toxicity risk from offgassing in smaller vehicles (less dilution volume). [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Of the 33 subsystems, nine were acceptable at 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2 with no modification, and only three, the Pressure Control Assembly (PCA), the Crew Active Dosimeter (CAD) and the Hybrid Electronic Radiation Assessor (HERA), at 8.2 psia/34 to 40 % O2; all others need more analysis, testing and/or design changes for Exploration. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The same three (PCA, CAD, HERA) are the only assessed subsystems with no performance, thermal or material impact (Finding F-1). [CAB-02 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flammability of ISS ECLSS heritage materials at 8.2 psia was of particular concern: NASA has flammability data for many materials at 30 % O2 but limited data above that level, and many commonly used ISS materials are flammable above 30 % O2; not reported in this statement: total pressure, test method, gravity level. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This requires a change of materials in 21 % of the assessed subsystems at 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2 and in 70 % at 8.2 psia/34 % O2; alternative materials meeting performance and flammability requirements exist in limited cases, but for most 8.2 psia/34 % O2 cases they will have to be developed. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The performance, thermal and materials impacts will carry over into Exploration vehicle mass, volume, power and schedule; no substantial mass or volume impact was found for any subsystem except possibly the Sabatier Carbon Dioxide Reduction Assembly, and power impacts arise mainly from running fans and blowers faster to offset lower air density. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Schedule impacts vary; historical experience shows seemingly small changes can bring significant challenges, cost and schedule growth (refs. 81–83). [CAB-02 p.13 · CITED]
- Clear schedule risks lie in hardware that needs testing to choose mitigations and understand performance, and in recertifying all equipment for its intended conditions; Section 8.3 holds the NESC recommendations for analysing and testing critical components at Exploration conditions. [CAB-02 p.13–14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
