### Fans, blowers and cabin air properties at reduced pressure
- A fan or blower is a constant-volume device: each rotation moves the same volume, which leaves at an increased relative pressure. [CAB-02 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fans or blowers that must deliver a constant mass flow for convective cooling in both ISS and Exploration atmospheres will need to spin faster by the ratio of the atmospheric densities. [CAB-02 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Air pressure (density) sets key fan design features such as blade attack angle and cross-section diameter, and poor aerodynamic blade optimisation can cause excess noise, heat of compression, higher power consumption and/or shorter life. [CAB-02 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most ISS fans and blowers were designed for 14.7 psia and 21 % O2, some certified for lower-pressure operation during contingency events. [CAB-02 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- That design atmosphere gives an air density of about 0.075 lbm/ft3 (1.2 kg/m3); temperature and humidity not stated in the pages read. [CAB-02 p.25 · MODELED]
- Running ISS fans and blowers outside their certification parameters, e.g. in Exploration atmospheres, will likely cause performance impacts such as excess noise, higher power consumption and/or shorter life (F-2). [CAB-02 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Cabin air heat capacity per unit volume and thermal conductivity are not highly sensitive to the composition changes of the Exploration environments (Appendix A items c and e, Table A-1). [CAB-02 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Appendix A gas composition: O2 mole fraction specified as 21 % at 14.7 psia, 26.5 % at 10.2 psia and 34 % at 8.2 psia; water mole fraction from a set temperature and relative humidity; N2 as yN2 = 1 − yO2 − yw; molecular weight and specific heat as molar averages; Table A-1 values are all calculated at 40 % rH and 22 °C for three columns, nominal ISS cabin 14.7 psia/21 % O2, Exploration cabin 8.3 psia/34 % O2 and Exploration cabin 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2. [CAB-02 p.98 · MODELED · nominal, ctx; CAB-02 p.99 · Table A-1 · MODELED · nominal, ctx]
- With the proposed Exploration atmospheres, the ability of ECLSS equipment to move or dissipate heat by forced air convection will be significantly reduced, because lower cabin pressure lowers air density. [CAB-02 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 1, steady-state 1-D internal-flow heat transfer: Q = A * V * ρ * Cp * (T1–T2), with Q heat rejected from the fluid, A duct cross-section, V fluid velocity, ρ density, Cp specific heat, T1 inlet and T2 outlet temperature (units and fitted range not stated). [CAB-02 p.30 · Eq. 1 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1 is applied to cabin air flowing through a generic air/water heat exchanger (HX): Fig. 2 shows an HX air duct from inlet T_air,1 to outlet T_air,2 with air velocity V_air over an HX cold plate. [CAB-02 p.30 · MODELED; CAB-02 p.31 · Fig. 2 · MODELED]
- Air density varies linearly with pressure while specific heat stays nearly constant (Table 6); combining Eq. 1 with Table 6 gives Eq. 2, QExp = QNom * PExp/PNom (QNom and PNom at 14.7 psia, QExp and PExp at 10.2 or 8.2 psia; fitted range not stated), so heat rejection falls in direct proportion to cabin pressure (Table 7); O2 concentration, temperature and humidity behind Table 6 not stated in the pages read. [CAB-02 p.31 · Eq. 2 · MODELED]

| Ambient pressure (psia) | Air density ρ (Table 6) | Specific heat Cp (Table 6) | Heat rejection (Table 7) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14.7 | 0.0743 lbm/ft3 (1.191 kg/m3) | 0.2396 Btu/lb/°R (1.0025 kJ/kg/oK) | QNom | [CAB-02 p.31 · Table 6 · MODELED; CAB-02 p.31 · Table 7 · MODELED] |
| 10.2 | 0.0515 lbm/ft3 (0.825 kg/m3) | 0.2395 Btu/lb/°R (1.0022 kJ/kg/oK) | QExp = 0.694 * QNom | [CAB-02 p.31 · Table 6 · MODELED; CAB-02 p.31 · Table 7 · MODELED] |
| 8.2 | 0.0418 lbm/ft3 (0.67 kg/m3) | 0.2395 Btu/lb/°R (1.0020 kJ/kg/oK) | QExp = 0.565 * QNom | [CAB-02 p.31 · Table 6 · MODELED; CAB-02 p.31 · Table 7 · MODELED] |

- From Eq. 1, the lost heat rejection can be offset by a higher air inlet velocity V. [CAB-02 p.31 · MODELED]
- For an air/water HX this means a higher fan speed, which raises the inlet volume flow (Vdot = V*A), with calculations in Appendix A; Exploration atmospheres have a lower per-unit-volume heat capacity from the lower air density (F-9), which shows up as a lower ability to reject heat by convection (F-10), most likely mitigated by running HXs at higher fan speeds. [CAB-02 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Concerns with higher HX fan speeds: more acoustic contribution and electric power use, and possibly reduced fan performance (Vdot) at lower pressure. [CAB-02 p.31–32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Cabin acoustics and audible alarms at 10.2 and 8.2 psia
- Lower cabin pressure than on the ISS is generally expected to change the habitat acoustic environment: noise sources radiate less efficiently in lower-density gas, giving lower sound pressure levels, though strongly frequency-dependent (high frequencies can seem louder from lower absorption attenuation); this affects both unwanted equipment noise and wanted sounds such as voice and audible alarms. [CAB-02 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Skylab crewmembers reportedly found the 5 psia environment quiet but needing extra effort to talk (anecdotal, ref. 84). [CAB-02 p.29 · CITED]
- Human hearing and measurement microphones are expected to be only minimally affected because eardrums and diaphragms are back-vented for pressure equalisation. [CAB-02 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A microphone's response at its resonance frequency rises at lower pressure (less damping), while its broad frequency response does not change significantly (ref. 85). [CAB-02 p.29 · CITED]
- Faster fans needed at lower pressure complicate any prediction; 10.2 or 8.2 psia is expected to have both beneficial and detrimental effects on crew noise exposure and on voice and alarm communication, and the net effect cannot be predicted with certainty without accurate modelling of the specific vehicle and systems (F-7). [CAB-02 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Toxic offgassing in smaller vehicles and at 8.2 psia
- Offgassed-species concentrations are inversely proportional to vehicle volume, so a material mass acceptable for toxic offgassing in a large vehicle like the ISS may not be acceptable in smaller ones. [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Example: concentrations in the MPCV crew module (CM; internal free volume 530 ft3/15 m3) would be a factor of 8 higher than in the ISS (free volume used for offgassing calculations 4167 ft3/118 m3). [CAB-02 p.32 · MODELED]
- MAPTIS (NASA Materials and Processing Information System) reports offgassing data as maximum limit weights for the ISS and MPCV volumes, and assembled-item tests as the maximum number of units that can fly in the ISS or MPCV; both can be converted to limit weights or unit counts for Exploration vehicle volumes. [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Toxic offgassing rates were historically expected to depend little on pressure until molecular flow begins (e.g. <1 E-3 torr). [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Limited unpublished White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) data suggest a significant pressure effect in much higher pressure regimes: initial measurements gave offgassing levels 1.5-2 times higher at 8.2 psia than at 11.9 psia; not stated in the pages read: materials tested, O2 concentration, temperature, test duration. [CAB-02 p.32 · CITED · single-test]
- WSTF uses 11.9 psia as its standard offgassing test pressure because of its low ambient pressure; other organisations typically tested at 14.7 psia. [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Offgassing at 14.7 and 10.2 psia has always been assumed equivalent without problems, and WSTF data at 11.9 psia, midway between, are adequate for either without correction; the effect is significant at 8.2 psia, and more empirical data are needed to establish whether a correction factor can be applied to existing data for 8.2 psia environments (F-11). [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA-STD-6001 recommends retesting materials whose data are over 10 years old, because of analytical-instrument improvements and changes in material processing parameters; using existing MAPTIS data is not prohibited. [CAB-02 p.32 · CITED · nominal]
- Existing MAPTIS data have not led to known problems, and the report's offgassing assessments did not exclude them, though new programs may adopt the 10-year data-age recommendation; data older than 10 years, especially from the 1980s and 1990s, may not reflect current materials because of better instrument sensitivity and manufacturing changes (O-2), yet their continued use has caused no known toxicity problems in pressurised spacecraft. [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Acceptable offgassing quantities on the ISS are driven by its bulk volume and the dilution it allows; current ISS hardware may offgas too much for smaller vehicles and will offgas more at 8.2 psia than at standard test pressures (O-3). [CAB-02 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Material flammability in the Exploration Atmospheres
- Flammability of polymeric materials depends strongly on O2 concentration (percentage) and more weakly on O2 partial pressure. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA has extensive 1-g flammability data on polymeric materials at 24.1 % O2 and 14.7 psia (e.g. the ISS maximum O2 other than in the airlock during EVA prebreathe) and at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia (the worst case for materials flammability in the SSP orbiter, the ISS airlock during EVA prebreathe, the MPCV CM and CCP vehicles); essentially all existing flammability test data for flight materials come from 1-g testing. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- NASA has limited material flammability data at O2 concentrations above 30 % (F-12a); not reported in this statement: total pressure, test method. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because essentially all flight-material flammability data come from 1-g testing, minimal flammability data exist at varying O2 concentrations in partial-gravity environments (O-4). [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The maximum O2 concentration is not yet defined for all habitable Exploration elements that will operate on the lunar or Martian surface. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- HEO-DM-1006 (ref. 15) specifies a nominal total cabin pressure of 8.2 psia and O2 of at least 33.7 % for Exploration missions with high-frequency EVA. [CAB-02 p.33 · CITED · nominal]
- Allowing for O2 control bands and sensor accuracy, the maximum O2 at a nominal 8.2 psia could lie between 36 and 40 %, depending on the vehicle design and hardware; the assessment therefore evaluated hardware and material flammability up to 40 % O2 for the 8.2 psia environment. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Many ISS materials have been shown to meet flammability requirements at 10.2 psia and 30 % O2 but are unlikely to meet them at higher O2 concentrations; test method and sample form not stated for this statement in the pages read. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials in this category: polymeric materials, foam thermal insulations (e.g. Armaflex and Solimide AC-550 polyimide), Bisco HT-200 sound-block silicone, Soundcoat HT polyimide foam, Black KB 10 tape, blue duct tape, silicone-fiberglass insulations, flammable paint on metallic substrates, Nomex, and polyethylene covered in aluminium foil tape. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Metallic materials are usually nonflammable even in 100 % O2 at ambient pressure (gravity level and test method not stated in the pages read), and relatively flammable metals such as aluminium and titanium will be nonflammable under standard flammability test conditions in the expected Exploration environments. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The impact of higher flammability depends on the hardware design; many custom ECLSS items are largely metallic and may be usable with minor modifications. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Armaflex foam thermal insulation on the ISS coolant lines is acceptable for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia (test method and sample form not stated in the pages read) but likely to be flammable in habitable Exploration elements. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No drop-in replacement exists; some foams such as Zotek F30 would meet flammability requirements but would need extensive machining (F-12b). [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A vacuum-exposure requirement adds difficulty: Armaflex, Zotek F30 and other closed-cell thermal-insulation foams can be damaged by vacuum, while open-cell foams, needed for acoustic insulation, survive vacuum but lack the thermal performance of closed-cell foams. [CAB-02 p.33–34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Some closed-cell foams exist that would meet flammability requirements in habitable Exploration elements, but apart from Solimide HT-340 no suitable open-cell foam exists at this time (F-13). [CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Bisco HT-200 sound-block silicones, used extensively in ISS ECLSS hardware, are acceptable for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia (test method and sample form not stated in the pages read) but will likely be flammable in habitable Exploration elements (F-12c). [CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware usually has polymeric rather than metallic cases and so is more likely to be flammable in Exploration environments; relatively minor changes, such as covering exposed polymeric surfaces with aluminium tape, may sometimes protect it; with a metallic case the internal materials can usually be shown to be self-extinguishing, but polymeric cases will likely be flammable in habitable Exploration elements. [CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Programs with up to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia have historically accepted some flammable hardware by material usage agreement (MUA) because it is largely crew-tended in use and stowed in a nonflammable container otherwise; some flammable COTS hardware may be accepted the same way at higher O2, but many items accepted for the ISS are unlikely to be acceptable for Exploration without modification. [CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Example: the cordless vacuum cleaner is flammable hardware accepted for the ISS but, being fairly large, is unlikely to be acceptable for Exploration atmospheres without modification, whereas the CADs are small enough that they may be acceptable regardless of flammability. [CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Avionics Air Assembly (AAA) (section 7.2.1)
- Fig. 3 loop: cabin air enters at 72 °F, leaves the hardware rack at up to 109 °F, passes the AAA fan and heat exchanger (HX, cooled by moderate-temperature-loop (MTL) coolant) and returns to the cabin at 68–72 °F. [CAB-02 p.35 · Fig. 3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- Without aerodynamic optimisation of blade angles, AAA fan performance will drop at low pressure (F-1); convective heat transfer in the HX and avionics racks falls with air density, which may be overcome by changing fluid velocities and/or HX area, and more volumetric flow and power (higher fan speed) will be needed through the racks (Appendix A items i and j). [CAB-02 p.35 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Lower-density air has a lower heat capacity per volume while specific heat per mole barely changes, so to sink the same heat load within the same temperature limits the volumetric flow must rise in proportion to the density and heat-capacity change, possibly more to offset lower effectiveness (Appendix A item j): upwards of 40 % more volume flow through the racks at 10.2 psia (item a) and upwards of 80 % at 8.2 psia (item b). [CAB-02 p.35 · MODELED]
- Materials: missing materials data limited the AAA evaluation; the AAA is mostly metal and its bulk material is not expected to need redesign; thermal insulation was not evaluated because the AAA is cooled by the ISS MTL, which keeps cabin temperatures above the dew point, and is expected to be cooled the same way in Exploration vehicles. [CAB-02 p.35 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Brine Processor Assembly (BPA) (section 7.2.2)
- Cabin pressures below the BPA certification pressure may make brine weep through the device's bladder (F-15). [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BPA avionics are cooled by cold plates, natural convection and forced convection by process air (ref. 9). [CAB-02 p.37 · CITED · nominal]
- Lower forced- and natural-convection heat transfer at low pressure may raise the steady-state touch temperature, which more ventilation (AAA flow) could mitigate. [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The BPA bladder is flammable in ISS environments and sits inside an aluminium box with airflow below 10 cfm. [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- It was accepted for the ISS on JSC 29353 data (ref. 21) showing that a vented aluminium container with a constant 10 cfm airflow can contain an internal fire. [CAB-02 p.37 · CITED]
- That acceptance holds for environments up to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia; more flammability testing is needed to know whether the hardware is acceptable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia (F-15). [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The brine processor bladder was specifically tested for offgassing for the ISS, and the results show it is acceptable for offgassing in smaller-volume vehicles. [CAB-02 p.37 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The other BPA materials were verified for the ISS from MAPTIS data but would need reassessment and, depending on vehicle volume, offgassing tests as an assembly for Exploration vehicles. [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On the ISS the BPA has caused odour problems and trace-contaminant build-up above the odour threshold (ref. 90). [CAB-02 p.37 · CITED]
- The effect will be stronger in Exploration-sized vehicles with less dilution volume (O-5) and will likely require trace-contaminant control by a GAC bed; it matters most for the BPA among cabin-venting ECLSS hardware because of its high vent flow (10 cfm, 0.283 m3/min) and near-continuous operation (~26-day dewatering cycles). [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Common Cabin Air Assembly (CCAA) (section 7.2.3)
- The CCAA (Fig. 5, ref. 22) controls cabin air temperature and humidity and ventilates to mix constituents in microgravity; it can serve a volume equal to the ISS U.S. Lab Module while keeping margin on fan RPM. [CAB-02 p.37 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The CCAA is certified to operate at 10.2 psia/30 % O2 in the ISS airlock (refs. 7, 23). [CAB-02 p.37 · CITED · nominal]
- The airlock is a smaller volume than one CCAA usually serves, but its certification there gives insight into fan performance and materials compatibility; specific CCAA requirements will depend on vehicle size, architecture and mission. [CAB-02 p.38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In nominal operation, fans pull cabin air in, combine it with moisture-laden air from CDRA and TCCS and pass it through a condensing heat exchanger (CHX); the cooled, saturated air returns to the cabin with a slip-stream fed to CDRA (refs. 7, 13). [CAB-02 p.37 · CITED · nominal]
- Without aerodynamic optimisation, fan performance will suffer at lower pressure, needing more volumetric flow to keep the crew within temperature limits (F-9, F-10); this is likely manageable at 10.2 psia thanks to the CCAA fan RPM margin, while 8.2 psia may need a larger or redesigned fan. [CAB-02 p.38 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the CCAA is primarily metallic, so flammability and toxic offgassing should not be a concern for those parts; its foam insulation is a silicone of unidentified type, and the exposed foam carries a fire-retardant coating for the ISS 24.1 % O2, which suggests it will be flammable in all Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Foam that is internal, between the metallic hardware and the case, may be an acceptable configuration although flammable, but the foam exposed on the rear of the CCAA CHX is unlikely to be acceptable for Exploration because of flammability and exposed area (F-16b). [CAB-02 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A relatively simple fix is to replace all HX foam with Zotek foam, nonflammable in Exploration environments, though toxic offgassing would have to be re-evaluated for vehicles smaller than the ISS whatever foam is used; a vacuum-exposure requirement would be a problem for closed-cell foams, and open-cell Solimide HT-340 should be acceptable for flammability but has unacceptable thermal performance. [CAB-02 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Each CCAA bacterial filter element is pleated borosilicate HEPA media with 0.3-μm pores in a rectangular aluminium frame; pleated glass is nonflammable in the Exploration atmospheres and will be acceptable. [CAB-02 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The inlet ORU acoustic enclosure is graphite composite with rubber (e.g. Bisco HT-200 sound blocker, probably flammable in HLS-type atmospheres but acceptable for 30 % O2, 10.2 psia) and felt bonded inside; the HX ORU inlet duct has a thin, fragile, nonstructural graphite-composite acoustic cover likely acceptable for flammability to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but possibly needing replacement at higher O2. [CAB-02 p.39 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly (CDRA) and 4BCO2 (section 7.2.4)
- CDRA desorbs a CO2-laden zeolite bed by heating it to 400 °F (204 °C) under vacuum; a blower drives cabin air through the beds during adsorption, process air cools desorbed beds back towards adsorption temperature (minimum about 50 °F, 10 °C, during adsorption), and CDRA is certified for nominal ISS environments; the next-generation 4BCO2 keeps the same basic architecture with many design improvements (refs. 16, 24). [CAB-02 p.40 · CITED · nominal; CAB-02 p.41 · CITED · nominal]
- The CDRA blower, or the mag-lev 4BCO2 blower under development, will likely not deliver the required volumetric flow in Exploration environments: the CDRA blower has no minimum specified operating pressure (ref. 25, 2K-070836-rev2 Table 5-6), and the 4BCO2 blower minimum pressure requirement is well above the reduced pressures evaluated. [CAB-02 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials that will not meet Exploration flammability requirements in CDRA: black KB 10 tape, blue duct tape, Armaflex AP pipe insulation and the silicone-fiberglass insulation blanket. [CAB-02 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Armaflex AP pipe insulation on CDRA passes flammability at 30 % O2, but covered by black KB 10 tape the configuration is flammable (F-12d, ref. 92); not reported in this statement: total pressure, test method. [CAB-02 p.41 · CITED · single-test]
- The KB 10 and blue duct tapes on the silicone-fiberglass blanket over the desiccant/adsorbent ORU would have to be replaced for Exploration and the blanket itself may need replacing; all other exterior hardware is metallic and nonflammable. [CAB-02 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Acceptable modifications are feasible for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia, but Armaflex AP is likely flammable at higher O2 (F-12a); replacing KB 10 with L-T-80 aluminium tape may be enough to control flammability in Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- 4BCO2 uses similar materials, including Armaflex insulation and KB10 tape on the low-temperature loop (LTL) lines. [CAB-02 p.41 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Carbon Dioxide Reduction Assembly (CRA, Sabatier) (section 7.2.5)
- The CRA reduces metabolic CO2 by the Sabatier reaction: CO2 from CDRA is stored at high pressure in an accumulator, H2 comes from OGA water electrolysis, the gases react over a Ru/Al2O3 catalyst in a packed bed to methane and water, methane is vented to space and water goes to the WPA via the wastewater bus (refs. 29, 30). [CAB-02 p.41 · CITED · nominal]
- The exothermic reaction needs high temperature to start but converts well at lower temperature (ref. 31); on the ISS, AAA air keeps an axial reactor temperature gradient with a hot inlet and cooler outlet. [CAB-02 p.41–42 · CITED · nominal]
- The reactor runs below cabin pressure (~11-13 psia) so that H2 or methane cannot vent or leak into the cabin (refs. 20, 21). [CAB-02 p.42 · CITED · nominal]
- Keeping that sub-ambient approach in Exploration would put the reactor below 10.2 or 8.2 psia (F-18a); an alternative is a pressure dome like OGA's as a containment layer for positive gauge pressure, at a mass penalty, with trades depending on the mission. [CAB-02 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The AAA air that holds the reactor temperature gradient has less heat capacity per volume and will need more volume flow, likely enough to control temperature depending on specifics such as the coolant-air flow path. [CAB-02 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials information was too limited for a full assessment; exposed materials appear metallic except Teflon-insulated wiring, the Dapco 2030-coated fiberglass-epoxy composite compressor acoustic cover and a silicone duct, and the cover and duct are nonflammable at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but likely flammable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia. [CAB-02 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Internal materials appear acceptable for flammability to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia, but how the housings would protect flammable internals at higher O2 is unclear; the CRA compressor is a high flammability risk because of its nonmetallic acoustic cover and the many polymeric materials inside it (F-12a). [CAB-02 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The Sabatier was verified for toxic offgassing in the ISS volume by analysis of materials data, which is likely inadequate for Exploration vehicle and habitat volumes. [CAB-02 p.42 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Portable fire extinguishers (PFE) (section 7.2.6)
- The MPCV PFE (Fig. 7, ref. 33; the Fig. 7 caption reads "ISS Water-Mist PFE Development Unit") is a water-spray extinguisher certified for the CM and was analysed because of its intended use at reduced cabin pressure and increased O2 (ref. 34); the ISS PFE uses water mist instead, and both are certified for 10.2 psia and 30 % O2 (ref. 24). [CAB-02 p.43 · CITED · nominal]
- Lower-pressure Exploration atmospheres could change water-spray PFE plume dispersal, water flow rate, required water quantity and tank size (F-19). [CAB-02 p.43 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Higher O2 concentrations could reduce the ability of water-spray and/or water-mist PFEs to extinguish a fire (F-20). [CAB-02 p.43 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No thermal impacts are apparent for either PFE in Exploration environments. [CAB-02 p.43 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The MPCV PFE exterior is metal or painted metal (red epoxy paint on a titanium pressure vessel): nonflammable for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia and possibly nonflammable for 34-40 % O2 at 8.2 psia, though no flammability data exist for flammable paint on metallic substrates at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia (F-12e). [CAB-02 p.43 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS PFE is a titanium tank in a red Nomex cover, certified for 30 % O2, 10.2 psia and, except for the cover, expected to be acceptable at the highest Exploration O2 levels. [CAB-02 p.43–44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The Nomex cover will not meet flammability requirements at the highest Exploration O2 concentrations (F-16f) but may be acceptable if treated with a fire retardant; PFE toxic offgassing should not be a concern for Exploration vehicles and habitats. [CAB-02 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Emergency mask, fire and ammonia cartridges (section 7.2.7)
- The emergency respirator cartridges remove contaminants from the crew's breathing gas in emergencies with adsorbents and catalysts (refs. 28, 35-37); the fire cartridge (Fig. 8, ref. 38) oxidises CO to CO2 and filters other contaminants from ISS cabin air after a fire for up to 90 minutes, using a gold-nanoparticle and iron-oxide catalyst, a GAC layer and a PTFE particulate filter to capture fire products, ammonia and particulates (ref. 26). [CAB-02 p.44 · CITED · nominal]
- The fire cartridge is certified for the ISS airlock at 10.2 psia and 30 % O2. [CAB-02 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Lower pressure is not expected to change adsorbent or catalyst capacity, since particulate-filter capacity depends on the absolute amount of particulate a fire produces, but kinetic or pressure-drop changes may reduce cartridge performance and require filter geometry changes for 8.2 psia. [CAB-02 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Less cooling of the beds by lower-heat-capacity breathing air could raise their steady-state temperature and, if high enough, reduce capacity at 8.2 psia, but the effect is likely negligible because the bed is small relative to the crew respiratory rate. [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ammonia cartridges that attach to the mask are flammable but acceptable in Exploration atmospheres for contingency use. [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The fire cartridges passed flammability testing in the ISS 24.1 % O2 atmosphere (total pressure not stated in this statement). [CAB-02 p.45 · MEASURED · single-test]
- They would not be expected to pass at higher O2 concentrations, but may use the same contingency rationale as the ammonia cartridges; the orange Nomex bags that store masks and cartridges are nonflammable up to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but would need modification (e.g. fire-retardant treatment) for 34-40 % O2 at 8.2 psia (F-12f). [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The emergency mask, mainly a Nomex-based layup, passed flammability in 24.1 % O2 but has large areas of material that are flammable in 24.1 % O2 (e.g. neck dam, visor); total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-02 p.45 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The masks are likely flammable in all Exploration atmospheres but may be acceptable for contingency use, during which they are effectively crew-tended at all times. [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A toxic-offgassing test on the emergency mask limited the total number of masks to 38 for the ISS volume (ref. 93). [CAB-02 p.45 · CITED]
- Mask offgassing may be too high for Exploration vehicles and habitats and could prevent carrying enough masks for an emergency (O-3a): only four masks would be allowed for the MPCV volume; if needed, the hardware may be baked at a moderate temperature (e.g. 120 °F) to reduce offgassing. [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Orion smoke-eater filter (OSEF) (section 7.2.8)
- The OSEF provides on-orbit post-fire cleanup of particulates and harmful gases in the MPCV CM: it installs directly in the CM particulate air filter, a detachable prefilter catches particulates and a primary filter of sorbent and oxidation catalyst removes contaminant gases; it is certified for 10.2 psia, 30 % O2 (ref. 39). [CAB-02 p.45 · CITED · nominal]
- At 10.2 psia/30 % O2 there is no concern since it is certified there (ref. 29); pressure changes are not expected to alter adsorbent capacity, catalyst performance or particulate-filter performance and capacity. [CAB-02 p.45 · CITED]
- The design would likely keep the same volumetric flow at 8.2 as at 10.2 psia for the same air volume, but velocity-related kinetic effects may require sorbent or catalyst bed dimension changes, and the lower heat capacity of the process air may raise steady-state temperatures and reduce sorbent capacity or catalyst performance. [CAB-02 p.45 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The OSEF has not been tested or certified for 8.2 psia (F-12). [CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The OSEF is certified for flammability in 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia. [CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- It may be acceptable for flammability at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia: the only exposed non-aluminium material is the prefilter element, borosilicate fiberglass with a proprietary fluoropolymer coating; fiberglass can burn because of its sizing, but the coating may not be flammable at these O2 levels; toxic offgassing is not a concern. [CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Intermodule Ventilation (IMV) fan (section 7.2.9)
- The IMV mixes cabin air between ISS modules so gases mix properly, e.g. O2 released by OGA, humidity from the Urine Processor Separator Plumbing Assembly (SPA), the BPA and the crew, and CO2 for removal by CDRA (ref. 8). [CAB-02 p.46 · CITED · nominal]
- The IMV blower provides constant-volume mixing and the air volume to move is not expected to change for Exploration, so no low-pressure operating impact is expected; the controller, cooled by the process gas, may run hotter because of weaker natural and forced convection (F-12, F-13) and may need another cooling approach. [CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No IMV materials evaluation was possible for lack of data. [CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Oxygen Generation Assembly (OGA) (section 7.2.10)
- The OGA makes crew O2 with a cathode-feed water electrolyser (Fig. 9, ref. 40): a rotary separator removes H2 from the circulating feedwater, and O2 forms on the anode side of the cell stack and is vented to the cabin. [CAB-02 p.46 · CITED · nominal]
- A pressure dome held under vacuum stops product H2 from diffusing or leaking into areas with cabin air (O2), preventing combustion hazards; the water recirculation loop runs outside the dome to recycle unreacted water through the stack, and electrostatic forces drive much of the species migration and separation across the stack (ref. 41). [CAB-02 p.46–47 · CITED · nominal]
- Fig. 9 schematic: a hydrogen-sensor ORU checks for H2 in the O2 sent to the cabin, downstream of a water absorber on the O2 outlet; a nitrogen-purge ORU purges the stack with N2; H2 is vented to space or to the Sabatier; the stack sits inside the pressure dome. [CAB-02 p.47 · Fig. 9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The O2 side of the stack sees cabin pressure through the O2 vent, so Exploration atmospheres lower the O2-side pressure; the larger anode (ambient) to cathode (26-28 psia) pressure difference may affect the system, possibly overcoming protonic drag in the stack and releasing liquid water into the O2 product stream (F-22a). [CAB-02 p.47 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the OGA rack, the AAA disperses any O2 leak, diluting it to a maximum local concentration of 29 %, which is acceptable in the ISS cabin at a nominal 21 % O2. [CAB-02 p.47 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In Exploration atmospheres with elevated O2, an OGA O2 leak could create an unacceptable hazard inside a rack, and another hazard mitigation would be needed (F-22b). [CAB-02 p.47 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- If the wastewater-bus pressure falls (section 7.2.5) and with it the recirculation-loop pressure, dissolved H2 may come out of solution in the loop, the rotary-separator accumulator high/low setpoints may need changing and sensors may go out of range (F-22c). [CAB-02 p.47 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- None of these impacts should affect O2 production at the required rate; they are safety and operational concerns, and lowering the O2-side (anode) stack pressure with a back-pressure regulator on the outlet is one possible fix, with its own consequences and materials concerns. [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- H2 sensors in the O2 vent stream shut the OGA down if H2 reaches a hazardous level; water deactivates them, so a water absorber sits upstream, and lower cabin pressure may degrade the sensors or cause premature failure through more water in the product O2 (F-22d). [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The mostly liquid-cooled OGA is less thermally affected; weaker convection with ambient air may raise steady-state temperatures, which more coolant flow could offset. [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The OGA is sealed inside a metallic pressure dome, and its parts exposed to elevated O2 (up to 100 %) have been verified acceptable (ref. 94). [CAB-02 p.48 · CITED]
- The major components outside the dome are in metallic boxes and unlikely to be a flammability concern; polymeric materials outside the boxes are Teflon-insulated wiring (nonflammable in Exploration environments) and other insulation (likely flammable), so the OGA may be acceptable for all Exploration environments with insulation changes. [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Shutdown hazard on the ISS: the recirculation loop is not purged and holds product H2 and unreacted water; product O2 from the O2 side can diffuse into the loop, where O2 and H2 react to liquid water that condenses and lowers the loop pressure, which can draw ambient air in; at start-up that O2 could collect in the separator with residual H2 and create a flammability and/or explosion hazard (F-22e). [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors see reason to think this risk is lower in Exploration atmospheres because the pressure difference driving air into the loop is smaller, though the concentration gradient driving O2 diffusion stays the same because the O2 partial pressure is constant. [CAB-02 p.48 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Pressure Control Assembly (PCA) (section 7.2.11)
- The PCA has high-pressure N2 and O2 tanks, a pressure control panel (PCP) and a vent relief valve: the PCP reads total and partial pressures and commands the tank valves (off, on or partial-on), flow passes an orifice for accurate control, and the PCA supplements OGA O2 and makes up lost N2 (refs. 42-44). [CAB-02 p.48–49 · CITED · nominal]
- No performance, thermal or materials impacts were identified (F-1a): few or no performance impacts are expected, though flow-rate correlations for the lower ambient pressure and vent resizing may be needed, and no thermal impacts are anticipated. [CAB-02 p.49 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No detailed materials assessment was done: the PCA is predominantly metallic with Teflon-insulated wiring to the controllers, all electronics should be in metallic boxes or housings, and no flammability or toxic-offgassing issues are anticipated in Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.49 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Trace Contaminant Control System (TCCS) (section 7.2.12)
- The TCCS removes the trace contaminants emitted by equipment offgassing and human metabolism to keep cabin concentrations within maximum allowable limits for the mission duration; without active control they may build up to toxic levels. [CAB-02 p.49 · CITED · nominal]
- In the ISS TCCS (Fig. 10, ref. 45) a fan pulls cabin air through a fixed GAC bed that removes high-molecular-weight contaminants and ammonia (bed flow set by the ammonia load); two-thirds of the air then returns to the cabin and the rest is heated in a regenerative HX and sent to a high-temperature catalytic oxidiser for low-molecular-weight contaminants (flow and split set by the formaldehyde load); a granular LiOH bed downstream removes acidic byproducts, and the exhaust joins the ventilation upstream of the CCAA. [CAB-02 p.49 · CITED · nominal]
- Some trace contaminants are removed incidentally in humidity condensate, but best-practice design of active trace-contaminant control takes no credit for it (ref. 46). [CAB-02 p.49 · CITED · nominal]
- Fig. 10 labels: cabin air inlet 15.3 cubic m/hr; fixed charcoal bed 22.7 kg; blower with speed sensors; flow meter; orifice plate with 10.7 cubic m/hr bypass; catalytic oxidiser 0.5 kg of 0.5 % Pd on alumina, 673 K operating and 811 K maximum temperature, with temperature sensors; postsorbent bed 1.4 kg LiOH; cabin air outlet (to THC); process sample lines. [CAB-02 p.50 · Fig. 10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Lower pressure is not expected to reduce carbon-bed capacity or catalytic-reactor performance, but the bed may need a different aspect ratio to keep the residence time needed for proper kinetics (F-5), and the fan will have aerodynamic performance impacts. [CAB-02 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Future TCCS designs are expected to use offgassing rates per unit of internal nonstructural equipment mass plus human metabolic emissions, as for the ISS, adjusted for flight experience (ref. 95); for the same per-unit rates the same effective active flow is needed. [CAB-02 p.50 · CITED · nominal]
- Emission rates need no adjustment for total cabin pressure because they come from diffusion processes insensitive to pressure; the longer mean free path at lower pressure may raise linear diffusion velocities and help disperse contaminants. [CAB-02 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The bed's heat of adsorption and the blower's heat of compression leave with the process air; lower air density may raise the carbon-bed steady-state temperature and slightly cut capacity (F-5), an effect expected to be negligible because the contaminants are dilute; the catalytic reactor may need less heater power, since heating the same air volume means heating less mass (less N2). [CAB-02 p.50 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the TCCS exterior is primarily metallic, with electronics in a metallic box and Teflon-insulated wiring, so no external flammability or offgassing concerns are known for Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.50–51 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The internal activated-carbon bed is flammable but assumed acceptable because no ignition sources are present; the ISS bed is not regenerated, but regenerative carbon beds carry a fire risk unless they cool to ambient temperature before being exposed to cabin air again. [CAB-02 p.51 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Urine Processor Assembly (UPA) (section 7.2.13)
- The Separator Plumbing Assembly (SPA) separates free water from the Distillation Assembly (DA) vent gases (Fig. 11, ref. 47); the liquid joins the distillate stream and the gases are vented to the cabin. [CAB-02 p.51 · CITED · nominal; CAB-02 p.46 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because the DA is fed pretreated urine, this vent gas carries trace contaminants; at its low flow rate SPA venting may cause odour and contaminant build-up in Exploration-sized vehicles, so cabin venting may need source (point-of-use) contamination control (O-5). [CAB-02 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The UPA is mainly liquid-cooled by process fluid, with some natural and forced convection, so lower air density may raise hardware steady-state temperature, which AAA cooling could mitigate. [CAB-02 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The UPA is predominantly metallic apart from Teflon-insulated cables, with Solimide AC-550 polyimide thermal insulation and Bisco HT-200A barium-sulfate-filled silicone acoustic insulation inside. [CAB-02 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Solimide AC-550 and Bisco HT-200A are nonflammable to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but likely flammable at 34-40 % O2, 8.2 psia (F-12c); they may still be acceptable because the metallic exterior contains them. [CAB-02 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Silicones are usually flammable at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia, but Bisco HT-200A is nonflammable to at least 34 % O2 (pressure not stated in this statement); the UPA is acceptable for toxic offgassing in Exploration vehicle volumes. [CAB-02 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Where nonflammable thermal insulation is required, Solimide AC-550 in the UPA and WPA could be replaced by Solimide HT-340 or Zotek F30, which existing data show acceptable for 34-40 % O2, 8.2 psia environments (UPA section) and for Exploration environments (WPA section) (ref. 96). [CAB-02 p.52 · CITED; CAB-02 p.56–57 · CITED]

### Universal Waste Management System (UWMS) (section 7.2.14)
- The air-cooled urine/air separator motor and electronics will lose convective cooling and likely run hotter, possibly beyond component specifications or touch-temperature limits (F-9, F-10); higher airflow needed for capture may mitigate this, but more AAA flow may be required depending on usage frequency. [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The GAC bed may be less cooled by natural and forced convection, run hotter and possibly lose capacity (F-4), an effect likely negligible and mitigable by more cooling (e.g. higher velocities, AAA flow). [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The commode structure is aluminium, but several exposed polymeric materials are potential issues for Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The UWMS is certified for 24.1 % O2 at 14.7 psia and, possibly except the urine hose assembly, is acceptable to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia. [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The fecal canister lid is likely flammable beyond 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but may be small enough to be acceptable; the urine hose appears to be covered by Halar sleeving and is likely acceptable for 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but likely flammable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia; the Velcro strips inside the fecal canister are longer than the standard Velcro rules allow (ref. 21) but, being internal, are not considered a concern. [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The UWMS will need toxic-offgassing reassessment for volumes smaller than the ISS, and some or all components will likely need component-level testing for Exploration vehicles and habitats (O-3b). [CAB-02 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Water Processor Assembly (WPA) (section 7.2.15)
- In the WPA, wastewater passes the Mostly Liquid Separator (MLS), a rotary separator that removes gas bubbles (the gas is filtered of odorous compounds and vented to the cabin); the water then passes two HXs, is preheated, injected with O2 and sent to a packed-bed catalytic oxidiser that oxidises low-molecular-weight compounds to CO2/carbonate/bicarbonate, and a membrane gas-liquid separator removes unreacted O2 and vents it to the cabin (refs. 51, 52). [CAB-02 p.55–56 · CITED · nominal]
- The Gas Liquid Separator (GLS) is a membrane separator that removes excess O2 from the catalytic-oxidiser effluent, using cabin air as sweep gas and venting to the cabin. [CAB-02 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Lower gas-side pressure in the GLS raises the pressure gradient across the membrane and likely improves separation, but catalytic-oxidiser efficiency may drop and flow problems may arise in the water-processing loop; how these competing changes net out for WPA performance is not clear. [CAB-02 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The WPA, its components and avionics are largely liquid-cooled by the process fluid, but the GLS will lose convective cooling from the lower-density AAA air, mitigable by more AAA flow or possibly more coolant in the liquid HXs. [CAB-02 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the WPA is mainly metallic; its Teflon-insulated cables are nonflammable beyond 40 % O2, its internal Solimide AC-550 polyimide insulation is nonflammable to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but flammable in Exploration environments (34-40 % O2, 8.2 psia), and its Bisco HT-200A is likely flammable; both are likely acceptable because the metallic exterior contains them. [CAB-02 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The WPA would likely be acceptable for toxic offgassing in all Exploration vehicle volumes. [CAB-02 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Crew Health Care System (CHeCS): scope and calibration (section 7.3)
- The ISS CHeCS is the medical and environmental hardware that keeps the crew healthy and safe, in four subsystems: the Countermeasures System (CMS); the Environmental Health System (EHS), which monitors chemical and microbial species in air, water and surfaces and the acoustic environment (also to catch changes in fan performance); the Health Maintenance System (HMS); and the Radiation System (RAD). [CAB-02 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- ISS hardware is certified to operate safely at nominal conditions, typically 14.7 psia with 21 % O2; hardware used during EVA prebreathe must be certified for a minimum 9.5 psia and a maximum 100 % O2, and the Portable Oxygen Monitor (POM) in EHS is the only CHeCS item used during prebreathe. [CAB-02 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- ISS and Exploration missions levy different requirements: size, operational concept, maintenance logistics, operating pressure and O2 concentration will change, so some ISS CHeCS hardware will be unusable even if compatible with an Exploration atmosphere. [CAB-02 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Not assessed: CHeCS hardware with known obsolescence issues, consumables (e.g. syringes, sample hardware, pipettes and tips, likely to change and need recertification), HMS medical diagnostic hardware, and the current ISS CMS exercise hardware (size, logistics, obsolescence); the flywheel exercise device in development was attempted, and radiation monitoring was limited to the CAD and HERA on the information available. [CAB-02 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.58 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most CHeCS hardware are analytical instruments whose calibration translates electrical signals into a physical property; accepted best practice is to calibrate at operating conditions to account for differences between laboratory (in-shop/bench) and field use (ref. 53), so all Exploration analytical instruments are assumed calibrated at their intended operating conditions. [CAB-02 p.58 · CITED · nominal]
- Alternatively, instruments calibrated at 14.7 psia and 21 % O2 can apply correction factors for operation at lower pressure and higher O2, weighing the difficulty of calibrating at those conditions against that of generating correction factors; field calibration is impractical in flight (crew time, materials, hardware, complexity), so in-shop/bench calibration, at operating conditions or with correction factors, is the most viable option (refs. 54, 55). [CAB-02 p.58 · CITED]

### Acoustic Monitor (AM) (section 7.3.1)
- The ISS AM is a COTS kit made by Svantek (Fig. 14 labels: microphone/pre-amp assembly 7052E/SV15, acoustic monitor SV102A+, windscreen SA25, belt pouch SA49, mini USB cable SC56). [CAB-02 p.59 · Fig. 14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The AM was not certified for pressures or O2 concentrations beyond the nominal ISS 14.7 psia and 21 % O2 (ref. 56), but the same hardware is planned for future Artemis missions, with delta certification testing planned. [CAB-02 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The lower pressure and higher O2 of an Exploration atmosphere are expected to have minimal impact on AM performance; performance tests at 8.2 psia/34 % O2 and 10.2 psia/26.5 % O2 within the Artemis delta certification are to establish the size of all impacts. [CAB-02 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- No information was available to assess thermal impacts of an Exploration atmosphere on the COTS acoustic monitors. [CAB-02 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the aluminium case suggests the AM would be acceptable for Exploration flammability; the microphone/preamp and mini USB cables are flammable, and a more robust wrap (Nomex overwrapped with Nitto P-212 glass-cloth tape) works up to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but probably not at higher O2; the belt pouch is flammable in Exploration atmospheres but acceptable to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia, and a custom pouch would be needed above that. [CAB-02 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Offgassing testing was not required for the ISS but is probably necessary for Exploration vehicle volumes (O-3c); all parts of the kit were assessed for flammability. [CAB-02 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Anomaly Gas Analyzer (AGA) (section 7.3.2)
- The AGA (Fig. 15 photo: mounted in the MPCV CM) is a portable, battery-powered analyser that combines two spectroscopies: a Teflon integrating sphere as a multi-pass optical cell measures CO2, O2, hydrochloric acid (HCl), hydrofluoric acid (HF) and ammonia (NH3) by absorption, and a photoacoustic cell measures CO, hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and hydrazine (N2H4); it also monitors cabin pressure, temperature and water vapour. [CAB-02 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.60 · Fig. 15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Two crew-selectable modes each run at least 10 hours without changing batteries: post-landing mode shows CO2, NH3 and N2H4; on-orbit mode shows CO, HCl, HCN, HF, CO2, O2 and NH3. [CAB-02 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Tunable diode lasers (TDLs) are matched to the absorption wavelength of each target gas: in the integrating sphere, absorption lowers the light intensity, related to concentration by Beer's Law; in the temperature-regulated, vibration-isolated photoacoustic cell, the laser-gas interaction creates a pressure wave whose magnitude, measured by a transducer, gives the concentration. [CAB-02 p.60 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- TDL spectroscopy is very stable in calibration, so no periodic recalibration is needed for currently planned mission durations, thanks to robust solid-state optics and the optical platform design. [CAB-02 p.60–61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS POM, which uses TDL spectroscopy with a multi-pass cell, has kept a stable calibration for at least 3 years under current maintenance logistics, and the AGA lasers are enclosed in the photoacoustic cell or integrating sphere inside the AGA structure (ref. 58). [CAB-02 p.61 · CITED]
- The AGA end-item specification requires an operating pressure range of 10.2-15.2 psia and does not require operation at O2 concentrations other than the nominal ISS 21 % (ref. 59). [CAB-02 p.61 · CITED · nominal]
- Key AGA components (TDLs, photodetectors, pressure transducers, photoacoustic cell) are not expected to be significantly affected by an Exploration atmosphere. [CAB-02 p.61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Preliminary tests of the AGA at lower pressure (10.2 psia) and elevated O2 (~28 %) suggested that higher O2 may make it under-report contaminants through effects on the photoacoustic signal (F-26, ref. 97), postulated to come from a change in pressure-wave velocity across the photoacoustic cell caused by more O2 molecules (ref. 60). [CAB-02 p.61 · CITED · single-test]
- Lower pressure is expected to affect the pressure wave and acoustic monitor the same way, and the authors conclude the AGA's initial calibration under its use conditions should account for the lower pressure and higher O2 of an Exploration atmosphere. [CAB-02 p.61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Thermal: internal fans keep the AGA at operating temperature, and the TDLs and photoacoustic cell use thermo-electric plates (conduction); lower pressure and higher O2 are assumed not to significantly affect the fan cooling. [CAB-02 p.61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the metallic box will probably be acceptable for flammability, but the internal electronics are flammable and the fan cooling makes it somewhat uncertain whether the box can contain a fire in Exploration atmospheres; the AGA is not yet M&P certified and, being planned for ISS and MPCV, its final design has to meet flammability and offgassing requirements in the MPCV worst-case 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia (O-3d). [CAB-02 p.61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Air Quality Monitor (AQM) (section 7.3.3)
- The AQM (Fig. 16 photo: AQMs in ISS Node 2) is a gas chromatograph-differential mobility spectrometer (GC-DMS) that analyses trace volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in cabin air. [CAB-02 p.61 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.62 · Fig. 16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Its requirement and verification document (ref. 63) requires an operating pressure range of 10.2-15.2 psia and no O2 concentration other than the nominal 21 %. [CAB-02 p.62 · CITED · nominal]
- On the ISS, dust-clogged vents reduced internal cooling so the GC column could not cool to its starting temperature in the allotted time, causing missed cabin analyses; crew vent cleaning, typically by vacuum, restored full thermal regulation (ref. 98). [CAB-02 p.63 · CITED]
- GC column cooling will be less efficient in reduced-pressure Exploration environments, lengthening the sample time for cabin gas analysis (F-27b). [CAB-02 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the aluminium housing should be acceptable; the polycarbonate display window will be acceptable to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but flammable at higher O2, and with about 24 square in. of exposed area it does not meet the JSC 29353 small-quantity exemption, though it may be accepted by MUA on separation from credible ignition sources; the Teflon-insulated power cables are acceptable, but the polyimide flag labels are flammable and need replacing. [CAB-02 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On existing offgassing data, a single AQM is acceptable for vehicles larger than 20 m3, with reassessment needed for smaller vehicles and habitable structures (O-3e). [CAB-02 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Crew Active Dosimeter (CAD) (section 7.3.4)
- CADs are COTS direct-ion dosimeters (ref. 65) that measure radiation exposure, digitise it and send it by Bluetooth low energy to a powered laptop; they are carried in a pocket or clipped to clothing, with a visual display for the crew. [CAB-02 p.63 · CITED]
- Overall the CAD (Fig. 17 photo: lab unit) is not expected to be affected by low-pressure, increased-O2 environments (F-1b). [CAB-02 p.64 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.64 · Fig. 17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The CAD was accepted for the ISS through a simplified certification process for COTS technology (ref. 66), with no certification testing outside the ISS nominal 14.7 psia and 21 % O2. [CAB-02 p.64 · CITED]
- Its performance is not expected to change because measurement takes place in an enclosed, hermetically sealed chamber; CADs are planned for future Artemis missions with delta certification before flight, which is also expected to cover thermal impacts, since no thermal information was available. [CAB-02 p.64 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The CAD body is Ultem 1000, not flammable in 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but flammable in 34-40 % O2 at 8.2 psia; flammability is still not expected to be a concern given its 0.67 x 1.46 x 0.33 in. size, no propagation path or ignition source, and a size below the NASA-STD-6016 threshold for IVA flammability control; its size also makes toxic offgassing unlikely to be a concern. [CAB-02 p.64 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Colorimetric Water Quality Monitoring Kit (CWQMK) (section 7.3.5)
- The CWQMK is a COTS diffuse-reflectance spectrophotometer that measures iodine in water from the ISS potable water dispenser (PWD), using reagent-impregnated membranes bought from the manufacturer (refs. 67-69; Fig. 18 photo: spectrophotometer for biocide analysis). [CAB-02 p.64 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.65 · CITED; CAB-02 p.65 · Fig. 18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Overall no performance, thermal or materials impacts are expected from lower pressure or higher O2 (F-1c); an Exploration atmosphere is not expected to affect its operation, but its materials will need re-certification for the elevated O2. [CAB-02 p.65 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The CWQMK was certified not to create a hazard at low pressure during depressurisation, but had no certification testing for operation away from the nominal 14.7 psia and no requirement to operate away from 21 % O2 (ref. 70). [CAB-02 p.65 · CITED]
- Membranes: iodine membranes (ISS U.S. segment) are coated with polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), silver membranes (ISS Russian segment) with DMABR/Brij-30 (5-(p-dimethylaminobenzylidene) rhodanine and polyoxyethylene (4) lauryl ether). [CAB-02 p.65 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Thermal impacts are unknown because the kit was never required to work away from 14.7 psia and 21 % O2, though effects on the spectrometer are unlikely. [CAB-02 p.65 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: the kit's pouch has an outer Durette fabric acceptable for flammability up to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but not above, and most items inside are flammable even in the ISS environment. [CAB-02 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Use is limited (75 minutes a day, four times per year), crew-tended, and without credible ignition source (alkaline batteries lack the power to ignite solids), so the flammable contents are assumed acceptable in all Exploration atmospheres through operational controls; only the outer pouch fabric would need changing above 30 % O2, and standard textiles meeting Exploration flammability requirements are expected to be available. [CAB-02 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On existing offgassing data for the kit (ref. 99), no known Exploration vehicle is assumed to have an offgassing issue with it. [CAB-02 p.66 · CITED]

### Flywheel exercise device (MPCV, in development) (section 7.3.6)
- The flywheel device serves one crew member at a time, suited or unsuited: pulleys and a flywheel (Fig. 19, ref. 71) provide the loads, with straps, harnesses and an exercise bar; exercise needs no vehicle power, only the sensors measuring displacement, load and power do. [CAB-02 p.66 · CITED]
- Fig. 19 labels: Orion Flywheel Device with exercise bar and foot guard, step surface, resistance selector, exercise bar, strap, footplate. [CAB-02 p.67 · Fig. 19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Its requirements call for operation at 9.5-15.6 psia and do not require operation in elevated O2 (ref. 72). [CAB-02 p.67 · CITED · nominal]
- An Exploration atmosphere is anticipated to have no impact on its function, while its thermal load and thermal impacts are unknown and therefore uncertain (F-29). [CAB-02 p.67 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials: a full assessment was not possible for a device in development; its mainly metallic exterior will likely be acceptable; the crew's nylon strap is flammable but acceptable for MPCV 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia because it is crew-tended in use and otherwise inside the flywheel housing with only about 2 in. exposed at the handle connection, a rationale that may also hold at higher Exploration O2. [CAB-02 p.67 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The other straps are flammable but enclosed in the aluminium housing; toxic offgassing for Exploration vehicles and habitats is unknown. [CAB-02 p.67 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Hybrid Electronic Radiation Assessor (HERA) (section 7.3.7)
- HERA is an active ionising-radiation area monitor for the habitable volume, distributed as HERA sensor units (HSUs) and HERA processing units (HPUs) with their mounting hardware and cabling to the MPCV power and data units. [CAB-02 p.67–68 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- It first flies on Artemis I and, linked to vehicle caution and warning, on Artemis II and beyond; no performance, thermal or materials impacts are expected from reduced pressure and increased O2. [CAB-02 p.68 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- HERA must operate from space vacuum to 17.2 psia and over 0-40 % O2 to be accepted or flight-qualified, and no Exploration-atmosphere performance impact is expected (ref. 73). [CAB-02 p.68 · CITED · nominal]
- The same range (space vacuum to 17.2 psia, 0-40 % O2) is in RDWK-10108 Project Technical Requirements Specifications, which covers the whole system of HSUs and HPUs, and no thermal impact is expected. [CAB-02 p.68 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.69 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- HERA is certified for flammability in 40 % O2 for use in an MPCV avionics bay with no fire detection or suppression, so it would be acceptable for flammability in Exploration atmospheres at or below that O2; its offgassing certification shows substantial margin for the MPCV, so offgassing will be acceptable for Exploration vehicles. [CAB-02 p.68 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### MinION sequencer and Biomole Kit (section 7.3.8)
- MinION is a COTS genetic sequencer by Oxford Nanopore Technologies that reads genetic sequence with functionalised nanopores (refs. 74-76); it is part of the Biomole Kit (Fig. 20, ref. 77) with flow-cells, calibration cells, a mini polymerase chain reaction (PCR) device, magnetic beads and stands, pipettes and tips, and the reagents for sample preparation and analysis. [CAB-02 p.69 · CITED]
- Fig. 20 shows the device, magnetic stands for sample preparation, USB cables, a calibration cell, pipettes and tips, the PCR device and its power supply. [CAB-02 p.69 · Fig. 20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The MinION/Biomole Kit was not tested beyond the nominal ISS 14.7 psia and 21 % O2 (ref. 78); it will be used on future Artemis missions and needs delta certification testing. [CAB-02 p.69 · CITED]
- Its requirements and verification documents (ref. 79) require it to work in atmospheres up to 30 % O2 and, with no operating pressure specified, to work after exposure to 0 psia. [CAB-02 p.69–70 · CITED · nominal]
- No testing has been done, but lower pressure and higher O2 are not expected to affect its performance. [CAB-02 p.70 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- MinION hardware is flammable in the ISS environment but was accepted because it is stowed when not in use, lacks a credible internal ignition source and has all flammable cables wrapped (ref. 100). [CAB-02 p.70 · CITED]
- Its clear PMMA (acrylic) case will not be acceptable for Exploration environments because of flammability; a polycarbonate case, cables wrapped in an existing overwrap design demonstrated to prevent fire propagation in 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia (or Teflon cables) and no flag labels may make it acceptable for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia, but higher O2 would require a redesign (F-30). [CAB-02 p.70 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- MinION contains over 20 pounds of polymeric materials; accepted for offgassing on the ISS, its final configuration would need offgassing tests (with heaters powered) for smaller Exploration vehicles; all its components were assessed. [CAB-02 p.70 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Cordless vacuum cleaner (section 7.4.1)
- The ISS-certified cordless vacuum is the COTS Makita 18V LXT Lithium-Ion (36V) Brushless Cordless Half-Gallon HEPA Filter Backpack Vacuum (P/N XCV09Z), also certified to fly on CCP vehicles if soft-stowed in a nonflammable cargo transfer bag (ref. 101); its batteries charge through an adapter cup in the ISS Universal Battery Charger. [CAB-02 p.70 · CITED]
- Table 8 (Makita Vacuum Components) has 14 rows (P/N, part name, OpNom, mass, dimensions); only the battery and charger rows were transcribed, the others being the vacuum cleaner, flex hose, bent pipe, HEPA filter, dust bag, crevice tool, round brush, shelf brush, flex tool adapter and hose cap. [CAB-02 p.71 · Table 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| P/N (Table 8) | Part name | OpNom | Mass lbs (kg) | L x W x H in (cm) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LithiumBat-001 | Makita 18V LXT Li-Ion 2.0 AH Battery | 2.0 Ahr Makita Battery Pack | 0.8 (0.36) | 4.24 x 2 x 2.87 (10.77 x 5.08 x 7.29) | [CAB-02 p.71 · Table 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| UBC-SP-200 | Makita Vac UBC Battery Adapter | Makita Battery Pack Universal Battery Charger Adapter | 1 (0.45) | 2.7 x 2.4 x 1.6 (6.86 x 6.1 x 4.06) | [CAB-02 p.71 · Table 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| DC18RD | MAKITA 18V LXT Li-Ion Dual Port Rapid Optimum Charger | Not Applicable – Ground Units | 4.95 (2.25) | 8 x 14 x 4.25 (20.32 x 35.56 x 10.8) | [CAB-02 p.71 · Table 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| DC18RC | Makita 18V LXT Li-Ion Rapid Optimum Charger | Not Applicable – Ground Units | 2.5 (1.14) | 11 x 5 x 10 (27.94 x 12.7 x 25.4) | [CAB-02 p.71 · Table 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |

- Fig. 21 battery callout: Makita 18V LXT Li-Ion 2.0 AH battery pack, uses 2 batteries; 2AH batteries were used to mitigate battery propagation testing (total energy under 80Wh). [CAB-02 p.72 · Fig. 21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The vacuum may need higher fan speeds to clean adequately at reduced pressure, adding acoustic risk; other performance concerns may exist, but no data are available. [CAB-02 p.72 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In Makita battery testing at JSC/ESTA (WO 1908028) the 4-ampere-hour (AH) battery failed thermal-runaway testing, so only the 2.0 AH battery (PN BL1820B) was approved for the vacuum, which is not stowed with the battery installed; ambient O2, pressure and test platform not stated in the pages read. [CAB-02 p.72–73 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Touch-temperature tests (WO-2001004) for 0 % and 100 % blockage, covering the worst-case thermal extremes in medium- and high-power modes on the ISS, stayed below the 113 °F worst-case metal-surface allowable. [CAB-02 p.73 · MEASURED]
- When certified for the ISS, the polymeric materials of the vacuum, its attachments (flex hose, bent pipe, crevice tool, round brush, shelf brush, flex tool adapter, vac hose tethered cap), filter bags, HEPA filters and batteries were assumed flammable in 24.1 % O2 at 14.7 psia; it must be stowed in a nonflammable locker or container when not in use (ISS Operational Control Agreement Database (OCAD), Fire Event on Board ISS), is crew-tended in use, and has its battery removed for stowage. [CAB-02 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- These controls are reasonable at the ISS's relatively low O2, but for this relatively large item their acceptability is uncertain at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia, and modifications would almost certainly be needed at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia (F-31). [CAB-02 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The vacuum with accessories passed toxic-offgassing testing for the ISS volume and is acceptable in Exploration vehicle and habitat volumes; no components were left unassessed. [CAB-02 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Crew Quarters (CQ) (section 7.4.2)
- The CQ, in Node 2 rack Bay 5, is a permanent personal space for sleep, recreation, communication and stowage of personal items, built as a 6061 aluminium rack exoskeleton with a composite substructure mainly of ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE); six interface cables from Node 2 power lighting, laptop, fans, command and data handling (C&DH) and Audio Terminal Unit (ATU) voice communication. [CAB-02 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Passive ventilation is by air exchange with the node aisle, and two redundant fans give controllable ventilation and CO2 removal, with fan speed and diffuser orientation used for heat removal; audio annunciation devices (AADs) sound Class 1 alarms, the ATU speaker gives audio and Class I, II and III alarms, and removable acoustic blankets cover the CQ (Fig. 22 photo: CQ flight unit SEG32109500-301 in the rack handling adapter during acoustic testing). [CAB-02 p.73 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.74 · Fig. 22 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- ISS-CQ interfaces: cabin air, electrical, caution and warning (C&W), data management, access for a PFE, and structural. [CAB-02 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Acoustic, light, visual-isolation and radiation-protection performance is not expected to change with the cabin atmosphere, unless materials have to change for flammability or offgassing; the Solid State Lighting Assembly (SSLA) lights are certified after hard-vacuum exposure and not expected to be affected by reduced pressure. [CAB-02 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Each CQ has an intake and an exhaust fan giving a combined maximum of 95 CFM and minimum of 58 CFM; with one fan failed the minimum drops to 44 CFM, above the 30 CFM minimum rating (ref. 102). [CAB-02 p.74 · CITED · nominal]
- The fans will give the same volumetric air exchange at reduced pressure, adequate for CO2 washout. [CAB-02 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The temperature difference between Node 2 and the CQ must stay below 9 °F with the crew awake and below 5 °F with the crew asleep. [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The CQ fans will need a design change to move more air for crew comfort, possibly a specialty design. [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The CQ side walls and kick panels are 1-in.-thick sandwich composite panels with a Nomex honeycomb core, acceptable for flammability in 30 % O2, 10.2 psia, where the composite showed no signs of burning (ref. 103); gravity level, test method, ignition method and duration not stated in the pages read. [CAB-02 p.75 · CITED · single-test]
- On that result there is a good chance the panels are acceptable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia, and alternate composite constructions exist that meet flammability requirements for all Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The radiation-shielding back wall is 2-in.-thick polyethylene covered with aluminium foil tape, which protects the flammable polyethylene up to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia; acceptable operation at 34-40 % O2 is possible (F-12g), but no empirical data are currently available. [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Acoustic and padding blankets with Nomex HT90 and Gore-Tex expanded PTFE outer layers will be acceptable to 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but are unlikely to be at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia, where a fire-retardant treatment of the Nomex may suffice; the ventilation-system acoustic abatement, mainly Soundcoat HT polyimide foam, may be acceptable to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia but not at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia (F-12c). [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The composite sandwich panels were baked out to meet offgassing requirements in the ISS volume, suggesting offgassing may be a problem in vehicles and habitats smaller than the 118 m3 standard ISS volume used for offgassing assessment (O-3f). [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Galley rack: potable water dispenser (PWD), FRIDGE and Galley food warmers (section 7.4.3)
- The Galley rack is a modified Express Transportation Rack consolidating crew food preparation and storage: the PWD, two refrigerated/frozen stowage volumes (Microgravity Express Rack Locker/INcubator (MERLIN) units, replaced in 2020 by FRIDGE units) and two rack-mounted food warmers (Fig. 23 photo, before late 2020: two MERLIN lockers top left, PWD top right, two Galley food warmers below them, storage at the bottom). [CAB-02 p.75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.76 · Fig. 23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The rack is cooled by the U.S. Laboratory MTLs, gets smoke detection through air exchange with Node 1, and was designed for a minimum operating pressure of 13.9 psia, deactivating automatically below it. [CAB-02 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- FRIDGE holds internal temperatures from -4 to +118 °F (-20 to +48 °C), needs no airflow and is isolated from the cabin except when opened (ref. 80). [CAB-02 p.76 · CITED · nominal]
- FRIDGE holds wall temperature with a thermoelectric cooler and cools contents by convection inside the compartment, so bulk and content cooling rates may drop with air density while absolute cooling capability is likely unaffected (F-32). [CAB-02 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The Galley Food Warmer (GFW) target is 180 °F (82 °C), not settable, with internal temperatures of 145 to 190 °F (63 to 88 °C) during warm-up; at reduced pressure the target may still be reached but contents may take longer to warm. [CAB-02 p.76 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The PWD draws cooling air from the Node 1 aisleway and discharges it warmed into the rack, and uprating the PWD fan is an in-work design consideration for Exploration; the food warmers also dump heat into the rack, which has no AAA fan, so a similar rack in Exploration vehicles and habitats will need forced-convection or water-loop cooling (F-33). [CAB-02 p.77 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- PWD materials: front panel, locker, chassis and most internals are aluminium or metallic; the internal heater assembly (Kapton heaters, Aerogel blanket, melamine foam insulation) is acceptable because the flammable materials are enclosed by the nonflammable Aerogel blanket and an anodised aluminium housing, which would contain an internal fire even if one propagated; front-panel items such as the polycarbonate window would be flammable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia but are small with no credible ignition source, so the PWD is acceptable for flammability in Exploration environments. [CAB-02 p.77 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The PWD would need offgassing tests for small Exploration volumes (e.g. the 15 m3 MPCV CM): its melamine foam, a formaldehyde concern, is assumed too small in quantity to matter, but the Aerogel blanket may be a problem on its materials-certification data (O-3g, ref. 104). [CAB-02 p.77 · CITED]
- The rack food warmer is mostly aluminium; its main flammability issue is the melamine-foam thermal insulation inserts, acceptable at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but flammable at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia, with Solimide HT-340 a possible replacement; a "polyimide enclosure" at the heater element listed in the MIUL may be acceptable at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia but likely not at 34-40 % O2 and 8.2 psia; flammable Nitto P-213 tape sits on an aluminium heat sink, and P-212 tape, nonflammable at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia, is a possible alternative; other flammable materials are in acceptably small quantities or surrounded by nonflammable materials. [CAB-02 p.77 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The melamine foam is an offgassing issue in volumes smaller than the ISS (O-3h): melamine foams tend to release formaldehyde, especially when heated to 185 °F (85 °C), and this foam passed an offgassing test at 190 °F (88 °C) in 1995 (ref. 105), before the standard test reliably detected and quantified formaldehyde. [CAB-02 p.77 · CITED]
- An alternative melamine foam (e.g. Basotect-W coated with Viton, used in the MPCV food warmer) could replace it; other polymers are assumed not to be an offgassing concern, and the Teflon-insulated DC power cable is assumed acceptable for flammability and offgassing in Exploration environments. [CAB-02 p.77 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### ISS suitcase food warmer (ISSFW) (section 7.4.4)
- The suitcase-style ISSFW (Fig. 24 photo) heats crew meals: an aluminium case with two latches and a handle holds four heater assemblies between two aluminium plates and two foam inserts (lid and base) of melamine foam with a Mosites coating against moisture absorption that restrain the food packages; the four heating elements each have a central thermal sensor, four thermostats sit under two white Teflon shields along one plate, and an insulation border under the hinge and near the handle protects the lid side. [CAB-02 p.78 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.78 · Fig. 24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- It must heat food packages to at least 145 °F (63 °C) in about 45 minutes and was certified for a minimum operating pressure of 13.9 psia; thermal and pressure differences would lengthen heating times, with no other thermal impacts expected. [CAB-02 p.78 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Materials: the aluminium shell is acceptable; the Mosites 10298-coated melamine foam is a flammability concern at 34-40 % O2, 8.2 psia but not at 30 % O2, 10.2 psia, and an offgassing concern in both; Basotect W would not change flammability but would make offgassing acceptable in both; the melamine foam is an offgassing issue in volumes smaller than the ISS (O-3i), other polymers are assumed not to be a concern, and no components were left unassessed. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
