# FILE: CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2
# CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2 — Exploration-atmosphere hardware impacts (NESC summary and appendix), fire-resistant textiles for 37 % O2, and planned lunar cabin and suit atmospheres

## Scope
Covers: the end of the NESC assessment CAB-02 (ISS and MPCV sleeping bags, consequences for Exploration design, the Table 9 impact summary, definitions, findings F-1 to F-34, observations, recommendations R-1 to R-6, Appendix A cabin-air property calculations and Table A-1, the AAA temperature estimate and the informal 2021 meeting notes); CAB-03 on qualifying fire-resistant cabin textiles for 37 % O2 at 8.2 psia (Test 1 as used for textiles, layup effects, crew clothing, CTBs, sleeping bags, PBI shirt, patches, the NESC textile strategy); CAB-04 on lunar surface-vehicle and suit atmospheres for Artemis; the cabin-atmosphere blocks of OVR-03 (2008) and OVR-13 (2026 slides).
Not here: CAB-02 sections 1 to 7.4.4 (scope, method, Table 1 vehicle atmospheres, ISS control bands, the subsystem-by-subsystem assessment and Tables 3 and 5) and CAB-01 Table 1 (see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1); the Test 1 method, MOC and acceptance rules in NASA-STD-6001B and JSC 29353 (see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1, MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2); OVR-03 and OVR-13 flame-spread and flammability-limit results in microgravity, lunar and Martian gravity and the FM² plan (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2).

## Findings

### CAB-02: ISS and MPCV sleeping bags (section 7.4.5)
- The ISS Sleeping Bag Assembly was developed for the Commercial Crew Program (CCP), first flew on the SpaceX Demonstration-2 mission, and consists of a sleeping bag with a replaceable liner and eight ties that tether the bag in place. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The bag measures 84 in. long × 27 in. wide × 1 in. thick and weighs about 6.6 lb with its liner; it is meant mainly for the crew quarters (CQ) but may be used anywhere in Exploration vehicles and habitats. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Construction: outer shell of royal blue Nomex, insulation layer of Thinsulate FR-120, inner layer of elastic (Interlock) Nomex, and a replaceable white cotton batiste #128 liner held by Velcro and toggle-style buttons and meant to be changed monthly. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Other features: expandable gussets (blue Nomex side and bottom panels), a head pocket, pillow accommodation in the liner, arm and foot openings, a nylon zipper with a cotton liner strip (0.2 in. wide × 45 in. long), nylon-webbing internal body restraints, vents with blue Nomex covers, external pockets sized for a notebook or iPad Air, and 22 Nomex webbing attachment loops around the perimeter. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Accessories: eight Vectran-cord ties per bag (24 in. long × 0.15 in. diameter) and an optional debris screen (27 × 24 in.) that the crew may use to cover the face during sleep; bags, liners, ties and debris screens are soft-stowed for launch. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-02 expects neither the performance nor the thermal performance of the sleeping bag to be affected by the reduced pressure or the higher O2 of the Exploration atmospheres. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS sleeping bag is probably too bulky for Exploration vehicles, and its materials would need special operational controls for flammability at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The lighter MPCV sleeping bag is certified for 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia, on condition that it is stowed in a nonflammable container when not in use. [CAB-02 p.79 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Neither the ISS nor the MPCV (Orion) sleeping bag design is acceptable for flammability at 8.2 psia and 34–40 % O2 (finding F-34 words it as 34 %+ O2), because royal blue Nomex is the main exposed material (F-12f, F-34). [CAB-02 p.79–80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS and MPCV sleeping bags were baked out at 195 °F (91 °C) for 5–6 days to bring toxic offgassing down to a level that allows up to six bags in the MPCV volume (530 ft3 / 15 m3) and in the CCP volume (388 ft3 / 11 m3); CAB-02 expects a similar bakeout to be needed for Exploration vehicles. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Components not assessed for the sleeping bags: none. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02: consequences of the reduced-pressure atmospheres for Exploration design (section 7.5)
- The assessment did not identify definitive, quantitative "best" mitigation strategies for the performance, thermal and materials impacts it found (summary chart, Table 9); CAB-02 leaves the choice to the developers of Exploration systems and vehicles, who can trade them within their own architectures and mission priorities. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-02 still draws common themes on mass, volume, power and schedule from the assessment, to give program managers some perspective on risk. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mass: no substantial mass impact was found for any subsystem or item, with the possible exception of the Sabatier CRA if an enclosing dome is chosen for hazard control. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mechanical parts inside components (e.g. fans and blowers, relief valves, bellows tanks) will likely need modification or replacement, but they are usually a small fraction of system mass, so CAB-02 regards these changes, with reasonable confidence, as a low risk to system mass. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Many items contain acoustic and/or thermal insulation that will likely have to be replaced to meet flammability requirements at high O2 concentrations. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Insulation is generally light, but because no materials are currently suitable for O2 approaching 40 % at 8.2 psia and insulation is used throughout a vehicle or habitat, CAB-02 sees a possible integrated, substantial mass impact that deserves continued management attention. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Volume: no substantial impact for any subsystem or item except the Sabatier CRA if a dome is adopted; fans and blowers that must deliver a defined mass flow rate (as many convective-cooling fans do) may see notable growth of their external envelope if the chosen mitigation is a larger internal fan-blade assembly diameter. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Insulation changes may affect volume noticeably, possibly more than mass, given how widely insulation is used in vehicles and habitats; mechanical part changes inside components are expected to have little if any discernible effect on subsystem envelopes. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Power: the potential impacts come mostly from fans and blowers if higher operating speeds are chosen to keep mass flow rate at the lower cabin pressures (air densities); because so many fans and blowers deliver defined mass flow rates for equipment and environmental cooling, CAB-02 says managers should consider a possible substantial integrated power impact for a vehicle or habitat. [CAB-02 p.80 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Schedule: impacts are varied; human space system development has several cases where a perceived "simple" design change caused serious program schedule effects, and assembly and integration schedules can hinge on the delivery of a single item. [CAB-02 p.81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For these reasons CAB-02 asks managers and designers to give constant, diligent attention to identified or proposed changes to ISS ECLS equipment for Exploration vehicles and habitats. [CAB-02 p.81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Substantial schedule risk lies wherever testing is needed to: provide data for mitigation choices (e.g. how lower-pressure operation would affect Sabatier CRA performance); understand performance (e.g. CDRA under the combined effects on blower efficiency, bed heating and cooling, and adsorption/desorption kinetics), or for the PFE, AGA and AQM, how effectiveness changes at higher O2 concentration; and identify and certify alternate materials and recertify equipment, by test and/or analysis, for its intended Exploration operating conditions. [CAB-02 p.81 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02: definition of the Exploration atmospheres
- CAB-02 section 13.0 (Definition of Terms) defines an Exploration Atmosphere as a habitable-volume atmosphere held nominally at 8.2 psia / 26.5 % O2 or 10.2 psia / 26.5 % O2, and defines Exploration Mission(s) and Exploration Vehicle by the same two points as an assumed nominal or temporary operational cabin environment. [CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- For planning and for this assessment, CAB-02 considered nominal cabin atmospheres of 10.2 psia with 26.5 % O2 and 8.2 psia with 34 % O2, which it calls "Exploration Atmospheres" to tell them apart from the ISS nominal atmosphere. [CAB-02 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, ctx; CAB-02 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, ctx]

### CAB-02: report terms and nil statements
- In CAB-02, a Finding (F-n) is a relevant factual conclusion and/or issue within the assessment scope that the team rigorously based on data from its own analyses, tests, inspections and/or reviews of technical documentation. [CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- An Observation (O-n) is a noteworthy fact, issue and/or risk not directly within the assessment scope that could become a separate issue if not addressed, or alternatively a positive acknowledgement of an organisation's operational structure, tools and/or support. [CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A Recommendation (R-n) is a proposed, measurable stakeholder action directly supported by specific findings and/or observations, intended to correct or mitigate an identified issue or risk. [CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Sections 9.0–12.0 of CAB-02 report no alternate technical opinions, no hardware, software or data packages disseminated outside the report, no recommendations for the NASA Lessons Learned database, and no recommendations for NASA standards, specifications, handbooks or procedures. [CAB-02 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02 findings and observations: material flammability and ISS hardware at elevated O2
- F-12: NASA has limited empirical material flammability data at O2 concentrations above 30 %, but from an analysis of material characteristics many ISS materials are unlikely to meet the requirements at 32–40 % O2: (a) polymeric materials; (b) foam thermal insulations such as Armaflex and Solimide AC-550 polyimide; (c) Bisco HT-200 sound-block silicone and Soundcoat HT polyimide foam; (d) black KB 10 tape, blue duct tape and silicone-fiberglass insulations; (e) flammable paint on metallic substrates; (f) Nomex; (g) polyethylene covered in aluminium foil tape; not reported in this finding: total pressure. [CAB-02 p.83–84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-13: some closed-cell foams exist that would meet flammability requirements in habitable Exploration elements, but apart from Solimide HT-340 no open-cell foam with suitable performance exists at this time. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O-4: minimal flammability data exist at varying O2 concentrations in partial-gravity environments. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-1: no performance, thermal or material impacts were identified for three subsystems: the Pressure Control Assembly (PCA), the Crew Active Dosimeter (CAD) and the Hybrid Electronic Radiation Assessor (HERA). [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-16: the CCAA will not meet performance, thermal or material flammability requirements for the Exploration atmospheres: (a) its slurper bars may lose efficiency because the airflow drag force falls with atmospheric density; (b) the CCAA CHX ORU has foam fully exposed on the rear of the hardware and is unlikely to be acceptable for Exploration because of the material's flammability and surface area. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-18: the CRA may not meet performance requirements and its components will not meet material flammability requirements in the Exploration atmospheres: (a) if sub-ambient-pressure operation is kept as the hazard mitigation for Exploration Sabatier hardware, the reactor pressure would have to drop below 10.2 or 8.3 psia, lowering the Sabatier reaction rate and the performance of the life-support gas-liquid separators; (b) the CRA compressor is a high flammability risk because of its nonmetallic acoustic cover and the many polymeric materials inside it. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-30: the MinION case, cabling and labels are not suitable for the elevated Exploration O2 concentrations. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-31: the ISS risk-acceptance rationale for the flammable vacuum cleaner may not hold at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia and almost certainly will not at 34–40 % O2 and 8.2 psia, because the item is relatively large. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02 findings: fire extinguishers, emergency systems and the O2 Generation Assembly
- F-19: low-pressure atmospheres could change water-spray PFE characteristics, including plume dispersal, water flow rate, required water quantity and the corresponding tank size. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-20: increased O2 concentrations could reduce the ability of all PFEs to extinguish fire. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-21: the designs of the ISS emergency systems are poorly documented in internal and external NASA literature, leaving minimal data from which to assess the existing hardware. [CAB-02 p.85 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-22: the OGA may see significant performance and safety impacts in the Exploration atmospheres: (a) the higher pressure drop across the OGA cells may overcome the protonic drag in the cell stack and let liquid water into the O2 product stream; (b) where cabin O2 is already elevated, an O2 leak from the OGA could create an unacceptable hazard inside a rack, so another hazard mitigation would be needed; (c) a lower recirculation-loop pressure could bring dissolved H2 out of solution, require new rotary-separator accumulator high/low setpoints and push sensors out of range; (d) lower cabin pressure may degrade the OGA H2 sensors and/or make them fail early because of more water in the product O2; (e) ambient O2 in the recirculation loop could collect in the separator during start-up and combine with residual product H2 into a flammability and/or explosion hazard. [CAB-02 p.85 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02 findings and observations: offgassing, monitors and reduced air density
- F-11: more empirical data on how pressure affects toxic offgassing rates are needed to establish whether a correction factor can be applied to existing data for 8.2 psia environments. [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O-2: MAPTIS offgassing data older than 10 years, especially from the 1980s and 1990s, may not reflect current material characteristics because analytical instrument sensitivity and material manufacturing have changed. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O-3: hardware offgassing may be too high in smaller vehicles (11–18 m3), where less volume is available for dilution, and will also be higher at 8.2 psia than at standard test pressures; of particular concern are (a) emergency masks, (b) UWMS hardware, (c) the acoustic monitor, (d) AGA hardware, (e) AQM hardware, (f) CQ composite sandwich panels with Nomex honeycomb core, (g) the Galley Rack PWD aerogel blanket, (h) the Galley Rack Food Warmer melamine foam and (i) the ISS Suitcase Food Warmer melamine foam. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O-5: gas streams that vent to the cabin and carry trace contaminants will raise the risk of odour build-up in Exploration-sized vehicles. [CAB-02 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-26: preliminary testing showed the AGA photoacoustic response is affected at O2 concentrations above 21 %, so contaminants are under-reported; not reported in this finding: total pressure. [CAB-02 p.85 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-27: the AQM may suffer functional and thermal performance impacts in the Exploration environments: (a) elevated O2 may disturb the chromatographic separation and ionization that together set AQM performance; (b) GC column cooling will be less efficient at reduced pressure, so cabin gas analyses will need longer sample times. [CAB-02 p.85 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-28: lower pressure and/or elevated O2 may harm the reagents of the CWQMK and MinION by (a) interfering with the chemical reactions the CWQMK relies on and (b) shortening the shelf life of CWQMK and MinION packaged reagents through faster oxidation. [CAB-02 p.85 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-2: running ISS fans and blowers outside their certification parameters (e.g. in the Exploration atmospheres) will likely cause performance impacts such as excess noise, higher power consumption and/or shorter life. [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-5: a filter whose fibrous structure and porosity are unchanged will have the same or slightly better filtration efficiency at Exploration pressures. [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-6: mechanical devices that reference the cabin atmosphere to operate (e.g. valves, regulators, sensors, bellows and gas-liquid separators) will not perform as expected outside their designed, calibrated and qualified pressure. [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-9 and F-10: the Exploration atmospheres have a lower heat capacity per unit volume because the air is less dense, and they will reduce the ability of equipment to reject heat by convection. [CAB-02 p.83 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- F-14: the AAA fan will not meet thermal performance requirements in the Exploration environments: for the same heat load and temperature limits, the racks will need upwards of 40 % more volume flow at 10.2 psia and upwards of 80 % more at 8.2 psia; not reported in this finding: O2 concentration. [CAB-02 p.84 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-02 Appendix A: how the cabin air properties were calculated
- Density comes from the ideal-gas equation of state, P = ρRT rearranged to ρ = P/(RT), with P the total pressure, ρ the molar density (mol/m3), R the universal gas constant and T the temperature; units of P, R and T and the valid range are not stated. [CAB-02 p.97 · MODELED]
- Water vapour pressure comes from the Antoine equation, log10 P = A − B/(C + T) with T in °C, using A = 8.07131, B = 1730.63 and C = 233.426 for water over T = 1–100 °C; the unit of P is not stated. [CAB-02 p.97 · MODELED]
- Heat capacity uses the polynomial c_P (J/(mol·K)) = A + BT + CT² + DT³ with constants from Perry's Chemical Engineering Handbook, and the gas mixture's heat capacity is taken as the molar average of its constituents; the unit of T and the valid range are not stated. [CAB-02 p.97 · MODELED · nominal]

| Species (unlabelled constants table, from Perry's) | MW | A | B | C | D | Cp at 22 °C (J/mol-K) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| O2 | 32 | 28.11 | -3.70E-06 | 1.75E-05 | 1.07E-08 | 2.99E+01 | [CAB-02 p.97 · CITED] |
| N2 | 28 | 31.15 | -0.01357 | 2.68E-05 | -1.17E-08 | 2.92E+01 | [CAB-02 p.97 · CITED] |
| H2O(g) | 18 | 3.22E+01 | 0.001924 | 1.06E-05 | -3.60E-09 | 3.36E+01 | [CAB-02 p.97 · CITED] |

- Relative humidity: the dew point follows from the modified Raoult's law P·y_w = P_w^sat(T)·γ_w·x_w (P total pressure, y_w mole fraction of water in the gas, P_w^sat the saturation pressure of water from the Antoine equation, γ_w the activity coefficient for non-ideal mixtures; x_w not defined in words); only liquid water is taken as condensable, so γ_w = 1 = x_w and the saturation partial pressure equals the Antoine vapour pressure; then %rH = P_w / P_w^sat(T) × 100 % and y_w(rH, T) = (%rH/100)·P_w^sat(T)/P_total (P_w not defined in words). [CAB-02 p.97–98 · MODELED · nominal]
- Gas composition: the O2 mole fraction is specified (21 % at 14.7 psia, 26.5 % at 10.2 psia, 34 % at 8.2 psia), the water mole fraction follows from a chosen temperature and RH, y_N2 = 1 − y_O2 − y_w, and the mixture MW and c_P are molar averages (Σ y_i·MW_i, Σ y_i·C_p,i). [CAB-02 p.98 · MODELED · nominal]
- Specific humidity, the mass of water vapour per mass of dry air on a 1-mol basis, is sH = y_w·MW_w / (y_O2·MW_O2 + y_N2·MW_N2). [CAB-02 p.98 · MODELED]
- CAB-02 notes that specific humidity is hard to compare between atmospheres of different composition (there is less absolute N2 in the Exploration atmospheres), which is why it also uses absolute humidity, the total mass of water vapour per unit volume. [CAB-02 p.98 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Absolute humidity on a 1 m3 basis: n_total = P_total/(RT), n_w = n_total·y_w and aH = n_w·MW_w, in g/m3. [CAB-02 p.98 · MODELED]
- Psychrometric charts were generated with these equations for each cabin pressure and O2 composition, with temperature on the x-axis, specific humidity on the y-axis and absolute humidity marked for one condition. [CAB-02 p.99 · MODELED · nominal]
- For the same temperature and RH, specific humidity (and the water mole fraction) changes with pressure while the dew-point temperature and absolute humidity stay the same in every atmosphere; Fig. A-4 shows this in three panels ("8.3psia", "10.2psia" and "14.7 psia saturation curve"; T in °F vs specific humidity in g H2O/g dry air; saturation and 20, 40, 60 and 80 % rH curves), each annotated "11.1g H2O/m^3 at saturation (55F)"; O2 concentration is not printed on the figure. [CAB-02 p.99 · MODELED; CAB-02 p.103 · Fig. A-4 · MODELED · ~fig]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

### CAB-02 Appendix A: Avionics Air Assembly (AAA) maximum air temperature
- Assuming a constant avionics heat load in the ISS and Exploration environments, the same blower volume flow through the racks (so a lower mass flow), steady-state heat transfer, the ISS nominal rack inlet of 72 °F and maximum outlet of 109 °F, density from the ideal-gas law at 22 °C, Cp from empirical data and a composition of 40 % rH at 22 °C, CAB-02 estimates the AAA maximum rack air temperature at 136 °F for 8.3 psia / 34 % O2, from ((41 × 29 × 20)/(23 × 29) + 22) × 9/5 + 32, and at 123 °F for 10.2 psia / 26.5 % O2, from ((41 × 29 × 20)/(29 × 29) + 22) × 9/5 + 32 (the inputs 41, 29, 20, 23 and 29 are printed without labels). [CAB-02 p.103 · MODELED · nominal]
- The calculation sets Q_ISS = Q_Exploration, i.e. V̇·ρ_ISS·c_p,ISS·ΔT_ISS = V̇·ρ_exp·c_p,exp·ΔT_exp, so ΔT_exp = ρ_ISS·c_p,ISS·ΔT_ISS / (ρ_exp·c_p,exp) and T_max,exploration = ΔT_exp + T_min,AAA; symbols are not defined beyond the assumptions (volume flow rate, density, Cp) and their units are not stated. [CAB-02 p.103 · MODELED]

### CAB-02 Appendix: informal meeting notes on hardware in the Exploration atmospheres
- Trace Contaminant Control System notes (05/05/2021): there is a small risk of a carbon-bed fire, particularly in a 34 % O2 environment, and a very large risk if regenerative beds are desorbed by temperature/pressure swing; total pressure not stated in these notes. [CAB-02 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.91 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The same notes recount, without a reference, a Mir case in which Russian beds were used regeneratively and cabin air was passed over a freshly regenerated bed before it had cooled enough: a bed fire broke out, causing a large cloud of smoke and CO poisoning of the crew; bed material, O2 concentration, total pressure and airflow are not stated. [CAB-02 p.109 · CITED]
- The same notes state that TCCS input loads, including crew and equipment offgassing, will not be affected by pressure, because appreciable increases in offgassing occur only near or at hard vacuum (outgassing). [CAB-02 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- O2 Generation Assembly notes (06/28/2021): the cell stack and RSA (not defined) sit in a dome exposed to vacuum for safety, and the N2, feedwater and recirculation-loop pressures are all above 20 psia, so no impacts are expected from low pressure and leakage in or out could even decrease; cabin O2 and total pressure not stated in this note. [CAB-02 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.90 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The OGA O2 outlet, and with it the O2 side of the cell stack, is open to the cabin atmosphere, so the lower pressure could affect the outlet H2 sensors and, unlikely, cell performance. [CAB-02 p.109–110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The OGA H2 sensors detect H2 from the temperature change of the O2/H2 reaction over catalytic beads and will likely need recalibration for the new thermal environment. [CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The simplest solution noted is a back-pressure regulator on the O2 vent to hold 14.7 psia, which could give a less than optimal design; a lower O2 vent pressure could lower the MDP (not defined) set by the initiating detonation pressure; vent pressure values not stated. [CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The detonation risk from ambient O2 leaking into the OGA needs to be understood with leak rates and material balances. [CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The AAA drives air through the OGA rack to dilute O2 in a possible loss-of-containment event, and the 06/28/2021 notes give a maximum O2 of 29 % after dilution in the rack, to be assessed and updated; cabin total pressure and cabin O2 for this value not stated. [CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.109 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- Notes of the NESC discussion with Boeing and Collins (01/02/2021) say the AAA mixing in the OGS rack (OGS not defined) keeps a potential O2 release below 28 % maximum concentration, and that this has to be updated for Exploration O2 concentrations (analysis); cabin total pressure and cabin O2 for this value not stated. [CAB-02 p.111 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The same 01/02/2021 notes on the OGA: a back-pressure regulator on the O2 vent could raise the anode cell pressure to its nominal ISS pressure, so the recirculation-loop pressure would not have to be lowered (lowering it would violate hazard controls); the hydrogen sensors in the O2 vent line need reassessment and possibly lower-pressure testing, depending on OGA configuration; the hazard analyses assume O2 vent or leak dilution in the rack keeps the environment safe, and dilution at lower pressure / higher O2 ambient needs to be evaluated (analysis). [CAB-02 p.111 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The same 01/02/2021 notes state that the AAA uses open-cell acoustic insulations that pass flammability only up to ~32 % O2, that this insulation is also used in many other hardware items, and that replacement materials need development and testing; total pressure, flammability test method, thickness and gravity level not stated. [CAB-02 p.111 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The same notes on air movers: the CCAA can nominally deliver 500 cfm but only 300 cfm in the airlock at 10.2 psia (density effects not counted) because the CHiPS filters (not defined) restrict it; the airlock CCAA is currently working well; a test up to 500 cfm at 10.2 psia would need the CHiPS filters replaced with HEPA filters; airlock O2 concentration not stated. [CAB-02 p.112 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.110 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- The IMV will not need higher speeds, because only a constant volume flow is required. [CAB-02 p.112 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
### CAB-03: why fire-resistant textiles matter in enriched-O2 cabins
- Material selection is a key part of NASA's spacecraft fire safety management plan; non-flammable textiles are needed so that large-scale flame propagation events do not occur inside a spacecraft, and fire-resistant textiles also serve as a hazard control that protects more flammable materials from ignition. [CAB-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Greater use of textiles and other softgoods (textiles valued in space for being light and flexible) is crucial for exploration spaceflight, to reduce mass and volume. [CAB-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Enriched-O2 cabins (>21 % O2) benefit exploration missions by allowing a shorter prebreathe before EVA, but materials become exponentially more flammable as O2 rises; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Recent agency testing revealed a lack of COTS materials that meet safety requirements in O2-enriched environments: the testing of the last three years found only limited COTS textiles that can be certified for use in up to 37 % O2; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-03 attributes this to the fact that most fibres and textiles developed for Apollo (100 % O2 cabin) and Skylab (>70 % O2 cabin) are no longer commercially available, because those programs ended and raw materials were discontinued or the original manufacturers closed. [CAB-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Commercial development of textiles with high flammability performance beyond 21 % O2 is usually not economical because the customer base is small: the fire-service market (clothing for firefighters, police and military; non-wearable fire barriers in commercial airplanes and batteries) is strong but never needs performance at 37 % O2, so textiles for the exploration atmosphere are a niche market. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As fire-resistant textiles are a key part of the fire-prevention strategy that includes materials selection, and NASA is returning to higher O2 inside spacecraft, development of in-cabin textiles for the lunar and Martian surface atmosphere has begun, reducing the highest risks first and favouring the development paths most likely to meet flammability and application requirements. [CAB-03 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-03: the exploration cabin atmosphere and the 37 % O2 certification target
- A 2021 memorandum of the Deputy Associate Administrator for Human Exploration and Operations (HEO) Systems Engineering & Integration (ref. [1]) set a common habitable atmosphere for human exploration and designated 8.2 psia total pressure with 33.7 % O2 by volume for operations on the lunar and Martian surfaces. [CAB-03 p.2 · CITED · nominal]
- The aim was to reduce flammability risk while keeping the prebreathe before EVA short, given the short missions planned on the lunar surface. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This atmosphere is a significant departure from the essentially Earth atmosphere kept in the habitable volumes of other current NASA crewed vehicles and programs such as the ISS, and it has serious implications for the flight materials now in use. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In 2024, Revision B of the Moon to Mars Architecture Definition Document (ref. [2]) listed "Non-flammable Materials, Additives, Coatings for Habitable Volumes" as an architecture-driven child gap within the overall gap of fire safety upgrades for surviving exploration mission environments. [CAB-03 p.2 · CITED]
- CAB-03 reads that listing as showing that the need to develop fire-resistant textiles persists. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With Artemis missions moving to high-O2 cabins (>30 % O2 by volume), CAB-03 sees a significant need for better fire-resistant textiles for in-cabin softgoods, to inhibit flame propagation in high-O2 atmospheres and keep the mission safe in the event of a fire; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The agency's focus is now on certifying textiles for 34 % O2 plus a 3 % margin, a target of 37 % O2; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### CAB-03: earlier enriched-O2 programs
- Artemis is not the first program with an enriched-O2 atmosphere: Apollo started in 100 % O2 and Skylab operated at >70 % O2, and in such atmospheres materials not normally considered flammable ignite easily and spread flame much faster than in Earth's atmosphere; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Fire-resistant textile development for Apollo began after the fatal Apollo 1 cabin fire, whose most probable ignition source was electrical arcing of wires carrying spacecraft power; that cabin held 100 % O2 at 16.7 psia, 2 psia above standard sea-level pressure and more than five times the 3 psia (21 kPa) O2 partial pressure of Earth's atmosphere. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### CAB-03: textiles in use on the ISS
- ISS nonclothing softgoods (acoustic blankets, cargo transfer bags (CTBs), webbings, sleeping bags) are made mostly of Kevlar, Nomex, Vectran and hybrid blends, and cotton is widely used for next-to-skin shirts. [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Because the ISS cabin atmosphere is the same as Earth's, ISS crew clothing uses polyester/cotton for daily wear and polyester/nylon for exercise; crew pants, for example, are 65 % polyester and 35 % cotton coated in Teflon for stain and wrinkle resistance, with several zippered and hook-and-loop pockets to hold small items on orbit. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- CAB-03 says most fabrics commonly used on the ISS may not be usable in their current form in the new exploration atmosphere because of its higher O2 (p.2), and that most ISS softgoods will not be usable for Artemis missions (p.4). [CAB-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- To close this gap for the first Artemis lunar-surface missions, textile and materials engineers have tested a significant number of textiles, individually and in layups that match specific applications. [CAB-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- New fire-resistant materials have been introduced for crew clothing, sleeping bags and CTBs and will fly for the first time on the coming Artemis missions; the textile engineering and development team sources existing COTS products, modifies COTS textiles and develops custom fire-resistant solutions to meet NASA flammability requirements at 37 % O2 and 8.2 psia. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### CAB-03: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 as CAB-03 describes it
- NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (Upward Flame Propagation) is the test NASA currently uses to evaluate and certify the flammability of materials for the habitable environments of spacecraft (ref. [9], NASA-STD-6001, revision not given). [CAB-03 p.3 · CITED]
- In Test 1 a vertical specimen (typical size 2.5 in × 17 in) is exposed at its bottom to a chemical igniter flame for about 25–30 s, in a closed 1400-liter chamber with O2 concentration and pressure controlled to represent spacecraft conditions. [CAB-03 p.3 · CITED · nominal]
- Pass criteria: none of the five required specimens burns more than 6 in, and no specimen propagates flame by transferring burning debris. [CAB-03 p.3 · CITED]
- Test 1 can be run as a single-setpoint test, with five consecutive specimens at a set O2 concentration and pressure to verify whether the material passes, and so can be certified for flight, at that atmosphere; or as a maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) test, with the chamber pressure fixed and O2 raised step by step until the sample fails, the MOC being the highest O2 percentage at which the material passes. [CAB-03 p.3 · CITED]
- A higher MOC indicates a more fire-resistant material. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The typical configuration, Standard Edge Ignition, holds the sample vertical and ignites its bottom edge; it is the most conservative method and suits all materials, especially composites or hard panels, but may be unrealistically severe for textiles because raw textile edges are usually not exposed in a softgoods assembly; it is recommended where the textile edge is directly exposed, as on a tether or tie-down strap. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most textiles that will be part of a softgoods assembly are tested in the "J"-configuration: the specimen hangs vertically with a J-shaped bend at the bottom, and the igniter at the bottom of the "J" ignites the specimen surface, giving fully vertical upward propagation without igniting the edge; a metal fixture can also shield the vertical edges when the material will have no exposed side or bottom edges in use. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The "J" set-up suits non-metallic materials with no exposed raw edges in use, and it needs additional verification of seam configurations. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-03: configuration and layup effects
- A July 2024 memo by Dr. Emily Hacopian, NASA Cross Program Flammability Subject Matter Expert (ref. [10]), captured the complexities of flammability in the exploration atmosphere and cautioned that materials may be more flammable in their as-used configuration, so test results must be interpreted with care. [CAB-03 p.3 · CITED]
- Recent coupon-level flammability testing at 37 % O2 (unpublished data) shows that propagation differs between configuration and layup tests and single-material tests; materials and forms, total pressure, gravity level and platform, diluent, flow, ignition method and location, enclosure, ambient temperature, one- or two-sided burning and test duration not stated. [CAB-03 p.3 · MEASURED]
- CAB-03 concludes that the combined performance of the textile components (e.g. zipper, thread, hook and loop), not only of the outermost layer, must be fire-resistant. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-03 notes that the PTFE fabric is less flammable than cotton, its layup partner in Fig. 1b. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Overall, recent testing found very few textiles able to pass NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at 37 % O2 and 8.2 psia, and textiles that pass on their own may still fail in a configuration with other textiles. [CAB-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Hardware used in flight as a fire hazard control to protect flammable materials from ignition (e.g. a CTB) must pass Fire Barrier Effectiveness Testing in addition to Test 1, and the Fire Barrier Effectiveness method is still being developed. [CAB-03 p.3–4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### CAB-03: crew clothing, CTBs, sleeping bags, shirts and patches
- Crew clothing is the specialised apparel and daily attire astronauts wear in the cabin during a mission, typically jackets, T-shirts and pants. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The new crew clothing was designed to maximise agility, comfort and functionality while meeting flammability standards in a high-O2 environment; after flammability, the top concern was offgassing, because low toxicity is critical for crew health in the closed cabin; fabrics also had to offer soft handfeel, comfort and light weight, which were deemed critical when candidates were compared. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The evaluation showed that a commercially available blend of para-aramid, meta-aramid and antistatic fibres can be a suitable candidate for outer garments such as jackets and pants. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This fabric is adequate for short-duration outer garments, but for long-duration missions (>9 days) a lighter, softer and more flexible fabric would be desired. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CTBs are softgoods containers used to stow, transport and protect hardware and supplies; on the ISS they have been used extensively for decades and are typically made of meta-aramid and polyester. [CAB-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In O2-enriched cabins CTBs are a particular fire safety challenge because they also act as a fire hazard control, protecting flammable contents from ignition and preventing large fire propagation when exposed to external ignition sources; so, besides NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 flame propagation testing, fire barrier effectiveness testing verifies that CTB materials protect the contents from an external ignition source. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- CTB materials must also be strong, durable, light and available in several colours for operational and human-factors needs, which makes suitable textiles for O2-enriched cabins hard to find. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The current CTB construction is mainly multilayer: outer and inner woven fabric layers sandwiching a felt layer. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- CTB candidates under evaluation: woven layers of para-aramid/meta-aramid/antistatic blend, 100 % meta-aramid, and PBI/Kevlar blend fabrics; felt layers of oxidized polyacrylonitrile (OPF), polyimide, silica, polyetherimide and various blends. [CAB-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- CTB down-selection also weighs dimensional stability, minimal foreign object debris (FOD) and the final bag weight, because with many CTBs manifested on some missions even modest increases in bag mass add up to a significant system-level weight; the development seeks to balance fire safety with mechanical robustness and mass efficiency. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The team is developing fire-resistant solutions for a sleeping bag that meets NASA flammability requirements at 37 % O2 and 8.2 psia. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The current ISS sleeping bag has Nomex attachment loops tied down with Vectran braid cord to attachment points in the cabin, a Nomex outer layer, a replaceable cotton inner layer secured with hook and loop, a head strap, a pillow pocket that can be stuffed with soft items, and arm and foot slits for air flow and for letting body heat and moisture escape. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The fire-resistant sleeping bag approach centres on a suitable layup with a soft, comfortable interior, a covered COTS narrow woven elastic webbing as head restraint, and alternative fire-resistant attachment loops and braid cord. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The team is working with vendors on a braid cord that meets NASA flammability requirements at 37 % O2; Kevlar EXO, "Poly-p- phenylenebenzioboxine" (PBO, as printed), PTFE and silicone-coated fiberglass are among the cord materials in the ongoing down-selection; total pressure not stated in this statement. [CAB-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Braid cord must also meet load requirements. [CAB-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For the next-to-skin crew T-shirt the team worked with a yarn-spinning vendor specialised in high-performance fibre spun yarns for the fire-service and safety-protection markets, with a rare worsted-spinning capability, and another vendor that, after several trials, knitted the 100 % PBI spun yarn into a soft, comfortable, relatively light 1×1 rib fabric. [CAB-03 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The PBI T-shirt is to replace the ISS cotton next-to-skin shirts, which are unsuitable for flammability on the high-O2 Artemis missions; besides its flammability performance, PBI offers good handfeel, soft touch and high moisture absorption, but its low fibre tenacity and reduced durability make it prone to pilling and less abrasion-resistant. [CAB-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-03: NESC strategy for nonflammable cabin textiles
- In November 2022 the Exploration Atmosphere Issue Resolution Team (ExAtm IRT) was formed after concerns about operating in O2-rich environments reached agency management; it sought a balance between competing mission variables such as vehicle atmosphere, flammability, decompression sickness risk, suit pressure and EVA duration. [CAB-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ExAtm IRT asked the NESC to set up an assessment and a multi-program strategy to develop high-priority nonflammable textiles for in-cabin softgoods at a minimum of 37 % O2 at 8.2 psia; programs such as the Human Landing System (HLS) and the Extravehicular Activity and Human Surface Mobility Program (EHP) can use these textiles to design hardware that inhibits flame propagation in enriched O2. [CAB-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The assessment plan had four tasks: identify stakeholders that need O2-enriched environments and collect their key performance and safety parameters; determine material requirements, applications and program priorities; assess the NASA and industry state of the art and opportunities for fire-resistant textiles; and develop a prioritised strategy and implementation plan. [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Stakeholders, broadly anyone with input into the strategy's priorities (flight operations, health and medical, softgoods, textiles, O2 and systems engineering), were queried in person to identify cabin applications, the material properties they need and top softgoods and textile priorities, capturing NASA's in-cabin textile needs at elevated O2. [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Textile priority considered how many applications use the textile, how much area or length is used in the cabin, whether an adequate solution exists, the impact on flammability risk, whether it is needed for government furnished equipment (GFE), and whether it or its application was a stakeholder concern; the list was split into Tier 1 (higher priority) and Tier 2 (lower priority). [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The state-of-the-art survey used textile SMEs' own knowledge, reviews of DoD, academic and textile-association fire-resistant developments, a contracted technology search, trade shows and about 30 domestic vendor visits, plus a review of Apollo- and Space Shuttle-era textile development to see which textiles are still available and which past resources were used. [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Over 100 supply-chain vendors were identified; after a discussion with each and brief interviews of a shorter list, the team down-selected about 30 high-potential US textile manufacturers for on-site visits, judging suitability mainly by textile capability (market-sector industrial scale, equipment versatility and R&D interests) and also by the ability to offer a low minimum order quantity (MOQ). [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The NESC strategy has three phases per textile: Phase 1, baseline testing of available COTS products to confirm whether any can be certified at 37 % O2 / 8.2 psia, with certification testing at White Sands Test Facility (WSTF); Phase 2, incremental improvement or modification of a COTS product when none passes NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 but a relatively small effort could raise its chance of passing, followed by re-assessment; Phase 3, a major custom development with an industrial partner when no COTS product passes and incremental improvement is not possible. [CAB-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- A go/no-go decision closes each phase and not every textile goes through all three: Phase 1 may be skipped when no COTS product exists or available products have already been tested; Phase 2 when no modification method is known or one is already identified and in use; Phase 3 when no industrial partner is willing to work with NASA on that textile or the first two phases met the need. [CAB-03 p.7–8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-03 concludes that fire-resistant textiles will stay a critical agency priority as NASA seeks to cut mass and volume in exploration vehicles with enriched-O2 cabins of up to 37 % O2 at 8.2 psia. [CAB-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA's textile team has made meaningful progress by identifying suitable COTS materials and advancing new textiles for urgent softgoods needs (crew clothing, CTBs, sleeping bags; the sentence is printed twice in a row), but further material optimisation is needed for durability, reliability and performance on extended-duration missions. [CAB-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- To close these gaps the NESC has completed an agency-wide assessment and developed the multi-program strategy, whose execution is the next phase, starting with the Tier 1 highest-priority textile systems. [CAB-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
### CAB-04: lunar surface-vehicle atmospheres, scope and open issues
- NASA and its commercial Artemis providers are still working to address and reduce flammability concerns at the atmospheres planned for lunar-surface vehicles. [CAB-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The difficulty lies in the tight coupling of materials flammability, ignition control, fire mitigation, human physiology and performance, and suit mobility and performance; earlier NASA recommendations on vehicle atmospheres flagged some of these as open work that was never funded to completion. [CAB-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-04 expects this work to shape the flight-certification path of the surface missions and to improve development and certification by covering partial-gravity effects on flammability, ignition guidelines, fire barrier effectiveness, vehicle configuration constraints and revised standards for materials flammability, so that later surface elements and missions can follow a similar process with shorter development, lower flammability risk and clear certification guidance. [CAB-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Recent vehicle and suit design work let the team question long-held norms and assumptions, potentially adding mission flexibility through better fire suppression, higher suit operating pressures and advanced vehicle environmental control systems. [CAB-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The team also found standards or guidelines lacking for cumulative mission decompression-sickness risk and for partial-gravity compensation factors. [CAB-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-04 abbreviations: Station = International Space Station; Station Suit = the ISS/Shuttle Extravehicular Mobility Unit; xEMU = Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit; MOC = Maximum Oxygen Concentration; HLS = Human Landing System Program; EHP = Extravehicular Activity and Human Surface Mobility Program. [CAB-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-04: sea-level, ISS and Artemis vehicle atmospheres
- CAB-04 calls the gas mixture inside a habitable volume or spacesuit its "atmosphere" and treats a safe, breathable one as essential to human spaceflight. [CAB-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At sea level Earth's air averages 14.7 psi (101.3 kPa) and is roughly 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen plus small amounts of other gases (ref. [1]). [CAB-04 p.3 · CITED · nominal]
- Spaceflight systems keep various pressures and gas ratios, set mainly by the O2 concentration, to suit their own needs. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The ISS keeps a near-sea-level atmosphere at around 21 % O2, while its EVA suits run on pure O2 at a much lower pressure. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Lower suit pressure makes moving easier for the astronaut, since the pressure difference to vacuum shrinks, but it is habitable only with an O2-rich gas; more O2 also raises fire risk, which suits counter with special materials and by limiting ignition sources. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- NASA is evaluating the atmosphere trade space across the many systems that must work together for Moon and Mars exploration, and choosing atmospheres and related procedures such as prebreathe protocols means balancing trade-offs for safety and operational flexibility. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For sustained missions, NASA Artemis requirements target an average of 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) with 34 % O2 as one answer to those trade-offs. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- CAB-04 notes that less is known about O2 concentrations above 30 %, which raises flammability concerns. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For that reason NASA teams have also tested with a vehicle atmosphere held under 30 % O2: an average of 9.6 psi (66.2 kPa) with 28.5 % O2 (ref. [2]). [CAB-04 p.3 · CITED · nominal]
- Fig. 1 compares sea-level air with an example lunar surface vehicle atmosphere as two pie graphics ("SEA LEVEL", "SURFACE HAB"), each split into O2, N2 and "other" slices over concentric 5-, 10- and 15-psi rings; the example's pressure and O2 are not printed, and read from the schematic the "SURFACE HAB" pie reaches about 9 psi (±2.5 psi) and its oxygen sector covers about 28 % (estimated ±3 percentage points; the "other" share cannot be read). [CAB-04 p.3 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ~fig]

### CAB-04: how the atmosphere drives material flammability
- Vehicle and suit atmospheres have to balance crew physiology, suit mobility, EVA duration and flammability, each of which affects crew health, safety and the ability to meet exploration goals. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flammability depends on the atmosphere: a material that is not flammable at sea level can be a hazard at another pressure or O2 concentration. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As an example, the Apollo 1 fire was made worse by the higher flammability of the command-module materials in its high-pressure, pure-O2 atmosphere (ref. [3]); materials, pressure value, flow and ignition not stated. [CAB-04 p.3 · CITED]
- In general, a higher O2 concentration and/or O2 partial pressure means a higher flammability risk. [CAB-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Historically, ISS on-board materials were tested to a 30 % maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) at sea-level pressure, a margin covering life-support control and error bands among other things (ref. [4]). [CAB-04 p.3 · CITED · nominal]
- Above 30 % O2, or at higher O2 partial pressure, some materials are less likely to pass testing because they become more flammable; materials, test method and pressure not stated. [CAB-04 p.3–4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For that reason, materials meant for the 34 % atmosphere have typically been tested up to 37 % O2; total pressure and test method of these tests not stated. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The chosen atmosphere and the construction materials inform each other: a desired O2 concentration or partial pressure may restrict material choice, and the atmosphere also sets the fire prevention and mitigation systems (ignition control, fire suppression). [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA and its partners are studying new materials, such as textiles, that are safer over a range of O2 concentrations, which brings many technical challenges; even with better materials, flammability stays a concern in high-O2 operation and will drive many EVA and cabin-atmosphere design considerations, requirements and procedures. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-04: crew physiology, prebreathe and spacesuits
- The life support system of a spacecraft or suit has to keep the crew safe and healthy for the whole mission: enough O2, and control of exhaled gases such as CO2, which is toxic in excess; O2 itself needs balance, since too little causes hypoxia and too much causes oxygen toxicity. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- N2 in the vehicle atmosphere can cause decompression sickness, so removing as much of it as possible from the body (denitrogenation) before an EVA is an advantage. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA O2 partial-pressure standards cap how hypoxic a crew atmosphere may be; they rest on limited historical flight and test data that do not try to quantify health or performance loss from long hypoxia exposure or from adjusted limits, and the NASA community is researching acceptable hypoxia limits. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Spaceflight systems must also limit the rate of pressure changes, because fast changes can injure the body, the ears and lungs among others. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On ISS expeditions the aim is science, mostly done inside the vehicle, with EVAs used mainly for replacements and repairs; on a surface mission EVAs are the main aim. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most tasks of an EVA day (private medical conferences, sleep, battery charging, suit and tool configuration) are set independently of the vehicle, but EVA preparation includes prebreathe, which depends on the vehicle atmosphere, O2 saturation and other factors (ref. [6]). [CAB-04 p.4 · CITED]
- Prebreathe is time spent at a higher O2 concentration so the body can expel dissolved N2 and avoid decompression sickness before an EVA ("the bends" to SCUBA divers). [CAB-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-04 p.4–5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Decompression sickness symptoms range from minor joint pain to neurological damage (ref. [7]). [CAB-04 p.5 · CITED]
- A lower vehicle pressure can shorten prebreathe by lowering the initial dissolved N2 in the body, but it usually needs a higher O2 concentration, and so a higher flammability risk, to prevent hypoxia; a shorter prebreathe translates directly into more EVA time. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Spacesuits often run a different atmosphere from spacecraft and habitats: higher suit pressure makes a suit stiffer and more tiring to work in, needs stronger brackets and hardware (more mass) and wears the hardware faster, so suits are best operated at the lowest possible pressure, which in turn needs higher O2 to avoid hypoxia. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| Suit (CAB-04) | Suit pressure | Suit O2 | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apollo suits | 3.75 psi (25.8 kPa) | 100 % | [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
| Station Suit (Extravehicular Mobility Unit of the Shuttle program and the ISS) | 4.3 psi (29.6 kPa) | 100 % (ref. [8]) | [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-04 p.5 · CITED · nominal] |
| Orlan (Russian, also used on the ISS) | 5.7 psi (39.2 kPa) | 100 % (ref. [8]) | [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-04 p.5 · CITED · nominal] |
| xEMU, under development and test by NASA and commercial partners for Artemis | test atmospheres from 4.3 psi (29.6 kPa) to 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) (ref. [9]) | not stated | [CAB-04 p.5 · CITED · nominal] |

- Fig. 3 shows the Apollo and Station (US) suit atmospheres as all-oxygen pie graphics against rings labelled 5, 10 and 15 psi. [CAB-04 p.5 · Fig. 3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- On 100 % O2, a higher suit pressure can shorten prebreathe, because less N2 has to be expelled, and so allow longer EVAs, but it costs suit flexibility and mobility. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Suited EVA performance tests repeated at several suit pressures could feed a cost function relating a suit-pressure increase to crew workload, fatigue and task duration, to be weighed against the prebreathe options in a risk trade; suit engineers and mission planners must balance decompression-sickness risk, the operational burden of prebreathe and suit mobility. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Suits for EVAs on planetary bodies have other mobility requirements than suits made only for microgravity, and design and atmosphere may differ by destination, e.g. Mars EVAs versus lunar EVAs. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-04: compatible atmospheres across the Moon to Mars architecture
- The Moon to Mars Architecture includes many human-rated systems from many providers and partners (Orion, the Human Landing System, the Pressurized Rover, spacesuits, surface habitats); because crews must move smoothly between them, their atmospheres must be compatible: vehicles that dock or berth in cislunar space (Orion, Gateway, HLS) need similar atmospheres for crew transfer, and lunar surface habitats need atmospheres that allow transfer into suits for EVAs. [CAB-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Moving between systems and atmospheres is an operational issue for the architecture: prebreathe length depends on how far the spacecraft and suit atmospheres differ, and since surface assets may run different atmospheres and EVA cadence varies, no single prebreathe protocol fits every case; a long prebreathe limits EVA opportunities, while a short one made possible by higher suit pressure can raise the risk of crew fatigue and injury. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA aims to minimise prebreathe time to maximise astronaut utilisation (e.g. science or technology demonstrations during an EVA) while keeping the crew safe (ref. [10]). [CAB-04 p.6 · CITED]
- NASA would ultimately like protocols comparable to SCUBA dive tables, giving a set of safe pressures, O2 concentrations and prebreathe times for planning EVAs across varied exploration needs. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The decompression-sickness risk-estimation tool being developed for this is the Aerospace Estimation Tool for Hypobaric Exposure Risk (AETHER) (ref. [11]). [CAB-04 p.6 · CITED]
- Decompression sickness combines a gas phase in the tissues (venous gas emboli) with the human perception of pain, so probabilistic models of decompression sickness and venous gas emboli need a large body of test data for validation (ref. [12]). [CAB-04 p.6 · CITED]

### CAB-04: design flow-down, partial gravity and Mars
- Atmosphere requirements flow down into overall system design and pre-flight testing; with several systems from different providers (launch vehicles, landers, habitation modules), compatible atmospheres become a key design concern, and spacecraft must monitor and adjust their gas ratios to hold the intended balance. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- More accurate and reliable ECLSS sensors and gas injection could shrink O2 concentration excursions and so narrow the boundaries used for material flammability testing, meaning more materials might pass; O2 and pressure values, materials and test method not stated. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Maximum-pressure requirements also influence the design and mass of a system's structure. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Suit pressure has to balance prebreathe needs against astronaut fatigue, mobility and suit life cycle (wear and tear), and these architecture factors, including the character of each destination, will drive many design choices. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-04 counts commonality across multi-system architectures, where practical, as a design factor, since atmosphere set points, the resulting prebreathe protocols and even fire mitigations chosen independently could add operational complexity in crew and ground-operator training. [CAB-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA has broad experience with microgravity spacewalks (e.g. in low Earth orbit) and a good understanding of crew physiology there, but far less operational experience in partial gravity, which comes only from the lunar landings of the 1960s and 1970s. [CAB-04 p.6–7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As partial-gravity experience grows, atmospheres (e.g. for the HLS and spacesuits) may change to better suit partial-gravity effects on the body and on surface assets; pressure and O2 values not stated. [CAB-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Many lunar systems carry over to Mars, but environmental differences may lead to design differences: Mars's atmosphere, with less pressure than Earth's but more than the lunar vacuum, may call for different habitat and suit atmospheres (values not stated); in Martian gravity the factors governing flame blow-off will differ (material, O2, pressure and flow not stated), and the suit's on-back mass and centre of gravity will weigh even more on crew fatigue during spacewalks. [CAB-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### CAB-04: early Artemis atmosphere options and conclusions
- For the first crewed Moon landings in over 40 years, NASA and its commercial Artemis providers are developing several architecture options to enable surface EVAs, and NASA has evaluated several prebreathe protocols for the early missions using the Table 1 variables. [CAB-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; CAB-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| CAB-04 Table 1 variable (group as printed) | Option 1 | Option 2 | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicle pressure (Vehicle Atmospheric Variables) | 8.2 psi | 9.6 psi | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
| Vehicle MOC (Vehicle Atmospheric Variables) | 37 % | 30 % | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
| Partial pressure of inspired oxygen, PiO2 (Physiological Variables) | 2.46 psi | 2.22 psi * (* being evaluated as a mildly hypoxic atmosphere, not yet approved) | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
| Suit pressure ("Suit Atmosphereic Variables" as printed) | 4.3 psi | 5.2 psi † († being evaluated as an elevated suit pressure, not yet approved) | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |

| CAB-04 Table 2 (early Artemis mission architecture examples) | Vehicle pressure | Vehicle MOC | PiO2 | Suit pressure | Prebreathe time | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture 1 | 8.2 psi | 37 % | 2.46 psi | 4.3 psi | ~50 min ‡ (‡ protocol based on modelling and indirect testing, not yet tested) | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
| Architecture 2 | 9.6 psi | 30 % | 2.46 psi | 5.2 psi | ~50 min | [CAB-04 p.8 · Table 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |

- CAB-04 concludes that no single atmosphere suits every vehicle and suit: a multi-partner architecture that keeps risk low and utilisation time high needs robust, flexible systems able to work in and connect with many others, so NASA should award contracts and settle standards with its providers with that flexibility in mind instead of dictating specific atmospheres or operational requirements. [CAB-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As NASA gains partial-gravity operating experience it will refine its approaches, which CAB-04 sees as enabling a lasting presence at the Moon Base and the first crewed trips to Mars. [CAB-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Key takeaways: vehicle and suit atmospheres are central to crew health and safety as the gas the crew breathes; choosing one means weighing risks such as fire and decompression sickness against suit mobility and EVA duration; exploration systems need safe, compatible atmospheres that let crews move between elements; partial gravity on the Moon or Mars may affect human physiology in ways NASA still has to understand, despite its long microgravity experience; and NASA will manage Artemis and Mars atmospheres through many trade-offs, keeping the flexibility to use a range of atmospheres for different uses. [CAB-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### OVR-03: cabin atmospheres and the normoxic curve (2008 view)
- For future missions NASA planned to raise the O2 concentration and lower the total pressure in the Orion crew exploration vehicle, the Altair lander and future lunar habitats (ref. 1). [OVR-03 p.5 · CITED · nominal]
- Such an atmosphere needs less inert gas (N2) mass, lowers vehicle internal pressures and shortens or removes the prebreathe needed to purge N2 from the blood before EVA, but its significant drawback is higher material flammability. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A major lesson of the Apollo 1 fire is that not every ignition source can be eliminated (ref. 2), so spacecraft fire prevention relies on material control and fire-resistant materials. [OVR-03 p.5 · CITED]
- Since Skylab, the Shuttle and the ISS have run at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21 % O2 / 79 % N2 by volume, 14.7 psia) apart from short pre-EVA periods at 30 % O2 with the total pressure lowered to 10.2 psia, so many Shuttle and ISS materials are tested and rated only to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Orion (the Crew Exploration Vehicle) and the Altair lunar lander were designed to operate at 8.0–14.9 psia, with maximum O2 concentrations of 30 % and 34 % respectively, and the shift from higher-pressure, lower-O2 to lower-pressure, higher-O2 atmospheres was to come as needs move from ISS crew exchange to lunar missions. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- As O2 concentration rises, the cabin pressure falls along the normoxic curve, which holds the O2 partial pressure at the sea-level air equivalent of 0.21 atm (3.09 psia); spacecraft O2 partial pressure will be controlled to 2.6–3.1 psia, a band of operating conditions on the hypoxic side of the normoxic curve. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

- The HLS, the lunar habitat and the pressurized rover will nominally use 8.2 psia with 34 % O2 and 66 % N2 to engineer out decompression-sickness risk, and their control bands are expected to allow up to 37 % O2. [OVR-13 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]
- OVR-13 states that humans do well at a constant O2 partial pressure even at reduced total pressure, whereas fire responds to the O2 concentration, so fire risk fixes the upper O2 limit and fire-safe materials become harder to find as O2 concentration rises. [OVR-13 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

# FILE: EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1
# EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1 — 1-g flammability limits versus microgravity: drop-tower limits, ground prediction methods, FLARE

## Scope
Covers: studies that compare solid-material flammability limits or flame spread on Earth with microgravity, from seven documents: OVR-03 (Olson et al. 2008: drop-tower 0g ULOI and MOC of Ultem 1000, Nomex HT90-40 and Mylar G against NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, the oxygen margin of safety ΔO2%0g–1g, and Kimwipes opposed and concurrent flame spread correlations along the normoxic curve); BAS-09 (Marcum et al. 2016: normal-gravity blowoff limits of cast PMMA rods correlated with the BASS-II microgravity boundary, and a proposed ground "upward flame spread test"); FLR-01 (Takahashi et al. 2024: JAXA FLARE ground-test prediction of filter paper limits versus 19 on-orbit SCEM tests); FLR-05 (Konno et al. 2023: ISO 4589-2 OI and ISO 4589-4 HOI tests on LDPE- and ETFE-insulated Cu and NiCr wires versus parabolic-flight limits); and general statements on why the 1-g Test 1 rating may not be conservative in space (BAS-04, CAB-02, CAB-04).
Not here: OVR-04, OVR-13, SAF-04, SAF-08 and SAF-09 (Martian and lunar limits, the oxygen margin at partial gravity, the reduced-pressure analog of Saffire II, the FM² plan), see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2; the BASS and BASS-II tests themselves, see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4; the Test 1 method and its 1-g parametric effects, see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1 and MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2; cabin atmosphere values, see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1 and CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2; Saffire large-scale fires, see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1 and LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2; SoFIE and Confined Combustion, see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1 and NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2.
