## Findings

### General statements: the 1-g Earth rating versus low gravity
- BAS-04 (citing NASA STD-6001B, 2011) describes Test 1 as the main method for judging the flammability of materials for habitable U.S. spacecraft: an upward flame propagation test started in a stagnant normal-gravity environment by a well-defined igniter flame at the bottom of a vertically mounted sample; a material passes if the vertical burn length stays under 15.2 cm (6 inches) with no transfer of burning debris, and it passes or fails at a given atmosphere (O2 concentration, pressure). [BAS-04 p.1 · CITED · nominal; BAS-04 p.10 · CITED]
- The test assumes 1-g upward flame spread is conservative relative to flammability in space; BAS-04 calls the assumption that it is the worst case problematic. [BAS-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BAS-04 states that recent research shows current normal-gravity flammability results are not conservative compared with ventilated microgravity or partial gravity, and that materials have kept burning in microgravity at or below Test 1 limits (no material, O2, pressure or flow named on those pages). [BAS-04 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BAS-04 asks whether materials might be intrinsically more flammable in space than on Earth because of reduced convective cooling with still adequate oxygen supply. [BAS-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-02 notes that essentially all flight-material flammability data come from 1-g tests, so data at varying O2 in partial gravity are minimal (its item O-4). [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Limited data (CAB-02 refs. 86–89) suggest materials will be more flammable in partial gravity, because gas velocities from natural buoyancy exceed the flow velocities of worst-case combustion. [CAB-02 p.33 · CITED]
- Further work on these differences is under way in support of the Human Landing System (HLS) Program, but CAB-02 states that definitive data will not be available in time to affect HLS. [CAB-02 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; CAB-02 p.90 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · ctx]
- CAB-04 sees the reduced lunar-surface gravity as a distinct challenge for fire extinguishment and propagation. [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-04 reasons that a flame can go out when cabin airflow is fast enough that reactants lack time to react while still hot, that this happens more easily on Earth because stronger gravity drives faster flows, and hence that a material self-extinguishing in Earth gravity may keep burning in lunar gravity (no material, O2, pressure or flow values given). [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-04 also reasons that, since airflow is needed to keep up the minimum O2 for propagation, a smouldering flame in microgravity may not spread without cabin ventilation (material, O2 and pressure not given). [CAB-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In lunar gravity, natural airflow might supply the extra oxygen a smouldering flame needs to spread (CAB-04 citing its ref. 5, a podcast; material, O2 and pressure not given). [CAB-04 p.4 · CITED; CAB-04 p.9 · CITED]

### Drop-tower 0g limits versus NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and the oxygen margin of safety (OVR-03)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Duration | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | thin fuels, 5 cm wide by 10 cm long, taped to the holder: Ultem 1000 10 mil film, Nomex HT90-40 fabric, Mylar G | 0g; low-speed flow tunnel on a NASA Zero Gravity Research Facility drop rig bus (modified flow system and software) | per test, 0 to 100 % O2 in diluent possible; diluent not named | 14.7 psia (Nomex), 10.2 psia (Ultem 1000, Mylar G); tunnel range 0 to 14.7 psia | forced, steady before release; concurrent 30 cm/s for the limit table (Ultem map also 10–30 cm/s concurrent and two opposed tests); tunnel range 0 to 30 cm/s | hot wire at the upstream or downstream end, energised in 1g with the sample in an enriched O2 above the 1g ULOI; the test O2 reached the sample shortly after release | 20 cm inside-diameter duct; 0.5 mm stainless-steel holder, cutout 5 by 10 cm, holder 20 cm wide and over 35 cm long, extending 12.7 cm upstream; test section vented to vacuum at the bottom to put the flame out | 5.18 s of microgravity; the flame had about 5 s in the test atmosphere | diluent, ambient temperature, one- or two-sided burning | [OVR-03 p.6–8 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal] |
- OVR-03 ran microgravity flammability and flame spread tests in a low-speed flow tunnel that simulates spacecraft ventilation flows; three thin fuels were tested for flammability (Ultem 1000 10 mil film, General Electric; Nomex HT90-40 and Mylar G, DuPont) and Kimwipes (Kimberly-Clark) for flame spread. [OVR-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; OVR-03 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal; OVR-03 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Tunnel changes: a second gas reservoir lets O2 (or diluent, or an extinguishing agent) change during a test; a new back-pressure valve gives up to 30 cm/s at up to 14.7 psia; higher-permeability porous plates and honeycomb improve flow distribution and laminarity; in Fig. 1, two bottles hold two mixtures, a critical flow orifice sets the flow and the back-pressure valve the chamber pressure. [OVR-03 p.6 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Imaging: two orthogonal colour video cameras with automatic gain; flame shape, size and spread rate measured with Spotlight software (ref. 10); a constant-brightness red LED in the image corner, which also flashes at release, gives a brightness reference; the green LED illumination makes Kimwipes look green. [OVR-03 p.7 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fuels: Ultem 1000, fire-retarded polyetherimide (PEI), 10 mil film; Nomex HT90-40, 12 mil fire-retarded aromatic nylon fabric that does not melt or drip; Mylar G, 5 mil polyethylene terephthalate film, not fire-retarded, that melts as it burns and was chosen mainly for not charring. [OVR-03 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors describe Kimwipes as thin cellulose that chars as it burns and has no fire-resistant treatment, tested to extend the thin-cellulose database and because it gives spread and extinction data within the short drop time; Ultem 1000 film as inherently flame-retarding and self-charring with very low smoke and smoke toxicity and a low heat-release rate, and Nomex fibres as swelling under heat to seal the gaps between fibres, stopping air movement through the fabric and thus inhibiting heat transfer through it. [OVR-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This was the first microgravity testing of Ultem 1000 and Mylar G. [OVR-03 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Test 1 and the 1g limits used for comparison (OVR-03)
- NASA tests materials with NASA STD-6001 Test 1 (OVR-03 ref. 3), an upward burning test at the worst-case atmosphere of use; materials that do not self-extinguish after 6 in. of burning need other special considerations or tests before use on spacecraft. [OVR-03 p.5 · CITED · nominal]
- Early in the Constellation Program (CxP), NASA Materials and Processes (M&P) staff saw that baseline O2 changes during development or between vehicles would force repeated testing of many materials, so NASA set out to find the maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) of a set of spacecraft materials, defined as the highest O2 at which a material passed Test 1 in 1 g. [OVR-03 p.5–6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Measuring the MOC with the Test 1 protocol has been evaluated (refs. 4–7) as a way to learn the material's flammability limits, not just pass or fail in the worst-case atmosphere, and so to understand its margin of safety in the real-use atmosphere. [OVR-03 p.6 · CITED]
- The MOC approach has not been formally approved as a standard test. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In this approach (ref. 5) the Test 1 O2 is reduced step by step to find the upward limiting oxygen index (1g ULOI) and the 1g MOC that consistently gives self-extinguishment; the 1g MOC is the O2 at which at least five samples passed the burn criterion (ref. 3) with at least one failure at 1 % more O2 by volume. [OVR-03 p.6 · CITED]
- OVR-03 defines the 1g ULOI as the O2 at which a material passes the Test 1 burn-length criterion about half the time. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Nomenclature: 1g normal gravity; 0g microgravity; LOI limiting oxygen index (downward or opposed); ULOI upward limiting oxygen index (burning); MOC maximum oxygen concentration at extinction; ΔO2%0g–1g the 0g mean limit minus the 1g mean limit (Eq. 1); CEV Crew Exploration Vehicle; CxP Constellation Program; EVA extravehicular activity; M&P NASA Materials and Processes; PEI polyetherimide; WSTF White Sands Test Facility. [OVR-03 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### 0g limits in the drop tower (OVR-03)
- Objective: to begin comparing Test 1 limits with concurrent-flow limits in microgravity, to see how 1g fire-safety margins change in real microgravity; from drop tests at several O2 levels on three fuels earlier tested by WSTF (ref. 8), OVR-03 defines an oxygen margin of safety for judging a material in its use atmosphere. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the drop (conditions C1) the established flame either went out in the new atmosphere (0g MOC) or shrank to a weaker burning state at the lower O2; the lowest O2 at which the flame lasted to the end of the drop is the 0g ULOI. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For Eq. 1, the 0g ULOI is the lowest % O2 at which the material burned for the whole test and the 0g MOC the highest % O2 at which it went out during the test. [OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Some flames might go out given longer time, so the authors call the drop-tower limits a conservative measure of the 0g limits; they are not identical to the 1g limits because of the short drop time, but a reasonable comparison. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- 30 cm/s is cited (ref. 11) as a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity. [OVR-03 p.7 · CITED · nominal]

[OVR-03 p.7 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that edge distortion acts by changing the flow around the burned edge: since oxygen transport is critical in microgravity, anything that reduces free oxygen flow past the sample lowers its flammability. [OVR-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Oxygen margin of safety ΔO2%0g–1g (OVR-03)
- Eq. 1: ΔO2%0g–1g = ((0gULO + 0gMOC)/2) − ((1gULO + 1gMOC)/2), the mean 0g limit minus the mean 1g limit, in % O2 (symbols as printed; the text names them 0g ULOI, 0g MOC, 1g ULOI, 1g MOC); Fig. 5 compares the Table 1 limits and gives this margin for the 1g Test 1 data. [OVR-03 p.8 · Eq. 1 · MODELED; OVR-03 p.8 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]
- A positive ΔO2%0g–1g means the flame spreads in 1g at lower O2 than in 0g; a negative value means it spreads in 0g at lower O2 than in 1g, a reduced margin of safety. [OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Ultem film is used on the Space Shuttle and the ISS, whose nominal atmosphere is 21 % ± 2 % O2. [OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Ultem's mean flammability limit is 25.25 % in 1g (Test 1, 10.2 psia), at least 2.25 % above that nominal range, and 22.5 % in 0g (drop rig, 30 cm/s concurrent, 10.2 psia), inside the range, so the material could burn if ignited; ΔO2%0g–1g = −2.75 %, a significant negative margin to weigh when deciding whether a material is safe for spacecraft use (see Conflicts). [OVR-03 p.7 · Table 1 · MEASURED; OVR-03 p.8 · MEASURED]
- As Fig. 5 shows, the 1g limits are generally not conservative for these materials, the negative ΔO2%0g–1g reaching −4 % O2 (Nomex at 14.7 psia, Ultem 1000 and Mylar G at 10.2 psia; 0g at 30 cm/s concurrent). [OVR-03 p.7 · Table 1 · MEASURED; OVR-03 p.8 · Fig. 5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors explain that in concurrent (upward) flow a material can reasonably burn at lower O2 in low g than in 1 g: without buoyancy the convective heat loss is much smaller, so the flame need not release as much heat to give the same heat flux to the unburned fuel; hence 0g limits below 1g limits, the general trend in Table 1, are not surprising. [OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The margin is being evaluated for other materials in concurrent flow, to be followed by opposed-flow limits; further evaluation of these and other materials continues, to understand 0g flammability and its effect on the oxygen margin of safety. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-03 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 5 legend: ◇ 1g ULOI, + 1g MOC, □ 0g ULOI, × 0g MOC, ▲ delta O2 %; left axis % O2, right axis delta O2 %; categories "Nomex HT90-40 14.7psia", "Ultem 1000 10.2psia", "Mylar G 10.2psia"; error bars from the ULOI–MOC differences. [OVR-03 p.8 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED]

- Example (Fig. 2a, b): a concurrent Kimwipes flame at 24 % O2, 30 cm/s and 6.4 psia, not near the limit, seen from the front and side, with flame tip, flame length, pyrolysis length, flame base, flow direction, igniter and a 10 cm scale marked (conditions C2) (test `OVR-03:nodate:KIMWIPES-FIG2:55df43b6`). [OVR-03 p.7 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]
- Kimwipes flames spread fast enough to give spread rates within the 5.18 s drop (conditions C2). [OVR-03 p.11 · MEASURED]
- Spread rates were measured from the video for each condition, the flame usually tracked in the edge view by hand or with a suitable threshold; a more detailed report is OVR-03 ref. 12. [OVR-03 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Cabin atmospheres that frame the tests (OVR-03)
- NASA plans higher O2 and lower total pressure for the Orion crew exploration vehicle, the Altair lander and future lunar habitats (OVR-03 ref. 1). [OVR-03 p.5 · CITED · nominal]
- As stated by OVR-03: since Skylab, the Shuttle and the ISS have run at sea-level air (21 % O2 / 79 % N2 by volume, 14.7 psia) except brief pre-EVA periods at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia, so many Shuttle and ISS materials are tested and rated only to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia; Orion (CEV) and Altair are designed for 8.0 to 14.9 psia at up to 30 and 34 % O2 respectively; the move to lower pressure and higher O2 comes as needs shift from ISS crew exchange to lunar missions. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- As O2 rises, cabin pressure falls along the normoxic curve, which holds O2 partial pressure at the sea-level air value of 0.21 atm (3.09 psia); spacecraft ppO2 will be held at 2.6 to 3.1 psia, a band on the hypoxic side of the curve. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The 0g ULOI and MOC quantify the 1g-to-0g difference in limits but not the difference in flammability above the 0g MOC; since exploration atmospheres will mostly lie on the normoxic curve, quantifying flammability along it would support trades between O2 and pressure. [OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- OVR-03 uses flame spread as the measure of relative flammability along the normoxic curve: it correlates spread rate with forced flow, O2 and pressure to collapse the data onto one curve, then extrapolates to normoxic conditions, studying how changing the atmosphere along the curve affects flame robustness. [OVR-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Correlations were built to capture the effect of flow, pressure and O2 on the measured spread rate. [OVR-03 p.9 · MODELED]

#### Opposed-flow correlation (OVR-03 Fig. 6)
- For normal-gravity downward (opposed) spread over thin fuels, earlier work (Magee and McAlevy, OVR-03 ref. 13) correlated spread rate with (O2)^0.9 (P)^0.05 (O2 mole fraction, P in atm), with only a slight pressure dependence, so O2 was the main influence in that buoyancy-controlled case. [OVR-03 p.9 · CITED]
- The new Kimwipes opposed-flow data (conditions C2) and earlier normal- and microgravity data (refs. 14–16) are well correlated by this relation except near the quench limit, where flow effects matter. [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · MODELED]
- Spread rate rises nearly linearly with O2 percentage while the pressure effect is quite weak in this range (Kimwipes, opposed flow, Fig. 6 data, conditions C2). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]
- By contrast, Bhattacharjee et al. (ref. 17) found a much stronger pressure dependence for a fuel four times thicker in quiescent conditions, tests shown to be near-limit, where losses such as radiation matter; even the near-limit data of refs. 14 and 15 fall off the correlation. [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · CITED]
- The authors therefore view the correlation as a worst-case (highest) spread-rate prediction for a given O2 and pressure. [OVR-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6 fits Kimwipes opposed-flow spread data from various atmospheres and gravity levels to the O2-pressure correlation based on Magee and McAlevy; y spread rate, cm/s (log, 0.1–10); x O2 (mole frac)^0.9 · P(atm)^0.05 (linear, 0–1). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · MODELED]
- Fig. 6 legend: ◇ 15 cm/s normoxic, △ 0g quiescent normoxic, ✳ 1g normoxic, ○ 0g quiescent 1 atm (Olson 1987), × 1g 1 atm (Olson 1987), + 0g forced flow 1 atm (Olson 1991), □ 0g forced flow 1 atm (Ferkul 1988), "all", and the line "Linear (all)", R² = 0.9536. [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]
- Below 40 % O2, opposed spread rate rises with forced flow up to an optimum velocity and falls above it; above 40 % O2 it does not depend on forced velocity (Kimwipes, opposed flow, conditions C2). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]
- Flow velocity is therefore not captured by the correlation, because of this non-monotonic dependence at low O2 (<40 %). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Concurrent-flow correlation (OVR-03 Fig. 7)
- OVR-03 found no published correlation of experimental concurrent spread data; Ferkul (ref. 18) fitted his numerical predictions of spread rate against O2 and forced flow with a polynomial and noted roughly linear growth with either flow or O2. [OVR-03 p.9 · CITED]
- The authors suggest the gap exists perhaps because normal-gravity concurrent spread is often accelerating. [OVR-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Correlation parameter (Fig. 7 x axis): x = O2 (mole fraction) × flow (cm/s) × P(atm)^0.5, capturing the observed linear effects of flow and O2 and a square-root pressure effect; y = spread rate, cm/s; it gave the best fit of the available data. [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 7 · MODELED]
- Fits to all the data (OVR-03 Kimwipes plus Grayson et al. and Pettegrew): linear y = 0.2498x + 0.4038, R² = 0.97 (legend 0.9696); power law y = 0.6763x^0.6187, R² = 0.93 (legend 0.9277), shown for comparison; fitted range not stated (data span x ~0 to ~12.6 on the plot). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 7 · MODELED]
- Fig. 7 shows all the concurrent data plus earlier near-limit data of Grayson (ref. 19) and Pettegrew (ref. 20); symbol size reflects error estimated from top versus bottom base spread rates; legend × normoxic data, ○ oxygen varies, △ velocity varies, ◇ pressure varies, □ other combination, ✳ Grayson et al., + Pettegrew-HW ign. [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED]
- Concurrent test matrix (Kimwipes, 0g drop rig, conditions C2): normoxic series from 24 % O2 at 12.8 psia to 85 % O2 at 3.6 psia, all at 30 cm/s; O2 varied 24 to 50 % at 10.2 psia and 30 cm/s; velocity varied 1 to 30 cm/s at 34 % O2 and 10.2 psia; pressure varied 5 to 14.7 psia at 40 % O2 and 30 cm/s. [OVR-03 p.9 · MEASURED]
- Over most of the range spread rate is linear in the correlation parameter, but at very low near-limit values the data fall off the linear fit, as predicted (ref. 21) (Kimwipes, concurrent, 0g, conditions C2). [OVR-03 p.9 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED]

#### Where concurrent spread outruns opposed spread (OVR-03 Fig. 8)
- Equating the two correlations and solving for the forced flow that makes the rates equal gives, against O2, the boundary above which concurrent spread is faster, for two pressures: the normoxic-equivalent pressure and 14.7 psia (1 atm); opposed spread is faster below the lines (Kimwipes, microgravity). [OVR-03 p.9 · MODELED; OVR-03 p.10 · Fig. 8 · MODELED]
- Over virtually the whole range of spacecraft atmospheres and flows (nominal ventilation 5 to 20 cm/s, ref. 11) opposed spread is faster, especially at normoxic conditions; between 20 and 25 % O2 the opposed and concurrent rates are similar, consistent with Fig. 4 (Kimwipes, microgravity). [OVR-03 p.9–10 · Fig. 8 · MODELED; OVR-03 p.11 · MODELED]
- The 5 to 20 cm/s nominal ventilation range is cited from ref. 11; Fig. 8 draws it as a dashed box from ~5 to ~20 cm/s and ~22 to 100 % O2. [OVR-03 p.9 · CITED · nominal; OVR-03 p.10 · Fig. 8 · CITED · nominal, ~fig]
- For a sample ignited in its middle rather than at an edge, the authors expect the flame to spread upstream, and any downstream flame to be further held back by the vitiated gas from the upstream flame. [OVR-03 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Opposed versus concurrent spread along the normoxic curve (OVR-03 Fig. 9)
- Along the normoxic curve, opposed spread rises quickly with O2, while concurrent spread rises more slowly because the falling pressure offsets the rising O2; the size of the change depends on spread direction (Kimwipes, correlation predictions). [OVR-03 p.10 · Fig. 9 · MODELED]
- Predicted opposed (upwind) spread rises from about 1 to 5 cm/s as O2 goes from 21 to 80 %, concurrent (downwind) spread at 30 cm/s forced flow only from about 3 to 4 cm/s; the gap between opposed and concurrent at 15 cm/s forced flow is larger still (Kimwipes, normoxic atmospheres). [OVR-03 p.10 · MODELED]
- The authors call for checking this trend with other materials. [OVR-03 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because the 0g limit data were taken mostly in concurrent flow and Fig. 9 shows clearly different concurrent and opposed spread rates, the authors find it plausible that 0g limits also differ, especially for materials whose limits lie at higher O2 along the normoxic curve, and leave this for future work. [OVR-03 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 9 plots measured and predicted Kimwipes spread rate (0–8 cm/s) against "%O2 normoxic" (10–100); legend ◇ 1g downward spread, ✳ 0g quiescent, △ 0g opposed 15 cm/s, ○ 0g concurrent 30 cm/s; dash-dot predicted concurrent 30 cm/s, dashed predicted concurrent 15 cm/s, solid predicted opposed. [OVR-03 p.10 · Fig. 9 · MEASURED]

#### Conclusions on the correlations (OVR-03)
- The spread tests yielded correlations for the effects of flow, O2 and pressure on spread rate; for opposed flow, an earlier correlation held away from the quench limit. [OVR-03 p.5 · MODELED; OVR-03 p.11 · MODELED]
- With no earlier three-variable correlation for concurrent data, the authors call theirs the first to combine O2, pressure and forced flow. [OVR-03 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Compared with 1g MOC trends of various materials against pressure and O2, lines of constant opposed spread rate agree best with the 1g MOC trends. [OVR-03 p.5 · MODELED]
- The authors read this as Test 1 upward limits being set essentially by the critical heat flux for ignition, where the flame's heat flux is too small to sustain burning. [OVR-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-03 p.11–12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Normal-gravity PMMA rod blowoff limits correlated with BASS-II (BAS-09)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | cast clear PMMA rods hung from a metal crossbar, radii 0.318, 0.476, 0.635, 1.270, 1.905 cm (a factor of six), initially flat-ended and burned to a rounded tip before each limit search | normal gravity, lab rig | calibrated premixed bottles of 14 to 18 % O2 by volume in balance nitrogen | not reported | upward axial stagnation flow (forced plus buoyant) from a 200 SLPM MKS mass flow controller and a flow straightener (uniform profile checked by hot-wire anemometer); maximum 165 SLPM (60.3 cm/s average tube speed) | lit by hand outside the apparatus, burned in dry shop air at the test flow, then the gas switched to the test bottle at the same flow | otherwise empty vertical quartz tube, 7.6 cm inside diameter, 25.4 cm long, exhaust snorkel above | total pressure, ambient temperature, test duration | [BAS-09 p.1–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- BAS-09 uses the same concurrent rod geometry as BASS-II, adding normal-gravity buoyant flow, to complement the flight results with ground blowoff limits. [BAS-09 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Procedure (conditions C3): the blowoff forced flow is found for each rod size and O2; each run first images a scale beside the rod and a card with the test conditions; dried shop air (O'Keefe dryer) is set to the test flow; once the flame is stable the gas is switched to see whether it blows off at that flow and O2; the lowest blowoff flow is found iteratively for each O2; matte black foil hides tube reflections and a colour video camera records through the tube. [BAS-09 p.1–2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors consider the rounded tip more representative of the steady shape of a burning sample. [BAS-09 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The 165 SLPM ceiling limited the O2 range over which blowoff could be reached; at 18 % O2 limits were found for only three radii (0.318, 0.476, 0.635 cm). [BAS-09 p.2–4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED]
- More than 280 runs (conditions C3) set the blowoff limits for each O2 and radius, each bracketing flow condition repeated at least once; Fig. 2 shows the flames just as blowoff starts, in a grid of 18, 17, 16 and 15 % O2 by the five radii (no 14 % row). [BAS-09 p.3–4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED]
- Blowoff (conditions C3) always began at the stagnation region; the flame then blew downstream; small holes could close ("heal") but a later larger one could destabilise the flame; the larger the radius, the larger the hole needed. [BAS-09 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the trigger to a flame hole at the stagnation region big enough to destabilise the flame base, and call the radius effect consistent with their ref. 13 on flame holes near a heat sink. [BAS-09 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At higher O2 and smaller radii (levels not given), the blown-off flame sometimes anchored briefly to the rod sides as a ring that oscillated with growing amplitude until it always blew off (conditions C3). [BAS-09 p.3 · MEASURED]
- In the Fig. 2 photographs the 0.318 cm flames at 18 and 17 % O2 show a bright white-orange zone and the others look blue; the flames widen with radius (a description of the photographs, not stated in the text; each at its blowoff flow, conditions C3). [BAS-09 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · ~fig]
- Fig. 3 plots each radius's blowoff boundary as O2 against forced flow velocity; each is roughly linear in flow, except at 14 % O2, where all radii collapse below 5 cm/s (conditions C3). [BAS-09 p.3 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
- The authors explain the 14 % collapse as air entering the tube top at low forced flow and raising the local O2 so the rod stayed flammable; the Fig. 4 caption puts the non-blowoff of the asymmetric 14 % quartz-tube flame down to ambient flow entrained back into the tube. [BAS-09 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-09 p.5 · Fig. 4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- Forced stretch rate a = 3/2 U/r (a_f on the Fig. 5 axis, s^-1), with U the average flow speed entering the tube at the lowest blowoff flow and r the rod radius (cm). [BAS-09 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; BAS-09 p.3 · MODELED; BAS-09 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]
- Fig. 5 plots blowoff forced stretch rate against r for each O2; at each O2 the data are fitted by a power law with a square-root exponent, and the inset shows the fit constant C varying linearly with O2, so blowoff stretch rate varies linearly with O2 as well as with the square root of radius (C3 conditions at 15 to 18 % O2). [BAS-09 p.3 · Fig. 5 · MODELED; BAS-09 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]
- The authors attribute the square-root exponent to stretch at the flame standoff distance rather than at the rod surface, and say these relations guided the later correlation. [BAS-09 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Standoff distance is estimated by the gas-phase thermal length δ = (α/a)^(1/2) (α gas thermal diffusivity; units not printed), so δ ∝ r^(1/2) at a given U. [BAS-09 p.3 · MODELED]
- Fig. 5 fits a_f = C r^-1/2 (a_f in s^-1, r in cm; fitted range not stated): C = 131.9 at 18 % (plotted at r = 0.318, 0.476, 0.635 cm), 89.64 at 17 %, 57.14 at 16 % and 13.08 at 15 % (each plotted at r = 0.318 to 1.905 cm); inset fit O2 (% by vol.) = 14.63 + 0.025C over the four constants (C units not printed). [BAS-09 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MODELED]

[BAS-09 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MODELED]
- The 16.5 cm/s agrees well with normal-gravity buoyant flow velocities of about 20 cm/s (the authors' ref. 16; material, O2 and pressure of those velocities not given). [BAS-09 p.7 · CITED]
- Fit to the shifted data (Fig. 6 "Linear (shifted data)", blue band): y = 0.0002x + 0.1343, R² = 0.9841, with y the O2 mole fraction (axis "O2 mole %") and x = ao + ab in s^-1; fitted range not stated. [BAS-09 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MODELED]
- The authors call the blowoff region inherently wide because blowoff is stochastic (their ref. 18). [BAS-09 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6 caption: the correlation accounts for flow acceleration from rod blockage, normalises all radii to ro through δ, and shifts by 78 s^-1 for buoyant stretch to align with BASS-II; open markers are the five radii unshifted, dots the shifted data, a line the BASS-II boundary, a band the linear fit. [BAS-09 p.7 · Fig. 6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- BASS-II boundary as drawn in BAS-09 Fig. 6 (ISS microgravity, concurrent, cast PMMA rods; diluent and pressure not reported by this source): ~16.5 % O2 at its left end (ao ~0 s^-1, top of the near-vertical low-stretch branch), its minimum at ~10 s^-1, and ~16.1 % O2 at its right (upper) end, ~160 s^-1. [BAS-09 p.1 · CITED; BAS-09 p.7 · Fig. 6 · CITED · ~fig]
- The authors find the linear trend of blowoff with O2 noteworthy and potentially useful for a better normal-gravity test of microgravity flammability. [BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Extrapolating the linear (shifted) normal-gravity blowoff boundary to zero stretch estimates 13.4 % O2 as the limiting oxygen concentration below which the cast PMMA rod cannot burn at any stretch rate (C3 data, shifted by ab = 78 s^-1 to stand for microgravity). (test `BAS-09:nodate:PMMA-ROD-BLOWOFF-BOUNDARY-ZERO-STRETCH-LOC:2163eb69`) [BAS-09 p.8 · MODELED]
- The authors call the 13.4 % estimate conservative from a fire-safety standpoint. [BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- BAS-09 calls the 13.4 % estimate still quite close to the 13.6 % O2 minimum needed for stable flames in BASS-II (ISS microgravity, concurrent, cast PMMA rods; flow speed, diluent and pressure not reported by this source). (test `BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-LOWEST-FINAL-O2-SUSTAINED:23bb3421`) [BAS-09 p.1 · CITED; BAS-09 p.8 · CITED]
- In BAS-04 (Olson and Ferkul 2015, the BASS-II paper BAS-09 cites as ref. 12), 13.6 % O2 is the minimum test point of the ISS concurrent cast PMMA rod boundary (radius and flow of that point not stated in the text; pressure not reported in the pages read). [BAS-04 p.1 · MEASURED · ctx; BAS-04 p.7 · MEASURED; BAS-09 p.9 · CITED]
- The authors judge the estimate good because the microgravity quenching boundary turns up away from the blowoff line only at low flow speeds, a very narrow part of the whole boundary. [BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Using an empirical shift presumes the microgravity boundary is already known, which is not generally so. [BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Alternative buoyant stretch from the authors' ref. 17: ab = K √(g/r) (ab in s^-1, g in cm/s^2, r in cm); with ab = 78 s^-1, g = 981 cm/s^2 and ro = 0.318 cm, K is estimated at 1.4 (cast PMMA rods, normal-gravity data aligned with BASS-II; K evaluated at this one point). [BAS-09 p.8 · MODELED]
- K is a density ratio (ref. 17). [BAS-09 p.8 · CITED]
- The authors expect similar critical temperatures at each O2 for materials with the same basic gas-phase chemistry, since K is a density ratio and blowoff may share one limiting reaction rate at a given flow (critical Damköhler number), so common C-H-O fuels should have a similar density ratio at blowoff; fuels with N, Br, Cl, P or other additives may not follow the same trends. [BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- How far K applies to other materials needs further research. [BAS-09 p.8–9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Conclusions: normal-gravity blowoff limits were measured for the rod in upward axial stagnation flow at five radii (0.318 to 1.905 cm) and five O2 levels (14 to 18 % by volume) (conditions C3). [BAS-09 p.8 · MEASURED]
- Converted to forced stretch rates, normalised with δ/δo = (r/ro)^1/2 to the base rod size (stretch at the flame standoff distance) and corrected for rod blockage, all the data fall on one curve (conditions C3). [BAS-09 p.8 · MODELED]
- The normal-gravity blowoff boundary of the rod is linear, with O2 directly proportional to flow speed (conditions C3; rod diameters 0.635 to 3.81 cm, 14 to 18 % O2). [BAS-09 p.1 · MEASURED]
- The authors find these blowoff limits compare favourably with BASS-II once buoyant stretch is included and the flow is corrected for the blockage of the fuel. [BAS-09 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The normal-gravity boundary runs parallel to the complete BASS-II microgravity extinction boundary (ISS) but at lower stretch rates; shifting it right by ab = 78 s^-1 (16.5 cm/s for the base rod) accounts for the extra buoyant stretch, in good agreement with buoyant flow estimates (conditions C3; BASS-II pressure not reported by this source). [BAS-09 p.8 · MODELED]
- The authors propose a normal-gravity "upward flame spread test": find the blowoff boundary of an axisymmetric rod in a forced flow tube, add the buoyant stretch to predict the microgravity blowoff boundary, and extrapolate the linear boundary to zero stretch to resolve microgravity limits, which they say current methods cannot do. [BAS-09 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For the authors, the axisymmetric rod in upward axial stagnation flow is a simple way to measure normal-gravity blowoff limits for comparison with the BASS-II results recently obtained on the ISS. [BAS-09 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Recent ISS testing (BASS-II) examined the oxygen-flow flammability boundary for three cast PMMA rod sizes. [BAS-09 p.1 · CITED]
- Hemispherical stagnation flow was shown early on (the authors' ref. 1) to be a good way to get flammability limits of fuels as a function of upward oxidizer flow; many heavier hydrocarbons had similar limiting O2 concentrations (13 %–14 %) and flame temperatures (1450–1500 °C) (gravity, diluent, pressure and flow speed not given). [BAS-09 p.1 · CITED]
- If proven for various materials, the zero-stretch extrapolation could give a conservative estimate of microgravity limits; it may work for many materials as long as their extinction boundaries have a similar shape, could give a tractable estimate of low-gravity flammability, and may improve spacecraft fire safety for exploration. [BAS-09 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; BAS-09 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### JAXA FLARE: ground-predicted versus on-orbit limits of filter paper (FLR-01)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Ambient temperature | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C4 | filter paper (Advantec No. 4A), 130 mm long, 40 mm or 20 mm wide, 0.12 mm thick, 96 g/m2, on a sample card held by electromagnets | microgravity; long-duration tests since May 2022 in the ISS/Kibo Solid Combustion Experiment Module (SCEM), a compact circulating wind tunnel on the Multi-purpose Small Payload Rack (MSPR), Insert 2 for flat samples | per run (adjustable 0 to 45 %); diluent not reported | 100 kPa (adjustable 0 to 101.3 kPa) | fan-driven, quiescent up to 25 cm/s, held constant or changed in steps; opposed (ignition downstream) or concurrent (ignition upstream) | electrically heated Kanthal wire 40 mm wide, on at T + 5 s for 10 s (video from T + 0 s), retractable after ignition | sample at the centre of a 14 cm × 14 cm test section | 298 K | diluent, one- or two-sided burning | [FLR-01 p.1–3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- One aim of FLARE, JAXA's fire-safety evaluation project, is to predict quantitatively the flammability limits of solid materials in microgravity from tests that can be run on the ground. [FLR-01 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- FLR-01 reports 19 opposed-flow flame spread tests (conditions C4) and compares the flammability limit curve predicted beforehand from ground tests with the flammability map measured in orbit. [FLR-01 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
- Effects of both radiative loss and blow-off were seen when the opposed flow was raised from 10 to 18 cm/s in 2 cm/s steps at 15.5 % O2 (conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.1 · MEASURED · single-test; FLR-01 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Against the orbital map, the original limit curve reproduced the blow-off branch well but overstated the flammable region at opposed flows below 10 cm/s (conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.1 · MEASURED]
- The authors trace the mismatch to insufficient account of how opposed flow velocity acts on the radiative quenching branch. [FLR-01 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Using the flow profile measured in orbit and modelling the effective opposed velocity at the flame front on both the radiative quenching and blow-off branches, the authors report a quantitative match to the orbital results. [FLR-01 p.1 · MODELED]
- FLR-01 draws from this that the limits of thin flat samples can be predicted accurately when the effect of the surface boundary layer is properly assessed. [FLR-01 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Past studies (FLR-01 refs. 3–11) report that the limiting oxygen concentration of materials falls in microgravity at low ambient flow (materials, flows, O2, pressure and platforms not given). [FLR-01 p.1 · CITED]
- Numerical and theoretical work (refs. 12–15) predicts that the limiting oxygen concentration rises, and spread is suppressed, at very low ambient flow or in quiescent air (materials, flows, O2 and pressure not given). [FLR-01 p.1 · CITED]
- Long-duration microgravity tests (refs. 16–18) have often shown flames under quiescent conditions spreading for a relatively long time before going out rather than at once (materials, O2, pressure and platforms not given). [FLR-01 p.1 · CITED]
- From these reports the authors conclude that, for flat solids in opposed flow, the limiting oxygen concentration generally traces a U-shaped curve against opposed flow velocity, explained by the blow-off limit and radiative extinction; a quantitative limit curve for a given material would let its fire safety be discussed in any environment. [FLR-01 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Takahashi et al. proposed obtaining the blow-off branch quantitatively from downward flame spread tests in fast airflow, a method standardised in the FLARE project as ISO 4589-4 (ref. 19). [FLR-01 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors therefore believe ground tests alone can predict the blow-off branch fairly accurately; the radiative extinction branch at low flow had been estimated from thermal decomposition tests and short drop-tower extinctions, so long-duration microgravity results were awaited. [FLR-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors improved their earlier model to predict limit curves under opposed flow more accurately. [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED]

#### Model of the opposed-flow limits (FLR-01)
- In the model, the flammability limits of flat solids in opposed flow come from coupling a blow-off branch and a radiative extinction branch. [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED]
- Fig. 1 sketches 2-D spread in opposed flow: relative velocity V_r = V_f + V_g ~ V_g; near the sample the velocity at the flame leading edge, V_g,eff, is below V_g; also marked are a height δ, preheat lengths L_gx and L_gy, sample half-thickness τ, the pyrolysis and preheat zones and the reference length x_d. [FLR-01 p.2 · Fig. 1 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1 (scale-analysis energy balance, refs. 10, 11): V_f ρ_s c_s τ (T_v − T_∞) + ε (1 − α_abs) σ (T_v^4 − T_∞^4) L_g = (1 − 1/Da) λ_g ((T_f − T_v)/L_g) L_g, with T_∞ = 298 K (α_abs in Eq. 1 is the gas absorption coefficient, a_abs = 0 in the nomenclature); symbols as in the nomenclature below; units not printed. [FLR-01 p.2 · Eq. 1 · MODELED]
- Gas preheat length L_g ~ α_g/V_g, with α_g evaluated at T_v; the solid preheat length is assumed equal to the gas one. [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED]
- Non-dimensionalised, the spread rate η depends on two numbers, Da (blow-off) and R_rad (radiative extinction); extinction occurs when R_rad + 1/Da reaches unity: Eq. 2, η + R_rad + 1/Da = 1, with η = V_f/V_f,th and V_f,th = (λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ)) · (T_f − T_v)/(T_v − T_∞). [FLR-01 p.2 · Eq. 2 · MODELED]
- Eq. 3: Da = B_1 · (α_g/V_g^2) ρ_g Y_O A exp(−E/RT_f) (B_1 not defined in the nomenclature); Eq. 4: R_rad = B_2 · ε (1 − a_abs) σ (T_v^4 − T_∞^4)/(ρ_g c_g V_g (T_f − T_v)), with B_2 = 4.2 and a_abs = 0; units not printed. [FLR-01 p.2 · Eq. 3 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.2 · Eq. 4 · MODELED]
- With V_f assumed slow, V_g is the opposed velocity seen by the flame front; R_rad counts only radiative loss from the preheated sample, not gas-phase radiation. [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED]
- Because V_g enters both Eqs. 3 and 4, the authors note that the equations need adjusting when the real velocity relative to the flame front differs from the bulk V_g. [FLR-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Nomenclature, regrouped: constants B_2 = 4.2 (Eq. 4), B_2' = 1.08 (Eq. 8), a_abs = 0 (gas absorption), T_∞ = 298 K, x_d = 0.04 m (blow-off reference location); Eq. 5 fit parameters A* (pre-exponential) and E* (activation energy); temperatures T_f (flame), T_v (pyrolysis), T_10 and T_50 (10 % and 50 % mass loss); velocities V_g (opposed), V_g,eff (effective opposed), V_f (spread) and V_f,th (spread in the thermal regime); gas properties at T_v: ρ_g, α_g, plus c_g and λ_g; solid properties ρ_s, c_s, λ_s, α_s (at T_v); others: Pr (Prandtl), R (gas constant), Y_0 (O2 mass fraction), ε (surface emissivity), η = V_f/V_f,th, σ (Stefan-Boltzmann), τ (sample half-thickness). [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED]
- A and E of Eq. 3 are hard to measure or estimate directly, so the authors obtain them from downward flame spread tests: the ISO 4589-2 test (ref. 20) and the ISO 4589-4 high gas velocity test (ref. 19). [FLR-01 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- From how sensitive the blow-off limit is to the surrounding flow, they fit experimental A* and E* that represent the blow-off limits quantitatively. [FLR-01 p.3 · MODELED]
- Eq. 5 (Eq. 3 modified for the boundary layer's effect on the velocity relative to the flame at blow-off, ref. 10): Da = Pr (x_d/V_g) ρ_g Y_O A* exp(−E*/RT_f), x_d = 0.04 m (from ref. 10); the arbitrary choice of x_d is absorbed by A*. [FLR-01 p.3 · Eq. 5 · MODELED]
- For the extinction branch, with slower flow and a larger flame standoff, the limit was estimated assuming plug flow, keeping the velocity relative to the flame equal to the bulk V_g. [FLR-01 p.3 · MODELED]
- Predicting a solid's limits from ground tests needs its Oxygen Index OI, High-velocity Oxygen Index HOI, thermal decomposition temperature T_v and flame temperature T_f. [FLR-01 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- T_v = (T_10 + T_50)/2, from TG-DTA (thermogravimetric-differential thermal analysis) tests; T_f is the adiabatic flame temperature from the material's composition, heat of combustion and the ambient atmosphere. [FLR-01 p.3 · MODELED]

- The SCEM O2 falls as a sample burns: one 130 mm × 40 mm filter paper sample lowers it by about 1 % (microgravity; initial O2, pressure and flow of this example not given). [FLR-01 p.3 · MEASURED]

#### On-orbit flammability map of filter paper (FLR-01 Fig. 5)

- Run #26 temperature profiles read from Fig. 7 (±5 mm, ±25 K; conditions C4): the T+20 s profile has a flat top at ~662 K over ~4 to ~8 mm (10 to 12 cm/s); the T+60 s peak is the highest, ~680 K at ~42 mm (14 to 16 cm/s); the T+20, 40, 70, 80 and 100 s peaks lie at ~655–665 K; the last profile, T+114 s, peaks at ~650 K at ~88 mm (18 cm/s). [FLR-01 p.5 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test]
- The authors' first report of this experiment (their ref. 18: Takahashi et al., Fire Technol. 2023, also the source of Table 1 and of the Fig. 9 velocity profile) already noted interesting flame behaviour. [FLR-01 p.3 · Table 1 · CITED; FLR-01 p.4 · CITED; FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 9 · CITED; FLR-01 p.8 · CITED]
- From the #10 versus #16 comparison the authors consider a 20 mm width wide enough for the conditions under which extinction occurs. [FLR-01 p.4–5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Run #26 sat at the border between the radiative extinction region and the blow-off region and showed features of both (conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors read Run #26 as crossing the flammability limit: radiative loss acted while the flame was briefly 3-D, but it finally went out as a 2-D flame, implying extinction at the blow-off limit. [FLR-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As predicted, the measured limiting oxygen concentration of filter paper falls below its ground OI (16.58 %) at opposed flows around 10 cm/s (conditions C4; Run #26 began at 15.5 %, about 1 % under the OI). [FLR-01 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors see the blow-off branch of Eq. 5, built from OI and HOI, as reproducing the observations accurately and quantitatively. [FLR-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Radiative branch, boundary layer and updated model (FLR-01)
- In the radiative extinction branch (opposed flow below 10 cm/s, conditions C4) the prediction and the tests disagreed. [FLR-01 p.5 · MEASURED]
- The pre-flight model expected a minimum limiting oxygen concentration of 14.0 % at 8 cm/s opposed flow and a much wider flammable range below 10 cm/s (Table 1 values, Eqs. 4 and 5, B_2 = 4.20; microgravity, T_∞ = 298 K). [FLR-01 p.2–3 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.5 · MODELED]
- Fig. 8 caption (Runs #01, #02, #30, #20, mild opposed flow): in each case the flame became 3-D while spreading, a sign of strong radiative loss, and, unlike Run #26, shrank in radius before going out; IR videos are Fig. S3 of the supplementary material. [FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED]
- The authors take Run #30 as showing a larger radiative-loss effect than projected, and judge that Eq. 4 over-weights a falling V_g, since it sets the velocity relative to the flame equal to the bulk V_g (plug flow). [FLR-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 4 assumes plug flow, with the opposed velocity relative to the flame set to the bulk velocity V_g. [FLR-01 p.5 · MODELED]
- In-orbit SCEM flow measurements (smoke tests) show that even at a low bulk flow of V_g = 4.5 cm/s the velocity at flame height (~5 mm) is below the bulk value because of the boundary layer (sample and O2 of the measurement not given). [FLR-01 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 9 shows the in-orbit vertical velocity profile from the smoke method (FLR-01 citing its ref. 18; bulk value marked 4.51 cm/s; axes Z location, mm, against velocity, mm/s) beside flame photos at several flows. [FLR-01 p.5 · CITED; FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 9 · CITED]
- Fig. 9 caption: the standoff distance grows as opposed flow falls, yet even at low flow the flame is expected to sit inside the boundary layer on the sample (photos: Run #31 at T+70 s, 26.0 %, 0 cm/s; Run #30 at T+70 s, 15.4 %, 8 cm/s; Run #28 at T+40 s, 15.9 %, 20 cm/s; conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 9 · MEASURED]
- From these results the authors conclude that even at low flow the flame front lies within the boundary layer, so the velocity facing the flame front must be estimated accurately. [FLR-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- To estimate the effective opposed velocity V_g,eff, the preheat zone length was measured from IR images for each condition and plotted against bulk V_g in Fig. 10; the preheat length runs from the maximum-temperature point on the unburned sample to the point where temperature has risen by 10 %. [FLR-01 p.5–6 · MEASURED]
- The original model has L_g ~ α_g/V_g (inverse to V_g), but a fit of the data above 6 cm/s bulk flow gives L_g roughly proportional to V_g^−0.43, close to an inverse square root (conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.6–7 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that the boundary layer affects the velocity facing the flame and therefore use V_g,eff instead of bulk V_g to evaluate L_g. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 6: V_g,eff ∝ V_g/(Pr Re^0.5), Re = x_d V_g/ν (x_d = 0.04 m; ν not defined in the nomenclature); Eq. 7: L_g ~ α_g/V_g,eff = sqrt(Pr x_d α_g/V_g); units not printed. [FLR-01 p.2 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.7 · Eq. 6 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.7 · Eq. 7 · MODELED]
- Fig. 10 shows the original L_g curve (gray) and the Eq. 7 curve (blue) against the data (axes preheat length 0–40 mm, opposed velocity 0–25 cm/s); the modified curve follows the measured trend better (conditions C4, opposed flow 0–24 cm/s, O2 15.5–34 %). [FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 10 · MEASURED · ~fig; FLR-01 p.7 · MEASURED]

- With V_g,eff from Eq. 6, R_rad of Eq. 4 becomes Eq. 8: R_rad = B_2′ · [ε (1 − a_abs) σ (T_v^4 − T_∞^4)/(ρ_g c_g (T_f − T_v))] · sqrt(Pr x_d/(V_g α_g)), with x_d the same 0.04 m length as in Eq. 5 (its arbitrariness absorbed by B_2′); units not printed. [FLR-01 p.3 · Eq. 5 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.7 · Eq. 8 · MODELED]
- B_2′ = 1.08 was set from the conditions at which 2-D spread could no longer be held at O2 above 21 % (on-orbit filter paper results). [FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED · nominal]
- The limit curve from Eqs. 5 and 8 is the blue "Updated curve with Eqs. 5 and 8" (the text says Fig. 2; the Fig. 5 legend carries it); Fig. 5 also shows the gray pre-flight curve (Eqs. 4 and 5) and two dashed curves where only B_2 of Eq. 4 is changed (6.0, red; 2.76, black), which, per the text and caption, do not represent the flammability map well. [FLR-01 p.4 · Fig. 5 · MODELED; FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED]
- Dashed-curve minima read from Fig. 5 (filter paper, microgravity; ±0.5 cm/s, ±0.25 %): B_2 = 6.0, ~14.6 % at ~11.5–12.6 cm/s, its steep low-velocity branch reaching 40 % at ~3.1 cm/s (`FLR-01:nodate:FILTERPAPER-LOC-ORIGINALCURVE-B2-6.0:ac71e5e0`, `…:afa59649`); B_2 = 2.76, ~13.3 % at ~5.5–7 cm/s, its steep branch at ~1.4 cm/s at 38 % (`FLR-01:nodate:FILTERPAPER-LOC-ORIGINALCURVE-B2-2.76:cd654ea0`, `…:49d75da2`). [FLR-01 p.4 · Fig. 5 · MODELED · ~fig]
- In the updated model radiative and kinetic effects weigh about equally near 16 cm/s opposed flow, consistent with Run #26 (Fig. 7) (filter paper, microgravity). [FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED]

- The modified curve represents the measured limits well, especially between 4 and 16 cm/s opposed flow, where both radiative extinction and blow-off act (filter paper, microgravity, SCEM). [FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED]
- The authors suggest that accounting for the boundary layer growing on solid samples allows accurate prediction of microgravity flammability limits; if B_2′ = 1.08 also works for other materials in coming orbital tests, limits of solids such as plastics could be predicted fairly accurately from ground data alone. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Caveat from the authors: the modified model predicts the minimum O2 concentration well, but flame behaviour at very low opposed flow needs care. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At low opposed flow the measured preheat zone length L_g is shorter than predicted (Fig. 10; conditions C4, O2 15.5–34 %). [FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 10 · MEASURED; FLR-01 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors' ref. 18 explains that L_g diverges in the 2-D flame model (~α_g/V_g) but stays finite, proportional to the flame radius, for round flames. [FLR-01 p.7 · CITED]
- The authors infer that once V_g falls below the 2-D spread limit (the blue curve) the flame turns round and 3-D, shortening L_g and cutting radiative loss, which lets it survive. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Conclusions: the long-duration ISS/Kibo filter paper tests were analysed in detail into a flammability map. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The limiting O2 concentration in microgravity was computed by modelling blow-off and radiative loss from OI and HOI tests, TG-DTA, the sample's composition and heat of combustion, and the resulting limit curve of filter paper was compared with the orbital map. [FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED]
- The blow-off branch was represented well quantitatively, but below 10 cm/s opposed flow the real limiting oxygen concentration was higher than the predicted curve (conditions C4). [FLR-01 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute this to the boundary layer on the sample, where the preheat length ahead of the flame varies inversely with the square root of opposed flow velocity, not with the velocity itself. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With the radiative loss term revised, the recalculated limit curve agreed quantitatively with the orbital map. [FLR-01 p.7 · MODELED]
- The authors conclude that assessing the flow facing the flame front in both the radiative quenching and blow-off branches allows precise prediction of the limits of thermally thin solids in microgravity, and so of solid-material flammability in space habitats from ground tests; the stated novelty is a flammability map from the first systematic long-duration SCEM tests of filter paper and models that predict the limit curves quantitatively through the boundary-layer effect, with the flow facing the flame front shown to vary inversely with the square root of bulk velocity even at low velocity. [FLR-01 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Supplementary material (IR videos: Fig. S1, Runs #16 and #29 and the #10 versus #16 width comparison; Fig. S2, Run #26; Fig. S3, the Fig. 8 runs) is online at doi:10.1016/j.proci.2024.105200. [FLR-01 p.4 · MEASURED; FLR-01 p.5 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED; FLR-01 p.5 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED; FLR-01 p.6 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED; FLR-01 p.8 · MEASURED]
- Standards and facility cited: ISO 4589-4:2021 (high gas velocity test), ISO 4589-2:2017 (ambient-temperature test), and JAXA's SCEM facility page. [FLR-01 p.8 · CITED]

- FLR-05 (Konno et al., accepted manuscript; doi:10.1016/j.firesaf.2023.103989, handle 2115/95976, CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0) applies the ISO 4589-4 high gas flow velocity oxygen index test, made for limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) of flat specimens in opposed flow, to electric wires, and compares ground data with microgravity data to check whether the minimum limiting oxygen concentration (MLOC) can be estimated from it. [FLR-05 p.1 · MEASURED; FLR-05 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Wires with LDPE and ETFE insulation on Cu and NiCr cores were tested over gas flow velocities of 4 to 100 cm/s. [FLR-05 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Abbreviations used by FLR-05: the polymers LDPE (low-density polyethylene) and ETFE (ethylene-tetrafluoroethylene); the oxygen measures OI (oxygen index), HOI (high gas velocity oxygen index), LOI (limiting oxygen index), LOC (limiting oxygen concentration) and MLOC (minimum LOC). [FLR-05 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors' highlights and abstract claim that the ISO 4589-4 test, as modified, determined wire LOCs accurately, that every wire tested is more flammable in microgravity than in normal gravity, and that the ground and microgravity LOCs are well connected. [FLR-05 p.3–4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Motivation and the FLARE MLOC method (FLR-05)
- For spacecraft fire safety the authors see a need to judge material flame retardancy for the atmospheres expected on missions. [FLR-05 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA-STD-6001B (FLR-05 ref. 1) judges material suitability for spacecraft by flammability, odour and offgas tests; despite its long record, scientists and engineers have recently raised issues (refs. 2, 3), one being that the standard does not consider the effect of gravity on material flammability. [FLR-05 p.5 · CITED · nominal]
- Because gravity matters in combustion with large gas density changes, the authors argue the gravity effect on flammability should be considered on a scientific basis. [FLR-05 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flammability is often judged from flame spread tests: NASA-STD-6001B Tests 1 and 4, the LOI test (ref. 4) and UL94 for plastics (ref. 5). [FLR-05 p.5 · CITED · nominal]
- The authors reason that real fire growth is governed by flame spread after ignition, so the critical condition for self-sustained burning after forced ignition is meaningful for flammability. [FLR-05 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Olson et al. (FLR-05 refs. 8, 9) observed opposed flame spread over 76 μm thin cellulosic paper in NASA Lewis (now Glenn) 2.2 s drop tower and 5.18 s Zero Gravity Facility tests and found a U-shaped relation between LOC (O2 at which spread is extinguished) and opposed flow velocity, so flammability is suppressed at both low and high flow and one flow gives burning at the lowest O2, the MLOC (lowest O2 for self-sustained burning, at a flow condition; definitions from ref. 2). [FLR-05 p.5–6 · CITED]
- The U shape is explained (refs. 10, 11) by gas residence time: at low flow (long residence) a quenching branch dominated by heat loss; at high flow (short residence) a blow-off or stretch-extinction branch dominated by reactant leakage from finite-rate chemistry. [FLR-05 p.6 · CITED]
- If a material's MLOC lies at a gas velocity below the buoyant flow induced by gravity, the authors expect its flame retardancy may worsen in reduced gravity, needing extra considerations in fire-safety standards judged on the ground. [FLR-05 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- JAXA's Flammability Limits at Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE, refs. 2, 12–14) aims to set up a method for estimating MLOC of various materials and propose it as a new option for spacecraft fire-safety standards. [FLR-05 p.6 · CITED · nominal]
- Takahashi et al. (refs. 15–19) built a semi-empirical model of LOC against opposed flow for thermally thin sheets and found that various materials have their MLOC at low flow in microgravity, where buoyant flow vanishes; their flammability map has a quenching branch at low flow and a blow-off branch at high flow, in a U shape. [FLR-05 p.6 · CITED]
- MLOC is estimated from a model of the extinction limit of opposed-flow spread over a thermally thin solid, with ground data used (refs. 17–19) to improve the quantitative prediction; tuning hard-to-know parameters (activation energy, pre-factor, solid emissivity) and extrapolating ground data predicted MLOCs for various materials. [FLR-05 p.6–7 · CITED · nominal]
- Recommended tuning data: the OI at low flow (4 cm/s, ISO 4589-2, ref. 4) and LOC at high flows (60–100 cm/s), where forced rather than natural convection controls the flow; the high-flow LOC method is newly standardised as ISO 4589-4 (ref. 20), the HOI test. [FLR-05 p.7 · CITED · nominal]
- The authors' reasons for high-flow data: with forced flow far above natural convection the experimenter controls the effective velocity at extinction, and extrapolating LOCs from different flows improves the MLOC estimate; LOC trends over a wide flow range also hint whether LOC falls or rises in microgravity; since flame-induced natural convection dominates at small forced flow, they recommend the HOI at 60–100 cm/s for predicting MLOC. [FLR-05 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 1 (concept, after Takahashi et al., refs. 17–19): O2 against opposed flow V_g with flammable and non-flammable regions split by a boundary that has a radiative extinction branch at low velocity and a blow-off extinction branch at high velocity; method steps: 1, OI by ISO 4589-2 at V_g = 4 cm/s; 2, HOI by ISO 4589-4 at V_g = 60–100 cm/s; 3, estimate LOC trends by theory; 4, find MLOC from the estimate; ground tests cover the higher velocities, microgravity (spacecraft, an upcoming ISS experiment) the lower ones. [FLR-05 p.7 · Fig. 1 · CITED]

#### Study scope and wire samples (FLR-05)
- ISO 4589-4 had so far been developed only for thermally thin sheets, and it was unclear whether the HOI test suits thermally thick or composite materials; the authors are now working on an MLOC method for electric wires, which they identify as the most likely cause of spacecraft fires, but no standard method exists for OI and HOI of wires. [FLR-05 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The study tests whether the ISO 4589-2 OI and ISO 4589-4 HOI tests can be applied to thin electric wires, and runs parabolic-flight microgravity tests to get LOC against opposed flow over a wide range including the MLOC condition. [FLR-05 p.8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Earlier data by Takahashi et al. (ref. 21) and Mizutani et al. (ref. 22) are also used to build the wire flammability maps and to judge whether the modified HOI test predicts wire MLOC. [FLR-05 p.8 · CITED]
- Wires with OI below and above the O2 level of air were chosen on purpose (LDPE and ETFE insulation; Cu and NiCr cores) to test the HOI method. [FLR-05 p.8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- ETFE, a flame-resistant polymer, has a high LOI of 30 % (ref. 23) against 18 % for LDPE (ref. 24) (form, gravity, pressure, flow and test method of these LOI values not given); ETFE's flame retardancy comes from halogen radical trapping (refs. 28, 29): halides recombine H radicals into H2 (H + HF → H2 + F), slowing the branching reaction H + O2 → O + OH and lowering O and OH. (tests `FLR-05:nodate:ETFE-LOI:3bda11ed`, `FLR-05:nodate:LDPE-LOI:89b0281b`) [FLR-05 p.8 · CITED; FLR-05 p.12 · CITED]
- H radicals also speed soot pyrolysis (ref. 28), so adding halogens is known to raise the sooting tendency of hydrocarbon diffusion flames (ref. 30). [FLR-05 p.12 · CITED]

#### Ground test procedure (FLR-05)
- Ignition and LOC determination follow ISO 4589-2 and ISO 4589-4, with the up-and-down method (ref. 25): O2 is raised or lowered a set number of times according to each spread result, giving the LOC in few tests; because the HOI velocity is the hot-wire anemometer value, not the bulk velocity, the volume flow rates that give the target velocity are recorded beforehand and the O2 and N2 rates set from them; before each run the analyser branch (V1) is opened while O2 and flow are set, then closed; the bypass (V2) and its control valve (V3) cut the test-section flow below 10 cm/s for ignition (conditions C5). [FLR-05 p.8–11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Pass/fail: a run counts as "flammable" if the flame spreads past a reference line 60 mm from the bottom edge of the holder plate and "not flammable" if it quenches before (Fig. 3 marks a transition region 215–180 mm, a test region 180–60 mm and a "not confidence" region 60–0 mm, plus the ignition position and the extinction location). [FLR-05 p.10 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED; FLR-05 p.11 · MEASURED]
- The 60 mm reference line is there to keep heat loss through the highly conductive core to the holder from affecting the extinction limit. [FLR-05 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Earlier wire temperature measurements (ref. 26) showed the hot region of a 0.5 mm diameter Cu core extending up to 40 mm upstream of the flame front in near-limit downward spread. [FLR-05 p.11 · CITED]
- The reference line is therefore set 60 mm from the holder bottom, a 20 mm safety margin included (conditions C5). [FLR-05 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Details of the flight setup are in FLR-05 refs. 22 and 27; earlier work (ref. 17) reported natural convection of about 3 cm/s from residual gravity during parabolic-flight spread tests, even on small flat sheets a few centimetres wide and under 1 m thick (as printed). [FLR-05 p.11–12 · CITED]
- The flight tests therefore used forced flows of 5–20 cm/s so that residual gravity would not dominate the spread (conditions C6). [FLR-05 p.12 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Flame spread rate against O2 (FLR-05 Figs. 5, 6)
- Spread rate Vf (ground and flight) was tracked from the leading edge of the visible flame; the front-position histories (Fig. 5) were nearly steady for every wire and condition, so Vf is the slope of a linear fit. [FLR-05 p.14 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 5 example runs (front position 0–80 mm over 0–80 s): (a) LDPE, Cu in μg at V_g 12 cm/s, Xo 0.197; Cu in 1 g at 100, 60 and 80 cm/s, Xo 0.200, 0.184, 0.192; NiCr in 1 g at 100, 60 and 80 cm/s, Xo 0.236, 0.214, 0.220; (b) ETFE, Cu in μg at 12 cm/s, Xo 0.390; Cu in 1 g at 80, 60 and 100 cm/s, Xo 0.442, 0.422, 0.466; NiCr in μg at 12 cm/s, Xo 0.271; NiCr in 1 g at 80, 60 and 100 cm/s, Xo 0.476, 0.442, 0.518 (sets C5 and C6). [FLR-05 p.14 · Fig. 5a · MEASURED · nominal; FLR-05 p.14 · Fig. 5b · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 6 plots Vf against O2 for every flow, the microgravity data included except LDPE–NiCr#2; since the ground and flight tunnels differ (75 and 60 mm inside diameter), data from an earlier 60 mm tunnel study (ref. 26, Konno et al. 2020) are added for comparison. [FLR-05 p.14–15 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors find little difference in Vf and extinction limits between the two tunnels, though only LDPE wires at 4 cm/s forced flow on the ground can be compared, and so judge the tunnel geometry not to affect the results significantly. [FLR-05 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Vf rose with O2 at every flow (sets C5, 4–100 cm/s, and C6, 5–20 cm/s); Cu-core wires, of higher thermal conductivity, spread faster than NiCr-core wires under the same conditions whatever the insulation, in line with earlier wire studies (refs. 26, 35–39). [FLR-05 p.15 · MEASURED]
- The authors conclude that a highly conductive core enhances steady flame spread. [FLR-05 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The minimum Vf of the Cu wires in Fig. 6 is larger than that of the NiCr wires for both insulations (the μg LDPE data are left out of this point, there being no LDPE–NiCr#2 Vf); Cu-wire Vf is also more sensitive to O2 than NiCr-wire Vf for both insulations, a feature the authors call unique to wire spread (sets C5, C6). [FLR-05 p.15–16 · MEASURED]
- Konno et al.'s theory (ref. 26) supports this: flames over highly conductive wires go out at a larger Vf because of heat loss from the unburned zone, a negative feedback that grows as the hot solid region lengthens at lower Vf and is stronger for a conductive core. [FLR-05 p.16 · CITED]
- The authors explain the O2 sensitivity by the bare metal core, heated by the downstream flame after the insulation burns off, recirculating heat upstream to the unburned zone, which makes spread more sensitive to flame temperature and length (ref. 39). [FLR-05 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Vf in microgravity was lower than in normal gravity for LDPE–Cu#2 but higher for ETFE–Cu#2 (sets C5, C6). [FLR-05 p.16 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the difference to the spread regime: the ETFE wire flame is in the kinetic regime, so its Vf rises as external flow falls, as in microgravity. [FLR-05 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 6 legend: circles Cu#2, triangles NiCr#2; μg data at 5 (red), 12 (magenta) and 20 cm/s (blue); 1 g data at 4 (yellow), 40 (green), 60 (teal), 80 (navy) and 100 cm/s (purple), plus "4 cm/s Konno et al. (2020)" (olive); hatched bars mark the flame spread limit; axes Vf 0–8 mm/s against O2 vol.% ((a) LDPE 14–26, (b) ETFE 20–60). [FLR-05 p.15 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]

- Fig. 7 plots LOC against opposed flow velocity; the OI test used 4 cm/s forced flow per ISO 4589-2. [FLR-05 p.16–17 · MEASURED · nominal]

(refs. 17–19); other results are plotted at their forced flow without buoyancy correction. [FLR-05 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

- The authors find the present flight data more consistent with the high-flow LOCs of the ground tests. [FLR-05 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[FLR-05 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Discussion and conclusions (FLR-05)
- The flammability boundary of flame spread over a solid is well established (ref. 9) to have two branches: a low-flow quenching branch governed by heat loss and a high-flow blow-off branch governed by finite-rate chemistry. [FLR-05 p.18 · CITED]
- Over the flows tested (μg 5–20 cm/s, 1 g 4–100 cm/s; sets C5, C6; for LDPE–NiCr#2 the μg points are Takahashi et al. (2013), ref. 21, Fig. 7b) no quenching branch was clearly seen at the low-flow side: LOC fell monotonically as flow fell, for all four wires. [FLR-05 p.17 · Fig. 7b · CITED · ~fig; FLR-05 p.18 · MEASURED; FLR-05 p.19 · MEASURED]
- The authors note that confirming a quenching branch for these wires needs forced flows below 5 cm/s, yet residual gravity and g-jitter in parabolic flight call for some forced flow for reproducible results; they consider their data the best obtainable from ground-based tests and see a need for on-orbit tests such as on the ISS (refs. 2, 12–14). [FLR-05 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Changing the core from Cu to NiCr changed how insulation flammability varies with flow: for NiCr wires the blow-off branch shifts to lower flows than for Cu wires, for both insulations (sets C5, C6; for LDPE–NiCr#2 the μg points are Takahashi et al. (2013), ref. 21, Fig. 7b). [FLR-05 p.17 · Fig. 7b · CITED · ~fig; FLR-05 p.18 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the shift to larger heat loss from stronger axial conduction along the Cu core, which moves the quenching branch to higher flows. [FLR-05 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In absolute terms NiCr wires had lower LOC than Cu wires at low flow, and Cu wires lower LOC than NiCr wires at high flow, for both insulations (sets C5, C6; for LDPE–NiCr#2 the μg points are Takahashi et al. (2013), ref. 21, Fig. 7b). [FLR-05 p.17 · Fig. 7b · CITED · ~fig; FLR-05 p.18–19 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that stronger axial conduction through the core can suppress insulation flammability at low flow and enhance it at high flow (refs. 26, 40). [FLR-05 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- ETFE LOCs fell markedly at low flow in microgravity compared with LDPE (set C6). [FLR-05 p.19 · MEASURED]
- Osorio et al. (ref. 27) and Mizutani et al. (ref. 22) also measured ETFE-insulated Cu wire in normal and microgravity and reported a large LOC drop in microgravity. [FLR-05 p.19 · CITED]
- The authors conclude that several studies show materials with enough flame retardancy on the ground becoming extremely flammable in microgravity, a serious threat to mission safety, so gravity effects on flame retardancy must be weighed in spacecraft safety design; the next step is to make MLOC predictable for many materials and identify which stay flame-retardant in microgravity. [FLR-05 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Conclusions (authors): the ISO 4589-4 HOI test, developed for LOC of thin sheets at high flow, was modified for wires, worked properly, and its data serve MLOC prediction; its validity is supported by the near-MLOC flight data agreeing with the HOI data. [FLR-05 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The LOC of every wire tested tended to fall monotonically with decreasing flow over the flows tested, so both LDPE- and ETFE-insulated wires should be more flammable without buoyant flow in microgravity than in normal gravity. [FLR-05 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For both insulations, NiCr wires showed lower LOC than Cu wires at low flow in microgravity, and the order reversed at high flow in normal gravity; since the same insulation behaves differently on different cores, the authors hold that a composite such as a wire should be rated as a whole, not by its insulation alone. [FLR-05 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- ETFE, flame-resistant on the ground, shows very low LOC (high flammability) at low flow in microgravity. [FLR-05 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2
# EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2 — Martian, Lunar and 0g limits vs 1g Test 1; Lunar-g evidence and the FM² plan; reduced pressure as a low-g analog

## Scope
Covers: OVR-04 (Olson and Ferkul 2012: Martian-g centrifuge limits of Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex HT90-40 compared with 1g WSTF, Lunar-g and 0g limits; oxygen margin of safety), OVR-13 (Ferkul et al. 2026 slides: why 1 g may not be the worst case, cited partial-g boundaries and spread rates, Lunar-g SIBAL tests, the FM² lunar-surface experiment plan and vent-gas estimates), SAF-04 and SAF-08 introductions (Earth test vs space), SAF-09 (Thomsen et al. 2018: reduced pressure as a ground simulation of reduced-gravity concurrent spread over 10 mm PMMA, compared with Saffire II sample 9).
Not here: BAS-09, CAB-02, CAB-04, FLR-01, FLR-05, OVR-03 and BAS-04 statements on Earth vs low-g limits (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1); the Test 1 method and 1-g parametric effects (see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1, MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2); cabin atmospheres (see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1, CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2); BASS results (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4); Saffire results (see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1, LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2).

## Findings

### Modified Test 1 protocol and the limit definitions (OVR-04)
- NASA STD 6001 Test 1, cited as the main method for judging materials for habitable volumes of U.S. spacecraft, is a pass/fail upward flame propagation test in the most severe flaming environment (O2, pressure) expected in the vehicle, e.g. 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia, the ISS pre-breathe environment for spacewalks; a material that does not self-extinguish after six inches of burning needs other special considerations and/or tests before use. [OVR-04 p.1 · CITED]
- The modified Test 1 protocol (refs. 2–4) relies on multiple 1-g tests. [OVR-04 p.1 · CITED]
- Instead of a pass/fail qualification in the worst expected environment, the modified protocol measures the actual upward flammability limit (akin to the Limiting Oxygen Index, LOI), so that the margin of safety in the real use environment can be assessed more accurately. [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.8 · CITED]
- More broadly, the authors see the protocol as a way to choose better or best materials by their margin of safety relative to the use environment, not only by a "pass". [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the modified procedure (ref. 2) the Test 1 O2 concentration is lowered step by step to find the 1g Upward Limiting Oxygen Index (1g ULOI) and the 1g Maximum Oxygen Concentration (1g MOC) that consistently gives self-extinguishment; 1g ULOI = the O2 concentration at which the material passes the Test 1 burn-length criterion about half the time; 1g MOC = the O2 concentration at which at least five samples passed the criterion and at least one sample failed at 1 % (by volume) more O2. [OVR-04 p.2 · CITED]
- Fig. 1 sketches, for an arbitrary material, the cumulative probability of burning (failing Test 1) against O2 concentration: ULOI at probability 0.5, MOC at probability 0, a "1 in 5 burn" point at 0.2, and a 1 % O2 interval between the MOC and the "1 in 5 burn" point. [OVR-04 p.2 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Reduced-gravity limits (asterisk) are defined slightly differently because the 1g definitions would need too many drop tests: MOC* = the highest O2 at which the flame was seen to self-extinguish within the drop time; ULOI* = the lowest O2 at which the flame survived the full drop time; Eq. 1 applies these to the 0g, Lunar-g and Martian-g drop tests. [OVR-04 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.4–6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors stress, three times, that the low-g extinction-limit criteria are not the same as the 1g ones because of the time limits of drop testing. [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The 1g comparison tests at NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) followed the STD-6001 Test 1 protocol but ignited the samples with a hot wire instead of a chemical igniter, and the atmosphere was varied to find ULOI and MOC; WSTF used Melinex 515, a very similar DuPont Teijin film, in place of Mylar G. [OVR-04 p.2–4 · CITED · nominal]
- The reason given for the hot wire: the chemical igniter heats for 25 s, while the longest low-gravity time is 5 s. [OVR-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The three fuels were evaluated for microgravity, Lunar and Martian limits to compare with the 1g ULOI and 1g MOC: Martian-g tests in the centrifuge, 1g tests at WSTF, microgravity tests with forced convection and Lunar-g tests at NASA GRC; the limits are tabulated to find the factor of safety tied to normal-gravity screening, the comparison being made against a modified NASA standard test protocol. [OVR-04 p.1–2 · MEASURED; OVR-04 p.1–2 · CITED; OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Test materials (OVR-04)
- Ultem 1000: fire-retarded polyetherimide (PEI) film, 10 mil thick, described by the authors as inherently flame-retarding and charring, with a very low smoke signature, very low smoke toxicity and a low heat-release rate. [OVR-04 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; OVR-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Nomex HT90-40: fire-retarded aromatic nylon fabric, 12 mil thick, that does not melt or drip as it burns. [OVR-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- When heated, Nomex fibres swell and close the spaces between them, which stops air moving through the fabric and so inhibits heat transfer through it. [OVR-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mylar G: polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film, 5 mil thick, not fire-retarded, melts as it burns, chosen mainly because it does not char. [OVR-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]

### Martian-g centrifuge apparatus and procedure (OVR-04)
- The Zero-Gravity Centrifuge was built for the NASA GRC Zero Gravity Facility drop tower within its size and volume limits: a flat circular turntable and a chamber dome (a chamber is needed because the tower is evacuated before a drop), designed for the largest rotation radius on the drop bus and strong enough for 2 atm absolute; the Fig. 2 photo labels Drop Bus, Pneumatic Lifters, Chamber Dome and Experiment Platform (Turntable). [OVR-04 p.2–3 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The fuel sheet lies parallel to the turntable near its outer edge, between two 0.005-in mica frames with a 5 cm × 15 cm opening, which are clamped between 0.010-in stainless-steel frames; a hot wire ignites it at the point farthest from the centre, which sets up concurrent-flow spread, the buoyant flow pointing toward the turntable centre (Fig. 3). [OVR-04 p.3 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The chamber is filled with the test atmosphere and spun for at least 5 min before the drop so the gas reaches solid-body rotation; 30.8 RPM gives Martian gravity (0.38 g Earth) at the radius of the igniter. [OVR-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; OVR-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Ignition was timed to occur at or just before the drop: Ultem and Nomex igniter current on 2.1 s before the drop for 3.5 s in total; Mylar (easier to ignite) 1 s before the drop for 2 s in total, helped by a 0.5-cm-wide strip of thin tissue (Kimwipes) for even energy input to the melting fuel. [OVR-04 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Mean igniter power was 58 W in all cases, and all Martian-g tests used the same igniter wire. [OVR-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
- Drop duration 5.18 s (Fig. 4 marks t = 5.18 s as the end of the drop). [OVR-04 p.4 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Footnote: the Martian-g flames were small relative to the sample and spread only a short way along the fuel during the 5.18-s drops. [OVR-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
- Because centrifugal acceleration scales with radius, such a flame stays in a region of nearly constant g (printed "(lunar g)"), whereas a flame spreading far along the fuel would feel an appreciably changing acceleration. [OVR-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
