### Interpretation of the margins (OVR-04)
- The authors conclude from Fig. 6 and Table I that the 1g limits are generally not conservative for these materials, as the negative ∆O2 % shows, by up to −5.75 % O2. [OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Their explanation for low-g concurrent (upward) flow: with buoyancy absent or reduced, convective heat loss from the flame zone falls, so the flame needs to release less heat than in 1g to give the unburned fuel the same heat flux; low-g limits lower than 1g limits are therefore the general trend and not entirely surprising. [OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Nomex and Ultem are charring fuels; char formation is a known fire-retardant mechanism because it reduces the heat release rate. [OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For these charring fuels (Ultem 10.2 psia, Nomex 14.7 psia) the 0g margin with concurrent forced flow is very close to zero, and the Lunar-g margin is ~2.5 % lower than 1g. [OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · CITED; OVR-04 p.7 · MODELED]
- The authors read the near-zero 0g margin as reduced charring in 0g possibly being offset by lower heat release in the weaker convective environment. [OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They add that materials may burn better with adequate but not excessive convection, as flammability maps predict (ref. 10). [OVR-04 p.7 · CITED]
- Mylar is non-charring; as in metals combustion (ref. 11), the absence of gravity-driven dripping keeps heated molten fuel in the flame zone instead of removing it. [OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As printed, the result for Mylar (5 mil film, 10.2 psia) is a significantly negative margin (~4–5 %) in Martian g, Lunar g and 0g. [OVR-04 p.7 · MODELED; OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Evaluation of ∆O2 % for other materials is continuing for concurrent limits, to be followed by opposed-flow limits; if proven for more materials, this may indicate the need for a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits. [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Martian-g flame behaviour near the limits (OVR-04)
- Fig. 4 shows front views of the Martian-g concurrent flames of Nomex HT90-40, Mylar G and Ultem 1000 (10 mil) at their ULOI* (O2 and pressure per Table I) just as the drop ends (t = 5.18 s), on the Zero-Gravity Centrifuge with hot-wire ignition at the outer sample end. [OVR-04 p.4 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED; OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · MEASURED; OVR-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At ULOI* the Mylar flame looked stable, while the Nomex and Ultem flames were growing dim and shrinking at the end of the drop (less than 1 cm long and getting smaller) (Martian g, concurrent flow). [OVR-04 p.4 · MEASURED]
- The authors judge that these very weak flames might have gone out given more time at Martian g, so the limits found are conservative. [OVR-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mylar G at the Martian-g ULOI* (18 % O2, 10.2 psi; 0.38 g Earth on the centrifuge; igniter 1 s before the drop for 2 s with Kimwipes; concurrent flow; 5 cm × 15 cm opening; 5.18 s drop): the igniter glows until ignition and then cools after power-off; the flame starts dim blue, brightens to yellow and appears to stabilise, and survives the whole drop without spanning the 5-cm sample width; Fig. 5 shows frames at 10 Hz, the last showing extinction caused by the impact of the experiment (test key OVR-04:nodate:MYLAR-MARTIAN-TEST:283be22d). [OVR-04 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; OVR-04 p.3–5 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- In another test at 17 % O2 (10.2 psi from the Table I Mylar column; Martian g, centrifuge drop) the Mylar flame went out (test key OVR-04:nodate:MYLAR-MARTIAN-TEST:5d39731d). [OVR-04 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test; OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · MEASURED]
- Near-limit flames in the reduced-gravity drop tests were generally small and confined to the upstream edge of the material, and any curling, swelling or contracting of the burned edge was seen to weaken the flame. [OVR-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- The weakening apparently acts through the flow around the burned edge; the authors infer that, since O2 transport is critical to low-gravity flames, anything that reduces free O2 flow past the sample reduces its flammability. [OVR-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Conclusions (OVR-04)
- Earlier microgravity and Lunar-gravity testing showed some materials burning to lower O2 concentrations in low gravity than in normal gravity (Table I conditions C3, C4). [OVR-04 p.1 · CITED; OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · CITED]
- Conclusions as printed: the upward flame spread O2 extinction limits at Martian buoyant-flow gravity were significantly lower than in normal gravity ("up to 5.75% O2 lower") and typically between the normal-gravity and Lunar-gravity values (Mylar G and Ultem 1000 at 10.2 psia, Nomex HT90-40 at 14.7 psia; drop-tower centrifuge, concurrent buoyant flow). [OVR-04 p.6 · Table I · MEASURED; OVR-04 p.8 · MEASURED]
- In Table I, the Martian ULOI* and MOC* lie between the 1g and Lunar values for Mylar and Ultem, while the Nomex Martian values (19.9, 19.0) are below its Lunar values (21.0, 19.9); the largest Martian ∆O2 is −3.35 % (Nomex), and −5.75 % is the Lunar Mylar margin (conditions C1–C3). [INFERRED from: OVR-04 p.6; OVR-04 p.8]
- The authors conclude that the Martian data suggest a gravity level below Earth's at which materials burn more readily than on Earth, and that the consistent negative margins indicate normal-gravity screening may not be conservative, so some materials tested safe for space may actually be flammable. [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The centrifuge reaches g-levels not easily attainable in simple drop-tower or aircraft experiments, and other projects could use the chamber. [OVR-04 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Cabin atmosphere background (OVR-04 introduction)
- For future missions it is often desirable to lower cabin pressure while keeping the O2 partial pressure; atmospheres are chosen on material flammability, decompression sickness, hypoxia and efficient crew transfers and excursions (ref. 5). [OVR-04 p.1 · CITED]
- Holding O2 partial pressure constant while lowering total pressure raises the O2 concentration, which raises material flammability. [OVR-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A major lesson of the Apollo 1 fire (ref. 6) is that ignition sources cannot all be eliminated, so spacecraft fire prevention relies on material controls near potential ignition sources and on fire-resistant materials. [OVR-04 p.1 · CITED]
- After Skylab, the Shuttle and ISS have operated at sea-level air (21 % O2, 79 % N2 by volume, 14.7 psia) except brief pre-EVA periods at 30 % O2 and 10.2 psia, so many materials used on the Shuttle or now on ISS are tested and rated only to 30 % O2 at 10.2 psia. [OVR-04 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Earth screening test vs space: general statements (OVR-13, SAF-04, SAF-08, SAF-09)
- NASA relies on a 1-g test to screen material flammability for flight: the material is ignited near the bottom and the flame spreads upward; a material that passes is considered safe for spaceflight, and one that fails has its use restricted (time, quantity, etc.). [OVR-13 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]
- The authors call this test a practical way to assess the great number of materials screened. [OVR-13 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- NASA rates materials for space use with a test performed on Earth (NASA-STD-6001B). [SAF-04 p.2 · CITED · nominal, slide]
- A material that passes that test is assumed safe in the microgravity environment of space. [SAF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- NASA screens materials for spacecraft cabins with an upward flame spread test (ref. 1). [SAF-09 p.2 · CITED]
- Concurrent (flow-assisted) flame spread is generally fast and so hazardous, which is why some material flammability tests use this mode to characterise fire hazard. [SAF-09 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Current material-selection standards (ECSS-Q-ST-70-21-C, ISO/TS 16697, NASA-STD-6001B) prescribe 1g fire tests on upright flat specimens. [SAF-08 p.2 · CITED · nominal; SAF-08 p.12 · CITED]
- The SAF-08 authors note that a spacecraft differs from such tests both in gravity and in the shape of the material. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- OVR-13: in the authors' reading, microgravity research hints that 1 g may not be the condition in which a material burns most readily; theory and experiment show some materials that do not burn in 1-g do burn in 0-g with low-speed flow, or at partial gravity such as Lunar-g; and growing evidence suggests a material that passes the NASA standard test might still fail below 1-g levels of gravity and flow. [OVR-13 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide; OVR-13 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- SAF-04: there is evidence that some materials that do not burn on Earth will burn in space under similar conditions. [SAF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- SAF-04: on Earth an upward-spreading (concurrent-flow) flame is nearly always more hazardous than a downward-spreading (opposed-flow) one; in reduced gravity, which configuration is more hazardous depends on flow speed, which complicates extrapolating Earth test results to space even further. [SAF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- SAF-09: spacecraft fire conditions differ greatly from those on Earth, especially for the space exploration atmospheres (SEA) NASA plans for future spacecraft, and testing in space is difficult and expensive. [SAF-09 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SEA conditions include microgravity, low-velocity flows and potentially low pressure (~60 kPa) with elevated O2 concentration (~34 %); they are designed to cut preparation time for spacewalks while keeping the O2 partial pressure acceptable for breathing (refs. 2, 3). [SAF-09 p.2 · CITED]
- Spacecraft ventilation induces flows of the order of 100 to 200 mm/s, while the buoyant flow induced by a spreading flame is of the order of 300 to 600 mm/s. [SAF-09 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flame-induced buoyancy makes the spacecraft environment, especially its low-velocity flows, very hard to reproduce on Earth, so fire testing of spacecraft materials needs either a reduced-gravity facility or another way of reducing buoyancy. [SAF-09 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-04: understanding ignition and flame growth feeds fire-safety protocols for space; spread and growth of a fire and its interaction with the vehicle cannot be expected to scale linearly from small-scale test data, which leaves a substantial gap in understanding fire behaviour in spacecraft. [SAF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide; SAF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- SAF-04 (2017): large-scale fire tests are common on Earth but had never been attempted in a space experiment, for obvious reasons of practicality and safety. [SAF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

### Limits of ground facilities and the case for lunar tests
- Drop towers and aircraft have given valuable information but are limited by duration and/or Coriolis-force effects. [OVR-13 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide; OVR-13 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- A drop tower limits experiment time to ~5 s, which may be long enough for the gas-phase response but is typically too short for the solid. [OVR-13 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Ground microgravity facilities such as drop towers and parabolic flights last a few seconds; space-based testing is very expensive and very limited in space and opportunities; concurrent spread tests in space are further limited by size and safety restrictions, and information on flame spread in spacecraft environments is still lacking. [SAF-09 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most experiments have been in microgravity with an imposed forced convection; the flow acting on a flame can be buoyancy, forced convection or both. [OVR-13 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The Lunar surface offers unlimited duration for studying flame spread and flammability, and tests on the Moon would resolve some important questions and set the primary benchmark for later tests. [OVR-13 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide; OVR-13 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

### Flammability boundary vs gravity or flow speed (OVR-13, cited T'ien 1986)
- Schematic cited from T'ien, "Diffusion flame extinction at small stretch rates: the mechanism of radiative loss", Combustion and Flame, 1986: % O2 (no scale printed) against gravity level (g/gEarth) or characteristic flow speed (cm/s), paired ticks 10^-4 / 1, 10^-2 / 4 and 1 / 20; a U-shaped boundary with a quenching branch on the low side and a blowoff branch on the high side, "Flame" above and "No Flame" below, and a hatched line at 1 with an arrow "1-g Studies" pointing to higher values. [OVR-13 p.17 · CITED · slide]
- In the p.18 version, the bottom of the curve is labelled "Critical Low Oxygen Limit" and sits between 10^-2 and 1 g/gEarth, with dashed lines marking the minimum and the level where the curve crosses the 1-g line. [OVR-13 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Model result shown: the O2 concentration needed for flammability reaches a minimum near g = gMoon (material, pressure and flow not stated). [OVR-13 p.17–18 · MODELED · slide]
- The authors state that numerical and experimental evidence suggests Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition. [OVR-13 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

[OVR-13 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Objective C: evaluate the hypothesis that some materials burning in partial g may be more flammable than in 1-g (other conditions not stated). [OVR-13 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Summary claims: FM² would give the first-ever observations and measurements of flame spread on the Moon and a bridge between 1-g and future partial-g environments. [OVR-13 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

[OVR-13 p.11 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]

### 1g upward vs microgravity concurrent burning of PMMA (SAF-08 introduction)
- In 1g a fire spreads mainly upward with the convective flow and barely downward against it; in microgravity with a forced flow the reverse holds, although the spread velocities differ. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors argue that slower spread and burning in microgravity do not mean lower hazard, because far more flammable flue gas is produced than on the ground. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They conclude that orbital-habitat fire safety needs the basic processes understood and standards derived from them, both to cut the chance of a fire starting and to allow sensible strategies that limit fire spread and its consequences. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- 1g mechanism described for PMMA: steep temperature gradients with buoyant convection create strong velocity gradients in both upward and downward burning, the flow is stretched and shear instabilities form vortices, giving the familiar flame flicker as air enters across the buoyant flow (Fig. 1). [SAF-08 p.2 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because air mixes in from more than one side, the pyrolysis gas always finds enough oxidant: the flame burns vigorously, flame length and pyrolysis area keep growing, and the pyrolysis area moves quickly up the sample surface; for PMMA the excess pyrolyzate burns almost completely, so hardly any soot or unburned MMA forms and the gases leaving the top are mainly CO2 and water. [SAF-08 p.2 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Microgravity with forced flow, which the authors call probably the most important difference: lacking weight differences, the flow stays layered and laminar through the reaction zone despite thermal expansion and local density gradients, so atmospheric O2 reaches the flame only from upstream. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With the layering preserved, only the flame base receives enough O2, and both the steady flame length and its burning rate are limited (ref. 4). [SAF-08 p.2 · Fig. 2 · CITED]
- Beneath the flame the material reaches pyrolysis temperature, but the flame shields the pyrolyzate from air and the flow carries it off, so besides exhaust gas a large amount of potentially combustible flue gas is produced (Fig. 2). [SAF-08 p.2 · Fig. 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With only the base well supplied, the burning zone cannot travel over the surface: the pyrolysis front grows until flame radiation can no longer bring the surface to pyrolysis temperature, and the flame base moves at the rate at which the leading edge is fully consumed. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- So, for given atmospheric conditions, the flame-base speed depends mainly on material thickness, and the burning zone travelling with the flow, normal on Earth, is rather unlikely in microgravity. [SAF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Raising the inflow velocity: beyond a certain speed the flame lifts off, jumps back to its base several times and then goes out; there might be a very narrow, sensitive velocity range in which a lifted flame is pushed slowly over the preheated surface without yet blowing off. [SAF-08 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Such a regime was not seen in microgravity blowoff tests on burning rod tips (ref. 4), where it was unstable and marked the transition to blowoff. [SAF-08 p.3 · CITED]

### Reduced pressure as a ground analog of reduced-gravity concurrent spread: rationale (SAF-09)
- Abstract: reducing buoyancy by lowering ambient pressure is a possible way to simulate on Earth the burning behaviour inside spacecraft. [SAF-09 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Objective: test that possibility by studying the effect of pressure on concurrent flame spread and, by comparison with microgravity data, see how far low pressure can replicate the spread characteristics seen in microgravity, here for upward/concurrent spread over 10 mm thick PMMA slabs. [SAF-09 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Given the cost and limits of experiments in a spacecraft such as Cygnus, the authors find it relevant to simulate reduced-buoyancy experiments on Earth, to cut testing cost and also to check the spacecraft tests and verify models. [SAF-09 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Tilting the surface to reduce gravity effects has problems: it changes the boundary-layer thickness and hence the flame-to-surface heat flux and spread rate, and hot pyrolyzate stratifies near the surface in a ceiling orientation or away from it in a floor orientation, changing pyrolyzate and air transport (refs. 19, 27); lowering pressure, and so density, is therefore the more promising route. [SAF-09 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Several studies have used the lower buoyancy at reduced pressure to simulate microgravity solid burning (ignition, opposed flame spread, extinction) (refs. 28–33). [SAF-09 p.3 · CITED]
- Mechanism (refs. 20, 26, 34, 35): concurrent spread depends strongly on the heat flux to the fuel surface, set by flame length and stand-off distance; because gas density changes with pressure, lowering pressure thickens the boundary layer, moves the flame away from the surface and cuts the heat transferred to it, so spread slows through both lower heat flux and a shorter flame; lowering pressure therefore acts on spread like lowering flow velocity (Fig. 1). [SAF-09 p.3 · CITED]
- The main constraint on reproducing spacecraft flame spread in normal gravity is that spacecraft flow velocities (~100 to 200 mm/s) cannot be reached because the flame's buoyant flow (~300 to 600 mm/s) overwhelms the forced flow, so reduced pressure is a potential way to simulate concurrent spread in reduced-gravity, low-velocity flows. [SAF-09 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 1 schematic of concurrent spread over a thick sample: spread rate V_f upward, gravity g downward, O2/N2 flow U_∞ upward, flame tip at x_f, pyrolysis front at x_p, pyrolysis length l_p = x_p, heating length l_h = x_f − x_p, heat fluxes q''_rs, q''_fr and q''_conv, sample thickness s, and a "Low P" label. [SAF-09 p.3 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This study examines concurrent spread over a thick PMMA sheet in normal gravity, mixed forced and free flow and a range of reduced pressures, the PMMA being chosen for comparison with microgravity tests, particularly Saffire II sample 9 (ref. 15); it follows the approach and analysis of the authors' thin-fabric tests (refs. 16, 17), so some information is repeated, given here in more detail. [SAF-09 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-09 p.3–4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire (ref. 13) carries out large-scale fire tests, or several small flame-spread tests of varied materials, in the uncrewed Orbital ATK Cygnus cargo vehicle after it leaves ISS and before it de-orbits; Saffire I and III were large-scale tests with a thin cotton/fiberglass fabric (Sibal) and Saffire II nine small-scale tests of different materials (refs. 13–15). [SAF-09 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors' normal-gravity variable-pressure tests supporting Saffire II used Sibal fabric (samples 5, 6; ref. 16), Nomex fabric (sample 7; ref. 17) and, here, a 10 mm PMMA slab (sample 9; ref. 15). [SAF-09 p.2 · CITED]
- Similar results were obtained by the authors with a thin composite cotton/fiberglass fabric (Sibal), reported elsewhere (ref. 16). [SAF-09 p.1 · CITED; SAF-09 p.16 · CITED; SAF-09 p.21 · CITED]

### Reduced-pressure tests and Saffire II sample 9: apparatus and methods (SAF-09)
- Normal-gravity apparatus (ref. 29; as in refs. 16, 17, adapted to thick PMMA): a laboratory-scale combustion tunnel inside a pressure chamber (Fig. 2), duct 125 mm × 125 mm and 600 mm long, the first 350 mm a flow straightener and the last 250 mm the test section; test-section walls normal to the sample of clear polycarbonate with low pins (~2–3 mm) holding the sample straight, walls parallel to it of 0.56 mm alkali-aluminosilicate glass for imaging. [SAF-09 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fig. 2a labels Air/N2 and O2 supply lines through control orifices, honeycomb, glass beads, perforated plates, upward air flow to the PMMA sample, alkali-aluminosilicate glass, pressure regulator, vacuum pump and camera. [SAF-09 p.4 · Fig. 2a · MEASURED · nominal]
- Sample: cast PMMA (McMaster-Carr) matching one Saffire II material (ref. 15), 150 mm long, 50 mm wide, 10 mm thick, vertical at the test-section midplane with both sides in the flow but only one side burning; a small groove on each side slides into a stainless-steel holder whose 25-mm sidewalls stop side air entrainment; shorter than the microgravity samples because that was the longest the apparatus could hold (Fig. 3, igniter holes at the upstream end). [SAF-09 p.4–5 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Ignition: a 29-gage Kanthal wire threaded along the upstream edge through 14 equally spaced holes in a ~5 mm tapered end, driven by a constant-current supply (BK Precision 1785) set to 68 W. [SAF-09 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The time needed to assure ignition was 10 to 50 s, longer at lower pressure (10 mm PMMA, normal gravity, air, 100 to 40 kPa, upward forced flow 200 mm/s). [SAF-09 p.4–5 · MEASURED]
- Compressed house air enters through critical nozzles (O'Keefe Controls) while the chamber is continuously evacuated by a vacuum generator (Vaccon JS-300) and mechanical regulator, and is delivered to the duct inlet at the bottom, keeping the duct flow fresh at constant mass flow; chamber pressure is monitored by a transducer (Omega PX303-015A5V). [SAF-09 p.4–5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Test matrix: air at 100, 80, 60 and 40 ± 2 kPa with a fixed forced flow of 200 mm/s directed upward (concurrent spread in mixed forced and free convection), the chamber sealed and set after placing the sample; ~40 kPa was the lowest pressure the apparatus allowed; 3 to 5 replicates per condition. [SAF-09 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Imaging: two 9000-lumen LEDs on a strobe circuit overpower the flame light to show the pyrolysis region; two cameras at 1920 × 1080 and 60 frames/s, a Sony RX10-III tracking the pyrolysis front and a Nikon D3200 recording visible flame length. [SAF-09 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Saffire II (ref. 15; details in refs. 13–15) on the Orbital ATK Cygnus: a rectangular flow duct 460 mm × 510 mm with fans at one end drawing air through, the sample holder mid-duct so air flows on both sides (Fig. 4c); nine samples 290 mm long by 50 mm wide (Fig. 4a), sample 9 being the 10 mm PMMA slab that gave the data used here; for concurrent spread a resistively heated 29-gage (0.286 mm) Kanthal wire through 18 closely spaced holes in the tapered upstream end across the 50 mm width was powered for 30 s (3.85 A, 97 W), more than in normal gravity, to assure ignition of the thick fuel; the sample burned in air at 200 mm/s and atmospheric pressure (test SAFFIRE-II:2-9). [SAF-09 p.5–6 · Fig. 4 · CITED · nominal, single-test]
- Saffire II instruments: two cameras at 30 fps in a dark duct, with green LED light for 0.4 s every 2 s to show the pyrolysis front; four radiometers viewing front and back; six thermocouples on and near the fuel and through the duct; O2, CO2 and pressure recorded just upstream of the fuel; plus vehicle smoke-detector data. [SAF-09 p.6 · CITED · nominal]
- Saffire II spread rate method: the flame location was taken from the dark images where pixel intensity drops sharply past a threshold, tracked over time, leaving out the initial ignition period (SAFFIRE-II:2-9). [SAF-09 p.6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Normal-gravity data: pyrolysis-front and flame-tip positions, from which the spread rate is extracted; the flame tip is located in dark frames (strobe off) where pixel intensity drops past 75 % of the flame-pixel intensity, and the pyrolysis front where the PMMA first visibly pyrolyses (bubbles) with the strobe on. [SAF-09 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The pyrolysis front could not be tracked in the Saffire II images because the flame covered the pyrolysis region and its light hid it (SAFFIRE-II:2-9). [SAF-09 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]

- C12 observations: after ignition the flame spreads to the end of the sample; the pyrolysis front was an inverted "U" in every test and the flame tip a flickering, flatter inverted "U"; flicker appears to decrease as pressure is lowered; an initial laminar spread usually turned into a turbulent flame (refs. 39, 40); much soot streamed from the flame tip and deposited along the sample; bursting PMMA bubbles (vapour jetting) distorted the flame more and more as the test went on (ref. 41). [SAF-09 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The decrease of flicker with pressure agrees with earlier studies of flicker in buoyant pool fires (refs. 36–38). [SAF-09 p.7 · CITED]
- Fig. 5 (C12 at 100 and 40 kPa, frames 100 s after ignition, strobe off for the flame tip and on for the pyrolysis front, 140 mm scale): at 40 kPa the flame and pyrolysis region are visibly shorter and the flame is mostly blue. [SAF-09 p.7 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED]
- Pyrolysis-front position vs time (Fig. 6a, C12, shaded bands = scatter among 3–5 tests): roughly linear within the sample length at every pressure, i.e. a nearly constant spread rate, and the front's spread slows as pressure falls. [SAF-09 p.7–8 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]
- Upward spread is usually acceleratory in normal gravity (refs. 43, 44), but over these short distances, with a weak dependence of spread rate on distance (ref. 43), the tests do not capture the transient character. [SAF-09 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[SAF-09 p.3 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-09 p.9 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED]
- The authors call the heated length an important spread parameter, and the values approximate (the flame tip is hard to fix and the flame changes character past the sample end) but helpful for interpretation. [SAF-09 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The heated length varies little along the sample but significantly with pressure, decreasing as pressure decreases (Fig. 9, averaged heated length vs pressure; C12). [SAF-09 p.9–10 · Fig. 9 · MEASURED]

- The colour difference suggests reduced pressure may not reproduce microgravity soot formation and flame temperature well. [SAF-09 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[SAF-09 p.11 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED]

- Fig. 11 readings are ±0.1 mm/s; unlabelled dashed straight lines run through the C12 data: through the pyrolysis-front points from ~0.29 mm/s at 40 kPa to ~0.97 mm/s at the 105 kPa plot edge, and through the flame-tip points from ~0.29 to ~1.20 mm/s. [SAF-09 p.11 · Fig. 11 · MODELED · ~fig]
- The flame-tip method gives higher rates, especially at ambient pressure, but the pyrolysis-front values carry more confidence given the flame-tip error; the microgravity rate (C13) is significantly lower than the normal-gravity rate (C12) at the same 100 kPa, and as pressure is lowered in normal gravity the rate falls toward the microgravity value. [SAF-09 p.11 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED]
- The authors take this as showing that buoyancy-induced flow plays an important role in normal-gravity concurrent spread. [SAF-09 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Model basis: the pressure dependence of Fig. 11 is correlated with a simplified analysis of concurrent spread over a thermally thick fuel (refs. 20, 34) combined with a mixed forced/free-flow analysis of flame-to-fuel heat transfer (ref. 19). [SAF-09 p.11 · MODELED]
- The same approach correlated pressure effects on concurrent spread over a thermally thin fuel (refs. 16, 17); here it is applied to a thick fuel, with a fuller justification of the simplifications. [SAF-09 p.11 · CITED]
- Spread is treated as a series of ignition steps in which the flame both heats and pyrolyses the solid and pilots ignition of the pyrolyzate/oxidizer mixture (refs. 20, 47–49); the spread rate is the ratio of the solid heating length downstream of the pyrolysis front to the time needed to heat, pyrolyse and ignite the solid. [SAF-09 p.11–12 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1 (thermally thick solid, ref. 20): V_f = l_h [π k_s ρ_s c_s (T_p − T_o)² / (4 (q''_fc + q''_fr − q''_rs)²) − (C x / U_m) φ(t_chem)]^(−1), with l_h the heated length downstream of the pyrolysis front, q''_fc the flame convective flux, q''_fr the flame radiant flux, q''_rs the solid re-radiation, U_m the mixed gas flow velocity, φ(t_chem) a function of the chemical time t_chem, ρ_s, c_s, k_s the solid density, specific heat and conductivity, T_p and T_o the pyrolysis and initial solid temperatures and C a constant (x not defined in the text; units not stated); the first term is heat transfer, the second gas-phase chemical kinetics. [SAF-09 p.12 · Eq. 1 · MODELED]
- Simplifications: flame convective and radiant flux and surface re-radiation uniform along the heated length (somewhat reasonable since the boundary layer, and so flame stand-off, grows only with a 1/2 to 1/4 power of distance from the leading edge, ref. 50); the solid ignites once its surface reaches pyrolysis temperature (reasonable for piloted ignition, the fuel rate following a temperature-sensitive Arrhenius law, the flame igniting the mixture once the lean limit is reached); 10 mm PMMA treated as thermally thick, which it approaches at least in normal-gravity flows (ref. 20); flame radiation to the surface taken as roughly balanced by surface re-radiation, because pressure and buoyant flow may alter soot and flame temperature (ref. 45). [SAF-09 p.12 · MODELED]
- The authors call the radiation balance a significant simplification that gives an analytical expression and that breaks down at low-velocity, low-pressure or microgravity flows. [SAF-09 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With it, the heat flux to the solid is mainly convective: q''_fc = h (T_f − T_p), with h the convective heat transfer coefficient, T_f the flame temperature and T_p the PMMA pyrolysis temperature (units not stated); the flame temperature, proportional to ambient O2 and only weakly dependent on pressure until chemical time exceeds physical time at fairly low pressure, is taken as constant since all tests are in air. [SAF-09 p.12–13 · MODELED]
- The chemical-kinetics term matters when the Damköhler number falls: at low O2, low pressure and large flow velocity (blowoff) (ref. 20), or at very low flow velocity in microgravity (diffusive transport and radiation losses) (refs. 51–54). [SAF-09 p.13 · MODELED]
- The authors state the present tests are away from those limits, so the spread rate follows the heat-transfer term of Eq. 1. [SAF-09 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 2: V_f ≈ l_h [4 (h (T_f − T_p))² / (π k_s ρ_s c_s (T_p − T_o)²)], so the spread rate is proportional to the heating length and to the square of the surface convective heat transfer coefficient, other properties held constant (units not stated). [SAF-09 p.13 · Eq. 2 · MODELED]
- h relates to flame stand-off and boundary-layer thickness through h = k/δ (k gas conductivity, δ boundary-layer thickness); δ follows the Reynolds number (Re) in pure forced flow or the Grashof number (Gr) in pure natural convection (ref. 50). [SAF-09 p.13 · MODELED]
- Eq. 3 (mixed forced and free flow, as in the normal-gravity tests; ref. 19): δ_m = C l_p [Re⁴ + Gr²]^(−1/8) Pr^(−1/3) = C l_p Re^(−1/2) [1 + 1/Fr²]^(−1/8) Pr^(−1/3), with Re = ρ U_f l_p / μ, Gr = g β ΔT l_p³ ρ² / μ², Fr = Re²/Gr = U_f² / (g l_p), U_f the forced-flow component, μ viscosity, ρ gas density, β thermal expansion coefficient, g gravity level, l_p the pyrolysis length as characteristic length, C a flow-type constant (Pr not defined in the text; units not stated). [SAF-09 p.13 · Eq. 3 · CITED]
- Eq. 3 reduces to pure forced flow at zero gravity (Fr = ∞) and to pure natural convection at zero forced flow (Fr = 0); similar boundary-layer thicknesses can be reached by trading Re against Gr. [SAF-09 p.13 · Eq. 3 · MODELED]
- Although l_p grows as the flame spreads, it is taken as constant and equal to half the sample length, giving an average boundary-layer thickness and heat flux consistent with Eq. 1. [SAF-09 p.13–14 · MODELED]
- Eq. 4, mixed-flow average convective coefficient: h = C (k / l_p^(1/2)) P^(1/2) U_f^(1/2) [g² l_p² / U_f⁴ + 1]^(1/8) Pr^(1/3), with P the pressure (units not stated); substituted in Eq. 2 it gives the spread rate in terms of the problem parameters, as done for a thin fuel in ref. 16 (not shown). [SAF-09 p.14 · Eq. 4 · MODELED]
- As mixed flow is hard to put into analytical spread models, most models use forced flow only (ref. 20); the alternative used here is a mixed-flow velocity that, applied as a pure forced flow, gives a boundary layer of the same thickness and so the same surface heat flux. [SAF-09 p.14 · MODELED]
- The authors hold the approach valid despite different velocity profiles, because h = k/δ and δ links to flow velocity through experimental correlations such as Eq. 3 that already include profile and temperature differences. [SAF-09 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 5 equates the mixed-flow boundary layer with the pure forced one (g = 0): C l_p (U_m P_0 l_p / μ)^(−1/2) Pr^(−1/3) = C l_p (U_f P l_p / μ)^(−1/2) [1 + g² l_p² / U_f⁴]^(−1/8) Pr^(−1/3); Eq. 6 then gives U_m = U_f (P / P_0) [g² l_p² / U_f⁴ + 1]^(1/4), with P_0 the standard Earth ambient pressure and U_f the forced-flow component at P_0 (units not stated). [SAF-09 p.14–15 · Eq. 6 · MODELED]
- Limits of Eq. 6: at zero gravity or large flow, U_m = (P/P_0) U_f; at elevated gravity and/or zero forced flow, U_m = (P/P_0) (g l_p)^(1/2). [SAF-09 p.15 · Eq. 6 · MODELED]
- U_m yields an equivalent forced-flow boundary layer of similar thickness and similar surface heat transfer coefficient, and by Eq. 2 flow conditions giving similar boundary layers and coefficients give similar spread rates. [SAF-09 p.15 · MODELED]
- Hence, the authors argue, spread in a pure forced flow such as in microgravity could be approximately predicted by a normal-gravity test with a similar mixed-convection boundary layer, or conversely. [SAF-09 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 7: h = (k / (C l_p)) Re^(1/2) Pr^(1/3) = C (k / l_p) (U_m P l_p / μ)^(1/2) Pr^(1/3); Eq. 8: V_f ≈ (l_h / l_p) [4 (C k (U_m P / μ)^(1/2) Pr^(1/3))² (T_f − T_p)² / (π k_s ρ_s c_s (T_p − T_o)²)] ≈ 4 C_1 k² (U_m P / μ) Pr^(2/3) (T_f − T_p)² / (π k_s ρ_s c_s (T_p − T_o)²), C_1 including the ratio l_h/l_p (units not stated). [SAF-09 p.15 · Eq. 8 · MODELED]
- l_h, the difference between flame length and pyrolysis length, grows weakly with time; an earlier application took l_h ~ l_p^c (refs. 20, 52); with l_p constant here, l_h is assumed constant and proportional to l_p, the proportionality going into C_1. [SAF-09 p.15 · MODELED]
- Eq. 8 resembles expressions for opposed spread over thick solids (refs. 20, 47–49, 53), the main difference being l_h (the heated length upstream of the flame front in opposed spread, the flame length beyond the pyrolysis front here), which the authors find understandable since the two modes share the same main controlling mechanisms (ref. 20). [SAF-09 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 12: the Fig. 11 spread rates correlate well with U_m from Eq. 6, and extrapolating to lower flow velocities (pressures) approximately predicts the microgravity data; as pressure falls, U_m and the spread rate fall toward the Saffire II rate, whose flow velocity was lower than the normal-gravity mixed-flow velocity (C12, C13). [SAF-09 p.15–16 · Fig. 12 · MODELED]

- Despite its simplifications, Eq. 8 predicts relatively well the rates measured at the lower pressures (80, 60, 40 kPa; C12) and the Saffire II microgravity rate (C13), although the values are somewhat under-predicted. [SAF-09 p.16–17 · Fig. 13 · MODELED]
- Caution: pressure changes also affect flame chemistry, and simulating microgravity would need pressures of the order of 30 to 20 kPa (p.16) or of 20 kPa (p.21), where some simplifications of the analysis may not apply; test methods relying only on pressure reduction to predict spread at other gravity levels need care. [SAF-09 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-09 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Validity of the analysis (SAF-09 discussion)
- The good correlation with pressure (buoyancy) and the apparent ability to predict microgravity concurrent spread at least approximately indicate, to the authors, that the description has merit; they find this somewhat surprising given the simplifications, but take the concepts and assumptions as reasonable at least for correlating the present tests with pressure. [SAF-09 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Neglecting chemical kinetics is an important simplification; kinetics matter when the Damköhler number falls so that the kinetic term of Eq. 1 becomes comparable with the heat-transfer term, with two limiting conditions. [SAF-09 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- First limit: at large flow velocities the chemical time exceeds the physical time and the spread rate falls with flow velocity until blowoff (refs. 5, 20). [SAF-09 p.17 · CITED]
- The authors judge the flow velocities of these tests too small for kinetics to affect spread near the blowoff limit, at least at elevated pressure; lower pressure slows reactions but also lowers the buoyant velocity and so lengthens the physical time, so reaching blowoff in these tests is unlikely. [SAF-09 p.17–18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Experiments of ref. 55 show chemical kinetics affecting the ignition of PMMA in air below 30 kPa. [SAF-09 p.18 · CITED; SAF-09 p.19 · CITED]
- The authors therefore take the analysis as valid down to about 30 kPa, and, since spread is linked to solid ignition and these tests were above 30 kPa, treat kinetics as not affecting spread through flame temperature, which is held constant over the test pressures. [SAF-09 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-09 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Second limit (refs. 5, 51, 56, 57): in microgravity and very low-velocity flows, less oxidizer reaches the flame, which moves outward seeking O2 while its temperature and soot drop; flame radiation to the surface falls until surface re-radiation matters, the spread rate decreases and the flame finally goes out (diffusion/radiation limit). [SAF-09 p.18 · CITED]
- In the present tests the gas velocity appears large enough for this effect not to matter, though it may become more significant if the pressure is too low. [SAF-09 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The analysis assumes flame-to-solid convection controls concurrent spread away from those limits of flow velocity, O2 or pressure, and the Fig. 12 correlation rests on convective heat transfer to the surface; to limit the role of radiation, flame radiation to the surface is taken as offset by surface re-radiation. [SAF-09 p.18 · MODELED]
- The authors find the convective control somewhat surprising, expecting radiation to matter more in concurrent spread: the visual changes with pressure (printed as Fig. 9) imply that soot, flame temperature and so flame radiation change with pressure, which refs. 45 and 46 on microgravity soot seem to confirm, so the radiant flux should vary with pressure and show in the correlation. [SAF-09 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In microgravity and very low-velocity flows, the flame stand-off may be large enough for surface re-radiation to exceed both convective and radiative heating from the flame (ref. 57). [SAF-09 p.18 · CITED]
- The good correlation suggests that the net flame-radiation minus re-radiation balance is small next to convection in these tests and that its variation with pressure is too weak to show, one possible reason being the small sample scale. [SAF-09 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With larger samples and more turbulent flames, radiation becomes more important and eventually dominates flame-to-solid heat transfer (ref. 53). [SAF-09 p.18 · CITED]
- Sample size also changes the flame and its convective heating: larger, turbulent flames change both the radiation and the turbulent convective correlations, so the small samples may explain the result and justify the radiant-flux assumption at least for these tests. [SAF-09 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Constant flame temperature is assumed, independent of pressure, which appears reasonable for not too low pressures because the flow O2 concentration is fixed (air). [SAF-09 p.18–19 · MODELED]
- Thermodynamically the adiabatic flame temperature is directly proportional to the flow O2 concentration and essentially independent of pressure for ideal gases; kinetically it depends weakly on pressure until chemical time exceeds physical time at relatively low pressure, when reaction rate and heat release drop. [SAF-09 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At fairly low pressure the molecular mean free path grows (λ ∝ 1/P), fewer collisions occur in the reaction zone and the flame sheet thickens (ref. 58); with lower O2 partial pressure this slows gas-phase reactions, lowering flame temperature, heat to the unburned solid and spread rate, effects that stay small until pressure is reduced significantly. [SAF-09 p.19 · CITED]
- Because V_f = dl_p/dt and l_p grows as the flame spreads, Eq. 2 predicts accelerating spread in mixed flow (depending on the relative gravity and forced flow) and in natural-convection upward spread, as observed (refs. 40, 43, 59), because the boundary layer grows more slowly than the flame heating length. [SAF-09 p.19 · MODELED]
- The models assume laminar flow and the tests used small samples; with a long enough sample the spread rate might become constant, as boundary-layer growth flattens and the flame turns turbulent with a nearly constant length, making the total heat flux and so the spread rate constant. [SAF-09 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For pure forced flow Eq. 8 predicts a constant spread rate, in line with boundary-layer models of concurrent spread (ref. 59): boundary-layer growth, which lowers the surface heat flux, is offset by growth of the flame heated length (ref. 19). [SAF-09 p.19 · MODELED]
- The Saffire II flame-tip data of Fig. 7 (C13 conditions: 10 mm PMMA, microgravity, air, atmospheric pressure, 200 mm/s concurrent flow) seem to confirm this approximately once the igniter's influence fades, an aspect that could not be checked before the Saffire II microgravity experiments. [SAF-09 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-09 p.9 · Fig. 7 · CITED · single-test; SAF-09 p.6 · CITED · nominal]
- Predicting the time dependence would need the transient conservation equations, beyond this simple analysis whose aim is the dependence of spread rate on buoyancy through pressure; for that aim, averages of the time-dependent controlling parameters are reasonable. [SAF-09 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The main simplification, an average pyrolysis length of half the sample length, implies average boundary-layer thickness, stand-off, flame-tip length, heated length and convective flux, consistent with the uniform-flux basis of Eq. 1 (refs. 20, 48); with constant average l_p, the flame-tip length (proportional to it, refs. 20, 52, 60) and the heated length are also constant. [SAF-09 p.19–20 · MODELED]
- Theory has boundary layer and flame stand-off growing gently along the sample, between the 1/2 power in forced flow and the 3/4 power in natural convection, so convective flux also falls gently (ref. 59). [SAF-09 p.20 · CITED]
- Taking half the sample length gives the heat flux at mid-sample, a zone of small variation (ref. 50), so the authors judge the impact small, adding that averaging h along a surface is common in heat transfer. [SAF-09 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The heated lengths measured in Fig. 8 indicate the constant-length assumption is reasonable for these test conditions (C12 conditions: 10 mm PMMA, normal gravity, air, 100 and 60 kPa, upward forced flow 200 mm/s). [SAF-09 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-09 p.9 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED; SAF-09 p.4–5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In Eq. 8 the ratio l_h/l_p multiplies the other terms, so even an inaccurate proportionality has a reduced effect on the predicted rate. [SAF-09 p.20 · MODELED]
- Sample length matters in a gravity field: a longer sample raises the average pyrolysis length, and buoyant velocity and spread rate increase with sample length, an effect captured approximately in Eq. 8 through the Froude number. [SAF-09 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Eq. 8 predicts the sample-length effect weakens as forced flow rises and as pressure or gravity fall; at g = 0 the spread rate is theoretically constant along, and independent of, the sample length; so Fig. 12 would show separate lines per sample length, farthest apart at 100 kPa and converging to the microgravity value, the separation shrinking with shorter samples, faster forced flow or lower gravity. [SAF-09 p.20 · MODELED]

### Concluding remarks (SAF-09)
- Concurrent spread rate and flame appearance over thick PMMA were studied at reduced pressure to find the effect of buoyancy, and to explore simulating reduced-gravity concurrent spread by lowering pressure. [SAF-09 p.20 · MEASURED]
- Lowering pressure lowers the concurrent spread rate over the thick solid and weakens the flame, giving dimmer blue flames at the lowest pressures, and the spread characteristics move closer to those seen in microgravity (10 mm PMMA, air; 1 g at 100 to 40 kPa with upward forced flow 200 mm/s vs Saffire II microgravity at 100 kPa and 200 mm/s). [SAF-09 p.1 · MEASURED; SAF-09 p.20 · MEASURED]
- The pressure dependence was correlated with a non-dimensional mixed-convection parameter (a mixed-flow velocity including gravity and pressure) describing the convective heat transfer from flame to solid, the main mechanism controlling spread; extrapolating the correlation to low pressure predicts the Saffire II microgravity spread rate fairly well, and the simplified thick-fuel expression predicts the measured variation with pressure and in microgravity fairly well (10 mm PMMA; microgravity at 100 kPa, air, 200 mm/s). [SAF-09 p.1 · MODELED; SAF-09 p.21 · MODELED]
- The flame-chemistry problem could be eased if microgravity tests were run at higher flow velocities, since the spread could then be simulated at higher pressures. [SAF-09 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At intermediate gravity levels such as the Moon or Mars, concurrent spread over thick solids could be simulated with an Eq. 8 formulation by lowering pressure until the mixed-flow velocity matches that at the reduced gravity; the simulation pressure would then be higher and kinetic effects smaller, so the analysis should apply better. [SAF-09 p.21 · MODELED]
- The analysis should also predict spread at other O2 concentrations through the dependence of flame temperature on the flow O2 concentration. [SAF-09 p.21 · MODELED]

# FILE: LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1
# LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1 — Saffire large-scale spacecraft fires: PSI records of Saffire I–III and Saffire IV–VI results

## Scope
Covers: the NASA PSI records of Saffire I, II and III (PSC-01: PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100); the Saffire IV–V fire-safety paper SAF-02 (which also tabulates the Saffire I–III thin samples); the Saffire VI preliminary results SAF-01; the Saffire IV–VI heat and smoke emission paper SAF-03; and the Saffire II sample-9 test description from SAF-09.
Not here: Saffire I–III flight results and slides (SAF-04), duct- and sample-size effects on concurrent spread over cellulose (SAF-06) and the Saffire V structured-PMMA analysis (SAF-08), all in LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2; the 1-g reduced-pressure analog of Saffire II (SAF-09 results) in EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2; BASS small-sample tests in BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4; the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method in MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1 and MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2; cabin atmospheres in CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1 and CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2; the other PSI records in PSI_CATALOGUE.

- The PSI-98 proposal title is "Characterization of Smoke from Microgravity Fires for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection". [PSC-01 p.53 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The PSI-99 and PSI-100 records point to an Experimental Details file in the Science document folder for sample and parameter details. [PSC-01 p.56–57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- All three records give the same two objectives: determine how fast a large-scale fire grows in low gravity, and compare low-g flammability limits with those from NASA's normal-gravity material flammability screening test. [PSC-01 p.53–54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.58–59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- All three records state the same hypothesis: because fire behaves very differently in normal and reduced gravity, designing spacecraft fire safety systems from terrestrial fires and fire standards carries an inherent vehicle risk from significant uncertainty; this has worked so far, but the uncertainty and risk grow as missions go farther from Earth with much longer return times. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The records state that spacecraft designers lack microgravity data on which to base fire safety designs and procedures, and propose large-scale fire experiments in an expendable spacecraft, with no risk to a crew, to close that gap. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Sibal is used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but keeps its structure after the cotton is consumed. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire II added samples to the Saffire I design, and Saffire III again used SIBAL but at 30 cm/s instead of the 20 cm/s of Saffire I. [PSC-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In all three records the instruments are: two cameras for flame images; thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperatures; two radiometers for flame radiation; solid-state sensors for pressure and CO2 and O2 mole fraction; two anemometers for flow velocity; all data compressed and downlinked. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; PSC-01 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- All three records describe the experiment as a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, impossible before because of the risk, with instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measuring oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth and two video cameras viewing the flame (PSI-100 names Saffire-I in this sentence, as printed). [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- All three records say the results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help validate NASA's material selection criteria and show how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size, and call the investigation crucial for current and future missions. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As Earth benefit, all three records name fire safety and prevention in small sealed spaces such as mines, airplanes and submarines. [PSC-01 p.54 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; PSC-01 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Programme aims and flight history
- SAF-02 judges that spacecraft fire risk assessment, prevention and response need a sound grasp of how fast fires grow and how they change the cabin environment, and that present understanding cannot reliably predict the growth, final size or vehicle impact of a spacecraft fire. [SAF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 states that, lacking such data, designers have relied on 1-g knowledge of flame spread, self-extinguishment, fire detection and suppression, and that the Saffire experiments target this risk at practical length scales and geometries. [SAF-01 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 states that the effect of a spacecraft fire on habitability had not been examined experimentally before the Saffire series began. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 states that no practical-scale fire test had been run in low gravity before the SAFFIRE series. [SAF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The goal of NASA's Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project was a series of large-scale tests of realistic spacecraft fires, run inside spacecraft. [SAF-01 p.1–2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-02 lists three objectives for the five flights Saffire I–V: watch realistic fires grow and spread in low gravity over thin and thick solid fuels in a range of atmospheres, including current and planned exploration ones; assess the fire's impact on the spacecraft and the transport of heat and smoke; demonstrate combustion-product measurement and post-fire cleanup technology. [SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]

| Flights | What the source reports | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Saffire I–III | flown 2017 to 2019; flights I and III studied spread and growth over large thin samples, flight II a set of smaller samples; the impact on the spacecraft was deliberately kept small | [SAF-03 p.2 · CITED · nominal] |
| Saffire IV and V | conducted in May 2020 and January 2021 on the NG-13 and NG-14 flights of the Northrup Grumman (as printed) Cygnus | [SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal] |
| Saffire IV–VI | planned as three flights; the concept was enlarged to release more of the fire's heat into the spacecraft and to add remote diagnostics and fire-response hardware elsewhere in the vehicle; SAF-02 covers IV and V | [SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal] |
| Saffire IV–VI | large thick samples burned for longer, releasing heat and smoke into the cabin; a remote diagnostics and filtration unit (Far Field Diagnostics, FFD) sat at the other end of the spacecraft and 6 sensors were spread over the open volume | [SAF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal] |
| Saffire VI | last flight of the series, on an orbiting Cygnus; SAF-01 presents preliminary results (its abstract says for one test) | [SAF-01 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal] |
| Saffire VI | in storage when SAF-02 was written; expected to add data that strengthen or clarify SAF-02's conclusions | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |

- SAF-01 considers the impact of the heat and pressure rise from a spacecraft fire hard to predict compared to the hazardous products. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- One major goal of Saffire VI was to compare the two. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-01 expects this comparison of fire impacts to guide spacecraft design. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 notes that in terrestrial fires smoke and its constituents are usually a greater hazard than heat, that in a confined orbiting spacecraft any of these hazards can become critical, and that a large temperature rise could cause thermal injury while rising CO2 and CO may be a more significant and acute crew hazard. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 names understanding the fire's effect on habitability as a major objective of SAFFIRE IV–VI, and says these tests made it possible to watch fires grow on large thick samples and assess their effect on the spacecraft. [SAF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 adds the time to smoke-detector alarm and the habitability state when the alarm triggers, comparing the fire-caused CO and CO2 changes with NASA exposure standards at alarm time. [SAF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 states that fire-response planning depends on knowing which hazards matter most, and that its results show the smoke-product hazard matters more than the heat and pressure rise. [SAF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Citing earlier Saffire papers, SAF-02 and SAF-01 report that the prior flights showed spacecraft fires can grow to significant size under typical spacecraft conditions, and SAF-02 adds that they lasted long enough to concern crew and vehicle and changed the understanding of spread and growth in long, large-scale experiments. [SAF-02 p.2 · CITED; SAF-01 p.2 · CITED]
- Citing the earlier flights, SAF-01 reports that their average temperature and pressure rise were not of particular concern, but the CO and CO2 increases were large enough to be a health concern. [SAF-01 p.2 · CITED]
- Citing Eigenbrod et al., SAF-03 reports a strong effect of rib surface structures aligned with the flow on SAFFIRE IV–VI flame spread. [SAF-03 p.2 · CITED; SAF-03 p.5 · CITED; SAF-03 p.9 · CITED]
- Citing SAF-02's authors, SAF-03 reports that concurrent spread on thick materials is suppressed at low flow by the "oxygen shadow"; flow speeds not reported by this source. [SAF-03 p.2 · CITED; SAF-03 p.9 · CITED]
- SAF-03 cites Fortenberry et al. for the measured aerosol and gas levels of SAFFIRE IV–V and Niehaus et al. for modelling their transport in the spacecraft. [SAF-03 p.2 · CITED; SAF-03 p.10 · CITED]

### Hardware, atmosphere set-up and diagnostics
- For Saffire IV–VI the Saffire Flow Unit (SFU) was close to the Saffire I–III unit, with side-view cameras added and gas sensors at the inlet and outlet to measure oxygen consumption and carbon-oxide production. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- To fit the second camera set, SAF-01 gives the duct half-height cut from 25 cm (Saffire I–III) to 15 cm (Saffire IV–VI), perpendicular to the sample, with the 45 cm width kept. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-02 states the same change as a duct height cut from 25 cm to 15 cm perpendicular to the sample surface, with the 45 cm width kept. [SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The Saffire IV–VI tests ran in a rectangular flow tunnel 30 cm high, 45 cm wide and 109 cm long, with the samples on a metal frame in the middle of the duct. [SAF-01 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Flow straighteners at each duct end fed plenums; the inlet and outlet ducts joined these plenums parallel to the flow duct, giving a folded geometry that mixed the flow and allowed temperature and O2, CO2 and CO measurement at inlet and outlet; SAF-03 states the straighteners gave flat, straight flow profiles and that CO2, CO and O2 were measured in the inlet and outlet ducts. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.3 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 and SAF-02 state that a fan in the inlet duct drove the flow and a vane anemometer at the inlet-duct entrance measured it; SAF-03 states that the fan was controlled from a rotary anemometer's output so the duct-entrance velocity stayed constant through each test. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Flow uniformity was checked with smoke traces from rosin beads on a heated wire at the start and end of the test sequence. [SAF-03 p.3 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 Fig. 2 shows flow entering at the bottom right, spread by a plenum on the left into the test section, then entering the outlet duct where species are measured and compared with the inlet; its labels are inlet rotary anemometer, humidity sensor, fan and O2 injection, inlet CO, CO2 and O2 sampling, temperatures at inlet, test section and outlet, in-situ temperature (6), radiometers (4), cameras (4), CO2 and acid-gas injection, and outlet CO, CO2, O2 sampling and temperature. [SAF-03 p.3 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- On each flight the samples sat on one flat frame and were ignited one by one in separate tests; Saffire IV and V cards held three or four samples set up for four ignitions, and the Saffire VI card held four samples set up for four ignitions. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Four video cameras imaged the sample top and edge (not the back); every 2 s green LEDs flashed on the surface for about 0.1 s, which let the pyrolysis-zone length be measured. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-03 tracked flames by thresholding the images, averaging the flame position over the central third of the flame (edge effects neglected), correcting for camera auto-gain and averaging over 2 s intervals. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In the SAFFIRE IV–VI images the trailing edge was generally very bright (soot) while the leading edge could be dim blue. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 defines flame length as the difference between the average positions of the leading and trailing edges. [SAF-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In Cygnus the SFU sat near the end cone (nadir), with its intake in the aft-port standoff and its outlet in the forward-port standoff; the standoffs carried air from the hatch area (zenith) to the end cone; the FFD, with the smoke cleanup system and smoke sensors, was in a mid-deck locker location next to the hatch. [SAF-01 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Six remote sensors, each a thermocouple and a CO2 sensor, were placed one in each of the four standoffs at the vehicle mid-plane, one in the end cone (nadir) and one in the hatch area (zenith); the figures mark the standoff sensors red and the end-cone and hatch sensors green, the standoffs being the triangular spaces along the vehicle at the ends of each row of cargo bags. [SAF-01 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Exhaust left the SFU into the forward-port standoff and the overall spacecraft flow carried it to the FFD in the hatch area; the FFD held aerosol and species diagnostics and a smoke cleanup system. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Cygnus was launched full of cargo, which the ISS crew replaced with material for disposal; SAF-01 calls the trash repacking essential to Saffire because filling extra volume let the experiment adjust the spacecraft oxygen concentration; SAF-03 Fig. 1 shows the SFU (A) and FFD (B) with no cargo and in the descent configuration loaded with trash. [SAF-03 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The hardware was installed before launch but unpowered until Cygnus had left the ISS; at the test orbit it powered up and stepped through the sequence, each test triggered separately by ground command with its detailed steps set in advance by a command file; SAF-03 adds that ground triggering ensured continuous telemetry and free drift with no thruster firings. [SAF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- After all tests the data were downloaded; bandwidth limits meant the video was compressed and only a reduced number of uncompressed images came down. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Before the tests the spacecraft free volume was measured by releasing a known amount of CO2 and following the concentration over time; SAF-03 says this was the first test sequence on each flight and also used the pressure change and the remote sensors. [SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The spacecraft started at the ISS pressure and oxygen concentration; the measured volume set a target pressure reduction and oxygen backfill, the Cygnus operators vented the vehicle to the requested pressure, and the experiment (SAF-03: the SFU) released oxygen to the target, which SAF-01 calls the desired condition of its Table 1. [SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The FFD held gas sensors for CO, CO2 and O2, the ionization sensor of a commercial smoke detector and a TSI DustTrak DRX 8533 that measures aerosol mass concentration by light scattering. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-03 refers to Fortenberry et al. for details of the FFD gas sensors. [SAF-03 p.4 · CITED · nominal]
- The FFD sat near the inlet of the Cygnus air circulation system, so it gave a good measure of habitability and of when a smoke detector would trigger as the circulation swept air to the intake. [SAF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-03 compares this with the ISS, where smoke detectors sit in front of air intakes. [SAF-03 p.4 · CITED · nominal]
- In the FFD, cabin air entered from the right past multiple sensors and left by one of three paths: direct bypass, smoke eater or CO2 scrubber; air took the bypass while a sample burned, the smoke eater ran after every test once the sample was out, and the CO2 scrubber ran only before Saffire operations and after one test because of its limited capacity; Fig. 4 labels the inlet sensors ΔP, CO, CPM, CO2, ION, TEMP, O2, HF/HCl and RH, actuators ACT1–ACT3, the DustTrak DRX, outlet CO, ION, TEMP and fan, and avionics. [SAF-03 p.5 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-03 measured cabin CO and CO2 continuously, plus aerosol concentration by light scattering, estimated the heat release of some tests by oxygen consumption calorimetry from O2 consumption and CO and CO2 production, and correlated these with distributed temperatures and the pressure rise. [SAF-03 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-02 lists the Saffire IV–V measurements as video, flame spread rate, flame temperatures and radiant output, energy release by oxygen calorimetry, CO2 and temperature at six places in the spacecraft, CO2, CO, O2, HF and HCl, vehicle pressurized volume and aerosol concentration, with a post-fire cleanup system, internal volume measurements and acid-gas (HCl, HF) transport also part of the experiments. [SAF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- On Saffire IV and V the outlet gas sensor had been moved away from the location where mixing had been verified, so it did not see fully mixed outlet flow and the gas measurements were not useful. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED]
- For Saffire VI the sensor was moved back to the verified location at the end of the duct, giving the oxygen consumption calorimetry needed for flame heat release, and SAF-01 says improvements were made on this flight to ensure accurate heat release measurement. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]

- SAF-01 Fig. 3 gives established-flame front views for Saffire VI test 2 (SIBAL), test 3 (2-sided PMMA) and test 4 (1-sided PMMA); in each the oxidizer arrives from the left at 20 cm/s. [SAF-01 p.4 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · nominal]

- In VI-3 (C2) the outlet duct temperature rose continuously (Fig. 4), and the oxygen consumption (Fig. 5) and the CO and CO2 at the SFU outlet (Fig. 6) rose continuously until the flow was reduced at 1120 s. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- At the same time the gas temperature at the SFU outlet was significant, 70 °C, while the temperature near the FFD (zenith) changed only slightly from its baseline (C2). [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The CO and CO2 were very high leaving the SFU but attenuated at the FFD (Fig. 6, C2). [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The heat release computed from oxygen consumption was consistent with the radiometer (Fig. 5, C2). [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- At the lower flow of 5 cm/s after 1120 s the outlet CO2 and CO increased (Fig. 6 caption, C2). [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-01 attributes this increase to the lower ambient flow. [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 attributes the dip at 1120 s in Fig. 5 to the transient flow change disturbing the oxygen sampling. [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 7 shows the FFD smoke concentrations and the response of a terrestrial ionization detector; the smoke levels rose fast and then fell (C2). [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-01 presumes the fall comes from particle loss by impaction on multiple surfaces. [SAF-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The SAF-01 captions state that the inlet and outlet traces end because the duct flow was reduced at 1120 s and stopped at 1420 s, that the forward-port sensor is the one nearest the duct outlet, and that the zenith sensor is near the far field device (C2). [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test; SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]

- In SAF-03 Figs. 6 to 8 the time axis starts at the experiment timeline start, about 10 minutes before ignition. [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In SAF-03 Fig. 6 (C3) the flame length and the radiometer signal agree very closely in the later part of the test. [SAF-03 p.6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Flame tracking stopped when the flow was cut to 5 cm/s at 480 s, because the flame had weakened greatly and shrunk (C3). [SAF-03 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test; SAF-03 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The purpose of the low-flow interval was to cool the sample and make sure it went out when the flow stopped (C3). [SAF-03 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]
- SAF-03 states that this was meant to avoid the issues seen in SAFFIRE IV-2, citing SAF-02's authors. [SAF-03 p.6 · CITED; SAF-03 p.9 · CITED]
- After the flow was reduced to 5 cm/s the radiometer signal did not drop at once but kept rising for another 50 s (C3). [SAF-03 p.6 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-03 explains this by two effects acting together: the weakened flame expanded thermally at the reduced flow, coming closer to the radiometers, and hot combustion products accumulated in the chamber at the lower flow. [SAF-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Smoke aerosol at the FFD followed the flame length with a minor delay (Fig. 7, C3). [SAF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-03 attributes the short delay to the direct path from the SFU to the FFD: though at opposite ends of the module, most of the flow went straight to the FFD without the extensive mixing found in geometries such as the ISS. [SAF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 therefore expects detection in this test to be faster than in many spacecraft. [SAF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 8 compares the HRR with the radiometer for the same test, and the peak HRR reached 3 kW (Table 1 prints 3240 W; C3). [SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-03 calls this substantial for a small spacecraft. [SAF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The temperature rise at the FFD was only 0.5 °C (Table 1, C3). [SAF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Citing SAF-01, SAF-03 gives a peak of 77 °C at the SFU outlet for this test. [SAF-03 p.7 · CITED · single-test; SAF-03 p.10 · CITED]
- SAF-03 says these outlet temperatures fell quickly through mixing and heat loss. [SAF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 Fig. 7 plots flame length, the FFD ionization smoke-detector signal and the total particulate matter (PM total) from the DustTrak DRX; Fig. 8 plots O2 consumed (mg/s), CO2 produced (mg/s), radiometer #4 (×10) and heat release rate (C3). [SAF-03 p.8 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-03 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-03 notes that the ionization chamber voltage falls as the aerosol concentration rises. [SAF-03 p.8 · Fig. 7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Heat release, temperature and pressure rise in the cabin
- In Saffire IV and V (Cygnus in orbit; per-test conditions in SAF-02 Table 1) the fire events had a measurable effect on vehicle pressure, temperature and CO2 and heat release rates reached up to 10 kW, yet average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels; which test reached 10 kW, the size of the effects and the acceptance levels are not reported by this source. [SAF-02 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 gives the Saffire IV–VI fires as 1.5 to 3.2 kW in free air volumes of 17 to 19 m3 (orbiting Cygnus; per-test oxygen, pressure and 20 cm/s concurrent flow in its Table 1). [SAF-01 p.1–2 · MEASURED; SAF-01 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- On p.4 SAF-01 gives the same fires (IV-1, V-2, VI-2, VI-3, VI-4; conditions in its Table 1) as generally 1.5 to 3 kW. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 calls this a small fire by terrestrial standards. [SAF-01 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 states that, apart from the thin cellulose samples of earlier flights, the heat release of the thick PMMA samples on Saffire IV and V was not determined; SAF-03 states that the HRR of SAFFIRE IV and V was not successfully determined, which made it hard to relate the products to fire size. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 judges that without heat release data for the PMMA (high heat release) cases, the earlier results were of limited use as reference data for model validation. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 computed heat release from oxygen consumption by the method of Huggett (Fig. 5), and its Table 2 also gives heat release from the fuel consumption rate for the thin materials. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Huggett's estimate, valid for a wide range of combustibles, is 13.1 kJ per gram of oxygen consumed. [SAF-01 p.4 · CITED]
- SAF-01 includes the thin cotton samples of each flight in its analysis. [SAF-01 p.3 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01's reason is that for thin fuels the heat release rate can be estimated from the spread rate. [SAF-01 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For thick materials SAF-01 states that much of the burning is on surfaces the cameras cannot see, so heat release cannot be estimated from the flame images. [SAF-01 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For VI-2 (SIBAL Cloth, 50 cm long, 41 cm wide, 20 cm/s concurrent, 54.1 kPa, 31.0 mol % O2, orbiting Cygnus; ambient temperature not reported by this source) both methods were applied and agreed within 15 %. [SAF-01 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-01 calls this agreement reasonable for this kind of analysis. [SAF-01 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 Table 2 lists, for IV-1, V-2, VI-2, VI-3 and VI-4 (conditions in its Table 1), the material, burn duration (s), oxygen-consumption peak (W) and total (kJ) heat release, fuel-consumption average (W) and total (kJ) heat release, maximum temperature at the SFU outlet and at the FFD or nearest location (°C), FFD inlet CO2 increase (ppm), CO2 partial-pressure increase (mmHg) and FFD inlet CO increase (ppm); it holds the thin-fuel results of Saffire IV and V and all successful Saffire VI ignitions, with the increases measured at the FFD. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED; SAF-01 p.6 · Table 2 · MEASURED]
- Empty cells in SAF-01 Table 2 are cases where the data were not available. [SAF-01 p.6 · Table 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 compared the flame heat release with the overall temperature rise in the spacecraft and the change in its CO2 and CO concentrations. [SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SAF-01 finds the spacecraft temperature and pressure rise less significant than the CO2 and CO increase. [SAF-01 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Over its seven long-duration low-gravity tests (Cygnus in low Earth orbit, cabin pressure and oxygen varied, samples 40 cm wide, PMMA 18 cm and fabrics 50 cm long; per-test values in SAF-03 Table 1; diluent and ambient temperature not reported by this source), SAF-03 found the pressure rise and temperature change small, while smoke particulate rose to substantial levels and the gaseous products reached hazardous levels. [SAF-03 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
