- NASA sets a Spacecraft Maximum Allowed Concentration (SMAC) for CO by exposure time: 425 ppm for 1 hour and 100 ppm for 24 hours; for CO2, which is common in crewed spacecraft, NASA-STD-3001 limits the 1-hour average partial pressure to 3 mm Hg at most. [SAF-01 p.5 · CITED; SAF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- SAF-03 names heat, smoke, HCN, CO and CO2 as the main hazardous products of fires. [SAF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CO2 was scrubbed only twice during the Saffire flights and CO removal was limited. [SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 therefore reports its CO and CO2 values as the increase in the average spacecraft concentration caused by each test. [SAF-01 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the Saffire VI tests (C5, C6) the CO and CO2 diluted quickly. [SAF-01 p.5 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 still judges the increases significant from a toxicology standpoint. [SAF-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 Table 2 (CO2 partial-pressure increase) shows the allowable CO2 level exceeded in both Saffire VI PMMA tests (C5, C6). [SAF-01 p.5 · MEASURED; SAF-01 p.6 · Table 2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-01 reports CO levels well above the 24-hour SMAC and close to the 1-hour level; the sentence names no test and follows the one on both Saffire VI PMMA tests (C5, C6). [SAF-01 p.5 · MEASURED]
- In SAF-03 the maximum increases of both SAFFIRE VI PMMA tests (C7; VI-3 2-sided, 544 mbar, 0.30 mol fraction O2; VI-4 1-sided, 550 mbar, 0.29) exceeded the 1-hour CO2 limit and the 24-hour CO SMAC. [SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.8 · MEASURED]
- The 24-hour CO SMAC was also exceeded for the SAFFIRE IV PMMA (C7; IV-2, 2-sided, 1000 mbar, 0.22) and the SAFFIRE VI SIBAL (C7; VI-2, 541 mbar, 0.31). [SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 attributes the high levels of the SAFFIRE VI PMMA and SIBAL cases most likely to their higher oxygen concentrations. [SAF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Taking 1 mg/m3 as a fairly tight alarm threshold, SAF-01 finds that the FFD detector reached it at 981 s in VI-3 (Fig. 7 elapsed time; C5). [SAF-01 p.5 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- By then much of the hazardous gas release had already occurred (C5). [SAF-01 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-01 finds this comparable to predictions based on smoke versus hazardous-product emission by overheated materials. [SAF-01 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 holds that the key measure is the concentration of hazardous products when the fire is detected, not the peak, and that ideally the detection threshold would be set so that, for the fires expected in the spacecraft, detection comes in time for an effective crew response. [SAF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 used 2 mg/m3 of total particulate matter on the FFD's DustTrak DRX as a reference alarm threshold (Fig. 7 shows an example) and tabulated the time to reach it with the CO2 and CO increase, flame length and HRR at that time (C7). [SAF-03 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]
- That threshold detected the fire before the SAFFIRE IV PMMA (C7; IV-2, 1000 mbar, 0.22) and SAFFIRE VI SIBAL (C7; VI-2, 541 mbar, 0.31) samples reached hazardous CO levels. [SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.9 · MEASURED]
- Both SAFFIRE VI PMMA samples (C7; VI-3, 544 mbar, 0.30; VI-4, 550 mbar, 0.29) were past the CO threshold at alarm, the 1-sided sample approaching the 1-hour SMAC, and the CO increase was larger for the 1-sided sample. [SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.9 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 concludes that this spacecraft configuration would need a lower threshold or more detectors. [SAF-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- Citing its Refs. 1 and 6, SAF-02 states that Saffire I–III showed duct size and boundary-layer development affecting flame spread and flame size. [SAF-02 p.7 · CITED]
- One Saffire objective, detailed in an earlier paper, was to find out whether thin fuels show steady concurrent flame spread. [SAF-02 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In all Saffire I–V tests (C8) the cotton and SIBAL samples settled to a steady spread rate and flame size (Fig. 9, Table 2); this sentence of SAF-02 prints "steady opposed spread rate". [SAF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Citing its Ref. 1, SAF-02 notes that upward spread is usually acceleratory in 1 g, and that 1-g ground tests with SIBAL cloth spread steadily when flame size was limited by heat loss or lower pressure (pressure values not reported by this source). [SAF-02 p.7 · CITED]
- The steady spread rate depended on oxygen concentration and flow rate (C8). [SAF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Citing Li et al., SAF-02 adds that it also depended on duct height: their numerical model showed that, for concurrent spread beyond a critical separation distance, a taller duct lowered the air velocity above the flame because the flame restricted the flow less, and since concurrent spread speeds up with air velocity, a taller duct slowed the spread. [SAF-02 p.7 · CITED]
- Saffire IV added another SIBAL sample in the reduced-height duct of Saffire IV–V, plotted with Saffire I–III in Fig. 10. [SAF-02 p.7–8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Its spread rate was about 100 % higher in the reduced-height duct than in Saffire I and III (duct heights 46 cm for Saffire I–III and 30 cm for Saffire IV in Table 2 and the Fig. 10 caption; C8). [SAF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- Citing its Ref. 1, SAF-02 reports a novel flame-size overshoot of about 30 % in Saffire I and III, attributed to boundary-layer development on the sample surface. [SAF-02 p.8 · CITED]
- No overshoot was seen on the Saffire II SIBAL samples, whose card position gave a long entrance length (II-5 and II-6: width 5 cm, length 30 cm, duct 46 cm, flow 20 and 25 cm/s, O2 21 %, pressure 100 kPa; C8). [SAF-02 p.8 · Table 2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-02's explanation: close to the duct inlet the boundary layer has not yet developed, so it is thinner and the air moves faster next to the sample, which speeds up the spread. [SAF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The steady flame lengths (Table 2) grew on Saffire IV and for the Saffire V cotton sample relative to Saffire I–III (C8). [SAF-02 p.8 · Table 2 · MEASURED]
- SAF-02 attributes this to the reduced duct height on Saffire IV and, for the Saffire V cotton, to a thinner material in higher ambient oxygen. [SAF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 judges these results significant for fire safety because concurrent flames over thin fuels reached a limiting size under a variety of conditions, unlike upward spread in normal gravity, where flames tend to keep growing. [SAF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The Saffire VI SIBAL sample (VI-2: SIBAL Cloth 50 cm long, 41 cm wide, 20 cm/s concurrent, 54.1 kPa, 31.0 mol % O2, orbiting Cygnus; diluent and ambient temperature not reported by this source) reached a steady size and spread rate quite quickly. [SAF-01 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-01 finds flame growth and spread on Saffire VI consistent with the earlier flights. [SAF-01 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 Fig. 9 plots pyrolysis length (mm) against time from ignition start (s) for Saffire I–V, with flame base and tip positions, cotton in blue and SIBAL in green, annotations "smaller duct height 20 cm/s", "25 cm/s", "20 cm/s" and "dashed: 30 cm long, 5 cm wide samples", and an unlabelled vertical red dashed line (C8). - Saffire IV and V included three successful PMMA-slab tests (Table 1; more detail in SAF-02 Refs. 2 and 3). [SAF-02 p.8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Both concurrent samples, IV-2 (C10) and V-3 (C11), did not spread appreciably: the flame stayed fixed at the leading edge and advanced only by surface regression. [SAF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SAF-02 calls this typical of thick fuels in low gravity and unlike normal gravity. [SAF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- These concurrent flames first grew, then held a steady size for the rest of the burn (C10, C11). [SAF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- The IV-2 flame, burning in air on both sides, grew to 9.5 cm after 400 s (C10). [SAF-02 p.8–9 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The V-3 flame, in 25.4 % oxygen, grew to 11 cm after 450 s (C11). [SAF-02 p.9 · MEASURED · single-test]
- In Saffire VI the two flat cast PMMA samples (VI-3: two-sided, 10 mm thick, 54.6 kPa, 30.3 mol % O2; VI-4: one-sided, 5 mm thick, 55.2 kPa, 28.8 mol % O2; both 18 cm long, 41 cm wide, 20 cm/s concurrent, orbiting Cygnus; diluent not reported by this source, nor the ambient temperature for VI-4) grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced. [SAF-01 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-01 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-01 p.4 · MEASURED]
- Citing its Ref. 2, SAF-02 reports that the two 5 cm wide two-sided PMMA samples of Saffire II grew to flame lengths of 8.0 cm (grooved sample) and 9.5 (flat sample; unit not printed); oxygen, pressure and flow not reported by this source. [SAF-02 p.8 · CITED]
- In all these cases (Saffire II, IV-2, V-3) the flame length reached an upper limit. [SAF-02 p.9 · MEASURED]
- Citing its Refs. 9–11, SAF-02 states that similar 1-g tests did not reach a steady length. [SAF-02 p.9 · CITED]
- SAF-02 finds this limit similar to the limiting size of the thin samples, and notes it may surprise for a thick solid, since an upward flame on a sample this size keeps growing in normal gravity. [SAF-02 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Citing its Refs. 12 and 13, SAF-02 states that the stop of the flame tip has been linked to the surface energy balance at the pyrolysis front (flame tip) region. [SAF-02 p.9 · CITED]
- SAF-02 reasons that, with convection as the main heat transfer mode, the gas-phase heat flux to the pyrolysis front falls with downstream distance; once it is comparable to the surface radiative loss, net heat feedback and local burning rate become vanishingly small, the flame tip quenches locally and the flame on a thick solid becomes stationary. [SAF-02 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 expects higher ambient oxygen to reduce the standoff distance and attributes the longer final V-3 flame to its higher oxygen. [SAF-02 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In SAF-03 (C12) the flames did not spread as in 1-g upward burning of thick PMMA; they stayed attached to the leading edge and advanced only as the surface regressed. [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- All PMMA samples (C12) showed periods of very linear flame growth lasting several minutes, with similar slopes of 0.22 to 0.38 mm/s. [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Citing Olson et al., SAF-03 reports that the SAFFIRE II 5 cm wide sample grew at less than 0.1 mm/s in air. [SAF-03 p.5 · CITED; SAF-03 p.9 · CITED]
- SAF-03 calls the SAFFIRE IV–VI growth significantly faster than that. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The 2-sided samples were still growing at the end of the test (around 500 s), while the 1-sided samples began to plateau around 380 s (SAFFIRE V) and 420 s (SAFFIRE VI); the sentence gives no time zero, and Fig. 5 counts from ignitor turn-off (C12). [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 does not know whether the 2-sided samples would eventually plateau and says longer experiments would help. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 offers enhanced back-side heat loss of the 1-sided samples, against none for the 2-sided ones, as a plausible cause of their earlier plateau, and edge heat losses of the much smaller SAFFIRE II samples as the likely limit on their growth. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Citing SAF-02's authors, SAF-03 states that the SAFFIRE thin samples all spread linearly; citing Fernandez-Pello and Hirano, it states that acceleratory growth is often seen in normal-gravity upward spread on thick fuels. [SAF-03 p.5 · CITED; SAF-03 p.9 · CITED; SAF-03 p.10 · CITED]
- SAF-03 concludes that in low gravity spread and growth are expected to be at most linear and may hit a limiting size; that linear growth implies no acceleration even at high oxygen; and that, given the lack of spread, thick-material flame growth differs strongly between low and normal gravity. [SAF-03 p.5–6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 gives the test conditions and summary results in Table 1 and plots flame length versus time for the four PMMA tests in Fig. 5 (legend S-IV 2-sided, S-V 1-sided, S-VI 2-sided, S-VI 1-sided, each trace with a linear fit over its steady-growth stretch); since the 1-sided samples needed 120 s of ignition, double the 2-sided ones, Fig. 5 alone sets time zero at ignitor turn-off (C12). [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.7 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED · nominal]

### Back-side heat loss of the 1-sided PMMA (SAF-03)
- SAF-03 considers back-side heat loss relevant to spacecraft, where isolated plates burning on both sides are uncommon, and its 1-sided set-up to represent a panel or box cover with little mass behind it. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Behind the 5 mm 1-sided PMMA the backing was a 0.1 mm mica sheet (thermal diffusivity ~0.6 mm2/s) and then a 0.8 mm aluminum card (thermal diffusivity ~97 mm2/s). [SAF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- By SAF-03's estimate the backing adds under 1 % to the assembly's total thermal resistance, because the mica layer is so thin and the aluminum so conductive, even though their diffusivities differ widely (0.1 mm mica plus 0.8 mm aluminum behind the 5 mm PMMA). [SAF-03 p.5 · MODELED]
- SAF-03 notes that the aluminum's high diffusivity spreads heat sideways across the back once the thermal wave has passed through the material. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 estimates a characteristic thermal penetration time τ = L²/α per layer (L thickness in mm, α thermal diffusivity in mm2/s, τ in s; fitted range not reported by this source): PMMA plate, 5 mm, α = 0.11 mm2/s, about 220 s; mica, 0.1 mm, ~0.017 s; aluminum card, 0.8 mm, ~0.007 s. [SAF-03 p.5 · MODELED]
- The assembly's characteristic time is thus set by the PMMA at about 220 s, so the backing does not meaningfully change the penetration timescale, and beyond ~200 s the thermal wave is expected to have crossed the whole assembly (5 mm PMMA, 0.1 mm mica, 0.8 mm aluminum). [SAF-03 p.5 · MODELED]
- SAF-03 states that the SAFFIRE VI growth rates in its Table 1 (VI-3 2-sided, VI-4 1-sided) show back-side heat loss had a significant effect on the growth rate. [SAF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- As not every configuration can be tested, SAF-03 suggests using growth rates from 2-sided burns as a conservative upper bound for 1-sided uses. [SAF-03 p.5–6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- SAF-02 calls assured extinguishment a central concern of any fire response: many thicker materials go out by themselves in quiescent conditions, but thin and bubbling materials can keep burning in some circumstances (gravity level and material conditions not given in that sentence). [SAF-02 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire V-2 (C13) showed this delayed extinguishment for a thin material. [SAF-02 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- It burned steadily for the first 300 s with the fan on; the fan was turned off at about 280 s and stayed off for 70 s, and when the flow came back the flame grew back and burned another 150 s until the material was consumed (times as printed; C13). [SAF-02 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test]
- SAF-02 concludes that flames on thinner materials can persist for an extended time without forced air flow. [SAF-02 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- When imaging stopped, about 10 s after the flow was turned off, both surviving small blue flamelets and glowing char embers were present; the last top-view image (Fig. 3, right) covers the last 20 cm of the sample (C13). [SAF-02 p.4 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-02 cannot tell whether flamelets, embers or both carried the flame through the next 60 s, but judges a surviving flamelet the likely cause of reignition, since embers usually sit isolated in charred areas while flamelets sit at the edge of unburned fuel. [SAF-02 p.4–5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| C17 | IV-2: 2-sided cast PMMA, 10 mm thick, 18 cm long, 40 cm wide | Cygnus in orbit after leaving the ISS | 22.0 mol % | 100.0 kPa | 20 cm/s concurrent, reduced to 5 cm/s at the event | igniter wires on the card (Fig. 2, Test 2) | flow tunnel 30 × 45 × 109 cm, sample frame mid-duct | diluent, ambient temperature | [SAF-02 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test] |
| C18 | V-4: structured PMMA, 1 cm thick, 20 cm long, 40 cm wide | Cygnus in orbit after leaving the ISS | 25.7 mol % | 72.6 kPa | 20 cm/s opposed | igniter wires on the card (Fig. 2, Test 4 and Test 1); ignition after a planned 10 min of preheating | flow tunnel 30 × 45 × 109 cm, sample frame mid-duct | diluent, ambient temperature | [SAF-02 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-02 p.7 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test] |

- Two Saffire samples, IV-2 (C17) and V-4 (C18), showed intense deflagration-type ignition, recorded both on video and by the radiometers. [SAF-02 p.5 · MEASURED]
- SAF-02 attributes both events to stratified mixtures, noting that buoyancy moves hot vapour away from its source in normal gravity, whereas in low gravity hot fuel vapour can accumulate more easily. [SAF-02 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- After the IV-2 flow was cut to 5 cm/s (edge view, Fig. 7), the flame persisted on the upper surface, pulsing as bursting bubbles of molten PMMA ejected MMA vapour, while on the lower surface it had gone out but vapour kept coming out (C17). [SAF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The flame then reached the lower side through a gap at the sample's leading edge; at once a strong deflagration spread below the sample, and the induced flow drove a strong flame above it as well (C17). [SAF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- In SAF-02 Fig. 7 (flow left to right at 5 cm/s) the first image shows a weak upper-surface flame just starting to reach the lower side, where the flame had been out for 6.4 s; 267 ms later the flame fills the whole region below the sample and has strengthened the flame above (C17). [SAF-02 p.6 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- V-4 deflagrated on first ignition (Fig. 8): with the gas flowing at 20 cm/s, ignition began on the underside and within 100 ms the flame had bloomed to fill the field of view; these images match the sharp radiometer peak at 645 s in Fig. 6 (C18). [SAF-02 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-02 p.7 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · single-test]
- SAF-02 did not expect a stratified mixture at this gas velocity and suggests the curled ash of sample V-2 gave enough recirculation for it. [SAF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 concludes that the ease with which such mixtures formed is a risk for fire-response strategies, since reduced air flow and complex flow obstructions can let fuel vapour build up into a readily ignited mixture able to produce a strong deflagration. [SAF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- Citing its Refs. 14, 12 and 13, SAF-02 suggests that the oxygen shadow, combined with the surface energy balance, may cause this extinction behind the flames. [SAF-02 p.9 · CITED]

- The flame spread faster on the thin ribs at the top of the image and more slowly as the ribs widened; spread-rate values not reported by this source (C19). [SAF-02 p.9 · MEASURED · single-test]

[SAF-02 p.9–10 · MEASURED]

[SAF-02 p.10 · Fig. 12 · MEASURED · nominal]

### Flow control, ignitability and NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
- SAF-02 reads its results together as showing the strong influence of the flow on flame spread and growth in low gravity: unlike normal gravity, where flames can drive substantial buoyant flow, low-gravity flame growth is controlled by the flow environment. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 states that this makes low-gravity fire growth harder to assess, because simple growth laws (e.g. t²) normally used for normal-gravity fires cannot be assumed. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 notes that the best prevention and the best extinguishment strategies may differ: quiescent conditions reduce air flow, yet bubbling or charring materials may go out faster with some convective cooling and mass transport; for ignition, quiescent conditions probably make a sample less ignitable than convection does. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Citing its Ref. 15, SAF-02 states that the most ignitable condition is likely a low flow rate, since at higher flow velocity ignition is delayed or prevented by heat loss from the fuel surface to the adjacent flow. [SAF-02 p.10 · CITED]
- SAF-02 describes NASA Test 1 as an upward flammability test in which a 30 cm long sample is ignited at the bottom and fails at that condition if the flame grows or spreads past 15 cm, citing NASA-STD-6001B with Change 2, "Flammability, Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures", NASA, 2016-04-21. [SAF-02 p.10 · CITED; SAF-02 p.12 · CITED]
- Citing the standard, SAF-02 adds that NASA-STD-6001 calls for the worst-case sample, which is usually the thinnest. [SAF-02 p.10 · CITED · nominal]
- SAF-02 judges that the Test 1 configuration does not match overall fire behaviour in low gravity: flames on thick fuels do not grow or spread concurrently in low gravity but advance by surface regression, and spread is more likely in opposed (downward) spread. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 states that this does not make the normal-gravity test useless, since it is quite successful at identifying highly flammable materials. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 cautions that a pass cannot be taken to show that a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-02 also stresses surface structure: although the V-4 sample was 10 mm thick, the dimension that mattered for its flame spread was the rib width, and SAF-02 concludes that relatively thin surface structures need to be considered. [SAF-02 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Authors' summaries and conclusions
| Topic | SAF-02 summary statement (Saffire I–V) | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Extinguishment | thin charring fuels at raised oxygen, and bubbling polymers, cannot be assumed to go out quickly in quiescent conditions; in some cases cutting the flow to a small value rather than stopping it may help disperse fuel vapour and cool the material so it goes out | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| Ignition | overheated materials in quiescent or low-flow zones in low gravity can form stratified fuel mixtures that deflagrate dramatically on ignition | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| Flow and configuration | spread over thin materials can depend strongly on how large the flow space is compared with the flame; close to the inlet of a flow space the boundary layer is not yet developed and flames can start out 30 % larger than in developed flow, until they spread into developed flow; ridges and other surface shapes can strongly change opposed spread over thick materials | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| Spread and growth | flames reached nearly steady lengths in all configurations (concurrent and opposed, thin and thick fuels), the steady size depending on oxygen and flow velocity, unlike the usual continued growth of normal-gravity upward spread; thick fuels in concurrent flow did not spread but stayed pinned at the leading edge and moved as fuel was consumed; in opposed flow flames spread toward the leading edge and became pinned there, without growing, their downstream tail going out behind them; once at its limiting size, an upstream flame's oxygen "shadow" inhibited or put out downstream flames; thick-fuel growth differed from NASA STD 6001 Test 1, which does not invalidate the test but changes how its results are read | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |
| Spread and growth, observation | in one case a flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap and ignited a previously warmed PMMA surface (V-3, per SAF-02 p.9) | [SAF-02 p.9 · MEASURED · single-test; SAF-02 p.11 · MEASURED · single-test] |
| Outlook | the results give new understanding of fire behaviour in low gravity in practical configurations and are to be built into fire safety requirements and guidelines for exploration spacecraft and habitats | [SAF-02 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION] |

- SAF-02's abstract states that the combined experiments give significant new understanding of how sample and flow-duct height affect spread and growth, and a better view of a fire's impact on a spacecraft. [SAF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 summarizes that practical-scale fires of 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with 17 to 19 m3 of free air, that the temperature rose significantly only very near the fire, and that ambient CO and CO2 rose significantly, the PMMA tests exceeding the 1-hour CO2 limit and the 24-hour CO limit. [SAF-01 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 adds that an ionization detector and a light-scattering system readily detected the smoke, but a typical alarm threshold was reached only at 981 s, after most of the hazardous gas release. [SAF-01 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 concludes that the human hazard of a spacecraft fire closely resembles that of terrestrial fires, where smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern than heat, and that this helps define spacecraft fire-response approaches. [SAF-01 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-01 states that extending these results to the partial gravity of future Moon and Mars missions needs further work, and that further analysis and modelling of these fires will follow. [SAF-01 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SAF-03 concludes that SAFFIRE IV–VI usefully validated that flame growth on flat materials can be expected to be linear, without the acceleration seen in 1 g, which it calls extremely significant for the timeline of a spacecraft fire response. [SAF-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Growth on the 1-sided PMMA samples levelled off at a limiting size (thickness 5 mm, length 18 cm, width 40 cm; V-3 at 745 mbar and 0.26 mol fraction O2, VI-4 at 550 mbar and 0.29; flow 20 cm/s, opposed per the table caption; low gravity, Cygnus; diluent and ambient temperature not reported by this source). [SAF-03 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-03 p.9 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 calls this even more significant, and notes the 2-sided samples may not have burned long enough to reach a limiting size. [SAF-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In this spacecraft set-up, alarming at 2 mg/m3 came too late to catch the fires before some cases exceeded the 24-hour CO SMAC, and only one case came near the 1-hour SMAC (Cygnus in low Earth orbit; total particulate at the FFD; per-test conditions in SAF-03 Table 1). [SAF-03 p.1 · MEASURED; SAF-03 p.9 · MEASURED]
- SAF-03 concludes that smoke detection in this spacecraft for these design fires would need a lower threshold or more detectors to cut transport time, that choosing detection and response systems depends on knowing whether a detector can find a fire before the spacecraft becomes uninhabitable, and that this needs analysis specific to the spacecraft volume and flow, using heat and smoke production data like these in a model of the planned spacecraft. [SAF-03 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2
# LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2 — Saffire I–II results, duct and sample-size effects on concurrent spread (Saffire I–V, BASS), and ribbed PMMA on Saffire V

## Scope
Covers three Saffire documents: SAF-04 (Ferkul et al. 2017, slides: the Saffire-I and Saffire-II flights, per-test conditions, Table I microgravity and 1-g results, silicone, cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL), PMMA–Nomex and thick PMMA samples, vehicle O2 and CO2, radiometer and tracking charts, the Cygnus backup slide); SAF-06 (Olson et al. 2022: concurrent spread over SIBAL and cotton in Saffire I–V and two BASS tests, duct and sample-size effects, flame and pyrolysis lengths, burnout time, surface temperatures, surface energy balance, core-flow acceleration model); SAF-08 (Eigenbrod et al. 2021: opposed spread along a ribbed PMMA slab on Saffire V).
Not here: Saffire IV–VI test matrices, heat release, smoke, gas species and the Saffire IV–V fire-safety implications, and the PSI-98/99/100 records (see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1); the 1-g reduced-pressure analog of Saffire II sample 9 (SAF-09) and general Earth-versus-space limit statements, including one block each of SAF-04 and SAF-08 (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2); the BASS and BASS-II campaign results (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4); confined-duct (baffle) tests in the ISS glovebox (see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2); the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method and 1-g threshold studies (see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1, MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2); cabin atmospheres (see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1, CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2).

## Findings

### Saffire-I and Saffire-II large-scale tests (SAF-04)

| Set | Material and form | Gravity and platform | Oxygen and diluent | Flow speed and direction | Ignition | Enclosure | Test duration | Not reported by this source | Citation |

#### Objectives and test platform

- SAF-04 names the needs as low-g flammability limits for spacecraft materials and a definition of realistic fires for exploration vehicles, including the fate of a large-scale spacecraft fire. [SAF-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The stated objectives were: Saffire 1, assess flame spread of a large-scale microgravity fire (spread rate, mass consumption, heat release); Saffire 2, verify oxygen flammability limits in low gravity; Saffire 3, the same as Saffire 1 at a higher flow speed; and evaluate NASA's normal-gravity material flammability screening test for low-gravity conditions. [SAF-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Data from the experiment are to be used to validate models of spacecraft fire response scenarios. [SAF-04 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The fires were set on purpose inside unoccupied ISS resupply vehicles: Saffire launched stowed on board and stayed dormant while the vehicle was berthed and unloaded; the crew then stowed ISS trash in the vehicle with room left for air circulation; after departure the tests ran and all data were relayed to Earth before the vehicle's destructive re-entry; an uncaptioned illustration slide shows the hardware module, the module inside the vehicle, the vehicle at the ISS and a burning sample with an "Air Flow" arrow. [SAF-04 p.5–6 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]

#### Hardware and sample card

- The sample stands on edge on the centre plane of the Saffire flow duct (18 in × 20 in), with air entering at one end; two cameras and four radiometers view it (fields of view drawn as blue and red cones), and each flight carried six sample thermocouples. [SAF-04 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- The Saffire-II card holds the nine 5 cm × 29 cm samples in three rows (2-1 to 2-3, 2-4 to 2-6, 2-7 to 2-9); red igniter marks sit at the lower end of samples 1–3 and 5–9 and at the upper end of sample 4, as drawn in the photo, whose orientation relative to the flow is not printed on that slide. [SAF-04 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal, slide; SAF-04 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Two uncaptioned slides show only drawings: a flow-duct drawing under the slide title "SIBAL Fabric Results (con’t)" with four coloured traces above and below the sample plane and four red-outlined markers on the duct walls (p.23), and a duct drawing with red lines from points on the upper and lower walls to the sample plane and green lines from the lower compartment into the duct (p.34); apart from that title, no axes, units, labels, legend or caption are printed. [SAF-04 p.23 · MEASURED · nominal, slide; SAF-04 p.34 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]

[SAF-04 p.29 · Table I · MEASURED · slide]
- Δ %O2 (footnote i) is derived from measured CO2 production and referenced to the initial O2 concentration reported by the ISS. [SAF-04 p.29 · Table I · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

#### Silicone sheets (SAFFIRE-II:2-1 to 2-4)

- In upward-burning 1-g tests (C3), the three thicknesses 0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm spanned the flammability limits from significant burn to partial burn to no burn: 0.27 mm samples were almost always completely consumed, 0.61 mm burned on average 7.6 cm of the available 30 cm before going out, and 1.03 mm would not burn at all. [SAF-04 p.11 · MEASURED · slide]
- In downward-burning 1-g tests (C3), 0.37 mm silicone was completely consumed and the next thicker one tested, 0.61 mm, would not burn. [SAF-04 p.11 · MEASURED · slide]
- The authors framed the flight question as how much of the available fuel would burn and whether microgravity would be more or less favourable to flame spread. [SAF-04 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- In microgravity (C2) none of the four silicone samples burned, a result the authors call convincing though rather anticlimactic. [SAF-04 p.12 · MEASURED · slide]
- After the igniter was switched off a tiny gas-phase flame remained but did not spread and soon went out; all igniters appeared to work normally, and the material was clearly damaged near each igniter (C2). [SAF-04 p.12 · MEASURED · slide]
- Not even the thin sample allowed any flame spread in microgravity (C2), although it was entirely consumed in normal gravity, which the authors found surprising. [SAF-04 p.12 · MEASURED · slide]
- Earlier experience with cellulosic fuels (paper, fabric) and even PMMA had suggested that a material whose flame persists in upward 1-g tests would also burn in microgravity at a moderate flow speed below typical buoyant flow speeds (no reference marker printed). [SAF-04 p.12 · CITED · slide]
- Burning silicone becomes quite irregular, cracking and flaking off in complex ways. [SAF-04 p.13 · MEASURED · slide]
- The authors call silicone's microgravity behaviour perplexing, perhaps because of its complex burning: the fine silica powder it produces could deposit on the fuel and impede pyrolysis, and the larger buoyant flow speeds in 1-g could sweep the silica away fast enough not to hamper combustion. [SAF-04 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- They add that surface-reaction details and geometry could strongly affect the results, that buoyant flow might aid the cracking and flaking and so expose fresh fuel, and that the buoyant versus forced-convection boundary layer may contribute to the flammability differences. [SAF-04 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- More work is needed on the 1-g versus µ-g flammability of silicone; the authors suggest repeating the tests in microgravity at a much higher flow speed of around 60 to 80 cm/s, more typical of 1-g (other conditions as C2). [SAF-04 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

#### SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric (SAFFIRE-I:1-1, 1-2; SAFFIRE-II:2-5, 2-6)

- The "SIBAL" fabric is a 75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass blend in a simple weave (60 × 40 threads per inch) with the two fibres intermingled, overall area density 18 mg/cm2, used in sizes (W × L) 40.6 × 94 cm and 5 × 29 cm. [SAF-04 p.15 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- Test 1-1 (C1): at ignition the flame was mostly bright yellow and relatively vigorous, then soon developed a blue base and a pattern of orange radiation from incandescent soot. [SAF-04 p.16 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Test 1-1 (C1): flame length and brightness first fluctuated strongly at about 1.4 Hz and became more stable at about 90 s; subtle fluctuations persisted for the rest of the test at a slightly slower ~0.75 Hz (30 Hz image sequence starting 24 s after the igniter was turned off). [SAF-04 p.16 · MEASURED · single-test, slide; SAF-04 p.18 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- The authors call the reason for the fluctuation unclear: it may be a flow oscillation present even in the cold flow, or the flame interacting with the flow field in the first part of the duct. [SAF-04 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Test 1-1 (C1): after the flame had passed, exothermic surface smolder spots burning some of the leftover fuel were visible. [SAF-04 p.16 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Test 1-1 (C1): the flame burned the whole allotted test time of about 7 min (total burn time 420 s), and when the air flow was shut off it went out immediately. [SAF-04 p.16–17 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Test 1-1 (C1) burned about 90 % of the fuel, leaving 10 % unburned, enough for a meaningful opposed-flow test (1-2) and for conclusions on opposed-flow spread and development. [SAF-04 p.14 · MEASURED · single-test, slide; SAF-04 p.16 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Images of test 1-1 (C1): a photo of the sample shows a red zig-zag line along the top edge and a flame across the bottom edge, and an image slide shows a montage of frames 40 s apart from the igniter edge onward, with an inset comparing concurrent- and opposed-flow images. [SAF-04 p.14 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test, slide; SAF-04 p.19 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Average flame spread rate (C1): 1.8 mm/s concurrent (1-1) and 1.3 mm/s opposed (1-2), as printed on the position plot; the position curves show steady spread for most of the tests. [SAF-04 p.17 · MEASURED · slide; SAF-04 p.20–21 · MEASURED · slide]
- Flame length (C1): the concurrent flame (1-1) reaches a plateau of around 40 mm; the opposed flame (1-2) is a bit shorter, 24 mm. [SAF-04 p.21 · MEASURED · slide]
- Estimated average flame power of test 1-1 (C1): 1200 ± 300 W. [SAF-04 p.8 · MODELED · single-test, slide; SAF-04 p.17 · MODELED · single-test, slide]
- Average flame power of the Saffire-II SIBAL samples (C2, 5 cm wide; sample number not printed): 200 ± 50 W. [SAF-04 p.8 · MODELED · slide]
- At the same 20 cm/s flow, the 5-cm-wide sample (2-5, C2) spread marginally faster than the 40.6-cm-wide one (1-1, C1): 2.1 versus 1.8 mm/s. [SAF-04 p.21 · MEASURED · slide]
- The authors attribute this partly to the slightly higher starting oxygen (22.1 % vs 21.7 %), and add that the narrow sample might also have spread faster through larger side-entrainment effects. [SAF-04 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Figure (left, p.20): flame-base and pyrolysis position (mm) and flame length (mm, right axis) versus time (s) for 1-1 and 1-2 at 20 cm/s; values read from the figure (C1; tolerance ±25 s and ±25 mm for position, ±2.5 mm for length) [SAF-04 p.20 · MEASURED · ~fig, slide]

#### PMMA–Nomex composite (SAFFIRE-II:2-7)

- Purpose: to see how a material rated "safe" by the NASA 6001 Test 1 standard test reacts to extended exposure to a flame in microgravity. [SAF-04 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test, slide]
- The fabric is Nomex HT90-40, a meta-aramid fabric commonly used on the ISS; a 0.8 mm PMMA sheet formed the first 5 cm, followed by an overlap about 7 mm long where PMMA and fabric were in intimate contact, and Nomex for the rest of the sample (C2). [SAF-04 p.24 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test, slide]
- On Earth, Nomex HT90-40 burns only if the oxygen concentration is raised to around 24 to 25 % (normal gravity; test method, pressure, sample size and source not printed). [SAF-04 p.24 · CITED · slide]
- In microgravity (C2) the PMMA took about two minutes to burn away (Table I burn duration 140 s), all the while the flame plume extended over and heated the base of the Nomex. [SAF-04 p.25 · MEASURED · single-test, slide; SAF-04 p.29 · Table I · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Average flame power from the PMMA, assuming complete conversion of the fuel: 460 ± 50 W (C2; "±" printed as an underlined "+"). [SAF-04 p.25 · MODELED · single-test, slide]
- Despite this significant heating load the Nomex fabric did not ignite (C2). [SAF-04 p.25 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- Damage: the first 1 cm of fabric was significantly damaged, the first 5 cm completely blackened, and the remainder carried a black streak down its centre (C2). [SAF-04 p.25 · MEASURED · single-test, slide]
- The authors note that part of this discoloration may be soot deposited from the PMMA flame rather than pyrolysis of the fabric itself. [SAF-04 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

#### Thick PMMA slabs (SAFFIRE-II:2-8, 2-9)

- Cross-sections: both samples are drawn 5 cm wide and 1 cm thick; in 2-8 the middle 1.8-cm-wide portion is only 0.4 cm thick, while 2-9 is a flat rectangle (C2). [SAF-04 p.10 · MEASURED · nominal, slide]
- The µ-g burn length of ~10 cm (footnote iii) is the length of fuel with significant visible damage (C2). [SAF-04 p.29 · Table I · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Footnote iv: the flames stayed anchored at the base of the sample, which regressed very slowly, 0.01 to 0.04 mm/s (C2). [SAF-04 p.29 · Table I · MEASURED · slide]
- Average flame power of the thick PMMA samples (C2; sample number not printed): 600 ± 100 W. [SAF-04 p.8 · MODELED · slide]
- SAF-04 states that the results of samples 2-8 and 2-9 are described in another paper at the same conference (not identified on the slide). [SAF-04 p.9 · CITED · slide]

#### The authors' conclusions

- For the first time a large-scale fire was set on purpose inside a spacecraft in orbit, and smaller samples of various materials were burned on a later flight. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Unlike in 1-g, a steady flame was achieved even on a wide sample burning in concurrent flow. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The flames spread more slowly than in earlier tests in smaller ducts, which the authors take as showing that confined spaces matter for potential spacecraft fires. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Silicone appears less flammable in microgravity than in normal gravity, at least at the flow speeds tested. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- Nomex, a common ISS material rated "safe", could not be ignited even when bathed by a pilot flame. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The Saffire project planned further experiments on the effects of enhanced oxygen at reduced pressure. [SAF-04 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

#### Scope, apparatus and imaging

- The Saffire series burns metre-scale fires aboard the habitable but uncrewed Cygnus vehicle to study such fires and their effect on the spacecraft; this paper takes the concurrent spread over SIBAL (Saffire IV) and pure cotton (Saffire V) and compares it with the earlier SIBAL flights. [SAF-06 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The new variables of Saffire IV and V are a lower duct, the material (SIBAL versus cotton knit, and sample length) and normoxic oxygen and pressure; Saffire IV repeats Saffire I's conditions in the smaller duct (C8 vs C4) as a test of the duct-size effect on concurrent spread. [SAF-06 p.3–4 · MEASURED]
- The authors chose the cotton of Saffire V, with the same total area density as SIBAL, to test the boundary-layer explanation of the transient excess pyrolysis length: cotton burns away completely, exposing the flame base to the free-stream velocity. [SAF-06 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The duct draws Cygnus cabin air through a flow straightener, and the flow leaves in +x through a second straightener back into the cabin, then winds among the refuse bags and discarded equipment before re-entering the duct; smoke-wire visualization during the flights confirmed a uniform flow. [SAF-06 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors expect this path to mix the large cabin volume well, so they treat the oxygen concentration as constant over a test of about three minutes. [SAF-06 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Fig. 1 shows the duct (L, W, H as in Table 1) and the sample cards: Saffire IV holds "SIBAL Fabric" (Ignition 1, upstream), "Nomex Fabric" (Ignition 3), "1-sided PMMA (0.5 cm thk.)" (Ignition 4) and "2-sided PMMA (1 cm thk.)" (Ignition 2); Saffire V holds "Cotton Fabric" ("Normoxic O2", Test 2, upstream), "Structured PMMA (1 cm thk.)" (Tests 1 and 4) and "1-sided PMMA (0.5 cm thk.)" (Test 3); the card lies on the mid-height plane of the duct over its full length and width, and the downstream samples are not treated in this paper. [SAF-06 p.6–7 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The cotton (Fig. 2a, Teloi) has an area density of 18.1 mg/cm2, picked to match SIBAL most closely; SIBAL (Fig. 2b) is a custom blend in which every strand mixes 75 % unbleached cotton and 25 % fiberglass, 18.05 mg/cm2 in total (13.54 mg/cm2 cotton); Fig. 2c shows the fiberglass matrix left after a ground burn (scale bar 4 mm, spread direction vertical). [SAF-06 p.7–8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In SIBAL most of the cotton burns during spread, and leftover fuel keeps smouldering in spots inside the fiberglass matrix once the flame has passed. [SAF-06 p.7 · MEASURED]
- SIBAL was easier to prepare: its stiffness made it sturdier and less likely to stretch, while the cotton stretches up to 40 % across its width and much less along the spread direction. [SAF-06 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Surface- and edge-view cameras were AVT Manta G-235c GigE (Bayer colour, 30 frames/s, automatic exposure up to 0.03 s, gain allowed to vary once the longest exposure was reached); green LED strips lit the sample for 3 frames every 2 s to show the pyrolysis front, the dark frames giving flame size and shape; gain ran from 40 down to 32 (Saffire IV) and 24 (Saffire V). [SAF-06 p.7–8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Images came down first as compressed jpg for operations, later as RAW converted to lossless tiff and corrected for lens distortion; tracking used the corrected tiffs (surface view 1638 × 1325 px, edge view 1982 × 609 px, 3.2 mm/pixel). [SAF-06 p.8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Thermocouples (type K) were woven into the sample centreline to read the fuel surface temperature at the Table 1 locations; the other data sources are the flame images, radiometers and the vehicle pressure transducer, whose reading did not change noticeably during the SIBAL tests. [SAF-06 p.8–9 · MEASURED · nominal; SAF-06 p.18 · MEASURED · nominal]

#### Flame images

- Saffire IV (C8), Fig. 3: in the LED-lit half the burnt and unburnt fabric contrast sharply, and soot streaks laid down during ignition cross the unburnt fabric; the thin, dim flame sheet only shows after strong enhancement of the dark half; the flame appears as long as the pyrolysis zone; the base, best seen in the lit image as a thin pink line under the sooty flame, leaves glowing smoulder spots in the fiberglass matrix behind it (forced flow upward in the image; sample 50 × 40.6 cm). [SAF-06 p.9–10 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Saffire V (C9), Fig. 4: the cotton burns away completely, unlike SIBAL, especially over the first half of the sample; the frames shown are earlier than those of Fig. 3 because the sample curled once the flame reached the thermocouple location, distorting flow and flame (the caption says earlier than Fig. 2). [SAF-06 p.11–12 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Saffire V (C9): char oxidation is visible upstream of the flame base and is incomplete, so residual char accumulates as the flame advances; in the dark image the flame is much longer than the lit pyrolysis zone. [SAF-06 p.12 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The authors suggest the longer cotton flame may come from more fuel released in pyrolysis (similar area densities, but 25 % of SIBAL is inert fiberglass) or from the different atmosphere. [SAF-06 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 5 shows smaller SIBAL samples 1.1, 2.2 and 5 cm wide (Table 1 lists 1.2 cm; see Conflicts); the 5-cm Saffire II flame (C5, C6) is strongly curved over its whole extent, and the narrower BASS flames (C10, C11) are strongly curved too; BASS had no LED to light the pyrolysis front. [SAF-06 p.11–12 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- The authors read the curvature as a three-dimensional flame with strong edge effects. [SAF-06 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Edge views exist for the BASS tests and two Saffire flights; in BASS (Fig. 6) the 2.2-cm sample (C11) gave a long sooty flame and the 1.2-cm sample (C10) an all-blue one. [SAF-06 p.12–13 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the all-blue narrow flame to its larger share of heat lost to the metal holder. [SAF-06 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The Saffire edge views integrate a very deep flame (~40 cm); lens distortion and view angle make quantitative analysis very difficult, but the views can be compared; the LED shows the SIBAL surface in these nearly edge-on views, but the pyrolysis zone is hard to place because the sample edges stay unburnt further upstream than the centreline. [SAF-06 p.13 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 7 compares edge views at about the same flame-base position, Saffire IV at 58 s and Saffire V at 63 s, each unenhanced and with a 2.5 gamma correction (3 cm scale mark; the panel labels print "Saffire IV Original" for both pairs). [SAF-06 p.13 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Saffire V cotton (C9) vs Saffire IV SIBAL (C8): the cotton image's LED light is hard to see without enhancement; unenhanced, soot glow hides the blue in both flames; enhanced, both blue tips look longer and the cotton flame much longer; the SIBAL flame base is tapered, its two sides split by the fiberglass mesh, while the cotton base is rounded, wrapping the exposed fuel edge; and the cotton flame (76 kPa) is thicker than the SIBAL flame (99 kPa). [SAF-06 p.13–14 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- The authors read this as a much brighter cotton flame at the higher oxygen despite the lower pressure, in line with spread scaling linearly with oxygen and with the square root of pressure (ref. [8]), and attribute the thicker cotton flame to the lower pressure. [SAF-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Flame tracking, spread rate and flame and pyrolysis lengths

- Method: NASA's Spotlight software tracked the dark and LED-lit frames separately, with automated filtering and a threshold to find the flame edge; the base was tracked in both frame types, the flame tip at the sample centre in contrast-enhanced dark frames, and the pyrolysis front at the centre in lit frames, with the tracking checked by eye as it ran; Lf and Lp in Fig. 8 are tip-minus-base differences, and the steady base position against time gives Vf. [SAF-06 p.14–15 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Saffire IV (C8): spread was very steady; flame and pyrolysis lengths peaked at about 105 mm early, at 30–40 s, with the base only 100 mm from the igniter, then shrank slowly; the tip ran fast during early growth and then slowed while the base moved steadily; the flame length was briefly steady after about 100 s before the tip hit the sample end; this sample was half as long as those of Saffire I and III. [SAF-06 p.14 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Saffire V (C9): the base spread steadily early on and the tip fast during growth before slowing, with large peak flame and pyrolysis lengths at 40 s (base 100 mm from the igniter); the flame then shrank, but after the base passed the surface thermocouple at 300 mm, charring and curling made it non-uniform, which disturbs the tracking; Vf comes from the base-tracking slope before 300 mm (< 100 s). [SAF-06 p.14 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Spread rates were close, 0.36 cm/s for SIBAL in Saffire IV (C8) and 0.34 cm/s for cotton in Saffire V (C9), although the atmospheres differed. [SAF-06 p.14 · MEASURED]
- Correlation used by the authors for concurrent spread: Vf ~ O2% × P^1/2 (Vf in cm/s, O2 in % by volume, P in kPa; refs. [8, 18, 24]). [SAF-06 p.14 · CITED; SAF-06 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- With that correlation, the ratio of the two spread rates matches the ratio of oxygen times the square root of pressure for Saffire IV and V, and the conclusions call the effect of the normoxic atmosphere consistent with the known oxygen and pressure dependencies. [SAF-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- For the cotton (C9), Lf and Lp were each fitted with a polynomial and the fits subtracted, because far fewer lit than dark frames were available; the difference settles at a constant 40 mm by roughly 60 s, before either length is steady and before the cotton starts to curl (after 100 s). [SAF-06 p.15–16 · Fig. 9 · MODELED · single-test]
- The cotton flame is longer than its pyrolysis zone (C9), whereas the two lengths match for the SIBAL fabric in all SIBAL tests (Saffire I–IV, C4–C8). [SAF-06 p.15 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- The authors offer several reasons, also restated in their conclusions: cotton holds 25 % more fuel, so at a similar spread rate it burns faster and the extra pyrolysate lengthens the flame; pure cotton has a higher specific heat than the blend, which should slow spread and lengthen the preheat zone; the lower pressure thickens the flame, which may cut the heat flux to the preheat zone; and SIBAL's hot fiberglass and smouldering residue upstream form an extended thermal boundary layer, whereas the cotton flame base meets the ambient-temperature core flow. [SAF-06 p.15–16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 10 tracks Saffire I–III (series "tip" and "base" labelled "25 cm/s" and "20 cm/s", plus "30 cm long, 5 cm wide samples"); the wide samples follow the same trends as Saffire IV and V, and Table 1 lists the rates, lengths and sizes of all five flights. [SAF-06 p.16–17 · Fig. 10 · MEASURED]

#### Pyrolysis length and burnout time

- Fig. 11 plots the pyrolysis-length histories of Saffire I–V (series I, III, II-5, II-6, IV, V; notes "Cotton", "smaller duct height 20 cm/s", "25 cm/s", "20 cm/s", "dashed: 30 cm long, 5 cm wide samples"; axis printed "fpyrolysis length, mm"); all but the 5-cm samples peak at ~40 s, when the 5-cm samples seem to reach a steady size, and the longest full-width samples (C4, C7) are steady by about 100 s. [SAF-06 p.17 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED]
- Saffire IV seems to level off at about the same time, but the Saffire IV and V samples were too short to show the plateau clearly, and the curling cotton later distorted its pyrolysis-length measurement. [SAF-06 p.17 · MEASURED]

| Fig. 11 series (read ±5 mm, ±12.5 s; time from ignition start) | Reading | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| I (C4) | peak ~62 mm at ~40 s; ~55 mm at its end, ~420 s | [SAF-06 p.17 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test] |
| III (C7) | peak ~82 mm at ~30–40 s; ~55 mm at its end, ~322 s | [SAF-06 p.17 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test] |
| V, cotton (C9) | peak ~146 mm at ~40 s | [SAF-06 p.17 · Fig. 11 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test] |

- Saffire I and III (C4, C7) showed strong transient excess pyrolysis lengths (overshoots); the smaller Saffire II samples (C5, C6) did not, nor did the BASS samples (ref. [12] as printed); the Saffire II tests at comparable flow levelled off smoothly to the same steady pyrolysis lengths as Saffire I and III by 100 s. [SAF-06 p.17 · MEASURED]
- A transient excess pyrolysis length (flame-length overshoot) also appeared on the cotton that burned away (C9), larger than on SIBAL. [SAF-06 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.18 · MEASURED]
- The authors explain the missing overshoot on small samples by three factors: the Saffire II flame sits deep in the boundary layer half-way down the duct; hot gas can expand sideways as well as downstream (Saffire II and BASS); and oxygen reaches these three-dimensional flames from the sides as well as from above, so they grow smoothly to a steady size. [SAF-06 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors define burnout time as the pyrolysis length divided by the flame spread rate. [SAF-06 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As an equation, tb = Lp/Vf (tb in s, Lp in cm, Vf in cm/s); each test's Vf turns its pyrolysis-length history into a burnout-time history. [SAF-06 p.17 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 12 plots the burnout-time history of each Saffire test (series I, III, II-5, II-6, IV dashed, V; groups "Cotton", "Long, wide SIBAL", "Short, narrow SIBAL"; y pyrolysis length/spread rate, s; x time from ignition, s). [SAF-06 p.18 · Fig. 12 · MEASURED]
- The SIBAL tb histories of Saffire I, III and IV (C4, C7, C8) collapse onto one curve: tb rises almost 1:1 with time after ignition up to a peak, then decays slowly to a steady value in the longer tests; the steady tb of SIBAL in atmospheric air is about 22 s. [SAF-06 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.17 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
- The authors name the peak the transient excess burnout time, by analogy with the transient excess pyrolysis length. [SAF-06 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The tb histories of the small Saffire II samples (C5, C6) approach their steady values without a peak. [SAF-06 p.17 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute this to better oxygen transport across narrow samples and hence more heat feedback to the fuel (ref. [17]). [SAF-06 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire V (C9), with no boundary layer upstream of its flame since the fuel burns out, had the largest transient excess in burnout time and in pyrolysis length; the peak came at ~35 s after ignition for the SIBAL samples and slightly later, ~40 s, for cotton. [SAF-06 p.18 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.28 · MEASURED]
- The authors relate the larger and later cotton peak possibly to its higher fuel burning rate, and add that its different oxygen and pressure may affect the size and timing of the peak. [SAF-06 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire IV (C8), in the smaller duct, had a slightly lower peak burnout time than Saffire I (C4): ~30 s against ~35 s for Saffire I and III. [SAF-06 p.18 · MEASURED]
- The authors credit the faster core flow in the smaller duct, which speeds up spread and so the development of the preheat and pyrolysis zones; the same faster core flow makes the actual peak excess pyrolysis length larger. [SAF-06 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In the smaller duct the peak transient excess pyrolysis length of SIBAL was about twice as large (C8 vs C4). [SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
- Because the cotton (C9), which burns away and leaves no boundary layer upstream of its base, also overshoots, the authors conclude the overshoot cannot come only from the flame moving into a growing boundary layer on the sample (ref. [17]); something else must act. [SAF-06 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.28–29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Surface temperatures

- Fig. 13 (a: against time from burnout, b: against distance from burnout, c: against distance over Lp, which equals t/tb; series Saffire I TC1 and TC4 20 cm/s, Saffire III TC1 and TC4 25 cm/s, Saffire II Samples 5 and 6, Saffire IV TC1 and TC4 20 cm/s; dashed line near 400 °C): the SIBAL traces are aligned so that burnout is at x = 0, and the pyrolysis temperature, where the traces change slope, is 400 °C. [SAF-06 p.18–20 · Fig. 13 · MEASURED]
- Apart from the small Saffire II samples (C5, C6) the traces are alike, Saffire I and III (C4, C7) very close and Saffire IV (C8) with a slightly longer preheat time; against distance, Saffire IV shows a much longer preheat length. [SAF-06 p.18–19 · MEASURED]
- The authors find the longer Saffire IV preheat consistent with a faster core flow in the smaller duct. [SAF-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Saffire IV's sample length and thermocouple positions could not capture the early preheating, but did capture its longer pyrolysis length of 85 mm (Table 1, C8); Saffire I and III catch the early preheating at the downstream-most thermocouple, and Saffire I–III have similar pyrolysis lengths, 40 mm at 20 cm/s and 50 mm at 25 cm/s (C4–C7). [SAF-06 p.19 · MEASURED]
- On the x/Lp axis (Fig. 13c) pyrolysis starts at a non-dimensional burnout time of one for the SIBAL tests, and the profiles of all Saffire SIBAL samples share one shape across the pyrolysis zone. [SAF-06 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.19 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that burnout time mainly reflects the pyrolysis time rather than the preheat time, which differs between tests, so the excess pyrolysis length may stem from heat-flux changes mainly in the pyrolysis zone. [SAF-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 13c also shows a higher temperature across the pyrolysis zone for Saffire IV (C8); relative humidity was 37 % on Saffire IV against 47 %, 45 % and 46 % on Saffire I, II and III. [SAF-06 p.19 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest a faster core flow in the lower duct raising the heat flux, and partly the drier air, since water hydrogen-bonded to the cellulose takes part of the flame heat flux to evaporate, more so at higher humidity. [SAF-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Surface energy balance in the preheat zone (Saffire I)

- Eq. 1, the surface energy balance per side: q̇f″ = ρs τs(t) Cs(t) dTs/dt (heat-up of the fuel) + ε σ (Ts^4 − T∞^4) (re-radiation from the surface) + Lv(T) ms(t) As e^(−Es/RTs) (latent heat of vaporization, first-order pyrolysis model) + τs d/dx(k dTs/dx) (conduction in the solid from the pyrolysis zone to unheated fuel; this term is printed struck through); ms(t) is not defined in the nomenclature. [SAF-06 p.21 · Eq. 1 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors drop the conduction term because, at the velocities studied, conduction along the thin burning solid is much smaller than convection by the gas flowing along the surface. [SAF-06 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Inputs: half-thickness area density ρsτs(t) 0.009 g/cm2 at the start, falling as the cotton vaporizes; Cs(t) the mass-weighted mean of fiberglass (0.7 J/g K) and cotton (1.26 J/g K), with the cotton share falling; ε = 0.8; σ = 5.729 × 10^-12 W/cm2 K4 (stated as experimental); Lv = 300 + (Cp,f − Cs)(Ts − 300) J/g (ref. [31]); As = 1.626 × 10^11 s-1, Es = 1.6144 × 10^5 J/mol, R = 8.3145 J/mol K (ref. [30]). [SAF-06 p.21 · MODELED · nominal]
- Since all SIBAL thermocouples scale alike, the heat flux was estimated from the test with the longest preheat record, Saffire I (C4, slow spread), using its furthest downstream surface thermocouple (Fig. 15a: surface temperature and polynomial fit against time; Fig. 15b: net flame heat flux, surface radiation, sensible heat and heat of vaporization against distance from burnout, with "Pyrolysis" and "Preheat" regions split by a dashed line at 4 cm). [SAF-06 p.22 · Fig. 15 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The temperature history was fitted with a polynomial (coefficient of determination close to one), differentiated to give a smooth dTs/dt for the first term of Eq. 1 (C4). [SAF-06 p.22 · MODELED · single-test]
- Results (C4): the flux rises slowly far ahead of the flame and steeply within a few centimetres of the flame base; radiation and sensible heat absorb the flame flux in the preheat zone, latent heat exceeds sensible heat only in the last centimetre before burnout, and at burnout all of the flame flux leaves as re-radiation; in the preheat zone the flux heats the material until surface radiative loss balances it. [SAF-06 p.2 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.22–23 · MODELED · single-test; SAF-06 p.30 · MODELED]
- Preheat length is taken as the distance from pyrolysis onset to where the net flux falls to ~10 % of its value at onset (definition from ref. [9]). [SAF-06 p.22 · CITED]
- On that definition the preheat length is ~10 cm (C4), 2.5 times the pyrolysis length. [SAF-06 p.22–23 · MODELED · single-test; SAF-06 p.29–30 · MODELED · single-test]
- By 100 s, at steady state, the Saffire I base had reached 20 cm, with a pyrolysis length of only ~4 cm (C4). [SAF-06 p.22–23 · MEASURED · single-test]
- The Eq. 1 flux at the pyrolysis front (onset of pyrolysis) lies in the range of the critical heat flux for ignition of cellulose (C4). [SAF-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- That critical heat flux is 1–1.3 W/cm2 (ref. [32], White and Dietenberger). [SAF-06 p.23 · CITED; SAF-06 p.32 · CITED]
- The model of ref. [17] gives the same general shape of net flux but puts its peak, near 1 W/cm2 (0.25 cal/s cm2), at the flame base rather than near the pyrolysis front. [SAF-06 p.23 · CITED]

#### Duct and sample size effects

- Table 1 covers three duct sizes and five sample sizes (C4–C11). [SAF-06 p.23 · MEASURED]
- The spread-rate data of ref. [3] differ for each duct and SIBAL sample size at the same forced flow. [SAF-06 p.23 · CITED]
- Spread rate and flame length depend strongly on duct size even for ducts more than 30 cm tall: in the 30.5 cm duct of Saffire IV (C8) the steady spread rate (0.36 vs 0.18 cm/s), the pyrolysis length (8.5 vs 4 cm) and the flame length were about twice those in the 51 cm duct of Saffire I (C4). [SAF-06 p.2 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.23 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 16 (spread rate against duct height, by sample width 40.6, 5, 2.2 and 1.2 cm; BASS in the smallest duct, Saffire in the two larger; dashed trend line, no equation printed) shows spread rising as duct height falls, except for the narrow BASS sample (C10). [SAF-06 p.23 · Fig. 16 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest side heat losses to the holder slowed that narrow flame. [SAF-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Ref. [19] predicts spread rates and pyrolysis lengths falling as the inverse of duct height for ducts 4 to 9 cm tall. [SAF-06 p.23 · CITED]
- The authors call so large an effect in ducts this big surprising and not expected. [SAF-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They list the sensitivities: duct geometry (height, aspect ratio, length), sample geometry and burning mode (width, complete burnout or a fiberglass residue upstream) and flame size in the duct, itself possibly set by ambient oxygen, pressure, mean flow velocity and fuel area density. [SAF-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Model results of ref. [17] (its Fig. 6) compare wide and narrow samples at three heights above the fuel: the oxygen deficit is far larger for the wide sample at every height; at 0.9 cm the flow turns around the flame more strongly for the wide sample while the narrow one's streamlines straighten; the 0.0001 reaction contour has a similar wing shape at 0.3 cm for both, is much thicker in the flow direction for the narrow sample at 0.6 cm, and thickens for the wide sample only at 0.9 cm. [SAF-06 p.24 · CITED]
- That model also predicted a pyrolysis length shrinking as the flame advances into the thickening boundary layer, which none of the long-sample tests showed (Saffire I and III, C4, C7). [SAF-06 p.24 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest differing exit boundary conditions between model and experiment. [SAF-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Their hypothesis for the overshoot: after ignition there are no pyrolysis or preheated zones yet, so burnout takes very long until these develop, a post-ignition growth transient of the essentially two-dimensional flames; in the full-width samples, core-flow acceleration from thermal expansion and wall boundary-layer growth makes a very long flame until preheat and pyrolysis lengths form and tb reaches a steady value, while in narrow samples (BASS, Saffire II) lateral expansion and lateral oxygen transport damp the acceleration and the flame grows smoothly in three dimensions. [SAF-06 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SAF-06 p.28–29 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A two-dimensional transient model (ref. [16]) describes the overshoot similarly: in thin solids nearly all heat comes from the gas, as mean heat flux times preheat length; early the flux is high and the preheat zone short, later the zone is long and the flux low, and the product peaks during flame growth. [SAF-06 p.24 · CITED]
- The authors find this consistent with the burnout-time histories of Fig. 12. [SAF-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Earlier work cited in the introduction: Markstein and de Ris (ref. [5]) first showed steady, constant-size upward spread over very large samples (up to 91.4 cm wide); concurrent spread over thin fuels has a limiting length (ref. [16]); scaling analyses (refs. [8, 23–26]) identified Grashof, Reynolds, Planck and Nusselt numbers as the governing groups; models (refs. [13–15, 19–22]) show duct size matters; upward spread can reach a steady size at reduced pressure in 1 g (refs. [6, 24, 27]). [SAF-06 p.3–4 · CITED]
- Cited duct studies: Shih and T'ien's 3-D steady model (ref. [13]) gave slower spread in narrow channels at higher velocity, but at low velocity lateral oxygen diffusion raised spread even in small ducts; Shih and Wu's parallel-sheet 1-g tests (ref. [15]) and Shih's 2-D model (ref. [14]) closed the sample spacing from 150 mm (tests) and 500 mm (model) down to quenching at a few centimetres, with spread first rising (flow accelerated by thermal expansion, more radiant exchange) then falling as oxygen consumed at the flame base fails to enter the channel, so a maximum appears at intermediate heights, which the experiments confirmed although the model did not converge at some heights; Li and co-workers' ISS duct tests and 3-D transient model (refs. [19–22]) found spread non-monotonic with duct size, faster from thermal expansion as the duct shrinks, then slower from limited oxygen and heat loss to the closer walls. [SAF-06 p.4 · CITED]
- In microgravity the upstream fan sets the oxygen supply, whereas in 1 g a growing flame can draw in more and more oxygen. [SAF-06 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Cited sample-width and atmosphere work: Honda and Ronney (ref. [23], widths 4–100 mm) found spread varying with the cube of width and convectively stabilized below about 10 mm, and with the square root of width and radiation-stabilized above; Li et al.'s model of Saffire I and II (ref. [17]) predicted the overshoot on wide samples, attributed to the growing boundary layer, and its absence on narrow samples lying deep in the boundary layer half-way down the duct; the Grashof scaling P²g correlated upward spread (ref. [25]); concurrent spread has been found linear in flow rate (over the range tested) and oxygen but varying with the square root of pressure (refs. [8, 24]); early 2-D models gave spread linear in flow and oxygen (ref. [9]), a recent 3-D model linear in pressure and flow but quadratic in oxygen (ref. [18]); Zhao et al. (ref. [29]) fitted upward spread over narrow samples with power laws of pressure at five oxygen levels. [SAF-06 p.4–5 · CITED]

#### Core-flow acceleration estimate (thermal expansion and boundary layers)

- Aim: correlate spread rate with an effective flow velocity that accounts for duct and flame size, through two effects, flow acceleration by the flame's thermal expansion and extra core-flow acceleration by growing boundary layers; the duct inlet flow is assumed fixed, unaffected by the flame or boundary-layer growth. [SAF-06 p.24 · MODELED]
- Saffire V (C9) is kept in the analysis with caveats: the cotton burns away, so there is no boundary layer over the holder except on the first 3 cm of card (neglected), and its pressure, oxygen and fuel differ, which may confound the correlation even though its oxygen partial pressure is close to the air of the other tests. [SAF-06 p.24 · MODELED]
- Per the model of ref. [17] (its Fig. 5a), thermal expansion builds a local high-pressure plateau that slows the incoming flow and diverts streamlines at the flame base (a drag like a porous body), which may change the spread rate, and accelerates the flow inside the flame. [SAF-06 p.24–25 · CITED]
- The authors expect this acceleration to act strongly on the preheat zone downstream of the flame, especially in a smaller chamber, both effects depending on sample size relative to the chamber. [SAF-06 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Thermal expansion is estimated as isobaric ideal-gas expansion of a box-shaped flame Lf × w × 2Hf (visible flame height doubled to include the inner and outer halves of the thermal field), with a mean temperature Tmean = 1050 K from a 1400 K flame temperature (8 mm and 1 cm thermocouple readings in Saffire I, III and IV) and a 700 K pyrolysis temperature: Eq. 2, Ve = Lf · w · 2 · 2 · Hf · Tmean / T∞ (cm3, both sides of the sample); Eq. 3, Ue Aduct = ((Ve + Vduct)/Vduct) U Aduct, with U the inlet velocity (Aduct cancels). [SAF-06 p.25 · Eq. 2 · MODELED · nominal; SAF-06 p.25 · Eq. 3 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Hf is the only input not measured, for Saffire I–II as printed in the text, because those flights had no side-view cameras; estimated values marked in Table 1 are used (see Conflicts for the flights marked). [SAF-06 p.25 · MEASURED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Thermal expansion raised the core flow negligibly for the smallest flames in the largest ducts but by 113 % for the largest flames, an effect that is local and travels with the flame (Table 1 tests C4–C11). [SAF-06 p.25 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.30 · MODELED]
- The authors suggest this partly offsets the growing boundary layer over the sample, which may explain steady rather than slowly shrinking flame lengths (ref. [17]). [SAF-06 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Sample centres lie at 0.7–1.1 L/DH (DH the duct hydraulic diameter), well inside the entrance region, at 10–13 % of the entrance length from the correlation EL/DH = 0.06 ReD. [SAF-06 p.25 · MODELED · nominal]
- Entrance-length correlation used: EL/DH = 0.06 ReD (EL entrance length, ReD Reynolds number on DH). [SAF-06 p.25 · CITED]
- The authors therefore treat the flow away from the surfaces as an inviscid core that the boundary layers on four duct walls and two sample faces accelerate along the duct. [SAF-06 p.25–26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Boundary-layer equations: Eq. 4, δ = 5 (νx/Ue)^1/2; one third of every boundary-layer volume (δ* ≈ δ(x)/3 on a flat plate) displaces the core flow, and volumes add because the core is inviscid; Eq. 5, VBL = Σ(0..Lholder) δ(x)/3 (wΔx · 2) + Σ(0..Lduct) δ(x)/3 (WΔx · 2) + Σ(0..Lduct) δ(x)/3 (HΔx · 2), dimensions from Table 1, Δx = 0.1 cm; Eq. 6, UBLn = Vduct/(Vduct − VBLn) · Ue; Eq. 7, δn = 5 (νx/UBLn)^1/2; Eqs. 5–7 are iterated, converging at n = 4; for the cotton test the first term of Eq. 5 is zero (fabric burns away; the 3.3 cm upstream card is neglected), and since displacement grows along the duct the core accelerates as it goes. [SAF-06 p.26 · Eq. 4 · MODELED · nominal; SAF-06 p.26 · Eq. 5 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.26 · Eq. 6 · MODELED]
- Boundary-layer displacement raises the core velocity to 112 % for the largest duct (109 × 46 × 51 cm) and 135 % for the BASS duct (17 × 7.6 × 7.6 cm), worded on p.27 as a share of the initial duct volume and in the conclusions as an increase "by" 112 % and 135 %; the abstract and conclusions add that this simple estimate seems to explain the spread trends across three duct sizes and several sample sizes. [SAF-06 p.2 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.27 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.30 · MODELED; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest the rising core velocity along the duct raises momentum and heat transfer (ref. [33]), which may partly offset the predicted decay of pyrolysis length (ref. [17]) as the flame enters a thicker boundary layer. [SAF-06 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 17 plots spread rate against the accelerated flow UBL4 for all tests (series BASS-II, Saffire I, II-5, II-6, III, IV, V); the linear fit covers only the ~20 cm/s tests, cotton included, with R² = 0.9683 printed and no equation, while the 25 cm/s tests (C6, C7) do not correlate well. [SAF-06 p.27 · Fig. 17 · MODELED]

#### Local flow at the flame base and flame height

- Using the Blasius flat-plate solution, the authors compute the forced-flow speed felt at the flame base, taken 0.2 cm above the fuel surface (kinematic viscosity 0.16 cm2/s), from the accelerated velocity UBL4: Eq. 8, η = y (UBLn/(νx))^1/2, solved for x with Eq. 7 at n = 4. [SAF-06 p.28 · Eq. 8 · MODELED · nominal]
- Fig. 18 (left axis local velocity at the flame base, y = 2 mm; right axis boundary-layer thickness from Eqs. 4 and 5; x distance from the holder's leading edge; series BASS 2.2 cm, BASS 1.2 cm, Saffire I, II-5, II-6, III, IV and "Hf vs Vf*t_ss"): the local velocity at the flame base drops steeply over the first 10 cm as the boundary layer grows and is quite low away from the leading edge for the SIBAL fabrics (C4–C8, C10, C11). [SAF-06 p.28–29 · Fig. 18 · MODELED]
- The Table 1 flame heights are plotted at the base position Vf × tss, with tss the time the pyrolysis length stabilized (Fig. 11): about 110 s for the full-width samples, much earlier for the 5-cm samples, which burned in a boundary-layer flow from the start, and very soon for the small BASS samples. [SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
- The flame heights follow the boundary-layer thickness quite well. [SAF-06 p.29 · MODELED]
- Fig. 18 local velocity at the flame base, read from the figure (±1 cm/s, ±2.5 cm): ~28 cm/s at the leading edge (highest curve, BASS 2.2 cm), ~6–7.5 cm/s at 10 cm and ~2–2.5 cm/s at 100 cm from the holder's leading edge (C4–C8, C10, C11). [SAF-06 p.28 · Fig. 18 · MODELED · ~fig]
- Fig. 18 flame-height points at Vf × tss, read from the figure (±2.5 cm, ±0.1 cm; marker-to-series match low confidence): ~37 cm for Saffire V (Hf 3.5 cm) and ~40 cm for Saffire IV (Hf 2.7 cm); ~20 cm for Saffire I (Hf 2.0* cm), ~25 cm for Saffire III (Hf 1.8* cm), ~10 cm for Saffire II (Hf 1.0* and 0.9* cm), ~2 cm and ~3 cm for BASS (Hf ~0.6 and ~0.4 cm); * values estimated (Table 1 footnote). [SAF-06 p.28 · Fig. 18 · MEASURED · ~fig; SAF-06 p.9 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- In their conclusions the authors compare the 40 × 50 cm SIBAL and cotton samples of Saffire IV and V with the 40 × 90 cm SIBAL samples of Saffire I–III, flown in a larger duct, and with the much smaller BASS samples and duct. [SAF-06 p.29 · MEASURED]
