### Terms, acronyms and document titles defined in the sources
- CAB-01 Appendix C, fire barrier: an obstruction (such as a partition) that prohibits or tends to inhibit the propagation of burning; it may be internal or external in configuration. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, fire break: a gap, an opening or a nonflammable material between flammable materials that would prevent the propagation of burning. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, fire containment: the situation in which a fire and/or burning particles do not progress in any manner beyond the confines of a configuration. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, sealed containers: containers enclosed adequately enough to preclude replenishment of a combustible atmosphere under fire conditions. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, vented containers: containers that are unsealed and permit atmosphere exchange. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, heat sink: a structure or panel of high thermal conductivity, in intimate contact with a burning material, that extracts enough heat by conduction to lower the temperature below the ignition point and extinguish burning; an effective heat sink could limit initial ignition. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, ignition source: a heat source intense and localized enough to induce combustion; for flammability considerations any electrical wire or elevated-temperature component is considered an ignition source, and monopropellants, strong oxidizers, bases, etc. must also be considered. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, positive igniters: igniters that produce a controlled flame. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, propagation paths: the paths a flame front takes outside (or inside) an enclosure that represent fire paths between flammable materials; they are not necessarily straight or coplanar. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- CAB-01 Appendix C, void space: unoccupied volume in a container. [CAB-01 p.52 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Specification titles as CAB-01 Appendix B lists them: L-T-80, "Tape, pressure-sensitive adhesive (aluminum backed)"; ANSI/NEMA-WC-27500, "Standard for Aerospace and Industrial Electrical Cable" (formerly MIL-C-27500F, "Cable, electrical shielded and unshielded, aerospace"); SAE-AS-22759, "Wire, electric, fluoropolymer-insulated, copper or copper alloy" (formerly MIL-W-22759); SAE-AS-81044, "Wire, electric, crosslinked polyalkene, crosslinked alkane-imide polymer, or polyarylene insulated, copper or copper alloy" (formerly MIL-W-81044). [CAB-01 p.51 · CITED]
- Acronyms and abbreviations as CAB-01 Appendix D expands them: ABS, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene; ECTFE, ethylene chlorotrifluoroethylene; ETFE, ethylene tetrafluoroethylene; FEP, fluorinated ethylene propylene; TFE, tetrafluoroethylene; mil, milli-inch (0.001 inch); scfm, standard cubic feet per minute. [CAB-01 p.53 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2
# MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_2 — NASA-STD-(I)-6001B screening rules and test methods; Test 1 limits vs sample length

## Scope
Covers: the interim standard NASA-STD-(I)-6001B (OVR-06): its status and applicability, evaluation and acceptance rules, required and supplemental tests by environment (Tables 1 and 2), system evaluation after a Test 1 failure, the LOX/GOX oxygen-compatibility route, general test rules and specimen quantities (Table 3), Tests 1, 4, 10, 17, 18, 2 and 3, the Appendix A ignition and combustion tests, facility certification, the test-code key, and the acronyms, symbols and terms the standard defines (sections 3.1 and 3.2, Test 2 and Test 18 definitions); and two OVR-13 slides: the Test 1 description and the cited Test 1 MOC/ULOI-vs-sample-length table at 10.2 psia.
Not here: flammability configuration analysis (JSC 29353B) and 1-g parametric effects on Test 1 limits (see MATERIAL_ACCEPTANCE_1); exploration cabin atmospheres and material qualification for them (see CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_1, CABIN_ATMOSPHERES_2); 1-g vs reduced-gravity limits (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2).

## Findings

### Status and applicability of NASA-STD-(I)-6001B
- NASA-STD-(I)-6001B, *Flammability, Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures*, is an interim NASA technical standard (cover: approved 04-21-2008, expiration date 04-21-2010) that supersedes NASA-STD-6001, with measurement system metric (inch-pound). [OVR-06 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- History log: baseline release approved 02-09-1998; interim revision A approved 04-21-2008; interim revision B approved 11-10-2009, which updated the foreword and sections 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1 and 2.4 to NTSP's current template and made no technical change except correcting the units in Table 5; the foreword is signed by NASA Chief Engineer Michael Ryschkewitsch with approval date 11-10-2009. [OVR-06 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- It has the consensus of its developing Technical Working Group but not the Agency-wide concurrence a NASA Technical Standard requires, and a statement on every page says it does not yet have final NASA approval. [OVR-06 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- It is issued to give uniform engineering and technical requirements for urgent program and project needs, is approved for NASA Headquarters and Centers (including Component Facilities and Technical and Service Support Centers) and may be cited in contracts, programs and other Agency documents as a technical requirement. [OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- NASA-STD-6001 was previously published as NHB 8060.1, *Flammability, Odor, Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures for Materials in Environments that Support Combustion*. [OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Purpose: requirements for evaluating, testing and selecting materials so that unsafe conditions from flammability, offgassing and fluid compatibility are precluded, covering materials for space vehicles, their GSE and facilities used in assembly, test and flight operations, with requirements, criteria and test methods for flammability, offgassing and compatibility. [OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Its provisions will be included, as applicable, in all future contracts and programs involving space vehicles, payloads and support equipment, and other program or Center documents may add material performance requirements. [OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Materials for space vehicles, specified test facilities and specified GSE shall meet it, Center M&P organizations shall put its applicable requirements into their materials control programs, and it may apply to JPL, other contractors, grant recipients or agreement parties only as far as their contracts, grants or agreements specify. [OVR-06 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Requirements are numbered and use "shall", guidance is in italics from section 4 on, and tailoring for a program or project shall be formally documented in its requirements and approved by the Technical Authority. [OVR-06 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Cited documents are requirements as cited, their latest issues apply unless a version is designated, and not using a designated version needs approval by the responsible Technical Authority. [OVR-06 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Applicable documents are available through the NASA Technical Standards System (http://standards.nasa.gov), where feedback on the standard is also submitted, or from the standards bodies and distributors. [OVR-06 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The standard does not supersede or waive Agency requirements in other documents, and conflicts with other requirement documents shall be resolved by the responsible Technical Authority. [OVR-06 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Appendix C lists the referenced editions (latest at publication): JSC 29353A (2007) *Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications*, ISO 14624-4:2003 (upward flammability of materials in pressurized gaseous oxygen or oxygen-enriched environments) and ISO/IEC 17025:2005 (competence of testing and calibration laboratories); a different version needs specification or approval by the responsible Center M&P organization. [OVR-06 p.107 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Evaluation and acceptance rules (sections 4 and 5)
- Materials in habitable areas of spacecraft (spacecraft materials, stowed equipment, experiments) shall be evaluated for flammability and offgassing, all materials in other areas for flammability, materials exposed to LOX, GOX or other reactive fluids for compatibility with that fluid in their application, materials exposed to pressurized breathing gases also for offgassing, and electrical insulation also for arc tracking. [OVR-06 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Material suitability shall be evaluated in the worst-case anticipated use environment: the most hazardous pressure, temperature, material thickness and fluid exposure conditions (4.1 f; the 3.2 definition reads "and/or"). [OVR-06 p.15–16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Materials shown to meet the required-test criteria are acceptable for further design consideration, and where possible materials already shown to meet them in the use environment should be selected. [OVR-06 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Existing test data are compiled in the NASA MSFC Materials and Processes Technical Information System (MAPTIS, http://maptis.nasa.gov/). [OVR-06 p.16 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Systems with untested materials, or with materials failing the required-test criteria, shall be verified acceptable in the use configuration by analysis or testing and documented in a Materials Usage Agreement (MUA) per NASA-STD-(I)-6016 (flight hardware) or NASA-STD-(I)-5005 (GSE) that records the acceptance rationale and is submitted to the responsible Center M&P organization for approval. [OVR-06 p.16–17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The applicable test depends on the exposure environment (habitable environments, LOX and GOX systems, breathing gases, reactive fluids); required tests shall be run in the applicable exposure conditions, and a material must pass them to be acceptable for use without restriction. [OVR-06 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Nonmetals tested to NASA-STD-(I)-6001 should be retested every 10 years or as the responsible Center M&P organization requires. [OVR-06 p.17 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Materials that fail the required-test criteria but remain candidates shall be verified acceptable in the use configuration by analysis or testing and specifically approved by the responsible Center M&P organization. [OVR-06 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- When that organization specifies it, materials shall be batch/lot tested until composition and processing variations are shown to be insignificant for the characteristics evaluated. [OVR-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

[OVR-06 p.36 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.43–44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.55 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### System flammability evaluation after a Test 1 failure (sections 6 and 6.1)
- System evaluations shall show that configurations using flammable, incompatible or offgassing materials are acceptable. [OVR-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Under section 6.1 (system flammability in low-pressure air or oxygen-enriched environments, including habitable ones), a system flammability evaluation shall be conducted when materials failing the Test 1 criteria are proposed for human-occupied spacecraft, specified test facilities or specified GSE, and it can be done by analysis or by testing. [OVR-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- JSC 29353, *Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications*, gives guidelines for hardware flammability assessment and mitigation. [OVR-06 p.19 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Analytical route (6.1.2): four fire control guidelines shall be addressed and the results documented and submitted to the responsible Center M&P organization for evaluation: (a) amount and arrangement of flammable materials controlled so fire cannot spread in the vehicle, with any fire isolated in well-defined areas by firebreaks or other techniques and no propagation path to other areas; (b) ignition sources eliminated or controlled by design; (c) effects of an isolated fire on crew in habitable modules considered; (d) rate and size of pressure and temperature rise in any fire not causing structural damage to the vehicle. [OVR-06 p.19–20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Test route (6.1.3): materials failing Test 1 shall be evaluated by a configuration test such as Test 10, which evaluates the worst possible failure modes in the worst-case operating conditions. [OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- If the evaluation is inconclusive and a major assembly flammability test such as a crew module test is needed, the system design organization shall submit a test plan to the responsible Center M&P organization for approval before the test. [OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### LOX and GOX: material selection and oxygen compatibility assessment (section 6.3)
- Under section 6.3 (material and component compatibility in LOX and GOX environments), materials, components and systems in LOX and GOX environments (GOX: gas with ≥99.5 percent oxygen; LOX: cryogenic liquid with ≥99.5 percent oxygen) shall be evaluated by the Figure 1 approach. [OVR-06 p.14–15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- The need for an oxygen compatibility assessment (OCA) shall be addressed for compressed-air systems and pressurized systems containing enriched oxygen, i.e. >21 percent oxygen by volume (6.3.2 a; also Table 1 footnote 4 on the LOX and GOX and Breathing Gases rows), and if an OCA is judged unnecessary the responsible Center M&P organization shall concur. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.17–18 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Such systems are inherently less hazardous than systems containing pure oxygen, and the hazard increases with oxygen concentration and/or pressure. [OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- An OCA is a systematic approach to identify and address the fire hazards of an oxygen system that emphasises evaluating ignition mechanisms and applying materials test data; the process is described in NASA/TM-2007-213740. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The approach begins with pre-selection on flammability and combustion test data, then a flammability assessment; Figure 1 pre-selects on required Test 1 data [nonmetals in environments ≤345 kPa (≤50 psia)] or Test 17 data, plus supplemental autogenous ignition temperature (ASTM G72-01), heat of combustion (ASTM D240-02), oxygen index (ASTM G125-00) and ignition-mechanism test data. [OVR-06 p.20 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; OVR-06 p.22 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Section 6.3.3: materials found flammable shall get an OCA per NASA/TM-2007-213740, *Guide for Oxygen Compatibility Assessments on Oxygen Components and Systems*, which decides whether the material may be used or supplemental material, configuration or component testing is needed. [OVR-06 p.21 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Figure 1 logic: materials not flammable in the use configuration and environment go to "Is additional material control required?" (Note 3: requirements from sources other than NASA-STD-(I)-6001, such as corrosion), and are used if none is needed or evaluated if it is; flammable materials get the OCA, after which acceptable ones go to the material-control question, "not known" leads to material/configuration/component testing and unacceptable ones to "Select another material". [OVR-06 p.20–22 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In Figure 1, evaluation and testing both feed "Do changes/test results lead to acceptable materials?" (yes: the material-control question; no: select another material), and a newly selected material re-enters at the flammability question. [OVR-06 p.22 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Figure 1 Notes 1 and 2: flammability data must apply to the specific configuration of the parts, so data other than standard test data may be needed, and the responsible M&P organization is consulted on whether the flammability and ignitability data apply to the design configuration. [OVR-06 p.22 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Pre-selection (6.3.4 a): as a minimum, previously untested nonmetals shall undergo autogenous ignition temperature and heat of combustion tests. [OVR-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Pre-selection aims at materials with desirable flammability and combustion characteristics: materials that do not burn in the specific environment and configuration, and nonmetals with high autogenous ignition temperatures, low heats of combustion and high oxygen indices, are preferred for oxygen service, and data for specific ignition mechanisms (particle impact, gaseous fluid impact, mechanical impact) may also help. [OVR-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flammability assessment (6.3.4 b): data shall apply to the specific environment and configuration of the parts, materials of unknown flammability or configuration shall be considered flammable, and the responsible Center M&P organization shall be consulted on data applicability to the design configuration. [OVR-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- In general, all materials (metals, plastics, elastomers, lubricants, contaminants) become flammable in 100 percent oxygen as pressure increases, and almost all polymers are flammable in 100 percent oxygen at atmospheric pressure (not reported by this source: gravity, flow, ignition method, temperature, specimen form). [OVR-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flammability depends strongly on configuration: metals, even those normally highly resistant to ignition, are more flammable in oxygen in thin cross-sections (thin-walled tubing) or finely divided (wire mesh, sintered filters), so assessing flammability calls for a cross-sectional view of each component showing all its materials of construction. [OVR-06 p.23 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- OCA (6.3.4 c): the M&P organization shall be consulted on whether ignitability data apply to the design configuration, results shall be documented and submitted for concurrence (by MUA if applicable), and the hardware developer shall verify that the assessed materials reflect the as-built design. [OVR-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Supplemental tests (material, configuration or component tests) may be required as an aid to the OCA or as a result of its findings, and guidelines for them come from the responsible Center M&P organization. [OVR-06 p.18 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.24 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### General test requirements and minimum quantities (section 7, Table 3)
- Tests shall be performed by certified facilities that show good laboratory practice (including calibration and maintenance procedures) for accurate, repeatable data and demonstrate testing proficiency at least every 2 years per Appendix B. [OVR-06 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Identified test material shall come from the responsible NASA Center or the contractor hardware supplier with a test request form like Appendix D, or the requester may authorise a certified facility to procure it. [OVR-06 p.25 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Receipt and preparation requirements: materials accompanied by MSDSs (OSHA handling requirements); specimens visually inspected with flaws or contamination noted in the test report, prepared in the proper dimensions, weighed and identified individually, cleaned to end-use specifications and inspected after preparation; test fluids meeting or exceeding user specifications. [OVR-06 p.25–26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Contamination (solvents, cleaning agents, abnormal temperatures, humidity variations, environmental pollutants, particulates, handling) can significantly compromise material and configured-system characteristics, so it is important to control exposure to such sources enough to minimise variation in test results. [OVR-06 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A test that deviates from standard parameters, such as nonstandard specimen preparation or test conditions, shall be identified as nonstandard. [OVR-06 p.26 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Test 1 upward flame propagation (section 7.1, tailored ISO 14624-1)
| Set | Material, form | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Duration | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | candidate material, five specimens 300 mm by 65 mm (12 in by 2.5 in) tested one at a time, mounted vertically in a test stand, in the worst-case configuration | oxygen/nitrogen mixture with the highest oxygen the material could see in use (worst-case atmosphere), verified to +1.0 percent −0 percent of reading | worst-case atmosphere | air not allowed to flow during tests | ignition system at the specimen bottom | test chamber | each specimen burns until it self-extinguishes | gravity level and platform; temperature; one- or two-sided burning | [OVR-06 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; OVR-06 p.30–31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal] |
- Purpose (7.1.1): to determine whether a material exposed to a standard ignition source self-extinguishes and does not transfer burning debris that can ignite adjacent materials; section 7.1 is a voluntary consensus standard adopted and tailored, following ISO 14624-1:2003 (*Space systems — Safety and compatibility of materials — Part 1: Determination of upward flammability of materials*) with NASA exceptions, clarifications and additions, each naming the ISO section in parentheses. [OVR-06 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.27–30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Pass/fail (7.1.3): the specimens meet the acceptance criteria and count as self-extinguishing only if no material of the five standard-sized specimens burns >15 cm (6 in) and no specimen propagates flame by transferring burning debris; failure of any one specimen on either criterion fails the material in that test environment (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.29–30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- One test is five replicate, identical specimen ignitions, a specimen being one standard-sized section of the material (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Debris rule (ISO section 4): ignited specimens shall not ignite (flaming combustion) the paper below them, which would show that transferred burning debris has enough energy to ignite adjacent materials; once the paper ignites from debris, later burns in the same material test are run without paper because burning paper can inhibit burning of the specimen (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Burn length is the linear distance of consumed specimen (7.1.2 d), clarified for ISO section 3.1 as the distance from the specimen bottom to the farthest evidence of flame-consumption damage judged by visual observation, post-test examination, burn video and/or other means; burn length and whether burning debris ignited the paper are recorded in the test report. [OVR-06 p.28 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal; OVR-06 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Figure 2 (post-test specimen; front, section, side and isometric views) labels three damage zones from the bottom up: igniter flame influence, consumed material, heat damage area; it gives no scale or values. [OVR-06 p.29 · Fig. 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC, addition to ISO section 3.8): the highest oxygen concentration at which at least five specimens pass the acceptance criteria of this test; determining it is recommended when the worst-case environment is uncertain (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.30 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Atmosphere (ISO section 5.1 additions): test gases are mixed thoroughly before each specimen, premixed or mixed in the chamber, and in-chamber mixing uses a fan until a gas analyzer shows a homogeneous mixture (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Testing may be done in a fume hood in air if the above conditions are met and results are verified against test-chamber results (ISO section 6.1). [OVR-06 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- "Ambient conditions" (ISO section 6.3 clarification) means an oxygen concentration of 20.9 percent, a pressure of 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia) and a temperature of 23 (±5) °C [73 (±9) °F]. [OVR-06 p.31 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Procedure: Table 3 minimum quantities apply; every specimen is video recorded; the specimen is under vacuum no less than 1 min and no more than 3 min (ISO section 8.2.1); the igniter is retracted once it extinguishes; flames from the paper and flame jets and sparks from the specimen are observed and recorded; the paper rests on a non-flammable, non-conducting screen; the report goes to MAPTIS in the acceptable format (conditions C1). [OVR-06 p.31–32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- OVR-13 describes NASA's current flammability screening as NASA STD-6001 Test 1, an upward-burning test at the worst-case atmosphere in which the material will be used, historically 30% O2 at 10.2 psia, the shuttle pre-EVA atmosphere (not reported by this source: material, diluent, flow). [OVR-13 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]
- On that slide a sample burning more than 15 cm fails STD-6001 Test 1, with burn length taken as the length of consumed material, and the burn-zone sketch labels from the bottom an igniter-influenced region, consumed material and a heat-damaged area. [OVR-13 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]
- The slide's apparatus diagram (figure ID CD-99-78888) shows a test chamber with a vertical specimen in a frame beside a scale (and a substrate for testing coatings), specimen width "5 cm, typical", 33 cm from the holder top down to the specimen bottom at the igniter, 20 cm from there down to a paper sheet, and a 6-inch "limiting flame-spread height" measured up from the specimen bottom. [OVR-13 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal, slide]
- A photograph on the slide labelled as a sample failing NASA Test 1 shows a specimen burning with a tall flame in the Test 1 holder (atmosphere and material not stated). [OVR-13 p.27 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · slide]

- Purpose (7.4.1): to determine whether a wire insulation material exposed to a standard ignition source self-extinguishes and does not transfer burning debris that can ignite adjacent materials; 7.4 is a voluntary consensus standard adopted and tailored, following ISO 14624-2:2003 (*Part 2: Determination of flammability of electrical-wire insulation and accessory materials*) with NASA exceptions, clarifications and additions naming the ISO sections. [OVR-06 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.32–33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

[OVR-06 p.33 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

[OVR-06 p.34 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

[OVR-06 p.34–35 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

[OVR-06 p.35–36 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Test 10 configurational flammability (Appendix A.4)
- Test 10, formerly titled Simulated Panel or Major Assembly Flammability Test, is now a supplemental test (Appendix A.4) that may gather supplemental data when materials do not meet the Test 1 criteria. [OVR-06 p.44 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Purpose (A.4.1): to determine whether a hardware article exposed to a standard ignition source self-extinguishes and does not transfer burning debris that can ignite adjacent materials or other hardware. [OVR-06 p.74 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[OVR-06 p.74–75 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

- Test 17 determines the flammability of materials in GOX at the use pressure at ambient or elevated temperatures, and testing at other pressures can give supplemental information; 7.17 is a voluntary consensus standard adopted and tailored, following ASTM G124-95 (reapproved 2003), *Standard Test Method for Determining the Combustion Behavior of Metallic Materials in Oxygen-Enriched Atmospheres*, with NASA exceptions, clarifications and additions naming the ASTM section (conditions C3). [OVR-06 p.11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.55–56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- ISO 14624-4 (*Part 4: Determination of upward flammability of materials in pressurized gaseous oxygen or oxygen-enriched environments*) describes a similar test procedure. [OVR-06 p.56 · CITED]
- Criteria: a flammable material is defined as one that burns >3 cm (>1.2 in) (ASTM section 3 addition), a material is considered flammable at the maximum use pressure if at least one specimen burns >3 cm (>1.2 in) (7.17.3), setting a pressure at which it is not flammable needs at least 10 specimens tested without consumption >3 cm (>1.2 in) (7.17.2 e, 7.17.3 a), and a test is valid only if the promoter ignites, burns and detaches from the specimen (conditions C3). [OVR-06 p.56–57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Burn length is the specimen length consumed by combustion (7.17.2 d), computed as the pre-test specimen length minus the sum of the post-test specimen length and the promoter length (ASTM section 3 addition). [OVR-06 p.56–57 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Results depend on specimen configuration: specimens with high surface-area-to-volume ratios, such as filter materials, burn at lower pressures than bulk forms such as 0.32-cm (0.126-in) rods (conditions C3). [OVR-06 p.56 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A material that cannot be obtained or prepared as a cylinder gets a nonstandard specimen, which should have 0.32-cm (0.126-in) (±5 percent) sides and be at least 10.2 cm (4 in) (±5 percent) long; any deviation in specimen preparation, orientation, configuration, ignition source or test pressure makes the test nonstandard. [OVR-06 p.57–58 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Precision and reporting: initial test temperature recorded with ±5 percent of reading, pressure reading ±1 percent of reading, consumed length ±0.25 cm (±0.1 in); reports go to MAPTIS in the acceptable format. [OVR-06 p.57–58 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Test 3 flash point of liquids (Appendix A.2)
- Test 3 is now a supplemental test (Appendix A.2) giving supplemental information on the flash point of liquids: a specimen in a cup is heated at a controlled rate, with or without stirring, and a small flame is directed into the vapor space at regular intervals to see whether a flash occurs. [OVR-06 p.32 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Flash point is the lowest temperature, corrected to a barometric pressure of 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia), at which an ignition source ignites the specimen vapors under specified test conditions; it measures the tendency to form a flammable mixture with air under controlled laboratory conditions, is only one of several properties in the overall flammability hazard, and test criteria depend on the intended use. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.66 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Method selection follows ASTM E502-07 (selection of closed-cup flash-point methods), or by application an open-cup method, ASTM D92-05 (Cleveland open cup; D92-05a in section 2.3) or ASTM D1310-01 (Tag open cup, reapproved 2007); systems and procedures are those of the selected method(s), the report gives specimen identification, method, conditions, the flash point corrected to 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) and observations, and precision follows the ASTM method(s). [OVR-06 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.66–67 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Some pure materials, such as trichloroethylene, need large diameters for flame propagation: they do not propagate a flame in an apparatus the size of a flash-point tester, yet their vapors are flammable and burn when ignited in an apparatus of adequate size (not reported by this source: diameter values, gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, flow, ignition method, temperature, duration). [OVR-06 p.67 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Appendix A ignition and combustion property tests (A.8–A.11)
- A.8 autogenous ignition temperature: a material in a reaction vessel is exposed to a pressurized environment of 0.5 to 100 percent oxygen and heated at a predetermined rate, and the minimum temperature that causes spontaneous ignition, marked by a sudden temperature rise, is the autogenous ignition temperature (autoignition temperature: the lowest temperature at which a material spontaneously ignites under specific test conditions) (not reported by this source: pressure value, gravity, flow). [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.86–87 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Its criteria depend on the intended use as evaluated through hazard analyses and engineering assessments; it gives a numerical temperature at the onset of ignition under carefully controlled conditions and is only one of several properties in the overall ignitibility hazard. [OVR-06 p.86 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Conditions, specimen preparation, test system, pre-test and test procedures are those of ASTM G72-01 (*Standard Test Method for Autogenous Ignition Temperature of Liquids and Solids in a High-Pressure Oxygen-Enriched Environment*), with at least five specimens per test condition; the report gives specimen identification, method, conditions, ignition temperature, temperature rise on ignition and observations, goes to MAPTIS, and precision follows ASTM G72-01. [OVR-06 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.87–88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- A.9 heat of combustion: the heat evolved per unit mass when a nonmetal burns completely in oxygen, found by burning a weighed specimen in oxygen in a bomb calorimeter under controlled conditions and calculating from temperatures before, during and after combustion. [OVR-06 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Its criteria depend on the intended use as evaluated through hazard analyses and engineering assessments, and heat of combustion is only one of several properties in a material's overall oxygen compatibility. [OVR-06 p.88 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Gross heat of combustion is heat released per unit mass burned in a constant-volume enclosure with gaseous products except water condensed to liquid, net heat of combustion is burning at constant pressure with all products including water gaseous, and the gross value is the one determined experimentally while the net value is more commonly used. [OVR-06 p.88–89 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For polymers of interest in aerospace (especially oxygen systems) the gross heat of combustion is conservative relative to the net by ~0.6 MJ/kg (~150 cal/g) or less, and the gross value is adequate for evaluating oxygen compatibility (not reported by this source: specific polymers, test conditions). [OVR-06 p.89 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Conditions, specimen preparation, test system and procedures are those of ASTM D240-02 (reapproved 2007) or ASTM D4809-06 (bomb calorimeter, high-precision method), both titled for liquid hydrocarbon fuels, with at least five specimens per test condition (sections A.9.6 and A.9.7 are each printed twice); the report gives specimen identification, method, conditions, gross heat of combustion and observations, goes to MAPTIS, and precision follows those methods. [OVR-06 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.89 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- A.10 oxygen index (guidance): as part of pre-selecting previously untested nonmetals for oxygen service, they may be tested to ASTM G125-00 (*Measuring Liquid and Solid Material Fire Limits in Gaseous Oxidants*) or ASTM D2863-06 (*Measuring the Minimum Oxygen Concentration to Support Candle-Like Combustion of Plastics (Oxygen Index)*; D2863-06a in section 2.3). [OVR-06 p.10–11 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.90 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- A.11 electrical arc test: it determines the voltage and current needed to ignite nonmetals; with test pressure, oxygen concentration, specimen material and configuration, voltage and current set by the OCA or the test requester, a material fails at the test conditions if ignited once in a maximum of 60 tests and passes if not ignited in 60 tests, the current typically being varied to find the ignition threshold. [OVR-06 p.90 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Apparatus: specimen configuration specified by the OCA or requester (preparation may include fraying with a wire brush), a single wire strand in contact with the material (Figure 5: wire clamping mechanism, slide cover glasses, sample, specimen mounting plate), a stainless-steel cross chamber with four 10.2-cm (4-in) ports, pressurized as desired with oxygen or a specified gas mixture (system maximum 689 kPa (100 psia)), with gas inlet and outlet, a view window for normal and high-speed video, a mounting block with built-in heat exchanger for temperature control, a "TCe" (as printed) for temperature measurement, and power for the arcing from a supply that emulates batteries while allowing different voltages and currents. [OVR-06 p.90–91 · Fig. 5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Procedure: voltage set to the test condition and current slightly below it; wire sized and clamped; chamber sealed, purged and pressurized to the test pressure and oxygen concentration; current raised manually until the wire breaks and arcs; after an ignition testing continues at a lower current, and without ignition high-speed video and inspection confirm the wire broke in the desired place touching the specimen; each test is one wire-break event observed for ignition; the report gives material and configuration, test pressure, oxygen concentration and the current/voltage needed for ignition. [OVR-06 p.91–92 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Test facility certification (Appendix B)
- Certification is required for any facility performing the standard's required tests because their data are presented for materials selection approval; applicants submit detailed written procedures to the certification panel covering instrument calibration, specimen preparation, test chamber certification, test atmosphere analysis or verification, data analysis, report preparation, quality control, recording and archiving of test data, materials control and control of flight articles. [OVR-06 p.104 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Facilities certified to ISO/IEC 17025, *General requirements for competence of testing and calibration laboratories*, are considered to meet paragraph B.3. [OVR-06 p.104 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Certification is kept by performing the certified method and reporting its data to MAPTIS at least once within the last 18 months, taking part with other NASA-certified facilities in the latest round robin (round robins for Tests 1, 4 and 7 at least every 2 years), and having the data reviewed and approved by the panel or its designees. [OVR-06 p.105 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- All test instrumentation shall be in current calibration with documented traceability to national, international or intrinsic standards where available, and the facility certifies testing per approved plans and procedures, prepares complete records for each material or system, keeps test data for at least 15 years and submits records and data to MAPTIS. [OVR-06 p.105–106 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]

### Terms, acronyms and document titles defined in the sources
- Symbols as the source expands them (section 3.1): °C, degree Celsius; °F, degree Fahrenheit; ≥, equal to or greater than; ≤, equal to or less than; >, greater than; <, less than; µ, micro; %, percent; ±, plus or minus. [OVR-06 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Acronyms as the source expands them (section 3.1): ASTM, ASTM International (originally known as the American Society for Testing and Materials); CO2, carbon dioxide; GN2, gaseous nitrogen; GOX, gaseous oxygen; GSE, Ground Support Equipment; IEC, International Electrotechnical Commission; ISO, International Organization for Standardization; JSC, Johnson Space Center. [OVR-06 p.12 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- Acronyms as the source expands them (section 3.1): LOX, liquid oxygen; M&P, materials and processes; MSDS, Material Safety Data Sheet; MSFC, Marshall Space Flight Center; N2H4, hydrazine; NASA, National Aeronautics and Space Administration; O2, oxygen; OSHA, Occupational Safety and Health Administration; SAE, Society of Automotive Engineers International; STD, standard; TC, thermocouple; TM, technical memorandum. [OVR-06 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[OVR-06 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Other symbols and abbreviations as the source expands them (section 3.1): P, minimum contact pressure; RMS, root mean square; T, toxic hazard index. [OVR-06 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Symbols and units as the source expands them (section 3.1): V, volt; v, linear surface velocity; W, watt. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Ambient (room) temperature (section 3.2): room temperature is 23 (±5) °C [73 (±9) °F]. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Arc (section 3.2, repeated in the Test 18 definitions, 7.18.4): a continuous, luminous discharge of electric current crossing a gap between two conducting surfaces. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Arc tracking, also called arc propagation (section 3.2, repeated in 7.18.4): the phenomenon in which an arc between two or more wires, once initiated, sustains itself through a conductive path provided by degradation of the insulation for a measurable length. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.59 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Assembled article (section 3.2): an assembled article could be any component or assembly of components that is not a single material. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Degradation (section 3.2): an adverse physical or chemical change in a substance. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Gaseous fluid impact (section 3.2): heat delivered to a specimen by rapid fluid compression, which may also be called pneumatic impact, rapid pressurization or adiabatic compression. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mechanical impact (section 3.2): energy delivered by a plummet dropped from a pre-established height onto a striker pin in contact with a specimen. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Offgassed product (section 3.2): an organic or inorganic compound evolved as a gas from a material or assembled article. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Offgassing (section 3.2): the evolution of gaseous products from a liquid or solid material into an atmosphere. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Single-barrier failure (section 3.2): a leak through a barrier within a component that lets the fluid contact the materials directly behind the barrier; single barriers include mechanical joints (e.g. B-nuts), O-rings, gaskets and bladders, and metallic and nonmetallic diaphragms, while structural parts such as pressure lines and tanks, welded or brazed joints, and redundant seals in series that have been pressure-tested individually before use are not considered single barriers. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC; sections 3.1 and 3.2): the maximum concentration of an offgassed product allowed in the habitable area of the spacecraft for a specified duration. [OVR-06 p.13 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Technical Authority (section 3.2): it provides technical checks and balances by assuring that safety and mission success, relevant technical standards, engineering work, and safety and reliability analysis products are conducted properly in accordance with established, high-reliability processes independent of nontechnical program/project constraints. [OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Voluntary consensus standard (VCS; sections 3.1 and 3.2): a technical standard developed or adopted by voluntary consensus standard bodies, both domestic and foreign. [OVR-06 p.14 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.15 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Table titles (section 5): Table 1, Required Tests for Each Material Use, and Table 2, Supplemental Tests for Each Material Use, each give an environment, a test number and a title; the test methods of Table 1 are described in section 7. [OVR-06 p.17 · Table 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; OVR-06 p.18 · Table 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Effective heat of combustion (Test 2 definitions): the measured heat release divided by the mass loss for a specified time period. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Extinction coefficient (Test 2 definitions): a measure of the reduction of light transmission through a medium. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Heat flux (Test 2 definitions): the incident flux imposed externally from the radiant heater on the specimen. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Ignitability (Test 2 definitions): the propensity of a material to ignite, as measured by the time to ignition at a specified heating flux. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Rate of heat release (Test 2 definitions): the heat evolved from the specimen per unit time. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Smoke obscuration (Test 2 definitions): the reduction of light transmission by smoke, as measured by light attenuation, reported as the extinction coefficient. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Total heat release (Test 2 definitions): the quantity of heat released, determined by integrating the rate of heat release as a function of time. [OVR-06 p.63 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1
# NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1 — SoFIE-GEL: extinction of 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS

## Scope
Covers: SOF-02 (T'ien et al. 2025) and SOF-03 (Li et al. 2024), the SoFIE-GEL tests on 4-cm PMMA spheres in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack: hardware and embedded-thermocouple method, example time histories, the effect of sub-surface heating, the 1-atm extinction map (quenching, in-between and blowoff points), five oxygen-depletion cases, and the authors' conclusions.
Not here: SoFIE/RTDFS quiescent spread over PMMA sheets (SOF-04) and Confined Combustion (SOF-08) (see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2); BASS and BASS-II tests, including their 1-cm and 2-cm PMMA spheres (see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4); Saffire (see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1, LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2); general Earth-test versus low-gravity limit studies (see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1, EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2).

## Findings

### Campaign, sample and hardware
- SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) is a NASA-sponsored programme for solid-fuel combustion in microgravity with five sub-projects; GEL is the first sub-project, recently carried out on the ISS. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SOF-03 names the sponsor as NASA Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) and expands GEL as the Growth and Extinction Experiment, the first of SoFIE's five original experiments. [SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- GEL ran aboard the ISS from 13 January 2023 to 7 March 2024 with 17 PMMA samples and 54 tests, for a cumulative microgravity burning time of about 7 h. [SOF-02 p.1–2 · MEASURED]
- GEL aims to measure flame growth and extinction of a bulk solid (a PMMA sphere) against flow velocity, O2 percentage, pressure and the degree of internal sample heating in microgravity, and to build a numerical model that relates the microgravity results to normal-gravity ones. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 reports extinction limits from 35 of the tests, all at 1 atm, plus time sequences of several runs in which flow was changed mid-test (down to sub-buoyant values) and solid-temperature records from selected cases. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED]
- The 4-cm diameter gives a front stagnation-flow region well defined enough to keep flame-curvature effects small, while the sphere still fits the CIR test chamber. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- Each test regresses the surface so little that the sphere keeps roughly its shape and is re-used, typically three times, which reduces the samples flown and the crew's sample changes. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SOF-02 judges the sphere big enough for several embedded thermocouples to disturb it only minimally. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · nominal]
- SOF-03 chose the 4-cm sphere as a thick solid standing for the many non-thin materials used in spacecraft. [SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- PMMA is a common stand-in for non-charring solids in fire research and is used for spacecraft windows for its optical and material properties despite its flammability risk. [SOF-02 p.3 · CITED]
- Meisner Acrylic Casting cell-cast the spheres, and the CWRU Center for Imaging Research (CCIR) imaged them. [SOF-02 p.9 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The SoFIE insert sits inside the CIR aboard the ISS, which SOF-02's text calls the Combustion Integrated Rack and SOF-03 the Combustion Integrated Rig. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- CIR equipment per SOF-02: cameras, lighting, radiometers, power supply, filters, gas cylinders, vacuum source, cooling water, and sensors for O2, pressure, velocity, CO and CO2; SOF-03 names power supply, filters, lighting, gas-cylinder intakes, radiometers and the same five sensors. [SOF-02 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The insert's flow duct is square, 13.3 cm × 13.3 cm in cross-section and 24.6 cm long; the Fig. 1 diagram labels it 13 cm × 13 cm and shows the air-speed sensor, the duct fans and a 4-cm PMMA sphere with internal thermocouples. [SOF-02 p.2–3 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · Fig. 1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two fan banks drive a forced flow of 0.2–80 cm/s, read by a flow sensor at the upstream end of the duct. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Each sphere is held on a long stainless-steel tube of 6.35 mm diameter, and the samples sit 120° apart on an index system that is rotated to line one sample up with the duct (number of samples on the index: see Conflicts). [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The crew installs the hardware, changes consumables (fuel samples, oxidizer cylinders, filters, adsorber cartridges, igniters) and helps with debugging; everything else is run remotely in real time from the NASA Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- For ignition one sample sits on the duct centreline about 1 cm downstream of the duct exit; an electrically heated coiled wire near the sphere's upstream stagnation point ignites it and is then withdrawn, and the sample either stays at that spot for the whole test or is moved into the duct. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Four fixed cameras film the flame: three Sony FCB-MA130 units (1400 × 1200 pixels; SoFIE Cam1, Cam2, Cam3) along the duct, at right angles to an Allied Vision GC-1380CH ACME colour camera (1.4 megapixel, 1360 × 1024 pixels); Cam1 views the ignition position, Cam2 and ACME the position inside the duct, and Cam3 was off in the reported cases. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Extinction can be forced by lowering or raising the flow, by venting to lower chamber pressure, by adding nitrogen (lowers O2 while raising pressure), or by natural, gradual O2 depletion in the sealed CIR chamber (free volume 85.7 L). [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SOF-02's extinction data come from flow changes and from O2 depletion. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In SOF-03 every extinction was reached by natural, gradual O2 depletion in the sealed CIR chamber (free volume 85.7 L) while the flow was held constant. [SOF-03 p.1–2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- SOF-03 regards depletion as the least intrusive route, free of outside disturbance, which it considers important both for accurate limits and for seeing spontaneous cyclic extinction dynamics. [SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Reported O2 and flow come from sensors at the duct entrance, upstream of the sample, read in real time. [SOF-02 p.2–3 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 estimates the uncertainty of the flow and O2 measurements at ±0.25 %. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED]
- O2 is measured at several places in the chamber; SOF-02 uses the duct-entrance value because that is the O2 reaching the flame, and treats O2 depletion as a main route to the extinction limits. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Ground crews set the flow actively through the fan voltage; pressure could be adjusted but was left uncontrolled in SOF-02's tests, so all of them stay near 1 atm (1 ± 0.05 atm), the pressure rising by less than 5 % during a test from gas heating and product build-up in the closed chamber. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 considers the effect of that pressure rise on the results negligible. [SOF-02 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Two radiometers at two chamber locations have wide viewing angles not optimised for GEL; their traces serve only to time ignition, extinction and any near-limit perturbation or pulsation. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Each SOF-02 example run records ignition, flame growth, velocity, O2, pressure and radiometer histories, with the conductive heat flux into the solid at the forward stagnation region computed afterwards from the embedded thermocouples; the flame videos, showing colour, size, tip and base positions and standoff distance, are a main output. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Full videos of selected tests are in SOF-02's online supplementary material (doi:10.1016/j.combustflame.2025.114244). [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.9 · MEASURED]
- SOF-03 has five supplementary videos, S1 to S5, one per case; S1 is the Case #1 quenching sequence from the ACME camera (Fig. 2) and S2 the Case #2 blowoff from SoFIE Cam2 (Fig. 4). [SOF-03 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.4 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.6 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SOF-03 points to a SoFIE project description by P.V. Ferkul on NTRS (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20190030735/downloads/20190030735.pdf) and to its refs [14,15] for sample fabrication and the gradient method. [SOF-03 p.9 · CITED; SOF-03 p.2–3 · CITED]

### Embedded thermocouples and the qc method
- Each sphere is cast with five thermocouples: TC1, TC2 and TC3 lie on the centreline at different depths near the forward stagnation point and give the sub-surface temperature gradient, the measure of sub-surface heating, while TC4 and TC5 sit at an angle to the centreline. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Casting the thermocouples in gives excellent contact and avoids drilled holes, which disturb the solid when there are several sensors, at the cost of a tedious and expensive process; SOF-02 refers to its refs [13,26] for fabrication and gradient details. [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Every sample was CT-scanned after casting; Table 1 gives each thermocouple's angle from the centreline and depth below the initial unburnt surface, and only TC1–TC3, whose angles are all small and so roughly aligned with the flow, are used for the stagnation-region gradient. [SOF-02 p.5–6 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- The depths shift as the surface regresses during burning, but the spacing between thermocouples should stay the same. [SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED]

| Fresh sample | TC1 angle ° / depth mm | TC2 ° / mm | TC3 ° / mm | TC4 ° / mm | TC5 ° / mm | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1403 | 0.98 / 3.69 | 1.1 / 5.5 | 1.95 / 7.65 | 17.9 / 3.4 | 19.7 / 4.7 | [SOF-02 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED] |
| 1407 | 0.41 / 2.97 | 0.95 / 4.66 | 0.41 / 6.85 | 15.5 / 2.9 | 28.9 / 4.47 | [SOF-02 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED] |
| 1409 | 0.13 / 3.01 | 0.08 / 5.21 | 0.86 / 7.48 | 13.7 / 3.0 | 31.1 / 4.72 | [SOF-02 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED] |
| 1410 | 1.37 / 2.64 | 0.57 / 4.95 | 1.39 / 6.65 | 12.0 / 2.7 | 30.0 / 4.24 | [SOF-02 p.6 · Table 1 · MEASURED] |

- Fig. 5, a CT image with a 3.5-mm scale bar, shows TC1–TC5, a bubble layer, the cast PMMA and the support rod in a GEL sphere first burnt to quenching in normal gravity and later tested in microgravity in NASA's Zero Gravity Research Facility drop tower; burned flight samples are to be scanned the same way once back on Earth and compared with their preflight scans. [SOF-02 p.5 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- A bubble layer exists next to the burning surface. [SOF-02 p.5 · CITED]
- To locate the burning surface, an exponential curve through the TC1–TC3 temperatures (TC2 and TC3 only, when TC1 is exposed to the gas) is extrapolated to 380 °C, the assumed surface pyrolysis temperature; the fit then gives the TC1-to-surface distance. [SOF-02 p.5 · CITED]
- SOF-02 computes Δrs1, the TC1-to-surface distance at extinction, from this temperature curve built on measured TC1–TC3 data and the assumed 380 °C surface. [SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- qc = λs (∂T/∂r)surface, where the gradient is taken from the fitted curve at the surface, λs = 0.132 W/m K is PMMA's conductivity at the surface temperature, and qc is the heat loss into the solid interior in W/cm2. [SOF-02 p.5 · MODELED; SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Temperatures are good to ±5 °C, but the curve fit amplifies the error, so the surface gradient and hence qc may be uncertain by 20 %. [SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 nomenclature: a, strain rate of the stagnation-region flow (s−1); qc, rate at which the flame loses heat by conduction into the solid interior in the stagnation region (W/cm2); R, sphere radius (cm); U∞, upstream flow velocity (cm/s); Δrs1, surface-to-TC1 distance at extinction (mm); Δtie, total heat-up time from ignitor on to extinction (s), during which the ignitor and then the flame heat the solid; LOI, limiting oxygen index (molar percentage). [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-02 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-02 acronyms: BASS, Burning and Suppression of Solids; CIR, Combustion Integrated Rig (the text writes Rack); GEL, Growth and Extinction Limits; Mir, the Russian space station of 1986 to 2001; PMMA, polymethylmethacrylate; TC, thermocouple. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Extinction modes: background and definitions
- Blowoff and quenching are two distinct extinction modes; aerodynamic blowoff at short flow residence time is read through a critical small Damköhler number and is a flame-stabilisation problem. [SOF-02 p.1 · CITED; SOF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- Aerodynamic quenching in slow flow is a consequence of flame heat losses. [SOF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- In the authors' account, quenching comes from excessive flame heat loss and can also be reached aerodynamically in slow flow: combustion weakens, the ratio of heat loss (radiation, for example) to heat release rises, and the cooler flame goes out. [SOF-02 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- An earlier computation using flame stretch (flow strain) rate as the parameter gave a U-shaped extinction boundary with a blowoff branch and a quenching branch; the point where the branches meet, the minimum flammable condition with the lowest O2 limit, is called the fundamental limit. [SOF-02 p.1 · CITED; SOF-03 p.5 · CITED]
- That model was simple (one-step kinetics, a solid fuel with surface radiative loss), but bringing radiation into interactive flame calculations had broad consequences beyond solid fuels. [SOF-02 p.1 · CITED]
- Blowoff experiments are common, whereas aerodynamic quenching studies in open air (long residence time) are rare, especially for solid fuels. [SOF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors explain this by the flow needed for quenching usually being weaker than the buoyant flow always present in normal gravity, so mapping the whole boundary, including the low-strain limits, remains a challenge. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In normal gravity, low buoyant-stretch stagnation flames can be obtained only with very large solid samples or large-radius burners; "large bottom burning" has been proposed for this, and experiments with large PMMA samples or burners have been run. [SOF-02 p.2 · CITED · nominal; SOF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- Testing a sample of given size in low-speed flow therefore needs microgravity, where the imposed flow can be set independently. [SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Near-limit quenching can be slow (long residence time, possible instabilities), so it needs long-duration microgravity, and solids need even longer tests because of their thermal inertia. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Microgravity tests also serve spacecraft fire safety, because knowing extinction limits of solids helps interpret material screening tests run on Earth. [SOF-03 p.2 · CITED]
- Earlier work: drop-tower and aircraft tests had to use very thin cellulosic samples; shuttle tests on thicker solids showed extinction can be very slow; extinction has been forced by sudden gravity, velocity or pressure changes; long-duration tests used cylindrical rods on Mir and the ISS and wire samples in the ISS FLARE project. [SOF-02 p.2 · CITED · nominal]
- SOF-02 warns that limits obtained by abrupt changes may depend on the method, through rate-dependent hysteresis of a non-linear system, and may skip near-limit phenomena, especially in quenching. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A model of flame growth and retreat on a 2-cm sphere was compared with BASS results from the ISS; BASS preceded SoFIE-GEL with less instrumentation, diagnostics and flow control. [SOF-02 p.2 · CITED · nominal]
- Normal-gravity low-stretch flames over large PMMA samples or burners gave quenching limits in the range predicted for microgravity forced flow, but with different near-limit behaviour: flamelets in those tests, flame pulsation in microgravity. [SOF-02 p.2 · CITED]
- SOF-02 infers that, besides local strain rate, flame scale also affects extinction dynamics. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Around a sphere in a flow, stagnation-point flow forms in front; flames there are locally one-dimensional when the standoff distance (SOF-02) or flame thickness (SOF-03) is much smaller than the radius, so results can be compared with 1-D models in terms of strain or stretch rate. [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This front region is where the flame is stabilised and it governs extinction of the envelope flame, while the shoulder and wake regions add multi-dimensional features of extinction (SOF-02: and of flame growth). [SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-02 states that the region near the forward stagnation point controls extinction. [SOF-02 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Before extinction is imposed (flow decrease or increase, or O2 decrease), the ignitor and then the flame preheat the sample's surface layer; the degree of heat-up varies inversely with the flame's heat loss to the solid, which the embedded thermocouples near the forward stagnation point quantify (4-cm PMMA spheres, ISS microgravity). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Heating of the sub-surface layer by the adjacent flame differs from preheating by an outside source. [SOF-02 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- During the long transient heat-up of a bulk solid after ignition, gas–solid heat exchange varies: as the surface layer warms, the flame loses less heat to the solid and burns hotter. [SOF-02 p.5 · CITED]
- The extinction limit therefore depends on when extinction is imposed; the more the solid has heated, the smaller the flame's heat loss. [SOF-02 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The heat flux conducted into the solid is measured with the embedded thermocouples at the stagnation-point region, the flame stabilisation zone. [SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]

- Δrs1 can exceed the original embedded depth of Table 1 because a swollen bubble layer forms, as earlier work discussed and as seen in these spheres (Fig. 5) (conditions C2). [SOF-02 p.5 · MEASURED]
- qc versus time, from the TC1–TC3 surface gradient, is the thick red curve of Figs. 2–4; under steady conditions (flow and pressure especially) it is highest at ignition, falls with time and may level off (Figs. 2 and 4), but a large flow increase can raise it slightly as the gas-phase heat flux rises (Fig. 3) (conditions C2). ### Extinction boundary map at 1 atm (SOF-02 Fig. 8)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity and platform | O2 | Pressure | Flow | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | diffusion flame over a 4-cm PMMA sphere | microgravity, ISS, SoFIE-GEL in the CIR | percentage at the extinction instant, measured at the duct entrance | one atmosphere (1 ± 0.05 atm) | purely forced; upstream velocity, plotted on a log scale | diluent, ambient temperature | [SOF-02 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.6 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · nominal] |

- Fig. 8 maps extinction for 35 microgravity tests at 1 atm, O2 at extinction against upstream velocity, with numbers beside the points giving qc at extinction in W/cm2 (a smaller number meaning more solid heating) (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.6 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED]
- Some points carry no qc: on re-used samples more than two thermocouples were exposed to the gas so the solid temperature curve could not be computed, or repeated ignition made a simple exponential fit questionable. [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED]
- A secondary axis gives the strain rate at the upstream stagnation point, a = 3/2 (U∞/R), with a in 1/s, U∞ the upstream velocity (cm/s) and R the initial sphere radius (cm). [SOF-02 p.6–7 · MODELED; SOF-02 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MODELED; SOF-02 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- This strain rate leaves out curvature and standoff effects; strain rate has been used before to describe stretched diffusion flames locally. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Mapped as O2 against log velocity (or strain rate), the 1-atm limits do not form the sharp U of the steady model but cluster around a truncated U-shaped band, something like a hockey stick (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- The data stop near 80 cm/s (a ~60 s−1) because of the facility, and the SoFIE duct hardware prevents blowoff limits at higher flows (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- More points lie on the low-velocity side, and the log velocity scale was chosen to emphasise quenching. [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In Fig. 8, blue points are quenching at low velocity or strain, red points blowoff at higher velocity or strain; a red point with black outline (legend "stagnation blowoff") is the O2 limit for local blowoff at the stagnation point, a plain red point (legend "total blowoff") the wake blowoff that follows. [SOF-02 p.7–8 · Fig. 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Two extinction modes appear: quenching at low flow or small strain, and stagnation and wake blowoffs at high flow or strain (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED]
- The band holds points with different degrees of preheating; with a few exceptions, points with smaller qc tend to stay flammable at lower O2 than their neighbours, so less flame heat loss or more solid heating makes the solid more flammable and more preheat widens the flammable domain (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 calls this physically reasonable, since smaller qc means less flame heat loss and more solid heating, and sees its contribution as quantitative data for the comparison. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The quenching-branch trend, a higher O2 limit at lower strain, is due to flame cooling by radiative losses. [SOF-02 p.7 · CITED]
- As the strain rate a falls, standoff grows as 1/a^(1/2) and heat release falls (proportional to a), while the non-dimensional surface radiative loss grows as 1/a^(1/2) and the gas-phase radiative loss as 1/a^n, with n between 1/2 and 1 (1 for an optically thin flame). [SOF-02 p.7 · CITED]
- For a thick solid, SOF-02 concludes that conductive loss into the solid interior, on top of the intrinsic radiative losses, also moves the limits, especially on the quenching side. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The bottom of the band, where the blowoff and quenching branches merge, lies around 10 cm/s, a strain rate of 7.5 1/s, and the minimum O2 is slightly below 14 % (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- From the few points available, the blowoff boundary has a much lower slope, as an earlier study on cylindrical rods also noted (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- At higher velocities there are two blowoff limits, stagnation and wake; the second can follow the first after a long delay because the flame anchors in the slower, lower-strain wake (Fig. 3, test 1403C), so the limiting O2 is lower for wake blowoff (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.4 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
- The modes are told apart by the multi-dimensional dynamics: quenching begins with the flame tips shrinking toward the stagnation point and ends as a small, weak flame; blowoff begins with a hole at the upstream stagnation region, after which the flame retreats downstream and goes out. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Near-limit cyclic pulsation can occur in quenching at low enough stretch, where the downstream flame tip pulses, and in blowoff at high enough stretch, where the upstream front near the sphere shoulder pulses with small, circumferentially irregular amplitude; close to the quench limit the pulsation can sweep from the front to the back of the sphere (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- During pulsation the radiometer readings peak higher, and the advancing front glows bright with the look of a triple flame. [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 theorises that this is a partially premixed flame over solid still pyrolysing after heating by the retreated diffusion flame, too weak to sustain a steady diffusion flame, hence the periodic pulsation. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Toward the bottom of the boundary the average number and amplitude of pulsation cycles fall; at intermediate velocities there is neither tip pulsation on the low side nor hole opening and base pulsation on the high side (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 therefore sees the flame's response along the boundary as smooth and continuous from one branch to the other. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In a narrow band around 10 cm/s the videos cannot separate the two modes, and such points are plotted as open "in-between" symbols. [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The in-between points lie at the bottom of the boundary and are the lowest O2 that sustains burning of the sample, the fundamental limit (conditions C3, around 10 cm/s). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED]
- For PMMA the O2 limit at the bottom of the band is below 14 %, lower than values in conventional flammability tables but reported before, as this work and an earlier rod study show (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.7 · MEASURED; SOF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02 judges this sub-14 % limit considerably lower than the normal-gravity PMMA limiting oxygen index and upward-flammability values listed in conventional tables. [SOF-02 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The stretch rate at the O2 minimum, close to 7.5 1/s, is similar to that predicted by the earlier simplified model, although the model's O2 limit is off (conditions C3). [SOF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]

#### Case #1, sample 1409B: low-flow quenching (conditions C4, inside the duct)
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): From 500 s to extinction at 757.55 s the flow reading varies between 4.46 and 4.92 cm/s with a gradual upward trend while O2 depletes. [SOF-03 p.3 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): SOF-03 attributes the trend to a change in flow resistance, probably tied to a slight drop in chamber pressure during quenching as combustion products are filtered. [SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): As O2 slowly depletes the tip shrinks upstream; small fluctuations of varied amplitude and period follow, and large cyclic pulsation with retreat begins at about 744 s, each cycle leaving a shorter instantaneous flame until extinction at 757.55 s, when tip2 shrinks past the stagnation stabilisation zone. [SOF-03 p.3 · MEASURED · single-test]

[SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

[SOF-03 p.4 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED · ~fig, single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): Ten complete cycles of tip pulsation and retreat precede quenching (the flame reaching the back of the sphere); the downstream pulse takes longer in the first two cycles and then settles to a constant 0.4 s period, while each shrinking phase lasts 1.5 to 0.8 s, much slower than the pulse. [SOF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): Each cycle ends further upstream, so on average the flame length shrinks; the near-limit pulsation of Case #1 lasts only 18.84 s. [SOF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): The flame is brightest when the net downstream pulse speed peaks (Fig. 2(e)), in line with earlier work on blowoff oscillation over PMMA rods. [SOF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): SOF-03 suggests the asymmetry between the two tips may come from slightly asymmetric ignition or from the nature of near-limit flames. [SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): SOF-03 reads the brighter flame during the downstream pulse, compared with the CH* glow of the diffusion flame near the stagnation point, as a premixed flame, and the broadened image toward the back as a widened reaction zone; it hypothesises that after the tip retreats, fuel vapour leaking through the gap between tip and surface and pyrolysis gas from newly exposed hot solid form a combustible mixture of varying equivalence ratio, and takes the pulse reaching past the original diffusion-flame tip as support for the leakage source. [SOF-03 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #1, 1409B (C4): The downstream pulse speed is within the range of typical laminar premixed burning velocities. [SOF-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
