- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): At 200 s the flame tip bends slightly toward the centreline, and the flame turns blue as ambient O2 falls. [SOF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): SOF-03 attributes the bent tip to the flow restriction inside the duct and reads the yellowish flame at 200 s (16.6 % O2) as soot formation. [SOF-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): Extinction starts with a flame hole at the stagnation point, a local blowoff that occurs once O2 drops below 14.99 % at this stagnation strain rate of 25.7 s−1; the flame base then retreats into the slower near-wake region and pulses back upstream to the stagnation region, its base irregular and partly in the wake, partly in the shoulder region (Fig. 4(d)). [SOF-03 p.4 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): SOF-03 adds that after the base retreats the still-hot surface keeps releasing fuel vapour, which mixes with incoming O2. [SOF-03 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): There are only two base pulsation cycles, in which the base travels 5.4 cm on average; the upstream pulses last 0.41 s and the base retreats 0.21 s and 0.31 s, after which the flame spins azimuthally (a 3-D instability) for 3.18 s with its base anchored at the shoulder before complete blowoff. [SOF-03 p.4–5 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #2, 1408A (C4, 34.28 cm/s): As in Case #1, the upstream pulse speed is within the typical laminar premixed burning-velocity range. [SOF-03 p.4–5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]

#### Case #3, sample 1402C, and intermediate flows (conditions C4)
- Contrast of Cases #1 and #2 (C4): in quenching the flame tip shrinks upstream and pulsates, in blowoff the flame base retreats downstream and pulsates. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Intermediate flows (C4): several tests in the range of 9.22 to 11.5 cm/s (printed strain rates 6.92–8.23 s−1; see Conflicts) behaved alike: as O2 depleted the tip shrank without pulsating, and near extinction the base colour faded (a prelude to local blowoff or a hole) but the flame went out normally within one video frame, without base pulsation either. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Intermediate flows (C4): SOF-03 concludes that the transition from quenching to blowoff along the boundary is smooth, and gives Case #3 (1402C) as the representative intermediate case (video S3). [SOF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

#### Case #4, sample 1409C: ultra-low flow at elevated O2 (conditions C4, at the duct exit)
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): an ultra-low-velocity case in a relatively O2-rich atmosphere. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): The tip starts pulsing downstream at 311 s, right after the nominal flow is cut to 0.4 cm/s at 309 s, and keeps pulsing until quenching at 1237.88 s, 927 s in all; one side starts the cycles and the other joins only at about 1040 s (Fig. 5(a)). [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): O2 is 26.25 % when pulsation starts and depletes to 20.77 % at the quench, so most of the pulsation occurs at elevated O2. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Per the abstract, at very low flow (~0.4 cm/s) and elevated O2 the self-sustained cyclic tip pulsation lasts about 15 minutes. [SOF-03 p.1 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 expects the cycles would have lasted even longer without O2 depletion, and calls this a "self-sustained" pulsation, i.e. a limit cycle. [SOF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): The nominal flow is held at 0.2 cm/s during the pulsations (0.4 cm/s set in the first 10 s), while the sensor reads 0.16 to 0.5 cm/s, rising gradually during quenching as in Case #1, and from about 880 s oscillating in phase with the pulsation (Fig. 5(b), 10 s near extinction). [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 attributes the flow oscillation to flame–flow interaction: the flow is very weak, and the large pulsations change the duct's flow resistance. [SOF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Fig. 5 tracks the tip over the whole pulsation period (a) and over 10 s near extinction (b) with SoFIE Cam1, whose 30 frames/s resolve a single cycle well. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal, single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Each cycle is not sinusoidal: the tip spends much less time downstream than upstream. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 explains the shape by two time scales, propagation through the fuel–air mixture and preparation of a new mixture after the flame passes. [SOF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Fig. 5(b) shows the preparation time is the longer of the two, though of the same order, and close to the mass diffusion time. [SOF-03 p.5 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): The mass diffusion time is printed as D/δ², with δ the flame standoff and D the diffusion coefficient (units not stated). [SOF-03 p.5 · MODELED; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 suggests that in this low flow the fuel vapour escaping through the gap between tip and sphere may be the main source of the combustible mixture. [SOF-03 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Pulsation frequency starts at 1.4 Hz, falls gradually to 1 Hz, stays statistically constant from 640 s to 1200 s and drops to 0.8 Hz before the quench at 1238 s; in that quasi-steady period the amplitude grows (Fig. 5(a)) and each cycle's total time increases slightly. [SOF-03 p.5–6 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 ties the longer cycles mainly to the growing amplitude. [SOF-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Cycle-to-cycle variation means the stated frequency trend is a statistical average. [SOF-03 p.6 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Fig. 5 reads: pressure ~15 psi, nearly flat over ~311–1238 s (±2.5); tip2 typically ~90° before ~900 s and at most ~170° near 1230 s; tip1 at most ~20° at ~1237 s; over 1200–1210 s tip2 cycles from ~46° to ~137°, tip1 from ~−155° to ~−16° (tips ±30°) and the flow from ~3.0 to ~4.8 mm/s (±1 mm/s). - Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): Fig. 6 tracks tip1's travel in selected cycles, setting the tip position to zero at the start of each cycle and measuring the distance in later frames from that start. [SOF-03 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-03 p.3 · Table 1 · MEASURED]
- Case #4, 1409C (C4, duct exit): The pulse is slow at first, fastest mid-way and slows near its spreading limit, peaking at about 25 cm/s (solid line in Fig. 6), while the downstream pulse speed at the start of the cycles shows no significant differences; the shrinking is fast at first and slows near the stagnation region. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 judges the inner flame a weaker diffusion flame from its faint colour, as expected from the slower recirculating flow, and suggests this enveloping flame may occur only on blunt solids with flow separation. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): As in Case #2, local blowoff opens a hole in the front stagnation region; the flame then restabilises with its base anchored at the sphere's shoulder ("Fig. 11(b)" as printed). [SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 reads the intense colour as marking the anchored base, owing to high reactivity. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]

[SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): Per the abstract, in this second case at 50 cm/s the diffusion flame stabilises at the shoulder after local stagnation-point blowoff and, as O2 keeps falling, forms spinning flamelets. [SOF-03 p.1 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): SOF-03 explains the end: as more surface is exposed it cools until it no longer releases enough fuel vapour to keep burning. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION · single-test]
- Case #5, 1410C (C4, duct exit): The blowoff and spinning sequence is very dynamic (video S5). [SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test]

### Conclusions and implications
- SOF-02 presents SoFIE-GEL as a long-duration ISS experiment with an instrumented 4-cm PMMA sphere built to pin down extinction limits and near-limit events: varying the flow gave low-velocity quenching and higher-velocity blowoff limits, and O2 depletion gave the boundary at intermediate flows. [SOF-02 p.7–8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The sphere gives a well-defined stagnation flow for comparison with 1-D theory in terms of strain or stretch rate, and the flame dynamics around its sides add qualitative differences between quenching and blowoff. [SOF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A distinctive part of the work is the effect of sub-surface heating by the flame over the long transient burn: changing the burn time before extinction changed the heating, and the multiple thermocouples gave the stagnation-point surface gradient, a laborious measurement SOF-02 says had not been made before. [SOF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The boundary rests on 35 extinction-limit points from long-duration microgravity. [SOF-02 p.8 · MEASURED]
- SOF-02's novelty statement: the quenching process at low flow needs long-duration microgravity to develop, such data are rare, the project took more than 10 years, the blowoff–quenching boundary is given with flame-to-solid conductive heat loss as an extra parameter, and measuring that conduction from ignition to extinction with embedded thermocouples in cell-cast PMMA is new. [SOF-02 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The long, remotely run experiment lets the effect of purely forced flow on burning bulk solids be studied, especially at low velocities hard to reach in normal gravity. [SOF-02 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-03 is the first report of findings from this ISS experiment; using O2 depletion at fixed flows it shows the transient details of both low-flow quenching and high-flow blowoff. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Quenching is seen at low velocity as the tip shrinks upstream toward the stagnation region, extinction coming when the shrinking front flame is too small; blowoff begins when a hole opens at the forward stagnation point, in front of the envelope flame (4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, natural O2 depletion at set flows, one atmosphere). [SOF-03 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Neither process is quasi-static: in quenching the tip pulses downstream and shrinks upstream, the flame ending smaller after each cycle; in blowoff the base pulses between the hole and the downstream position, with far fewer cycles (same conditions). [SOF-03 p.1 · MEASURED]
- SOF-03 attributes the pulsations to a premixed flame front spreading into a combustible mixture. [SOF-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- An early quasi-steady model on a thin solid with surface radiative loss predicted the shrinking trend of quenching. [SOF-03 p.7 · CITED]
- SOF-03 finds that steady shrinking holds only for the average flame; the real quench is very dynamic, with local tip fluctuation and many downstream pulses reaching the back of the sphere, into a partially premixed mixture next to the hot surface made of fuel vapour leaking through the gap between tip and surface plus pyrolysis gas from the still-hot solid; in low-stretch flames that gap is large, raising the share of leakage. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Above 21 % O2 and below 1 cm/s flow, pulsating motion can persist for over 15 minutes (4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, one atmosphere; diluent not reported by this source). [SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED · single-test; SOF-03 p.1 · MEASURED]
- SOF-03 states that the implications for spacecraft safety need further study. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Blowoff starting with a hole at the stagnation region is well known and studied in detail before, and an early quasi-static thin-solid model predicted local stagnation blowoff and a possible side-stabilised flame as flow rises or the Damköhler number falls. [SOF-03 p.7 · CITED]
- In SOF-03's reading blowoff too is dynamic: cyclic upstream pulsation and base retreat can end with the flame stabilised at the sphere's shoulder, and once weakened by lower O2 it breaks into flamelets spinning azimuthally around the sphere. [SOF-03 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Other possible wake-flame configurations were not seen in this setup, possibly because of the sample support rod. [SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Although both modes show cyclic motion, the tip pulsates in quenching and the base in blowoff; the stagnation region is a flame stabilisation zone and the tip is not, but in both cases the hot surface supplies the fuel vapour for the pulsation. [SOF-03 p.7–8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Blowoff and quenching have also been studied with a PMMA cylinder aligned with the flow. [SOF-03 p.8 · CITED]
- SOF-03 sees its large sphere as giving better-defined stagnation, shoulder and wake zones, its embedded thermocouples as characterising preheat, and its low-velocity control as resolving the quenching limits better. [SOF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Low-stretch flames can be made with large samples in faster flows or with smaller samples in slower flows, and with large samples the flame breaks into flamelets (of diffusion-length size), strips or holes before the whole flame quenches. [SOF-03 p.8 · CITED]
- With the 4-cm sphere at low flow the quenching shows pulsation but no flamelets. [SOF-03 p.8 · MEASURED; SOF-03 p.7 · MEASURED]
- SOF-03 concludes that the same low stretch can give different near-limit details, that quenching and blowoff can be multi-dimensional and are not fixed by strain or stretch rate alone, and that another length scale may be needed. [SOF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- On the extinction criterion, SOF-03 argues that a single Damköhler number (chemical versus flow time) seems to apply to both modes in a 1-D view, but quantifying the reaction rate needs the actual flame temperature, which heat loss alters, so one or more non-dimensional heat-loss parameters would be needed. [SOF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In classical theory blowoff can occur even at the adiabatic flame temperature, with no heat loss. [SOF-03 p.8 · CITED]
- SOF-03 holds that the two modes are distinct: blowoff at high speed comes from short residence time in the stabilisation zone, heat loss modifying its boundary only modestly (small loss-to-generation ratio, small drop below adiabatic temperature), whereas at low stretch, with long residence time or large standoff, quenching occurs once heat loss becomes a significant fraction of heat release and cools the flame enough to extinguish it. [SOF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-03 claims GEL has shown both branches, their different mechanisms and transient responses, and clarified the flame behaviour where the two boundaries merge. [SOF-03 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-03 credits the long-duration microgravity environment with making these detailed extinction processes observable. [SOF-03 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

# FILE: NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2
# NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_2 — SoFIE quiescent PMMA sheets and Confined Combustion fabric between baffles

## Scope
Covers: two post-BASS ISS solid-fuel studies. SOF-04 (Carmignani et al. 2026): SoFIE/RTDFS quiescent flame spread, near-limit oscillation and radiative quenching over 0.05–1 mm PMMA sheets at 30 % O2 and 0.5 or 1 atm, with its radiative-loss model and predicted critical thickness, gas temperatures and radiative heat. SOF-08 (Li et al. 2020): Confined Combustion concurrent forced-flow spread over SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric between two parallel baffles in the BASS duct, with inter-baffle distance and baffle type as variables.
Not here: SoFIE-GEL PMMA-sphere extinction (SOF-02, SOF-03), see NEWER_ISS_SOLID_FUEL_1; the BASS and BASS-II tests themselves, see BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_1 to BASS_ISS_SOLIDS_4; Saffire large-scale fires, see LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_1 and LARGE_SCALE_FIRES_2; Earth ratings versus low-gravity limits, see EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_1 and EARTH_VS_LOW_G_LIMITS_2.

## Findings

### SoFIE/RTDFS hardware, data reduction and test matrix (SOF-04)
- SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) is a NASA project on several aspects of flame spread over solids; SOF-04 uses tests from its Residence Time Driven Flame Spread investigation (SoFIE/RTDFS), recently run on the ISS. [SOF-04 p.2 · MEASURED]
- The RTDFS investigation burned PMMA 0.05–1 mm thick in quiescent atmospheres of 30–40 % O2 by volume at 0.5 and 1 atm; most flames quenched before the sample end and oscillated near extinction, at times for relatively long periods. [SOF-04 p.2 · MEASURED]
- Guided by its Eq. (2) predictions, the RTDFS campaign varied fuel thickness, ambient pressure and O2 level. [SOF-04 p.2 · MEASURED]
- Matrix analysed in SOF-04: clear cast PMMA, 0.05–1 mm, initial O2 30 % by volume, quiescent, ISS; 12 tests at 1 atm and 6 repeated at 0.5 atm; the Fig. 4 legends list 0.05, 0.075, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 1 mm at 1 atm and 0.05, 0.075, 0.2, 0.5 and 1 mm at 0.5 atm. [SOF-04 p.2 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.4 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED]
- The SoFIE apparatus sits in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (free volume 90 L); a rotating holder, drawn carrying three samples, moves each sample to the middle of the tunnel before a test, so the chamber need not be opened between tests. [SOF-04 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Each 20 mm × 260 mm sample has an electrical igniter at each end, allowing several ignitions of one sample. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Coordinates: x runs along the sample, with x = 0 at the igniter facing camera S1; y is normal to the fuel surface. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Cameras: three top-view DSLRs (S1–S3, 53° field of view) about 110 mm apart cover the top of the sample with slight overlap; a side-view DSLR (ACME) images the central part; frame rate 10–30 Hz. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Radiometers: three, 23° field of view; R1 faces camera ACME (side view), R2 faces camera S1 (front view), R3 is on R1's side but nearer the duct inlet, beside camera S3. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.4 · Fig. 2 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Thermocouples: five K-type, 76 μm (0.003 in) in diameter, at nominal positions TC1 (x 50 mm, y 2 mm), TC2 (x 50, y 4), TC3 (x 100, y 2), TC4 (x 100, y 4) and TC5 (x 100, y 10). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Sensor records were aligned with camera frames by time stamp, t = 0 s at igniter power-on; after converting images to video in MATLAB, flame-front position, flame length and flame area were tracked over time with Flame Tracker, open-source image software with several colour-channel tracking methods. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]

### Quiescent spread model and predicted critical thickness (SOF-04)
| Set | Fuel | Gravity, flow | O2 | Pressure | Temperatures used | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | thermally thin solid sheet (τ_h ≈ τ), thickness varied | microgravity, truly quiescent (V_g = 0) | 21–100 % (Fig. 1 curves) | 1 atm, plus 0.5 atm for the 30 % curve | flame temperature 2700 K estimated for 30 % O2; properties evaluated at T_p = 400 °C | material named in the prediction, diluent | [SOF-04 p.2 · MODELED · nominal; SOF-04 p.3 · Fig. 1 · MODELED · nominal] |
- Thermal-regime opposed-flow spread rate (Eq. 1, refs [27, 28]): V_f,th = (π/4)·λ_g/(ρ_s c_s τ_h)·(T_f − T_p)/(T_p − T_∞), with λ thermal conductivity (s solid, g gas), ρ density, c specific heat, τ_h fuel thermal penetration thickness, T_f flame, T_p pyrolysis and T_∞ ambient temperature; units not stated. [SOF-04 p.2 · Eq. 1 · CITED]
- τ_h equals the fuel semi-thickness for a thermally thin fuel (nearly uniform temperature across the section) and scales as √(α_s t_res) for a thermally thick fuel (α_s solid thermal diffusivity, t_res residence time). [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Flow velocity V_g acts on Eq. 1 only through t_res ∼ L_g/V_g with L_g ∼ α_g/V_g, so τ_h is inversely proportional to flow velocity (α_g not defined in the pages read; units not stated). [SOF-04 p.2 · MODELED]
- Eq. 1 matches thermal-regime experiments, i.e. when the Damköhler number is high enough that finite-rate kinetics can be ignored [29]. [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED]
- Eqs. 2–3 rest on an earlier scaling expression for opposed-flow spread over thermally thin fuels in microgravity [19]: long residence time at low velocity makes radiation outweigh convection, so surface radiation loss was added to de Ris's otherwise unchanged assumptions [27], with a flame temperature like that of earlier thermal-regime analyses [19, 29]. [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED · nominal]
- The model neglects the transient local flows from hot-gas expansion and fuel-vapour jetting and sets V_g = 0 for a truly quiescent environment. [SOF-04 p.2 · MODELED · nominal]
- Eq. 2: η_f = V_f/V_f,th = 1/2 + (1/2)·√(1 − 4ℜ_0), dimensionless, V_f,th from Eq. 1 [19]; Eq. 3: ℜ_0 ≡ (1/F²)·(ρ_s c_s)/(ρ_g c_g)·(ε σ τ)/λ_g·(T_p⁴ − T_∞⁴)/(T_p − T_∞), with F = (T_f − T_p)/(T_p − T_∞) the temperature-difference ratio, ε the emissivity factor, σ the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and τ the semi-thickness; units not stated. [SOF-04 p.2 · Eq. 2 · CITED; SOF-04 p.2 · Eq. 3 · CITED]
- The radiation number ℜ_0 depends on gas and solid properties and on F; gas-phase and surface radiation effects on spread can be expressed by similar dimensionless numbers. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Bhattacharjee et al. [19] combined the two through an effective emissivity of 0.1 in ℜ_0. [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED · nominal]
- Predictions (C1): ℜ_0 is proportional to fuel thickness and inversely proportional to pressure; for ℜ_0 > 0.25 Eq. 2 yields a complex spread rate, read as extinction, so at every O2 level a critical thickness exists above which no real steady spread solution exists. [SOF-04 p.2 · MODELED]
- At extinction the predicted spread rate is half its thermal-limit value (η = 0.5 at every O2 level), and the critical thickness depends on O2 and ambient pressure (C1). [SOF-04 p.2 · MODELED; SOF-04 p.3 · Fig. 1 · MODELED]
- The authors call these results approximate but say the features they reveal do not depend on the property values chosen. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 1 plots "Normalized spread rate" against "Fuel thickness [mm]" (log axis): Eq. (2) curves for 21, 30, 50 and 100 % O2 at 1 atm and 30 % O2 at 0.5 atm, plus markers for experimental spread rates (1 atm filled circles, 0.5 atm open squares) divided by the Eq. 1 prediction. [SOF-04 p.3 · Fig. 1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Flame appearance, spread and quenching (SOF-04)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C2 | clear cast PMMA sheet, 20 mm × 260 mm, thickness per line | microgravity, ISS, SoFIE/RTDFS | 30 % by volume initial, decreasing as the flame spread (from ~1–2 % in shorter tests to 5–6 % in longer ones) | per line | quiescent | electrical igniters at both ends | mid-tunnel, chamber free volume 90 L | diluent, ambient temperature | [SOF-04 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED] |
- After the ignition transient most flames were blue and dim with minimal soot at both pressures; exceptions were brief yellow sooty zones in the outer flame over 0.05 and 0.075 mm sheets and local soot from vapour bubbles bursting at the surface of 0.5 and 1 mm sheets (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 3 (brightness and contrast enhanced) compares top and side views of flames spreading left to right over 0.05, 0.2 and 0.5 mm sheets at 1 atm and 0.5 atm; no full side view exists for 0.2 mm at 1 atm. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.4 · Fig. 3 · MEASURED]
- For every thickness, including the thinnest, the flame front ran well ahead of the burnout front (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors read this as preheating of a relatively large part of the solid before it burns. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The flames wrap the burnout front in a "C" shape whose leading edges stand farthest from the surface (standoff distance) (C2). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- At 0.5 atm the side view shows thinner flames standing farther ahead of the burnout front (C2, 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Over time the flames looked weaker and dimmer overall (C2, O2 falling during the test). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 4 plots flame-front position against time for each thickness at 1 atm (a) and 0.5 atm (b), with insets for the first 200 s; each line joins the three top cameras and averages the available repeats, the shaded band is the standard deviation among repeats and "X" marks flame extinction. [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.4 · Fig. 4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The results, which SOF-04 calls the first to vary fuel thickness systematically in quiescent microgravity, show much faster spread (steeper Fig. 4 slopes) over thinner sheets (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The 1 mm sheets break this trend: at 1 atm their position history is very close to that of 0.5 mm, and at 0.5 atm the 1 mm flame even outruns the 0.5 mm one; the 1 mm flames advanced mainly along the surface and left unburned material behind (C2). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors note this contradicts the inverse thickness dependence of Eq. 1 and suggest a different spread mode for these thicker sheets, with the limited regression in y typical of thermally thick fuels. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They liken it to BASS-II observations on 2 mm thick samples [31]. [SOF-04 p.3 · CITED]
- Flame-front positions oscillate throughout the tests, more visibly on thicker sheets (C2). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest the thermocouples may have weakened the flames and altered the Fig. 4 slopes, for example for 0.5 and 1 mm near x = 50 mm where TC1 and TC2 sit. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At 1 atm every flame over sheets thicker than 0.075 mm went out before the sample end (Fig. 4 "X"); at 0.5 atm only the 0.05 mm flame clearly crossed the whole sample and was the only sample fully consumed (C2). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Before quenching most flames oscillated along x (the position changes in Fig. 4) and across the sample width, which also shows as changes in flame area (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors call such flame-area changes typical of near-quenching flames. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Near extinction, after a period of steady or quasi-steady spread, flames suddenly began to oscillate or pulsate, with re-ignitions, sometimes for several minutes before quenching (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- The oscillation lasted 10–90 s on thinner sheets and up to 800 s on thicker ones (C2; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Some flames re-stabilised briefly before oscillating again and quenching; side views showed that oscillation could begin on either side at different times (C2). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Visually, the oscillations and re-ignitions resemble those modelled by Kumar and Kumar for thin fuels [23] and the near-limit flames of the BRE experiments [21]. [SOF-04 p.6 · CITED]
- At 0.5 atm flames took much longer, about twice as long, to cover similar distances; the 0.5 mm flame spread for about 16 min at 1 atm and over 30 min at 0.5 atm while advancing only about 150 mm in each case (C2). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- The authors call these durations remarkably long for this configuration. [SOF-04 p.3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Three flames over the thinnest sheets (one 0.05 mm, two 0.075 mm) also quenched; these tests were ignited at both ends at once, so the opposing fronts may have put one flame out; each time the flame that reached the thermocouples first died and the other burned through the remaining fuel (C2; pressure not reported for these three tests). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Because the surviving flame burned on, the authors consider a local O2 drop near the approaching flames or heat loss through the thermocouples more likely than the quenching mechanism of the thicker sheets. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 9 gives the spread rate close to extinction (left axis), computed from flame positions as in Fig. 4, and on the right axis η_f, each measured rate (V_f,exp) divided by its Eq. 1 prediction (V_f,th); some points carry error bars. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-04 p.7 · Fig. 9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The spread rate near extinction drops sharply with thickness at both pressures (C2). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]

- The authors find the quenching trend with thickness consistent with the Fig. 1 prediction. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They add that η_f values for the thicker sheets lose physical meaning because, per Fig. 1, those samples may start to act as thermally thick fuels, a transition the model may not represent well. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They also note the experimental rates were taken close to extinction, where flames oscillate and are unstable, which together with possible heat loss to the sample holder [26] could explain part of the gap between predicted and measured values. [SOF-04 p.6–7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Gas temperature and radiative heat (SOF-04)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | clear cast PMMA sheet, 20 mm × 260 mm, thickness per line | microgravity, ISS, SoFIE/RTDFS | 30 % by volume initial, decreasing during each test | per line | quiescent | electrical igniters at both ends | mid-tunnel, chamber free volume 90 L | diluent, ambient temperature | [SOF-04 p.2–3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED] |
- Thermocouple readings rose as the flame front approached (consistent with the camera images), but peaked at distances of order 5–30 mm beyond the flame front (C3; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED]
- Peak values were compared between x = 50 mm (TC1, TC2) and x = 100 mm (TC3–TC5), especially for quenching or unstable flames, and across conditions. [SOF-04 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Readings were corrected for radiation loss by balancing convection and radiation at the bead (Eq. 4): T_g = (ε_TC σ d_TC)/(Nu λ_g)·(T_TC⁴ − T_∞⁴) + T_TC, with ε_TC, d_TC and T_TC the bead emissivity, diameter and temperature, Nu the Nusselt number and λ_g the gas thermal conductivity; units not stated. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-04 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.4 · Eq. 4 · MODELED]
- With d_TC = 100 μm from image analysis, Nu = 2 (sphere without external flow) and an assumed ε_TC = 0.7, the correction raises the readings by 70–145 K (C3; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.4 · MODELED · nominal]
- Fig. 5 plots the corrected maximum temperatures against thickness, error bars showing variation across repeats; fill marks height (TC1 and TC3 at y = 2 mm empty, TC2 and TC4 at 4 mm light grey, TC5 at 10 mm dark grey) and shape marks x (circles 50 mm, triangles 100 mm); markers sit at 0.05, 0.075, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 mm in Fig. 5a (1 atm) and 0.05, 0.075, 0.2 and 1 mm in Fig. 5b (0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.4–5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-04 p.5 · Fig. 5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Maximum gas temperatures vary little with thickness: 1050–1180 °C at 1 atm and 1100–1200 °C at 0.5 atm after the Eq. 4 correction (the abstract gives similar maxima of 1050–1200 °C at both pressures), and not lower at 0.5 atm (C3). [SOF-04 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.5–6 · MEASURED]
- Values differ somewhat in y (TC1 vs TC2, TC3–TC5) with no clear trend with position; at 0.5 atm the spread is smaller except for 1 mm, where TC1 (y = 2 mm) reads lower than TC2 (y = 4 mm) (C3). [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- The authors suggest the y-variation may come from changes in flame standoff or from thermocouples shifting before the tests. [SOF-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

- Radiometers R1 (side) and R2 (front) view the same stretch of sample (Fig. 2e); their signals rise as the flame enters the field of view, oscillate around a mean while it spreads inside, then fall as it leaves, because flame size and position change the view factors; R3, tilted toward the S2–S3 camera region, had a view factor that varied more monotonically, rising or falling with spread direction; SOF-04 focuses on comparing R1 and R2 because they see the same region from two viewpoints (C3). [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- R1 and R2 traces had very similar time trends, but R1 generally read lower than R2 (C3; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- The part of the sample in the radiometer field of view reached about x ≈ 70 mm; for each test the heat flux was averaged over the time the flame spread within that field, then averaged over repeats at identical thickness, O2 and pressure, with a total standard deviation combining the oscillation within each test and the scatter of the repeat averages. [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The radiometers were about 150–160 mm from the flame, whose length was about 20–30 mm. [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- To a first approximation the flame is therefore treated as a point source, and the weak convective flows from vapour jetting or gas expansion are neglected so the radiometer flux is taken as purely radiative. [SOF-04 p.5 · MODELED]
- Eq. 5: Q̇_rad = 4πL²·q̇''_R, with L the flame–radiometer distance and q̇''_R the measured flux (Q̇_rad plotted in W); L is taken to the sample midpoint, L_R1 = 170 mm and L_R2 = 159 mm. [SOF-04 p.5 · Eq. 5 · MODELED · nominal]
- The authors note a finite flame thickness would shorten the effective L slightly, but measuring from the sample gives a more representative reference for surface radiation and for comparing tests. [SOF-04 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Q̇_rad is of order 20–30 W at 1 atm (C3, R1 and R2, Eq. 5). [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- SOF-04 finds this in line with a total heat release rate under 50 W from Snegirev et al. [26] (their conditions are not given in that sentence). [SOF-04 p.5 · CITED]
- At 0.5 atm the radiative heat is markedly lower than at 1 atm, about 50 % lower (C3). [SOF-04 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Apart from an initial rise from 0.05 to 0.2 mm, Q̇_rad does not change significantly with thickness (C3; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 6 plots Q̇_rad from Eq. 5 against thickness for R1 and R2 at 1 atm (markers at 0.05, 0.075, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 mm) and 0.5 atm (markers at 0.05, 0.075, 0.2, 0.5 and 1 mm), with error bars; Fig. 7 plots R2 − R1 for both pressures. [SOF-04 p.5 · Fig. 6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-04 p.6 · Fig. 7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Because only R2 sees the fuel surface, R2 − R1 estimates the surface radiation component. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Most R2 − R1 values lie between 2 and 5 W with no clear trend; two outliers are negative because for the thinnest sheets (0.05, 0.075 mm) R1 and R2 are similar, R1 being slightly larger in two cases (C3; 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the outliers possibly to the approximations behind Q̇_rad. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Surface radiation would be expected to grow with thickness through a longer pyrolysis region, but Fig. 7 varies little (C3; 0.05–1 mm, 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Surface radiation, as estimated, accounts for > 30 % of all radiant heat at 0.5 atm but < 20 % at 1 atm (C3). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]

- Possible causes of the lower heat at 0.5 atm discussed by the authors: more soot at 1 atm could explain a higher Q̇_rad, but with mostly blue, low-soot flames at both pressures soot is unlikely to be the reason; the lower gas density at 0.5 atm could alter the chemistry and lower the flame temperature, although the measured temperatures did not fall; or the emissivity may change with pressure. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Emissivity estimate: Hottel and Sarofim correlations for a CO2–H2O mixture (from partial pressures and a characteristic beam length), with stoichiometric burning of PMMA (C5H8O2) at x_O2 = 0.3, give p_CO2 = 0.217 atm and p_H2O = 0.174 atm at 1 atm total and half those values at 0.5 atm; at a gas temperature of 1100 °C (from the Fig. 5 thermocouples) the emissivity factor falls from about 0.11 at 1 atm to 0.075 at 0.5 atm (beam length value not stated in the pages read). [SOF-04 p.6 · MODELED]
- At these relatively low pressures the correction for overlapping CO2 and H2O absorption bands is negligible [32]. [SOF-04 p.6 · CITED]
- If emissivity alone caused the drop, Q̇_rad at 1 atm divided by Q̇_rad at 0.5 atm should be close to the emissivity ratio of 1.47. [SOF-04 p.6 · MODELED]
- Fig. 8 plots, for each radiometer, the radiative heat at 1 atm divided by that at 0.5 atm; the R1 points are drawn at 0.05, 0.075, 0.2 and 0.5 mm, the R2 points at 0.05, 0.075, 0.5 and 1 mm. [SOF-04 p.6 · Fig. 8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The R1 ratio is about 2.17 except for the 0.5 mm sheet; R2 ratios vary but stay of order 2 (C3). [SOF-04 p.6 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 8 reads (±0.1; C3): R1 ~3.8 at 0.5 mm (the exception; series max); R2 ~3.0 at 0.05 mm (series max), ~1.9 at 0.075 mm (series min), ~1.9 at the marker plotted at 0.5 mm and ~2.4 at the marker plotted at 1 mm. [SOF-04 p.6 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · ~fig]
- The authors conclude that emissivity change alone does not fully explain the drop: their estimate assumes a uniform gas temperature, set combustion products and a representative beam length, but because emissivity does not scale linearly with pressure they consider emissivity alone an unlikely cause, and suggest the rest may come from flame weakening and a smaller flame area, neither included in Q̇_rad. [SOF-04 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Authors' conclusions and stated significance (SOF-04)
- In microgravity, flames behave very differently than on Earth, which poses particular problems for spacecraft fire safety; without external or buoyant flow, spread is governed by diffusion and heat loss to the surroundings rather than by convection. [SOF-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Earlier radiative-loss analyses led the authors to expect quenching at fuel thicknesses that depend on ambient O2. [SOF-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The authors state that the experiments validate the predicted radiative quenching limits: only the thinnest sheets carried a flame to the sample end, and near quenching the dimensionless spread rate was about 0.5, as predicted (PMMA, ISS, quiescent, initial 30 % O2, 1 and 0.5 atm). [SOF-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-04 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They summarise that the maximum gas-phase flame temperature did not change between 0.5 and 1 atm while radiative heat fell by more than half at 0.5 atm, a fall partly attributable to lower emissivity of the combustion products. [SOF-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- They see the results as support for radiation-driven quenching over fuels of different thickness, and the long-lasting oscillations and re-ignitions as a safety concern for space missions, since flames may persist for long periods even without ventilation. [SOF-04 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Stated significance: the work links radiative-loss theory to rare ISS data, shows systematically how fuel thickness sets radiation-controlled extinction limits at elevated O2, gives an empirical basis for modelling fire behaviour off Earth, and can inform thickness-dependent flammability of materials for long missions. [SOF-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Background cited by SOF-04
- Fire safety is a basic requirement for crewed spacecraft [1], more so on long missions such as coming lunar missions, where suppressing or escaping a fire is severely limited. [SOF-04 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In reduced gravity, weak or absent buoyant convection changes combustion; without external flow, ignition and spread depend mainly on ambient O2 and pressure and on the heat-transfer modes between flame and surroundings; for solids, burning is usually limited by fuel vaporisation, which depends on heat transfer from flame to surface; fuel geometry matters too, and for flat fuels thickness is important for spread and extinction. [SOF-04 p.1–2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In quiescent conditions the relative motion between flame and fuel is just the spread rate, which allows basic study of the gas–solid coupling that controls spread and extinction. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- SOF-04 uses LOC for limiting oxygen concentration. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Microgravity flammability maps for PMMA cylinders show quenching at low enough external flow, through stronger surface radiative loss and weaker convective feedback [4]; the same studies show a lower LOC in microgravity than in normal gravity, attributed to reduced buoyancy and changed heat transfer [5, 6] (PMMA cylinders, low flow; O2 and pressure not stated in those sentences). [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED]
- At higher O2, the gain in spread rate under microgravity and low flow is smaller than in normal gravity [7] (material not stated in that sentence). [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED]
- Earlier scaling work on diffusive transport and flame radiative loss confirmed that microgravity flames can survive and spread where normal-gravity conditions would not sustain burning [8, 9] (quiescent; material not stated in that sentence). [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED]
- Because thermally thin fuels burn faster than thicker ones, the authors see them as suited to short microgravity facilities such as drop towers. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Longer quiescent tests on thin cellulosic fuels at high O2 [15, 16] found spread and quenching driven by radiative loss [17, 18] (gravity level and pressure not stated in that sentence); in microgravity a fuel can act as thermally thin or thick depending on ambient conditions [12]. [SOF-04 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors note that the small number of microgravity experiments makes model validation difficult. [SOF-04 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Confined Combustion hardware, baffles and procedure (SOF-08)
- Confined Combustion studies, on the ISS, how confinement affects concurrent, purely forced-flow flame spread in microgravity; SOF-08 presents results for a thin cotton-fiberglass blended fabric burned in a small flow duct in the MSG. [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.9 · MEASURED]
- The project refurbishes and modifies the BASS hardware to vary flow confinement and wall radiative reflection, and explores systematically the aerodynamic and radiative flame–wall interactions and the flame's fate (no ignition, growing flame, steady flame or extinction). [SOF-08 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors know of no earlier microgravity experiments aimed specifically at confinement effects on fire; the paper gives the concept and some initial data, and only selected SIBAL data. [SOF-08 p.2–3 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The experiment reuses the BASS flow duct [5, 6]: 20 cm long, square section 7.6 cm × 7.6 cm, flow up to 55 cm/s, operated in the MSG, which isolates the work volume aboard the ISS. [SOF-08 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Diagnostics: ISS environmental sensors plus an MSG O2 sensor (Quantek model 201, ±2 % of reading) that tracks O2 consumption during each test; a high-resolution video camera through the duct top window at 12.5 pixels/mm (0.08 mm/pixel) and 24 frames/s (~42 ms/frame), on automatic white balance, exposure and gain; occasionally an ISS camera downlink gave a second view through the MSG front window. [SOF-08 p.2 · MEASURED · nominal]
- As in BASS, each sample is clamped between two stainless-steel frames with a black-oxide finish; frame 13.8 cm × 6.1 cm, exposed fabric 10 cm × 2.2 cm; a 29-AWG Kanthal hot wire of ~1 Ω at the leading edge serves as igniter. [SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Two flat baffles of frame size (13.8 cm × 6.1 cm) sit parallel to the sample, one on each side, placed symmetrically; stacks of 5 mm spacers set the confinement; with inter-baffle distance D the fuel is D/2 from each baffle, and D varies by less than 3 % along the flow in all cases. [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.3 · Fig. 2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A custom transparent top window retrofitted to the BASS duct carries a magnetic mount for the baffle/sample assembly, which places the sample exactly mid-duct. [SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Fuels tested in Confined Combustion: SIBAL fabric (75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass), as in BASS [5], and 1 mm thick cast PMMA slabs. [SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Baffle types, chosen to change the radiative boundary: transparent general-purpose polycarbonate 1.6 mm thick, black anodized aluminum (reflectance ~0) and highly polished aluminum (reflectance ~1); surface properties were measured on the ground before flight. [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Specular gloss (Konica Minolta Multi Gloss 268A at 20°/60°/85°) was 1300/670/130 GU for the polished baffles and 0/0.3/1.3 GU for the black baffles (ground measurement). [SOF-08 p.3–4 · MEASURED]
- Polycarbonate transmittance, from a 5,500 K white LED and a UV-enhanced silicon photodiode with and without the baffle in the beam, averaged 92.5 % over three repeats (ground measurement). [SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED]
- These optical tests cover mainly visible light; flame infrared emission (2,500–3,000 nm from H2O and CO2, ~4,400 nm from CO2 [14]) may pass through the baffles at lower rates, and transmittance at longer wavelengths needs further testing. [SOF-08 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-08 p.4 · CITED]
- Manufacturer data [15] for 1 mm polycarbonate: transmittance about 90 % at 400–1,600 nm, about 40 % at 1,650 nm and back to 80 % at 1,750–1,950 nm. [SOF-08 p.4 · CITED]
- The aluminum baffles have far higher thermal conductivity than polycarbonate (200 vs 0.2 W/m/K) and higher volumetric heat capacity (ρ·Cp ~2.46 vs 1.44 J/cm³/K). [SOF-08 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In all tests MSG pressure and O2 stayed at ISS ambient values, 1.0 atm and ~22 %, with daily O2 between 21.3 % and 22.9 %; imposed flow 5–28 cm/s. [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED]
- Preflight calibration at D = 30, 40 and 50 mm and three stations (near entry, centre, near exit) showed slightly less flow between the baffles as D shrinks, about 28 % less from 50 to 30 mm at 7 cm/s imposed flow, with streamwise variation under 10 % of the mean. [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED]
- The assembly (6.1 cm wide) is narrower than the duct (7.8 cm), leaving ~0.8 cm gaps to the duct wall or window; an earlier numerical study [11] predicts flow diverting into these gaps, especially at small D (e.g. 1 cm). [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.4 · CITED]
- The authors say this adds to the lower flow measured between the baffles at small D. [SOF-08 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- The frame on the spacer side is ~0.3 cm narrower, so the top side gap is slightly larger than the bottom one; the spacer blocks are ~0.7 cm tall, giving block Reynolds numbers of 24–132 over the tested flows. [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.4 · MODELED]
- The authors expect the asymmetry to have minimal effect, if any, and judge that possible recirculation behind the blocks does not noticeably affect the flame. [SOF-08 p.4 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- In all tests the flame stayed at the centre of the frame, away from both side gaps, and neither the top view nor the occasional front view showed flame oscillation or consistent asymmetry (SIBAL, ISS MSG, 1.0 atm, ~22 % O2, 5–28 cm/s). [SOF-08 p.3 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED]
- Procedure: the flow is set first; the igniter current stays on until the sample ignites and an established flame is seen; ignition and growth are watched live and recorded through the top window, and post-burn images are taken; samples are lit at the upstream leading edge and allowed to burn to completion. [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal]
- Analysis code tracks the downstream flame tip and the upstream flame base; spread rate is the slope of a least-squares line through tip and base positions in the central 4–7 cm of the sample, avoiding growth and end effects, and flame length is the mean tip-minus-base distance over the same period. [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Steady versus growing flames and the representative case (SOF-08)
| Set | Material and form | Gravity, platform | O2, diluent | Pressure | Flow | Ignition | Enclosure | Not reported by this source | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C4 | SIBAL fabric (75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass), exposed 10 cm × 2.2 cm; flames on both faces | microgravity, ISS MSG | ~22 % (daily 21.3–22.9 %) | 1.0 atm | purely forced concurrent, speed per line | Kanthal hot wire at the upstream leading edge | two parallel baffles, type and D per line | diluent, ambient temperature | [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.5–6 · MEASURED] |
- Below 15 cm/s imposed flow the flame reached a steady length and spread rate in most tests (the abstract says for all tested inter-baffle distances) (C4). [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Above 15 cm/s the flame kept growing through the test without reaching steady state, except when D was small (< 3 cm), i.e. near the quenching distance (C4). [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.9 · MEASURED]
- The authors note this may be specific to the tested sample length, a longer sample possibly reaching steady state; the paper covers only steady cases. [SOF-08 p.5 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Representative case (Fig. 4: edge view through the top window, flow upward in the image at 5 cm/s, ignition at upper left, frames 2.4 s apart): black anodized aluminum baffles at D = 5.0 cm (C4). [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.5 · Fig. 4 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The igniter glow lights the duct in the first frames; after it is switched off and a short growth period, the flame settles at a limiting length and steady spread rate (C4, representative case). [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED]
- The flame has two layers: a thin yellow soot layer near the fabric and a thicker blue layer toward the baffles (C4, representative case). [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED]
- At the end the flame fronts reach the open downstream end of the sample and merge into one; shortly after, the sample is consumed and the flame quenches (C4, representative case). [SOF-08 p.5 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 5 (time 0 = igniter off; dashed lines = linear fits at steady state) prints for the representative case flame-tip V_f = 1.67 mm/s, flame-base V_b = 1.67 mm/s and flame length L_f = 1.93 cm (C4; black baffles, D = 5.0 cm, 5 cm/s; test key SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-BLACK-D5.0CM-5CMS:5f096889). [SOF-08 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED]
- Fig. 5 reads for the same case (C4; ±0.5 cm, ±2.5 s): at 0 s the tip is at ~3.2 cm and the base at ~1.3 cm; the tip jumps past the "End of the sample" line at ~38.5 s; flame length peaks at ~3.2 cm at ~39 s and the tip at ~11.1 cm at ~41 s; all three series end at ~46 s, flame length falling toward zero and the base at ~9.3 cm. [SOF-08 p.6 · Fig. 5 · MEASURED · ~fig]
- When the tip reaches the open downstream end, it accelerates, the flame suddenly lengthens and the left and right flames merge (Figs. 4–5; C4, representative case). [SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED]
- The authors' explanation: during spread the fuel vapour must diffuse across the viscous boundary layer to meet oxygen, so the flame follows the boundary-layer shape [1]; at the downstream edge the boundary layer breaks, the reaction zones of both sides can join, flow near the centre plane speeds up once the no-slip surface ends, and the baffles also end there, freeing the downstream flame from confinement (no O2 limit, no conductive loss to baffles); they suspect higher flow, extra O2 and less heat loss drive the tip acceleration. [SOF-08 p.6 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

| C5 | SIBAL fabric (75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass), exposed 10 cm × 2.2 cm; flames on both faces | microgravity, ISS MSG | ~22 % | 1.0 atm | purely forced concurrent, imposed 7 cm/s | at the upstream leading edge | two parallel baffles, type and D per line; "no baffles" = sample alone on its carrier, one face toward the duct interior and the other toward the transparent polycarbonate front window, equivalent to D = 7.6 cm (full duct width) | diluent, ambient temperature | [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.3–4 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · ~fig; SOF-08 p.8 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · ~fig] |

- Fig. 6 compares steady flame profiles with black anodized aluminum baffles at D = 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0 cm and with no baffles, five tests in all, with an overlay of the tracked outer flame edges and a 1.0 cm scale bar (C5). [SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- From no baffles to D = 2.0 cm, flame length first rises and then falls, peaking around D = 4.0 cm (C5, black baffles). [SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- At very small D (e.g. 2.0 cm), where the flame is small and weak, the camera struggles with white balance and the video colours are unrealistic and change frame to frame; the ISS crew reported the true flame colour during the burns to confirm or correct the video. [SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In the Fig. 6 discussion (black-baffle comparison), at D = 1.0 cm the flame went out right after the ignition energy was removed, and the post-burn sample showed it never spread past the ignition wire (burn length < 0.8 cm) (C5; test key SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-BLACK-D1.0CM-7CMS:2bac3957). [SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.7 · Fig. 6 · MEASURED · nominal]
- In the Fig. 7 discussion, ignition was not achieved at D = 1.0 cm for any baffle type (C5; test keys SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-REFLECTIVE-D1.0CM-7CMS:c0b3eeb2, SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-TRANSPARENT-D1.0CM-7CMS:25dd65d9). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The abstract states that for every baffle type a too-small distance (~1 cm) leaves the flame either unignited or extinguished before the sample end (SIBAL, ISS, concurrent forced flow). [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute this to reduced O2 supply to the flame zone and heat loss to the baffles. [SOF-08 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Across all tested flows and baffle types there is a quenching inter-baffle distance below which the flame failed to spread (SIBAL, ISS MSG, concurrent flow 5 to 25 cm/s, D 1 to 5 cm, 1.0 atm, ~22 % O2). [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.9 · MEASURED]
- The dashed "Quench limit" line in Fig. 7 is drawn at ~1.2 cm in the spread-rate panel (7a) and at ~1.5 cm in the flame-length panel (7b) (±0.25 cm) (C5; test key SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-QUENCHLIMIT-7CMS:7f052b21). [SOF-08 p.8 · Fig. 7 · MEASURED · ~fig]
- Both Fig. 7 quantities (error bars: 95 % confidence intervals) change non-monotonically as D decreases (C5). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- From no baffles (D = 7.6 cm) to D = 5.0 cm the black-baffle spread rate rises by a factor of ~1.5 (C5). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors find the rise inversely proportional to the smaller cross-section left for thermal expansion (V_f ~ 1/D), as Li et al. [9] predicted, implying that flow acceleration from combustion expansion drives the faster spread in this regime. [SOF-08 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- With reflective polished-aluminum baffles the gains in spread rate and flame length are larger still (C5). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the larger gain to extra radiative feedback reflected by the baffles. [SOF-08 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- As Li et al. [9] predicted, the optimal inter-baffle distance for spread is D = 4.0 cm, where spread rate and flame length peak for all baffle types (C5). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Below D = 4.0 cm the spread rate falls with D, and faster than the linear dependence on duct height predicted by Li et al. (C5). [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- The authors attribute the fall to O2 starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles [9]; they add that some flow may bypass outside the baffles through pressure build-up between them near the flame, an unintended limitation of the BASS-duct retrofit, so the flow entering the gap may be below the imposed value, especially with close baffles. [SOF-08 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Fig. 9 plots the spread rate with reflective or black baffles divided by that with transparent baffles at the same D, so the transparent case equals 1 at every D (y-axis printed "Flama spread rate ratio (V_f/V_f,transparent)"; error bars not read) (C5). [SOF-08 p.8–9 · Fig. 9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-08 p.9 · Fig. 9 · MEASURED · nominal]

- Fig. 8 compares steady flame profiles with reflective, black and transparent baffles at D = 4.0 cm (overlay of tracked outer edges, 1.0 cm scale bar): the flame is clearly longest with reflective baffles, as expected, and slightly longer with black than with transparent baffles (C5, D = 4.0 cm). [SOF-08 p.8 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.8 · Fig. 8 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors explain that part of the combustion heat leaves as radiation, which reflective baffles send back to the sample and gas flame while polycarbonate and black aluminum transmit or absorb much more of it; black baffles heat up and emit more surface radiation, and the slightly longer black-baffle flame likely reflects slightly higher reflection plus emission than with transparent baffles. [SOF-08 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At small D (e.g. D < 3.0 cm) black and reflective spread rates are similar to each other but differ from the transparent ones (C5). [SOF-08 p.8 · MEASURED]
- Extra radiation feedback from reflective baffles generally gives the highest spread rate, most strongly near the optimum D = 4.0 cm; at D = 3.0 cm the three baffle types give almost identical spread rates (C5). [SOF-08 p.8 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-08 p.8–9 · MEASURED]
- The authors infer that at such confinement burning is limited by the O2 supplied to the gap between the baffles. [SOF-08 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At D = 2.0 cm, the smallest distance at which a flame spread, transparent baffles give a slightly higher spread rate than the other types (C5). [SOF-08 p.9 · MEASURED]
- The authors read this as conductive heat loss to the close baffles cutting the spread rate [9, 10], the aluminum baffles, with their higher conductivity and heat capacity, being expected to draw more heat from the flame zone. [SOF-08 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- At equal D, flame length and spread rate are highest with polished aluminum and lowest with polycarbonate baffles, the difference being largest at intermediate distances, near the optimum; near the limit set by the reduced O2 supply, lengths and spread rates are similar for all baffle types (SIBAL, ISS MSG, concurrent forced flow, 1.0 atm, ~22 % O2). [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.9–10 · MEASURED]
- The authors say the ranking reverses at quenching for small D because transparent baffles conduct the least heat away from the flame. [SOF-08 p.10 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- For steady cases, confinement acts non-monotonically: as D decreases, flame length and spread rate first rise and then fall, giving an optimal inter-baffle distance (4.0 cm in this work) (SIBAL, ISS MSG, concurrent forced flow, 1.0 atm, ~22 % O2). [SOF-08 p.1 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.9 · MEASURED]
- The authors' reading: radiative feedback from the baffles should grow as D falls, but burning is limited by the reduced O2 supply; above the optimum, thermal expansion accelerates the flow and strengthens conductive feedback to the sample, raising the spread rate, while below it O2 starvation and extra heat loss to the baffles weaken the flame and slow spread. [SOF-08 p.1 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION; SOF-08 p.9 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]

### Comparison with BASS (SOF-08)
- Earlier BASS tests measured the spread rate of the same SIBAL material under similar conditions (1 atm, 21 % O2) with a slightly lower concurrent flow (5 cm/s). [SOF-08 p.7 · CITED · nominal]
- That BASS spread rate is ~42 % higher than this work's no-baffle case (Confined Combustion no-baffle data at 7 cm/s, 1.0 atm, ~22 % O2). [SOF-08 p.4 · MEASURED; SOF-08 p.6 · MEASURED · nominal; SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED]
- Hardware differences named: sample card width 3.6 cm in BASS vs 6.1 cm here, sample rotated 90° in the duct, and a changed sample-holder mechanism. [SOF-08 p.7 · MEASURED · nominal]
- The authors think several causes may combine; the wider card used here likely adds heat loss and reduces side O2 transport to the flame, both weakening it. [SOF-08 p.7 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- A wider card can raise the flow speed the sample meets [11], but this matters only in a low duct, near the thickness of the flow boundary layer. [SOF-08 p.7 · CITED]

### Background cited by SOF-08
- BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) burned thin cotton-fiberglass fabrics, Nomex, Ultem and PMMA slabs, rods and spheres in concurrent and opposed flow in a small flow duct (height 7.8 cm) in the ISS MSG [5, 6]; its cotton-fiberglass samples are called SIBAL. [SOF-08 p.1 · CITED · nominal]
- For SIBAL in BASS: steady spread in low-speed concurrent flow (~20 cm/s); flame length and spread rate rose with flow speed and with O2 up to the 22 % hardware limit; a low-speed quenching velocity was found that fell as O2 rose [5, 6]. [SOF-08 p.1–2 · CITED]
- In Saffire, large samples of the same fabric burned in a large duct (height 41 cm) inside the pressurized cabin of an uncrewed Cygnus ISS resupply vehicle; spread also became steady, but at clearly lower steady rates than in BASS at the same O2 and flow [7]. [SOF-08 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors suspected the different confinement of the large and small ducts behind the difference. [SOF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Shih and T'ien's two-dimensional steady CFD of concurrent spread over thin solids in a microgravity duct [10, 11] found flame length and spread rate first rising then falling as duct height decreases, from competing chimney effect, O2 restriction and wall heat loss; with wall radiation reflection included, some duct heights gave no converged solution. [SOF-08 p.2 · CITED]
- The authors suspect the flame keeps growing in such confinement, a transient a pseudo-steady model cannot capture. [SOF-08 p.2 · AUTHOR-INTERPRETATION]
- Li et al.'s three-dimensional transient model of the BASS geometry, with duct height 1–9 cm [9, 11], predicted an optimal height of 4.0 cm for fastest spread in 10 cm/s air flow; above it the chimney effect of expanding hot gas dominates and spread rate is roughly linear in the inverse duct height, below it spread follows the O2 supply and is roughly linear in duct height [11]. [SOF-08 p.2 · CITED]
- In normal gravity, fires in confined spaces such as parallel panels or channels can be longer and spread faster than in the open [12, 13]; in Shih and Wu's upward spread over parallel thin paper sheets [12], sheets more than 10 cm apart behaved like one sheet, closer sheets interacted and spread faster (chimney effect and radiation exchange between flames and samples both intensify the fire), and still closer sheets suffered O2 depletion and slower spread. [SOF-08 p.2 · CITED]
